identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a conference/program index entry and does not report an empirical study of a specific AI tool; it mentions web-based concordancing, virtual platforms, peer review, corpora, email, chat rooms, and related CALL practices in passing.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not a single empirical study of an AI tool; it is an index/listing of multiple language teaching and learning articles with brief summaries. No rigorous tool-specific methodology or outcome evidence is reported for a discrete system.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The excerpt contains no directly reported effect sizes or measured impact for a specific AI tool. At most, it suggests broad relevance of CALL/corpus-based practices, but the evidence is indirect and not attributable to one intervention.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of generating up-to-date, personalized reading comprehension exercises for middle school English learners, a task that teachers reported was time-consuming and difficult to scale with traditional materials. The authors explore whether ChatGPT can be used to generate reading passages and multiple-choice questions that are suitable for classroom use, and whether such outputs compare favorably with human-written materials and a GPT-2+PPLM baseline.

The intervention is a system that uses ChatGPT prompts to generate reading passages in zero-shot and one-shot settings, then creates associated multiple-choice questions and answers. The system was built for non-technical users with a graphical interface, and included a toxicity check before materials were shown to teachers or students. A GPT-2 model fine-tuned on teacher-collected Chinese middle-school reading materials served as the baseline.

The study context was Chinese middle schools, specifically English reading instruction for Grades 7-9 in Beijing. Evaluation combined automatic metrics, human ratings from Chinese college students and native English speakers, pairwise comparisons, and interviews with experienced middle school teachers who used the system for a week. The main findings were that ChatGPT-generated passages were generally judged high quality, often better than human-written passages on several dimensions, and highly suitable for the intended learners, while question generation was useful but still weaker than human-written questions, especially in the quality of distractors. Teachers reported that the system could reduce preparation time and support more personalized materials.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative conversational AI / LLM chatbot used to generate and adapt reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice questions.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a reading exercise generation system for Chinese middle school English learners, in zero-shot and one-shot prompting settings, to generate personalized reading passages and accompanying multiple-choice questions; also used with a toxicity check and editable UI for teacher review.

findings.finding_summary: Human and automatic evaluations found that ChatGPT-generated reading passages were high quality and often superior to human-written textbook passages. In Table 2, experienced Chinese student raters gave ChatGPT passages higher scores than human-written passages on readability (4.61 vs. 4.52), correctness (4.60 vs. 4.32), coherence (4.65 vs. 4.39), engagement (4.37 vs. 4.07), and overall quality (4.46 vs. 4.18); native speakers also rated ChatGPT highest overall (4.06 vs. 3.89 human-written).
findings.measure: Multi-dimension quality ratings of generated reading passages (readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, overall quality)
findings.sample_size: n=9 Chinese college students; n=364 native English speakers; 30 passages in Example Set 1

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise comparisons, evaluators preferred ChatGPT passages over human-written passages and often judged them as more human-like. Table 3 shows human vs. generated relative quality scores favoring ChatGPT (0.87 generated vs. 0.13 human in zero-shot; 0.80 vs. 0.20 in one-shot), and Table 4 shows lower model-generated scores for ChatGPT passages than human-written ones (0.30 generated vs. 0.53 human in zero-shot; 0.23 vs. 0.33 in one-shot), indicating they were less likely to be perceived as machine-generated.
findings.measure: Pairwise relative quality; perceived model-generated vs. human-written judgments
findings.sample_size: n=9 Chinese college students; 10 human-written passages plus generated counterparts

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed strong topic-following ability for reading passage generation. Table 5 reports topic coherence scores of 0.97 for ChatGPT in both zero-shot and one-shot settings, compared with 0.40 for the GPT-2 + PPLM baseline in the generated condition, suggesting that prompts effectively controlled passage topic alignment.
findings.measure: Topic coherence score for generated passages relative to target topics
findings.sample_size: n=9 Chinese college students; 10 topic-matched passages per condition

findings.finding_summary: Evaluators judged ChatGPT-generated passages to be suitable for middle school English learners. Table 6 shows generated suitability scores of 0.77 for both zero-shot and one-shot ChatGPT passages, compared with 0.37 for the GPT-2 + PPLM baseline, indicating the passages were considered appropriate reading comprehension materials.
findings.measure: Suitability score for middle school English learners
findings.sample_size: n=9 Chinese college students; 10 passages per condition

findings.finding_summary: For multiple-choice question generation, human-written items outperformed ChatGPT-generated items on all evaluated dimensions, though generated questions were still highly aligned with passage content. Table 7 reports Match 4.38, Useful 3.25, Suitable 3.48, and Generated-or-not 0.67 for generated questions versus 4.58, 3.93, 3.92, and 0.27 for human-written questions, respectively. The paper notes that teachers may need to select and edit generated questions because some are too straightforward or patterned.
findings.measure: Human ratings of generated multiple-choice question quality (match, usefulness, suitability, machine-like appearance)
findings.sample_size: n=9 Chinese college students; 10 exercises with generated and human-written question sets

findings.finding_summary: Experienced teachers reported that the system could substantially reduce cost and time while providing more diverse and personalized learning materials. In the system feedback section, teachers described it as a valuable tool and highly satisfactory overall, indicating operational benefits for lesson/material preparation rather than direct student outcome effects.
findings.measure: Teacher interview feedback on system usefulness and ease of use

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical system paper with mixed-method human evaluation, not a randomized controlled study or meta-analysis. It provides useful evidence on feasibility and perceived quality, but the sample is small and outcomes are mostly subjective ratings.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on passage quality and topic coherence are strong in the qualitative/ratings sense, and the system may improve instructional material production. However, direct student learning gains are not measured, so the broader educational impact remains modest/unclear.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and risks of large language models, especially ChatGPT, for education. The central question is how generative AI can be used to support learning and teaching while avoiding harms such as bias, overreliance, plagiarism, privacy violations, and misleading outputs. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, the paper synthesizes emerging literature and offers a conceptual analysis of use cases and constraints.

The paper discusses how large language models may support students through reading and writing assistance, summaries, explanations, quizzes, feedback, language practice, and remote tutoring. For teachers, it highlights possible uses in lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment support, exercise generation, and professional development. The discussion spans primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning contexts, with a particular emphasis on how these tools could affect literacy-related activities such as reading comprehension, writing quality, and critical thinking.

The authors conclude that large language models can be valuable educational tools only when integrated with strong human oversight, curriculum alignment, fact-checking practices, and clear policies for privacy, fairness, sustainability, and responsible use. They argue that effective adoption depends on educator training, institutional strategy, and pedagogical designs that preserve critical thinking and do not replace human instruction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative pre-trained transformer-based conversational AI system for human-like text generation, question answering, summarization, and dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses ChatGPT/GPT-style large language models as educational tools for generating content, quizzes, feedback, explanations, summaries, and personalized learning support, including literacy-related tasks such as reading comprehension question generation and writing assistance.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot used for language-based generation, tutoring, and feedback without a single evaluated product-specific system.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a position paper and broad review of large language models in education rather than an empirical evaluation of one generic tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and narrative overview, not an empirical study, RCT, or meta-analysis. It does not report original outcome data or effect estimates for a specific tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that LLMs may support literacy-related instruction through generation, feedback, and comprehension scaffolds, but it provides no measured impact in K-12 settings. The likely impact is plausible but unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: Integrating Generative AI in Knowledge Building
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can be integrated into K-12 knowledge-building instruction and how such use may support students’ emerging AI literacy. The authors focus on students’ nuanced processes of using GenAI for learning, rather than on short-term achievement outcomes, and ask how students incorporated ChatGPT into their knowledge-building work and how their AI literacy developed through that process.

The intervention was a classroom design experiment in a high school World Religions course using the Knowledge Building pedagogy. A teacher and the researchers collaboratively designed two phases of ChatGPT use: first, students used ChatGPT to generate essays and inquiry questions to critique, compare, and extend; second, they used a steering prompt to elicit brief answers, nuanced viewpoints, and follow-up questions, then fact-checked, discussed with peers, and posted reflections and knowledge-building notes. Students also used ChatGPT for writing support, brainstorming, and question generation, while the teacher explicitly modeled prompt engineering, source verification, and ethical citation.

The participants were 10 consenting high school students and one teacher at a private/international-style course drawing students from three schools in a major South American city. Data came primarily from semi-structured student interviews, supplemented by student artifacts and teacher planning/reflection documents. The findings suggest that ChatGPT was useful for rapid information search, idea generation, and mundane academic tasks, but students also encountered hallucinations, prompt-following problems, and citation challenges. Students developed a partial but growing understanding of AI mechanisms, strengths, weaknesses, risks, and societal implications, though their explanations were often still simplistic or incomplete. The paper concludes that effective and appropriate GenAI use in K-12 requires structured pedagogical scaffolding, explicit instruction in prompt engineering, fact-checking, and ethical use, along with spaces for critical reflection.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on large language models, capable of conversational text generation, question answering, and iterative prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by high school students in a world religions course to support knowledge building, generate ideas and questions, answer student questions, draft essay content, and support prompt-engineering, fact-checking, and reflective discussion.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative/mixed-methods classroom study with 10 high school students, ChatGPT was reported to support literacy-related work by helping students search for information, generate essay outlines, summarize texts, and correct minor writing mistakes. Students also reported that its usefulness depended on how they used it: some used it as a shortcut, while others used it as a supporting tool and maintained ownership of their writing.
findings.measure: Student interviews and analysis of student writing/artifacts related to writing assignments, essay outlines, and summaries

findings.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT supported knowledge building by offering diverse perspectives, surfacing new ideas, and helping them keep up with class discussion. The paper does not report quantitative effects; instead, it documents students' self-reported processes, including use of ChatGPT for idea generation, question generation, and collaborative discourse.
findings.measure: Student interviews and collaborative knowledge-building artifacts (Miro, Knowledge Forum)

findings.finding_summary: Students commonly described ChatGPT as improving efficiency in information searching and helping them complete mundane learning tasks more quickly. The paper reports that 70% of participants said ChatGPT improved information search efficiency, and about 60% used it for rapid access to information during class discussions, but no inferential statistics or effect sizes were provided.
findings.measure: Self-reported utility/efficiency in interviews

findings.finding_summary: The study reports emerging AI literacy across multiple dimensions, especially understanding of ChatGPT's mechanisms, strengths, weaknesses, risks, and societal implications. Most students had only a rudimentary and partly inaccurate understanding of how ChatGPT works, while a few articulated more sophisticated explanations involving probability and safeguards; the paper provides qualitative evidence rather than quantitative gains.
findings.measure: Interview coding of AI literacy dimensions (AI-mechanism, AI-strength, AI-weakness, AI-risk, AI-societal implications, AI-relationship)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small qualitative/mixed-methods case study with semi-structured interviews and artifact analysis, not an experimental efficacy study. It provides rich descriptive evidence but no causal estimate or quantitative effect size.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful support for literacy-related work, knowledge building, and AI literacy development, but the evidence is self-reported and non-quantitative. Reported impact is plausible and positive in places, but the magnitude cannot be established from the study.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks how generative AI may affect learning, teaching, and especially assessment in higher education. The authors frame the discussion around a broader history of educational technology hype, arguing that ChatGPT should be understood not as a complete disruption of education but as the latest in a long line of tools that can be overestimated if implementation and pedagogy are ignored.

The paper combines a desktop literature review with the authors’ own experimentation using ChatGPT. It reviews early peer-reviewed and preprint work on ChatGPT, GPT-3, and related AI writing tools, and then situates ChatGPT within existing Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd) frameworks. The discussion is organized around student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing applications, with emphasis on writing support, automated essay scoring, feedback, and assessment design.

The paper does not study a specific student sample; rather, it addresses higher education users broadly, including students, instructors, and institutions. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT has useful affordances for explanation, drafting, feedback, and experimentation, but also serious limitations in factual reliability, higher-order reasoning, and language quality in some contexts. The authors argue that institutions should adapt assessment and teaching practices, focus on more authentic and innovative assessment methods, and develop policies that guide appropriate use rather than simply banning the technology.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational AI chatbot built on GPT-family large language models, designed to generate text and respond to prompts in natural language.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviewed ChatGPT's functionality and experimented with it to test essay drafting, explanation quality, multilingual composition, and its potential implications for assessment and teaching in education.

findings.finding_summary: The paper does not report a controlled empirical study, but its review and experiments suggest ChatGPT is useful for quick conceptual explanations, basic problem solving, and drafting text, while performing poorly on higher-order analytical writing and some non-English composition tasks. The authors also note that it can generate passable prose quickly and may be difficult for plagiarism detectors to flag, but it can produce inaccurate, generic, or fabricated content.
findings.measure: Author observations from experimentation with ChatGPT; review of prior literature on educational uses and risks

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual review/article with informal experimentation, not a controlled empirical evaluation. It synthesizes early literature and author observations rather than reporting rigorous causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful effects on writing, assessment, and student support, but no effect sizes or controlled estimates are reported. The magnitude of impact is therefore unclear, though the authors indicate both useful and problematic capabilities.

paper_profiles.title: Performance of ChatGPT on USMLE: Potential for AI-assisted medical education using large language models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT, a general-purpose large language model, can answer high-stakes medical licensing exam questions accurately enough to be useful in medical education. The central question is not whether the model was taught with a specific educational intervention, but whether its generated answers and explanations demonstrate enough correctness, internal consistency, and useful reasoning to support learners.

The authors evaluated ChatGPT on 350 publicly available USMLE sample items spanning Step 1, Step 2 CK, and Step 3. Questions were presented in three formats: open-ended prompts, multiple-choice without forced justification, and multiple-choice with forced justification. Outputs were independently adjudicated by physicians for accuracy, concordance between answer and explanation, and the presence of nonobvious but valid insights. The study was conducted using USMLE sample questions, with no human student participants; the implicit audience was medical learners, especially medical students preparing for USMLE.

Results showed that ChatGPT often performed near or above the approximate passing threshold, with accuracy varying by question format and exam step. Explanations were highly concordant with answers, and many responses contained at least one significant insight. The authors conclude that large language models may have educational value as tools that can generate reasonably accurate, interpretable, and potentially teachable explanations, though they emphasize the need for future controlled studies and better validation before real-world educational deployment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model / chatbot that generates natural language responses from text prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated ChatGPT on USMLE sample exam questions to assess accuracy, concordance between answers and explanations, and the presence of nonobvious insights in its explanations as a proxy for medical education usefulness.

findings.finding_summary: Across 350 USMLE items, ChatGPT's accuracy varied by prompt format and exam step. With indeterminate responses censored/included, accuracy was 75.0%/45.4% for Step 1, 61.5%/54.1% for Step 2CK, and 68.8%/61.5% for Step 3 in open-ended format; 55.8%/36.1%, 59.1%/56.9%, and 61.3%/55.7% in multiple-choice no-justification format; and 64.5%/41.2%, 52.4%/49.5%, and 65.2%/59.8% in multiple-choice forced-justification format. The authors note performance approached the USMLE passing threshold (~60%) and was highest in some analyses on Steps 2CK and 3.
findings.measure: USMLE item-answer accuracy across Step 1, Step 2CK, and Step 3 under three prompt formats

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed very high answer-explanation concordance. Overall concordance was 94.6% across all questions, and concordance among accurate MC-J responses was 99.1% versus 85.1% among inaccurate responses (p<0.001).
findings.measure: Concordance between answer choice and explanation content

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT frequently produced novel, nonobvious explanations. At least one significant insight appeared in 88.9% of all responses, and mean density of insight was higher for accurate than inaccurate outputs (0.458 versus 0.199, p<0.0001). The authors argue this suggests the outputs could support human learning in medical education.
findings.measure: Presence and density of significant insights in explanations

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical performance study of ChatGPT on exam questions with physician adjudication, but it is not a randomized educational intervention or learner outcome study. The evidence is informative yet indirect for K-12 literacy use.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong model performance on a high-stakes text task and suggests potential educational usefulness, but it does not measure literacy learning gains or classroom implementation effects. The likely educational impact is therefore unclear for K-12 literacy instruction.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching with ChatGPT as a Linguistically Responsive Tool for Multilingual Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools, especially ChatGPT, are being integrated into K–12 multilingual learner (ML) instruction and asks whether these uses align with linguistically responsive pedagogy. Framed by translanguaging theory, the study is concerned with both the instructional purposes of AI and the conditions under which its use may support language and literacy learning for multilingual students.

The study analyzed classroom observations and post-observation interviews from two cohorts of in-service teachers enrolled in a professional development course on culturally and linguistically responsive pedagogy in Washington, DC public schools and public charter schools. Across 42 observed teachers, the author identified eight instances in which ChatGPT or related AI tools were used in literacy instruction. Uses included translating and transcribing speech and texts, differentiating reading level and content, scaffolding students’ prompting of ChatGPT, and a multimodal literacy activity using image generation.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can support MLs’ access, participation, and agency when used to facilitate communication, differentiate content, and promote production and co-labor. However, the paper also finds important gaps: there were no observed uses supporting translanguaging assessment or reflection, and there were limited examples involving family/community literacies or non-standard language practices. The author argues that effective and appropriate use of generative AI in K–12 literacy instruction requires explicit teacher guidance, critical AI literacy, and attention to bias, ethics, and sociopolitical language hierarchies.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI system for generating and transforming text, and related multimodal outputs, via natural-language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by K-12 teachers of multilingual learners to translate texts and vocabulary, differentiate reading level and content, transcribe and translate student speech, generate exemplar texts, scaffold prompting for student use, and support multimodal literacy experimentation with Dall-E.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative study of 42 observed K��12 teachers (with ChatGPT use identified in 8 observations), teachers reported that ChatGPT supported communication, differentiated content, and enabled structured prompting and multimodal literacy activities for multilingual learners. The paper does not report quantitative effect sizes; instead, it argues these uses may enhance access, participation, agency, and translanguaging-aligned pedagogy while noting gaps in assessment and reflection.
findings.measure: Observed instructional uses and interview-reported pedagogical affordances for literacy instruction
findings.sample_size: n=42 observed teachers; ChatGPT use in 8 observations

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods classroom observation and interview study, not an experimental efficacy design. It documents instructional uses and teacher perceptions rather than causal effects on student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports plausible instructional affordances and positive pedagogical alignment, but no quantitative student outcome data or effect sizes. Impact on literacy is therefore suggestive but unclear rather than measured.

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT responds to questions about science education and explores whether generative AI can support educators’ pedagogical work. The author’s central concern is not whether ChatGPT can directly improve student outcomes, but rather what kinds of science-education guidance it produces, how closely that output aligns with established research, and what risks arise when users treat it as an authoritative source.

The study uses a self-study methodology in which the author prompts ChatGPT with questions about effective science teaching, pedagogical choices, student failure, and classroom resource design. The paper also tests ChatGPT’s usefulness for generating a Year 7 science unit, a rubric, and a multiple-choice quiz, focusing on renewable and non-renewable energy sources as the example topic. The context is science education, with implications discussed for both classroom teaching and academic writing/research practice. No human participants were studied directly; the paper instead analyzes AI-generated text and the author’s reflections on using ChatGPT as a tool.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT often produces responses that align with familiar science-education themes, such as inquiry-based learning, differentiation, assessment, collaboration, and real-world connections. However, the author argues that the tool can present unsupported claims with an unwarranted appearance of authority, may reproduce bias, and can generate vague or generic educational materials that require expert review and adaptation. The paper concludes that ChatGPT may be useful as a starting point for lesson planning, rubric drafting, quiz generation, and editing, but only when educators use it critically, model responsible use, and consider ethical issues such as bias, copyright, and transparency.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on large language models, designed to generate human-like text and support conversational interactions across tasks such as question answering, summarization, writing, and drafting educational materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as an exploratory research tool and as a classroom-support tool to generate science teaching content, including responses to science education questions, a 5Es unit, a self-assessment rubric, and a multiple-choice quiz; also used for editing and rewriting text in the paper.

findings.finding_summary: This exploratory self-study found that ChatGPT's responses often aligned with key themes in the science education literature, but the paper also emphasizes that the outputs lacked evidence grounding and could present itself as an epistemic authority without sufficient qualification. The author further noted useful applications for lesson/unit design, rubric creation, quiz generation, and writing support, while cautioning that all AI-generated resources require critical evaluation and adaptation to context.
findings.measure: Alignment of ChatGPT responses with science education themes; usefulness for generating teaching resources and editing support; qualitative reflection on output quality and epistemic authority

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single exploratory self-study with qualitative reflection rather than a controlled evaluation of instructional effects. It does not report a rigorous empirical design or comparative outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful applications for generating instructional materials and supporting writing, but it provides no effect sizes or measured learner outcomes. Impact is therefore plausible but unclear rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Applications of ChatGPT to English Language Teaching: Opportunities, Challenges, and Recommendations
paper_profiles.venue: TESL-EJ (The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, may be used in English language teaching (ELT), with attention to both instructional opportunities and risks. The authors frame ChatGPT as a generative AI tool that can support language learning, but they also emphasize concerns about academic integrity, bias, misinformation, privacy, and the limits of automated feedback. The paper is positioned as a response to the rapid emergence of ChatGPT and the need for educators to think carefully about appropriate use in language classrooms.

The paper combines a literature-based discussion with the authors’ own classroom experimentation at Northeastern University. The intervention consisted of two in-class ChatGPT-supported activities: one in an undergraduate public speaking course focused on persuasive argumentation, and one in a graduate academic listening and speaking course focused on presentation skills. Students used ChatGPT to generate debate materials or respond to prompts about presentation strategies, then critically compared AI output with their own knowledge, revised ideas, and discussed the quality and limitations of the responses. The students in these activities were undergraduate and graduate international students in a university pathways program.

The authors report that ChatGPT can increase engagement, spark discussion, and serve as a useful launching point for critical thinking, comparison, and reflection. At the same time, they conclude that ChatGPT cannot replace human teachers and should be used with human oversight, explicit guidance, and careful pedagogical design. Their recommendations emphasize collaboration among educators, reflection with students about AI use and academic integrity, and redesign of learning activities and assessments to prioritize critical thinking, process-oriented learning, and responsible use of AI.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model interface that generates human-like text responses to prompts and can assist with conversation, feedback, writing, summarization, and content generation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviews ChatGPT's potential applications in English language teaching and reports the authors' classroom use of ChatGPT in undergraduate and graduate courses for persuasive argumentation and academic presentation skills, where students prompted the tool, analyzed its output, and compared it with their own knowledge.

findings.finding_summary: The paper is a conceptual/review article rather than an empirical evaluation, so it does not report original effect sizes or controlled outcome data. It synthesizes literature and the authors' classroom observations suggesting ChatGPT may support language practice, feedback, and critical comparison, while also raising concerns about inaccuracy, bias, cheating, and academic integrity.
findings.measure: Literature synthesis and classroom observations of engagement, critical analysis, and perceived usefulness

findings.finding_summary: In the authors' classroom implementation, students appeared more engaged, talkative, and willing to critically analyze AI output, compare it against their own ideas, and question accuracy and usefulness. These are qualitative observations from two courses and are presented as promising but not causal evidence.
findings.measure: Observed student engagement, interaction, skepticism, and critical analysis during in-class activities

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/recommendation paper with classroom examples, not a controlled empirical study. The evidence presented is qualitative and descriptive, so it does not meet criteria for higher-tier causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful instructional value for engagement, feedback, and critical thinking, but no quantitative effect sizes are reported. The observed impact is promising yet uncertain because it is based on anecdotal classroom observations rather than measured outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Creative Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.venue: Palgrave Studies in Creativity and Culture (Springer/Palgrave Macmillan)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length edited volume examines how artificial intelligence, especially generative AI and other AI tools, can be integrated into education with a focus on creativity, ethics, and human–AI collaboration. The opening chapter frames AI in education as both an opportunity and a challenge: it can support personalised learning, creative pedagogies, and hybrid intelligence, but it also raises concerns about privacy, bias, agency, and techno-solutionist assumptions about educational change.

The volume is organised into three parts. The first develops a theoretical account of creative engagement with AI and proposes a six-level model ranging from passive consumption of AI-generated content to expansive learning supported by AI. The second part presents concrete examples for K-12 education, including perspectives from educators and learners on AI use in school contexts. The third part extends the discussion to higher education and other educational settings, such as teacher education, professional training, games, and chatbots. Across these chapters, the book argues that AI should be used to augment, not replace, human agency and creativity.

Because the text provided is primarily introductory and chapter-level framing rather than an empirical study, the main conclusion is conceptual: effective use of AI in education requires critical, ethical, and learner-centred implementation. The editors emphasise that educators and learners need AI literacy and opportunities to co-design human–AI learning activities so that AI supports problem-solving, creativity, and expansive learning rather than narrowing pedagogy or shifting control away from teachers and students.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: Intelligent tutoring systems are AI-driven educational systems that provide individualized instruction, guidance, and feedback based on learner responses and performance.
identified_tools.use_case: The chapter is a literature review of AI in education that discusses ITS as a common class of AI tools in education, especially as the dominant form of current AI use at the second level of the chapter’s creative engagement model.

findings.finding_summary: The review characterizes ITS as the main AI application currently used in education, especially at the 'interactive consumer' level of the model. It notes that ITS can support learning by providing individualized assistance and feedback, but the chapter does not report quantitative effect sizes or sample sizes for ITS outcomes.
findings.measure: Individualized tutoring / learner support in education

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI refers to AI systems that produce text, images, or other content in response to prompts, including large language models and AI chatbots.
identified_tools.use_case: The chapter discusses generative AI tools such as ChatGPT as part of the broader AI-in-education landscape, emphasizing their potential for human-AI collaboration, creative pedagogy, and learner support rather than evaluating a single product.

findings.finding_summary: The chapter says generative AI may be used for composing written essays and other creative writing tasks, suggesting possible support for literacy-related production. It also emphasizes concerns about access, bias, privacy, and responsible use; however, it does not provide outcome data, effect sizes, or sample sizes.
findings.measure: Writing / essay composition and broader literacy-related support

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a chapter introduction/literature-review-style overview rather than an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. It discusses AI categories and conceptual models, but reports no study design, effect sizes, or sample sizes for tool outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter argues that AI and generative AI may influence learning and literacy through personalization, feedback, and content generation, but provides no empirical effect estimates. Any impact is therefore theoretical and unclear rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Traditional Teaching: The Potential of Large Language Models and Chatbots in Graduate Engineering Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) and chatbots may be integrated into higher education, with a particular focus on graduate engineering instruction. The authors frame the work as a response to broader technological disruptions in education and ask how LLM-based tools can support teaching, learning, and academic work while also introducing risks such as hallucinations, privacy concerns, overreliance, and biased outputs.

The paper combines conceptual discussion with a case study of a graduate fluid mechanics course at Michigan State University. The intervention/approach is the use of ChatGPT and related tools such as plugins (for example, Wolfram Alpha, ScholarAI, AskYourPDF), prompt engineering strategies, and the code interpreter to answer questions, generate quizzes, summarize papers, solve mathematical problems, and create visualizations. The paper also discusses custom instructions and different prompting strategies, including input-output, chain-of-thought, and tree-of-thought prompting.

The population and context are graduate engineering students and instructors, specifically in a graduate-level fluid mechanics course in the United States. The paper concludes that LLMs and chatbots can support self-paced learning, provide immediate feedback, reduce instructor workload, and extend classroom capabilities, but their effective use requires careful prompting, ethical oversight, instructor understanding of the technology, and curricular adaptation. The authors emphasize that these tools are complementary to human instruction rather than replacements and call for ongoing evaluation and responsible implementation.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot used for question answering, content generation, feedback, and interaction via plugins and custom instructions.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the central AI chatbot in a graduate fluid mechanics course case study to answer questions, generate quizzes and summaries, evaluate student responses, support prompting strategies, and demonstrate plugin-enabled functions such as Wolfram, ScholarAI, AskYourPDF, Retrieval, Browsing, and Code Interpreter.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT could answer specialized graduate fluid mechanics questions, generate summaries, quizzes, and project support, and provide feedback on student answers. It also states that in the question-bank evaluation, the results were 'encouraging,' but no quantitative performance results, sample sizes, or effect sizes are reported in the provided text.
findings.measure: Accuracy/performance on a graduate-level fluid mechanics question bank and qualitative usefulness for instruction

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/case-study paper rather than a controlled empirical evaluation, and the provided text does not report quantitative outcome estimates or comparison conditions. The methodology described is limited to a question bank and illustrative examples, so evidence strength is low.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful instructional utility for ChatGPT, including instant feedback and support for problem solving, but no effect size is reported. Because the reported outcomes are qualitative and the measurable impact is unclear, the impact is best coded as yellow.

paper_profiles.title: The Rise of Artificial Intelligence in Educational Measurement: Opportunities and Ethical Challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This white paper examines how artificial intelligence, including generative AI and large language models, is being incorporated into educational measurement and assessment. Rather than testing a single intervention, it surveys major application areas such as automated item generation, multimodal stimulus generation, automated scoring, and AI-supported score reporting and feedback, while emphasizing the ethical and psychometric issues that arise in each area.

The paper focuses on how AI tools can support assessment workflows by generating items, producing feedback, and scoring constructed responses more efficiently and at scale. It discusses implementation requirements such as human-in-the-loop oversight, multidisciplinary collaboration, representative training data, prompt engineering, transparency, explainability, and privacy protections. It also uses illustrative examples from AP Chinese Language and Culture and NAEP scoring challenges to show where AI and human judgments align or diverge.

The paper does not study a single classroom population or a specific K-12 intervention; instead, it is a conceptual and policy-oriented synthesis aimed at researchers, assessment specialists, educators, and policymakers. Its main conclusion is that AI can improve assessment efficiency and responsiveness, but only when used with careful validation, fairness checks, and strong human oversight. The authors argue that responsible deployment requires attention to bias, accountability, accessibility, and the educational purpose of the assessment system.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used for text generation, scoring, and feedback-related tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in an illustrative example to score AP Chinese writing responses, alongside a human rater, and to provide scoring rationales for those responses.

findings.finding_summary: In an illustrative comparison using 30 essay samples from 30 third-year college students, ChatGPT 3.5 and 4.0 produced scoring rationales that were internally consistent, but their scoring method differed from the human rater's. The paper reports that ChatGPT evaluated each rubric criterion independently and averaged the scores, whereas the human rater used a holistic approach; this methodological difference could lead to a different score distribution. No formal effect size or inferential test was reported.
findings.measure: AP Chinese writing scores and scoring rationales on a 0-6 scale

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI / large language model tools broadly used to generate text, items, feedback, and automated scoring outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a class of tools across automated item generation, multimodal stimulus generation, automated scoring, feedback enhancement, and automated writing evaluation; the paper synthesizes ethical considerations and implementation conditions rather than evaluating one generic tool empirically.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a white paper / conceptual review with one illustrative example and no rigorous empirical study design reported for the paper as a whole. The evidence is therefore not suitable for higher-confidence causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper describes potentially meaningful uses and implementation conditions for generative AI, but it does not report robust effect estimates for the paper's main claims. The only quantitative example is descriptive and provides no effect size.

paper_profiles.title: Inclusive education with AI: supporting special needs and tackling language barriers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews how artificial intelligence can support inclusive education, with a focus on two major barriers in K-12 settings: language differences and special educational needs. It asks how AI tools are being used in classrooms, what benefits they may provide, what limitations they have, and what implementation conditions are needed to use them responsibly and effectively.

The paper synthesizes recent literature, case studies, white papers, and policy reports from education, accessibility, and AI research. It discusses AI translation and captioning tools for multilingual classrooms, generative AI for bilingual materials, and assistive technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, adaptive learning platforms, VR/AR, robots, emotion-recognition tools, diagnostic systems, and accessibility features. The review frames these tools as supports for students with disabilities, multilingual learners, teachers, parents, and schools, primarily in K-12 contexts, though it does not report a single primary sample or intervention study.

The main conclusion is that AI can improve comprehension, engagement, access, and personalization, but only when used as a complement to teacher-led instruction and human oversight. The paper emphasizes that effectiveness depends on infrastructure, equitable access, cultural and linguistic accuracy, privacy protections, and thoughtful pedagogical use. It recommends gradual reduction of AI dependence over time, hybrid instructional approaches, and ethical implementation frameworks so that AI supports inclusion without widening existing inequities.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general category of generative AI tools and AI-enabled educational applications, including chatbots, translation apps, captioning/subtitling tools, adaptive learning systems, assistive technologies, and diagnostic platforms used to support inclusive K-12 education.
identified_tools.use_case: This is a review paper examining how generative AI and related AI tools are integrated into K-12 inclusive education, especially literacy/language support and special needs instruction. It discusses examples such as ChatGPT, DeepL, Google Translate, Duolingo, Otter.ai, Rev.com, and other AI-driven systems, but does not empirically evaluate a single named product as the study focus.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that AI-driven translation, captioning, bilingual content generation, and tutoring tools can improve comprehension, participation, engagement, and perceived inclusion for multilingual learners and students with disabilities. It also notes that benefits are contingent on careful implementation, human oversight, and equitable access; no pooled effect size is reported for the review itself.
findings.measure: Reported outcomes across included studies and case examples, including comprehension, participation, engagement, and inclusion

findings.finding_summary: The paper states that AI translation and bilingual content tools can support literacy-related skills by helping learners understand vocabulary, follow lessons, and perform closer to native-speaking peers in comprehension assessments. It also describes AI tools for reading support, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and adaptive literacy learning as promising for students with reading difficulties and language barriers.
findings.measure: Reading comprehension, vocabulary support, and literacy engagement across cited studies

findings.finding_summary: The review synthesizes evidence that AI language tools and chatbots can provide immediate feedback, simulated practice, and personalized pathways that support language learning and proficiency development. At the same time, it warns that overreliance may impede independent language skill development, so AI should complement rather than replace direct communication and traditional instruction.
findings.measure: Language proficiency, participation in language practice, and learner autonomy across cited studies

findings.finding_summary: Across special education applications, the review reports that AI-based assistive technologies, adaptive learning systems, interactive robots, VR/AR, and early diagnostic tools can improve accessibility, independence, engagement, and individualized support. The paper emphasizes that these gains depend on implementation conditions such as teacher training, infrastructure, data privacy protections, and context-sensitive use.
findings.measure: Accessibility, independence, engagement, individualized support, and diagnostic utility across cited studies

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/integrated review with examples drawn from many prior studies rather than a single empirical evaluation of one tool. The paper does not report a new controlled design or pooled quantitative estimate for the tools it discusses.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review describes potentially meaningful benefits for literacy, language support, and inclusion, but the evidence is synthesized from heterogeneous sources and many outcomes are qualitative or non-quantified. Because no single effect size is reported, the magnitude of impact is unclear at the paper level.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Today’s Education Landscape: Understanding and Managing Ethical Issues for Educational Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the ethical issues that arise when artificial intelligence is used in educational assessment. The authors argue that although AI can support assessment practices, there is a need to understand the boundary between ethically permissible and impermissible uses, especially given concerns such as fairness, privacy, cheating, bias, and inclusivity.

To investigate this, the paper uses a systematic literature mapping approach over 33 peer-reviewed studies published from 2018 onward. The review searches Scopus, applies PRISMA-based screening, and uses topic modelling and network analysis to identify major application areas and ethical issue clusters. The study is not an intervention study in a single classroom or school; rather, it synthesizes the broader literature on AI-enabled assessment systems, including assessment construction, personalized feedback, automated grading, proctoring, predictive analytics, and learning intervention.

The paper finds fourteen recurring AI use-case themes and ten ethical issue themes. It concludes that AI-based assessment research is highly interdisciplinary and still early in development, with computer science and education both prominent. The authors emphasize that effective and appropriate AI use in assessments requires explicit ethics governance, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and practical mitigation measures tailored to specific assessment contexts.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer-aided instruction or assessment systems that use AI techniques to support instruction, assessment, feedback, grading, or related educational tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a systematic literature mapping of AI applications in educational assessment, including automated grading, personalized feedback, intelligent tutoring, proctoring, and related assessment functions across K-12 and other educational contexts.

findings.finding_summary: Across the 33 included studies, the review identified 14 AI application sub-themes in assessment, with the most cited uses being AI-generated personalized feedback (55%), AI-derived learning intervention/assistance (52%), AI-based assessment construction/curation/delivery (45%), and AI-facilitated response and grading (30%). The paper synthesizes these as common mechanisms through which AI is integrated into assessment workflows, rather than reporting a single experimental effect.
findings.measure: Frequency of AI assessment use cases across included studies

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature mapping/review rather than a primary intervention study. It synthesizes themes and frequencies across 33 papers, but does not report a controlled causal evaluation of one tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports descriptive prevalence of AI assessment uses, not effect sizes on learner outcomes. As a result, the practical impact of any single tool or intervention remains unclear from this review alone.

paper_profiles.title: Impact of ChatGPT on ESL students’ academic writing skills: a mixed methods intervention study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can improve undergraduate ESL students’ academic writing when used as a formative feedback tool. The study is motivated by the lack of direct empirical evidence on generative AI tools in writing instruction, especially in relation to feedback, self-assessment, and peer assessment in large classes.

The intervention was conducted in a university academic writing course and compared an experimental group using ChatGPT for self- and peer-assessment with a comparison group receiving business-as-usual instruction. Students completed pre-, post-, and delayed post-tests on three paragraph-writing genres: process, comparison, and cause-effect writing. The experimental group also participated in short training on using ChatGPT and in focus group discussions about their experiences.

Participants were first-year undergraduate science and engineering students in India, all ESL learners aged 18–19. Quantitative results showed the ChatGPT group improved significantly more than the comparison group on immediate and delayed writing outcomes, with especially strong gains in content generation, organization, and grammar. Qualitative findings were broadly positive, suggesting ChatGPT supported idea generation, focus, collaboration, and grammatical accuracy, while some students worried about overreliance and reduced creativity. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can be a useful formative feedback tool in large ESL writing classes when students are properly trained.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model-based conversational AI chatbot for generating and refining text, answering questions, and providing interactive feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a formative feedback tool for self-assessment and peer assessment in an undergraduate ESL academic writing intervention.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed methods quasi-experimental intervention, the experimental group used ChatGPT for self- and peer-feedback during a six-hour academic writing unit on process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraphs. Writing scores improved substantially from pre-test to post-test and delayed post-test, and the experimental group outperformed the comparison group at both post-test and delayed post-test.
findings.measure: Writing test scores on three writing tasks assessed with rubrics covering content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary
findings.effect_size: F[2,72]=330.704; partial eta squared=0.902; pre-test vs post-test d=-3.300; pre-test vs delayed post-test d=-3.898; post-test vs delayed post-test d=-0.598
findings.sample_size: n=72 analyzed for repeated measures; EG n=37, CG n=35

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods quasi-experimental intervention rather than a randomized controlled trial, so internal validity is moderate but not strong. The paper reports clear pre/post and between-group tests, but the qualitative and intact-class design limits certainty.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are very large, with partial eta squared = 0.902 and large pre/post Cohen's d values. The experimental group also outperformed the comparison group at both post-test and delayed post-test, indicating substantial impact on writing performance.

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can serve as an effective tool for automated writing evaluation (AWE) in higher education English-as-a-new-language (ENL) instruction, and whether students prefer AI-generated feedback over feedback from a human tutor. The motivation is practical and pedagogical: as large language models such as GPT-4 become more accessible, educators need evidence on whether they can support writing instruction without harming learning outcomes.

The article reports two studies conducted at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region during Spring 2023. In Study 1, 48 ENL university students were placed into a control group receiving feedback from a trained human tutor or an experimental group receiving GPT-4-generated feedback over a six-week repeated-measures quasi-experimental design. Writing quality was assessed with pre- and posttests using an analytic rubric. In Study 2, a separate group of 43 ENL students received both AI and human feedback on weekly assignments and completed preference surveys plus open-ended responses.

Study 1 found no significant difference in writing gains between students who received AI-generated feedback and those who received human tutor feedback. Both groups improved similarly over time, suggesting that GPT-4-based feedback was not inferior to human feedback in this context, but also did not produce superior gains. Study 2 showed a near-even split in student preference between AI and human feedback. Students who preferred AI emphasized clarity, specificity, and availability, while those favoring human feedback valued interaction, engagement, and opportunities for follow-up. The authors conclude that a blended model combining AI-generated feedback with human tutoring may be the most beneficial approach.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based chatbot/LLM interface used to generate text feedback on student writing.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-4 within ChatGPT to generate corrective feedback on ENL students' weekly writing assignments and to compare AI-generated feedback with human tutor feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1 (n=48 ENL university students; analytic sample n=48 minus 1 posttest-only student), AI-generated feedback from GPT-4 did not produce superior writing gains relative to human tutor feedback. Both groups improved similarly over six weeks, and the group-by-time interaction was not statistically significant, F=3.094, p=0.085, partial eta squared=0.063.
findings.measure: Pretest-posttest writing scores on an analytic rubric assessing content, coherence, language use, and sources/evidence

findings.finding_summary: In Study 2 (n=43 ENL students; weekly survey responses varied from 32 to 41, average 37.7), student preference for GPT-4 feedback was nearly evenly split with preference for human tutor feedback. Grand means were very close across satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall preference, with slightly higher means for human tutor feedback on each paired item.
findings.measure: Weekly student preference survey on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall feedback preference

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single quasi-experimental study plus a survey/mixed-methods study, not a randomized trial or meta-analysis. The design is direct but has moderate methodological limitations, so the evidence is informative but not high-certainty.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports no statistically significant improvement in writing outcomes from AI-generated feedback over human tutor feedback, with a small interaction effect (partial eta squared=0.063). Student preference is mixed/even, suggesting unclear practical impact overall.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can generate high-quality reading comprehension materials for middle school English learners, and whether those materials are suitable for real educational use. The central question is not whether generative AI improves learning outcomes versus a control condition, but whether it can produce reading passages and multiple-choice questions that match or exceed the quality of human-written classroom materials.

The authors build a reading exercise generation system using ChatGPT, with prompts for zero-shot and one-shot passage generation and prompt-based multiple-choice question generation. A GPT-2 + PPLM baseline is used for comparison on passage generation. The study is situated in Chinese middle school English education, using reading materials collected from eight middle schools in Beijing, covering Grades 7–9. The paper evaluates output quality with automatic metrics, human ratings from Chinese college students and native English speakers, and direct comparisons against human-written textbook passages and exercises.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT-generated passages are generally rated higher than both human-written and GPT-2 baseline passages on several quality dimensions, including coherence, correctness, engagement, and overall quality, and are judged suitable for middle school use. However, the generated multiple-choice questions are weaker than human-written ones, especially in usefulness, suitability, and distractor quality. Experienced teachers who tested the system reported it as useful and promising for classroom resource creation, but the paper does not provide evidence of improved student reading or literacy outcomes relative to business-as-usual instruction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used to generate reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice questions from prompts, with zero-shot and one-shot prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper used ChatGPT to generate personalized reading passages and exercise questions for Chinese middle school English learners, and compared the outputs against human-written materials and a fine-tuned GPT-2+PPLM baseline.

findings.finding_summary: Human evaluators rated ChatGPT-generated reading passages higher than human-written passages on several quality dimensions. In Human Evaluation 1, Chinese students gave ChatGPT zero-shot passages the highest scores for readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, and overall quality (e.g., overall quality 4.46 vs 4.18 for human-written); native speakers also rated ChatGPT highest overall (4.06 vs 3.89).
findings.measure: Human ratings of reading passage quality across readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, and overall quality
findings.sample_size: n=9 Chinese college students; n=364 native English speakers; 30 passages per group

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise comparison, evaluators preferred ChatGPT passages over human-written passages. ChatGPT zero-shot passages received relative quality scores of 0.87 for generated passages versus 0.13 for human-written passages, and one-shot passages received 0.80 versus 0.20.
findings.measure: Pairwise relative quality preference between generated and human-written passages
findings.sample_size: n=9 students; 10 human-written passages plus generated counterparts

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT passages were judged to follow topic constraints well and to be suitable for middle school English learners. Topic coherence scores were 0.97 for both zero-shot and one-shot ChatGPT passages, and suitability scores were 0.77 for both settings, both higher than the GPT-2+PPLM baseline and in some cases higher than human-written passages.
findings.measure: Topic coherence and suitability ratings for reading passages
findings.sample_size: n=9 students; 10 topic-matched passages plus generated counterparts

findings.finding_summary: For generated exercise questions, ChatGPT-produced questions were rated as highly aligned with passage content and useful, though still below human-written questions. The paper reports a Match score of 4.38/5, Useful score of 3.25/5, and Suitable score of 3.48/5 for generated questions, versus 4.58/5, 3.93/5, and 3.92/5 for human-written questions.
findings.measure: Human ratings of multiple-choice reading comprehension question quality
findings.sample_size: n=10 exercises; human evaluation (number of raters not specified for this section)

findings.finding_summary: Experienced teachers reported that the system could reduce cost and time while providing more diverse and personalized learning materials. This was based on week-long first-hand use and interview feedback, not student outcome testing.
findings.measure: Teacher interview feedback on usefulness, ease of use, and expected efficiency gains

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an evaluation study of generated text quality and user feedback, not a controlled study of student reading outcomes. It provides no direct evidence of literacy gains versus business-as-usual or non-AI supports.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests high-quality output generation and promising usability, but it does not report effect sizes on learner achievement. Any impact on reading/literacy outcomes remains indirect and unmeasured.

paper_profiles.title: Impact of ChatGPT on Learning Motivation: Teachers and Students' Voices
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of English Studies in Arabia Felix
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT influences English language learning motivation, with particular attention to perceived effects on language skill development. Rather than testing achievement gains with an experimental design, the authors surveyed teachers and students shortly after ChatGPT became publicly available and asked for their views on its motivational impact.

The study used a quantitative questionnaire administered online to 80 participants drawn from English-language teachers/instructors and students. The instrument asked about ChatGPT’s perceived effects on macro-skills (listening, speaking, reading, writing), micro-skills (grammar, vocabulary), and motivation-related dimensions such as autonomy, self-confidence, interest, fun/enjoyment, interaction, and career-oriented motivation. Participants were geographically dispersed and responded via email and WhatsApp; the study appears to have been conducted in the early months of 2023 in Saudi Arabia-based institutions, with some author affiliations also in Yemen and India.

Findings were broadly positive. Respondents believed ChatGPT was especially motivating for reading, writing, grammar, and vocabulary, while views on listening and speaking were neutral. The strongest perceived motivational effects were on vocabulary, independent learning, and fun/enjoyment. ANOVA results indicated differences by teaching experience for perceptions of ChatGPT’s effects on listening and interest in learning English, with more experienced participants more likely to see benefits. The paper concludes that ChatGPT is viewed as a motivational tool for English learning, but it does not provide direct evidence of literacy outcome gains against a non-AI or business-as-usual comparison.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI conversational chatbot / large language model tool for dialogue, text generation, and assistance across tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a newly launched chatbot in English language learning; participants reported perceptions of how ChatGPT affects motivation and language-skill development.

findings.finding_summary: This paper reports teacher and student perceptions (n=80) that ChatGPT motivates EFL learners to develop reading and writing skills, with mean ratings of 4.02 (SD 1.0905) for reading and 3.92 (SD 1.01601) for writing. Participants were neutral on listening (M=3.32, SD 1.2806) and speaking (M=3.25, SD 1.2877), and also viewed ChatGPT favorably for vocabulary (M=4.45, SD 0.6731) and grammar (M=3.92, SD 0.9648).
findings.measure: Likert-scale questionnaire ratings of perceived impact on reading, writing, listening, speaking, grammar, and vocabulary

findings.finding_summary: Participants generally agreed that ChatGPT increases motivation-related outcomes including autonomy (independent learning M=4.025, SD 0.826385), self-confidence (M=3.975, SD 0.826385), fun/enjoyment (M=4.0, SD 0.954669), interest in learning English (M=3.55, SD 1.123962), interaction with others (M=3.875, SD 0.932874), and eagerness to get a job (M=4.0, SD 0.871489). The paper interprets these responses as positive expectations for ChatGPT's motivational effects.
findings.measure: Likert-scale questionnaire ratings of motivation-related constructs

findings.finding_summary: ANOVA found significant differences by teaching experience for perceived listening-skill impact (F=4.57817, p=0.0132231) and interest in learning English (F=8.04608, p=0.00067103). Tukey post hoc tests showed high-experience participants differed significantly from low-experience participants on listening (mean difference=1.21429, p=0.009), while effects on interest were significant for high-experience versus low-experience and high-experience versus students (mean differences 0.92857 and 0.87218, both p=0.001).
findings.measure: ANOVA and Tukey HSD comparisons of perceived effects by teaching experience
findings.confidence_interval: 95% CI for listening high vs low: 0.255 to 2.1735; interest high vs low: 0.3331 to 1.5241; interest high vs students: 0.3034 to 1.441

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional perception study using a questionnaire, not an intervention or causal evaluation. It provides descriptive and inferential evidence about attitudes toward ChatGPT, but no direct outcome gains for reading or literacy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived effects on reading and writing, with the strongest mean rating for vocabulary, but these are not measured learning gains and effect sizes for literacy outcomes are not reported. Evidence for direct K-12 reading/literacy improvement relative to business-as-usual is therefore unclear and modest at best.

paper_profiles.title: Not quite eye to A.I.: student and teacher perspectives on the use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and teachers view the appropriate use of generative AI (GenAI), specifically ChatGPT, across stages of the writing process. The authors focus on a practical question emerging from the rapid adoption of large language models in education: when is AI support acceptable, and when does it become inappropriate or dishonest? Rather than testing whether GenAI improves writing outcomes, the study investigates stakeholder perceptions of acceptable use in educational writing tasks.

The intervention/approach studied was a questionnaire built around six writing-process tasks: brainstorming, outlining, writing, revising, providing feedback, and evaluating. Participants read sample ChatGPT prompts and outputs for each task and rated four divisions of use: using AI when already competent, using AI as an idea/model generator, submitting AI output with disclosure, and submitting AI output without disclosure. The sample included 158 university students and 68 teachers, mostly undergraduates and higher-education educators, recruited from a U.S. public research university and multiple institutions worldwide. The teacher sample included only a small number of K-12 educators, but the study itself was primarily centered on higher education.

The main findings were that students and teachers broadly agreed that GenAI is most acceptable when it supports early-stage writing tasks or helps users model ideas without replacing their own work. Using GenAI to complete writing tasks, especially without disclosure, was seen as least acceptable by both groups. Some differences emerged: students were generally more accepting than teachers of undisclosed or directly submitted AI-assisted writing, while teachers were more accepting than students of using AI for feedback and evaluation as a model. The study concludes that institutions need explicit AI policies and teacher professional development, because nearly all respondents reported little or no training and little institutional guidance on acceptable AI use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model interface used to generate text, outlines, revisions, feedback, and evaluations from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper used ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-turbo) to generate example outputs for brainstorming, outlining, essay writing, revision, feedback, and evaluation prompts, and surveyed student/teacher perceptions of the appropriateness of these uses in the writing process.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey and perception study, not an outcome study of K-12 reading or literacy achievement. It does not test whether ChatGPT improves learner outcomes relative to business-as-usual or non-AI supports.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct impact on reading/literacy outcomes was measured. The paper reports attitudes about acceptable use in writing, so there is no evidence of learning gains or losses to rate for impact.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT and Academic Research: A Review and Recommendations Based on Practical Examples
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Education, Management and Development Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT can be used in academic research and writing, using a practical demonstration rather than an empirical evaluation. The authors ask whether a large language model can help with common research tasks such as generating ideas, drafting introductions, synthesizing literature, composing methodology sections, and supporting data analysis.

The intervention studied is not an educational treatment but the use of ChatGPT-3.5 as a writing and research assistant. The authors used a demo topic, "Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Higher Education," and prompted ChatGPT to produce different parts of a hypothetical manuscript. They assessed the outputs qualitatively, focusing on whether the chatbot could generate usable research ideas, problem statements, literature reviews with citations, and analyses.

The paper does not study K-12 learners or any student population; it instead addresses academic researchers in general. The context is a desktop/online AI writing workflow using secondary examples from published articles, websites, blogs, and other artifacts. The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can be helpful for brainstorming, outlining, and summarizing, but it is unreliable for rigorous literature synthesis, accurate citations, problem statements, and empirical analysis. The authors recommend using ChatGPT only as a supplementary tool with human oversight, and they call for clearer academic guidelines for responsible use of LLMs.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model/chatbot used to generate and transform text for a wide range of writing and reasoning tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper used ChatGPT 3.5 in a demo academic writing exercise to assess its ability to generate research ideas, introductions, literature reviews, methodology, and data-analysis outputs for a topic in higher education.

findings.finding_summary: This paper is a review/practical demonstration of ChatGPT, not an empirical evaluation of K-12 reading or literacy outcomes.
