It reports that ChatGPT was useful for initial idea generation and outlining, but was weak for problem statements, literature synthesis, citations/references, and empirical data analysis; no learner outcomes were measured.
findings.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a review/practical-examples paper with no experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation of learner outcomes. It provides descriptive observations about ChatGPT's writing capabilities only.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes or learner outcome measures are reported, and the paper does not study K-12 reading or literacy impact relative to business-as-usual or non-AI supports.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring students’ perspectives on Generative AI-assisted academic writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students perceive and experience generative AI (GenAI) when used to support academic writing. Rather than testing whether GenAI improves writing outcomes experimentally, the study asks what roles students expect AI to play, what benefits they perceive during writing, and what barriers they encounter while using it. The motivation is to better understand the student side of GenAI-assisted writing and to inform future educational AI and instructional design.

The intervention/context was a ChatGPT-4-embedded writing system called Writing With GPT (WWG), developed by the research team. Twenty students in higher education completed an English academic writing task with the system and then participated in semi-structured interviews. The participants were Chinese students at an English-medium international joint-venture university in Suzhou, mainland China, spanning bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral levels, with varying IELTS scores and AI literacy levels.

The study found that students expected GenAI to function as a multi-tasking writing assistant, a private virtual tutor, and a digital peer. They perceived benefits in ideation, planning, drafting, revision, writing quality, writing speed, topic knowledge, enjoyment, question generation, perceived support, and self-efficacy. At the same time, they identified substantial barriers, including hallucination, weak contextual and cultural understanding, limited higher-order thinking, lack of human/relationship/pedagogical awareness, interoperability issues, explainability gaps, and their own limitations in AI literacy, critical thinking, topic knowledge, and writing skill. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI can support academic writing, but its effectiveness depends on student capabilities and the system’s pedagogical and contextual fit.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot and writing assistant used for dialogue, drafting, feedback, and language support.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied a ChatGPT4-embedded writing system called Writing With GPT (WWG) to support students during an academic writing task; students used it for ideation, planning, drafting, revision, proofreading, and interactive support.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative mixed-methods interview study with 20 higher-education participants, not an experimental evaluation of outcomes. It provides direct evidence about student perceptions and experienced affordances/barriers, but not causal evidence of learning gains.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived advantages such as improved writing quality, speed, and self-efficacy, but it does not report quantitative effect sizes or comparative outcome data versus business-as-usual. As a result, impact on K-12 reading/literacy outcomes cannot be established from this study.

paper_profiles.title: E-EVAL: A Comprehensive Chinese K-12 Education Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in Chinese K-12 education. The authors argue that existing Chinese and general-purpose benchmarks emphasize advanced reasoning or professional knowledge, while overlooking primary-school content and the full span of K-12 subjects.

To address this gap, the paper introduces E-EVAL, a benchmark of 4,351 multiple-choice questions covering primary, middle, and high school levels across 23 subjects. The benchmark includes both arts and science domains, and the questions were sourced from regional homework, practice exercises, and mock exams. The dataset was manually processed and checked for duplicates, formula accuracy, and answer correctness, with separate dev, validation, and test splits.

The paper evaluates 15 LLMs, including commercial and open-source Chinese- and English-dominant models, using zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, and few-shot chain-of-thought prompting. Results show that Chinese-dominant models generally outperform English-dominant models on Chinese K-12 questions, arts subjects are easier than science subjects, and very strong models still struggle with simple primary-school math. Few-shot prompting helps modestly overall, especially for arts, while chain-of-thought tends to help only on more difficult science subjects and can hurt performance on arts subjects. The paper’s main contribution is therefore a benchmark and diagnostic analysis, not an intervention study on student learning outcomes.

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba's Qwen series of large language models for general-purpose language understanding, reasoning, and generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of 15 LLMs on the E-EVAL Chinese K-12 benchmark across arts/science subjects and prompt settings (zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, few-shot-chain-of-thought).

findings.finding_summary: Qwen-72B-Chat achieved the highest average accuracy among all tested models on E-EVAL, with 88.9% average accuracy. It also performed especially well on arts subjects (92.5%) and strong, though lower, on science subjects (84.0%), indicating better performance in arts than science.
findings.measure: Accuracy on E-EVAL multiple-choice questions

findings.finding_summary: Under prompt ablations, Qwen-72B-Chat scored 89.0% in zero-shot, 88.7% in five-shot-answer-only, and 88.8% in five-shot-chain-of-thought. The paper notes that few-shot and CoT did not improve this top model and slightly reduced performance in some settings.
findings.measure: Accuracy under zero-shot, five-shot-ao, and five-shot-cot prompting

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model for general-purpose dialogue and language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of the commercial LLMs on the E-EVAL Chinese K-12 benchmark across subjects and prompt settings.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT ranked below several Chinese-dominant models on E-EVAL, with 54.6% average accuracy. Its arts score was 60.5% and science score was 46.8%, showing substantially weaker performance than top Chinese models.
findings.measure: Accuracy on E-EVAL multiple-choice questions

findings.finding_summary: Across prompt settings, ChatGPT scored 54.5% in zero-shot, 56.9% in five-shot-answer-only, and 52.3% in five-shot-chain-of-thought. The paper characterizes few-shot as slightly beneficial overall for most models, but CoT as generally detrimental on average.
findings.measure: Accuracy under zero-shot, five-shot-ao, and five-shot-cot prompting

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model / generative AI chatbot without a specific named product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper benchmarks multiple LLMs on Chinese K-12 multiple-choice questions to assess general educational capabilities rather than a single product intervention.

findings.finding_summary: The benchmark study found that all evaluated models performed better on arts subjects than science subjects, and that Chinese-dominant models generally outperformed English-dominant models. The paper also reports that top models often did better in middle school than in primary school, and that the CoT prompt helped science more than arts while harming average performance overall.
findings.measure: Accuracy on E-EVAL across subject categories, school levels, and prompt types

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/evaluation paper, not a causal study of an AI tutoring intervention. It reports model accuracy on exam-style questions rather than student outcome effects relative to business-as-usual.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No evidence is provided that generative AI improved K-12 reading/literacy outcomes for learners. The paper measures LLM benchmark performance, so there is no educational impact estimate to score.

paper_profiles.title: Generating and Evaluating Tests for K-12 Students with Language Model Simulations: A Case Study on Sentence Reading Efficiency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of creating high-quality, parallel K-12 reading assessments more efficiently by using large language models (LLMs) together with student response data. The authors focus on silent sentence reading efficiency (SRE), a timed true/false reading task intended to measure how quickly and accurately students can process simple sentences. The broader goal is to reduce the cost and labor of writing, calibrating, and validating multiple equivalent test forms while preserving psychometric quality.

The intervention/approach has two parts. First, GPT-4 is used to generate candidate true and false sentences that meet constraints for age-appropriateness, simplicity, and diversity. Second, a fine-tuned LLM item-response simulator predicts how prior students would respond to unseen items, including both response accuracy and response time. Those simulated item parameters are then used to filter items and construct parallel test forms matched to a human-authored benchmark form. The paper evaluates this pipeline computationally, with crowdworkers, and in a real school deployment.

The population includes K-12 students from multiple U.S. schools for model training and evaluation, plus a school-based validation study with 234 students in grades 2-8 from a California public school; adult crowdworkers were also used for a separate comparison study. The authors report that AI-generated forms can closely match human-generated forms in total scores and difficulty, with very high score correlations in both crowdworker testing and the school study. They also find that the simulator predicts median response time better than standard readability metrics such as Flesch-Kincaid, and can flag ambiguous or problematic items before deployment. The paper concludes that LLMs can meaningfully support reading assessment construction, but human review remains necessary for safety and appropriateness.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used to generate and evaluate educational text items.
identified_tools.use_case: Used with GPT-4 to generate true and false sentence-reading test items for a K-12 sentence reading efficiency assessment, and to support filtering of potentially inappropriate items in the crowdworker experiments.

findings.finding_summary: The paper does not test learner achievement gains from using GPT-4; it tests whether GPT-4 can help generate and filter parallel reading test items. On the school deployment, 234 students in grades 2-8 completed a human-generated Lab form and a GPT-generated AI form, and total scores were highly correlated (r=0.93) between forms, suggesting the AI-generated items were comparable for assessment purposes rather than improving reading outcomes.
findings.measure: Correlation of total scores between human-generated Lab test form and GPT-generated AI test form

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta open-weight large language model family used here as the base model for a fine-tuned item-response simulator.
identified_tools.use_case: Fine-tuned with LoRA on student response data to predict unseen item response accuracy and response time, and to identify ambiguous items for calibrating and filtering generated sentence-reading test items.

findings.finding_summary: The fine-tuned LLaMA-based item-response simulator predicted unseen item parameters better than Flesch-Kincaid. In the school student evaluation, prediction correlations were 0.316 for accuracy and 0.509 for median response time, compared with Flesch-Kincaid correlations of -0.001 and 0.254, respectively.
findings.measure: Correlation between predicted and actual item accuracy; correlation between predicted and actual median response time
findings.sample_size: school study n=234; model trained on n=1,962 participants

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical single-study paper, but it is not an intervention study of student learning gains. The evidence is correlational/model-validation focused, with no randomized comparison of AI tutoring versus business-as-usual reading instruction.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are meaningful for assessment development and item calibration, not direct literacy improvement. The strongest reported association is a high form-score correlation (r=0.93), which indicates similarity between test forms rather than instructional impact on reading outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Are Large Language Models Fit For Guided Reading?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Bard are fit to support guided reading in children’s education. The author focuses on tasks that a reading guide or teacher would perform: generating meaningful questions from a text, producing questions that vary in cognitive difficulty, covering diverse topics within a story, and identifying portions of text a student should reread based on incorrect responses.

The study evaluates these LLMs on the FairytaleQA dataset of annotated children’s storybooks. The dataset includes storybooks for children from kindergarten through eighth grade, and the evaluation uses human annotations plus automated metrics such as ROUGE-L, BERTScore, and a diversity measure (Vendi score). The paper also compares ChatGPT and Bard against prior question-generation baselines trained specifically for FairytaleQA.

The main findings are that both LLMs can generate high-quality, semantically relevant educational questions and can recommend rereading sections of text effectively. However, their question diversity decreases as the input text grows longer, and they overproduce low-cognitive-demand questions relative to the baseline. The paper concludes that LLMs show promise as guided-reading support tools, but they need further validation before being deployed in educational settings.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model / chatbot used for generating and evaluating text-based outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as a guided-reading support tool for children’s storybooks, specifically for question-answer generation, question diversity, difficulty level of questions, and recommending text sections for rereading based on student responses.

findings.finding_summary: On the FairytaleQA validation/test set (46 storybooks), ChatGPT outperformed baseline question-generation models on BERTScore for generated questions, with reported validation/test precision 96.92/96.31, recall 95.03/96.01, and f-measure 95.96/96.15. The paper interprets this as ChatGPT generating meaningful educational questions that closely match the input text.
findings.measure: BERTScore for generated questions versus FairytaleQA reference questions

findings.finding_summary: For topic coverage/diversity, ChatGPT generated questions covering 61.4 sub-topics with one-paragraph input compared with a human diversity score of 66.8. Diversity dropped to 54.4 with two merged paragraphs and 49.4 with three merged paragraphs, indicating reduced coverage as input length increased.
findings.measure: Vendi Score-based topic diversity / sub-topic coverage

findings.finding_summary: In cognitive difficulty distribution, ChatGPT produced 3006 questions total, with 109 confirmative, 2003 explicit, and 894 implicit questions. The paper reports that 70.26% of ChatGPT's questions were low-challenge, about 20 percentage points above the baseline 53.22%, meaning ChatGPT over-generated low-challenge questions relative to human-generated baseline questions.
findings.measure: Question-type proportions (confirmative, explicit, implicit)

findings.finding_summary: For text recommendation, ChatGPT achieved very high overlap with the paragraph that had been intentionally obscured through wrong answers, with BERTScore precision 98.22, recall 99.1, and f-measure 98.65. The paper concludes that ChatGPT could summarize student responses and identify the section of text a student should reread.
findings.measure: BERTScore between recommended text and target paragraph

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational large language model / chatbot (Bard was the product name used at the time).
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as a guided-reading support tool for children’s storybooks, specifically for question-answer generation, question diversity, question difficulty, and recommending text sections for rereading based on student responses.

findings.finding_summary: On the FairytaleQA validation/test set (46 storybooks), Bard outperformed baseline question-generation models on BERTScore for generated questions, with reported validation/test precision 97.12/93.31, recall 95.43/96.34, and f-measure 96.27/94.80. The paper interprets this as Bard generating meaningful educational questions closely aligned to the input text.
findings.measure: BERTScore for generated questions versus FairytaleQA reference questions

findings.finding_summary: For topic coverage/diversity, Bard generated questions covering 64.2 sub-topics with one-paragraph input compared with a human diversity score of 66.8. Diversity dropped to 56.2 with two merged paragraphs and 48.2 with three merged paragraphs, indicating reduced coverage as input length increased.
findings.measure: Vendi Score-based topic diversity / sub-topic coverage

findings.finding_summary: In cognitive difficulty distribution, Bard produced 3546 questions total, with 97 confirmative, 2505 explicit, and 947 implicit questions. The paper reports that 73.38% of Bard's questions were low-challenge, about 20 percentage points above the baseline 53.22%, meaning Bard over-generated low-challenge questions relative to human-generated baseline questions.
findings.measure: Question-type proportions (confirmative, explicit, implicit)

findings.finding_summary: For text recommendation, Bard achieved very high overlap with the paragraph that had been intentionally obscured through wrong answers, with BERTScore precision 97.3, recall 98.7, and f-measure 97.99. The paper concludes that Bard could summarize student responses and identify the section of text a student should reread.
findings.measure: BERTScore between recommended text and target paragraph

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-paper evaluation of LLM outputs on proxy metrics, not a controlled study of student learning outcomes. It does not provide direct evidence that the tools improve K-12 reading/literacy relative to business-as-usual or non-AI supports.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong generation-quality and text-matching results, but these are task-performance proxies rather than learner outcome effects. No effect sizes on reading/literacy achievement are reported, so educational impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Can LLMs Grade Short-Answer Reading Comprehension Questions? An Empirical Study with a Novel Dataset
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative large language models (LLMs) can accurately grade short-answer reading comprehension responses, with a focus on formative assessment. The authors frame automatic short-answer grading as a way to reduce teacher workload and make open-ended literacy assessment more feasible in real-world classrooms, especially in under-resourced settings.

The study introduces a new dataset of reading comprehension responses from students in Ghana and then evaluates several GPT models, including GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, on their ability to classify student answers as correct, incorrect, or partially correct. The model is given the passage, question, and student answer, and its predictions are compared against expert human ratings. The paper also tests simple prompting strategies such as zero-shot versus few-shot prompting and compares using the full story versus the relevant passage.

Participants were school-age students in Ghana, spanning ages 9 to 18, with both written and spoken reading comprehension responses included in the dataset. The core educational context is reading/literacy assessment rather than instruction, and the work is positioned as relevant to K-12 literacy evaluation in low- and middle-income country settings.

The main finding is that GPT-4, especially with few-shot prompting, achieved very strong agreement with human raters and in the 3-class setting reached QWK 0.92, exceeding the agreement level of expert raters on that metric. Performance was weaker on partially correct responses than on clearly correct or incorrect answers, and GPT-4 outperformed GPT-3.5 across conditions. The paper concludes that generative LLMs show promise for automating formative literacy assessment, though the results come from a single-country dataset and should be interpreted cautiously for broader deployment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model/chatbot system used for natural-language prompting and classification/generation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as an automatic short-answer grading model to score student reading comprehension responses against expert human raters in a Ghanaian dataset; compared GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 under zero-shot and few-shot prompts.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4 with few-shot prompting achieved near-human agreement on the 3-class grading task, with QWK=0.92 on n=1,068 student responses. In the 2-class task it reached LWK=0.89, outperforming GPT-3.5 and matching or exceeding expert-human agreement on the 3-class metric.
findings.measure: Agreement with expert human raters on short-answer reading comprehension grading (QWK for 3-class; LWK for 2-class)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study, but it evaluates model agreement with human raters rather than a causal educational intervention. The methodology is clear, yet the paper does not test learner outcomes relative to business-as-usual or non-AI supports.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported agreement metrics are high, but they are not learner outcome effect sizes and do not directly demonstrate gains in reading achievement. The paper suggests operational usefulness for grading, not measured educational impact on students.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI writing assistant, CyberScholar, can support K-12 students’ writing through formative feedback aligned with teachers’ rubrics and classroom materials. The study is framed as an exploratory pilot intended to understand the tool’s potential rather than to test causal effects against a control condition. The authors are especially interested in how GenAI might contribute to writing development, self-regulation, metacognition, and AI literacy in school settings.

CyberScholar was piloted in four public schools in the United States: three high schools and one middle school. It was used in English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History classes with students in Grades 7, 8, 10, and 11. The study involved 121 students and 4 teachers, with data gathered through classroom observations, surveys, and interviews. The tool was configured using teachers’ instructional materials and rubrics through retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering so that the AI feedback would match classroom expectations.

Findings were based on thematic qualitative analysis of student and teacher responses. Participants generally viewed the tool positively, especially because it provided detailed and specific feedback, interactive clarification, and rubric-based ratings that made expectations more transparent. Students reported perceived improvements in grammar, transitions, clarity, and overall writing quality, and some revised drafts to improve rubric scores. The paper concludes that CyberScholar has promise as a complement to teacher feedback, but it does not provide direct evidence that GenAI improves K-12 literacy outcomes relative to business-as-usual or non-AI supports.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI writing assistant that provides automated formative feedback, suggestions for revision, and rubric-aligned commentary on student writing.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as CyberScholar, a piloted GenAI assistant for K-12 writing in grades 7, 8, 10, and 11 across English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History classrooms.

findings.finding_summary: This was a qualitative multiple-case study with 121 students and 4 teachers. Students and teachers reported that CyberScholar provided detailed and specific feedback, interactive clarification, and rubric-aligned ratings that were perceived as helpful for revising writing; 36 post-survey respondents said they would like to use it again, while 11 were hesitant. The paper reports some students saw improved rubric scores after revision (e.g., one student improved a 'Compare'/'Contrast' score from 0 to 2), but no inferential statistics or standardized effect sizes were reported.
findings.measure: Student perceptions of writing support; rubric-based revision outcomes; post-survey/interview themes

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The study uses a qualitative, exploratory multiple-case design with convenience sampling and no control group, so it does not provide causal evidence of reading or literacy gains relative to business-as-usual. Evidence is useful for implementation and perceived usefulness, but not for estimating effect size.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported impact is promising but unclear: students perceived better writing support and some rubric improvements, yet the paper does not report quantified learning gains or comparative outcomes. The strongest evidence is subjective and process-oriented rather than demonstrated academic impact.

paper_profiles.title: VNHSGE: VietNamese High School Graduation Examination Dataset for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VNHSGE, a Vietnamese High School Graduation Examination dataset created to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on educational tasks. The authors argue that existing benchmarks are dominated by English-language data and do not adequately capture the breadth, difficulty, and linguistic features of Vietnamese high school exams. As a result, they build a new benchmark spanning nine subjects and including both multiple-choice questions and literary essay tasks.

The dataset combines official and illustrative exam questions from the Vietnamese Ministry of Education and Training and similar exams collected from public sources. It includes 19,000 multiple-choice questions and 300 literature essays, with accompanying answers and step-by-step explanations. The paper describes the dataset structure in detail, including subject coverage, difficulty levels based on Bloom’s taxonomy, bilingual Vietnamese-English versions, and JSON/Word formats designed for LLM testing and evaluation.

The study evaluates ChatGPT and BingChat on the dataset and compares their performance against Vietnamese students’ score distributions. The main finding is that these LLMs reach human-level performance in some subjects and question types, especially literature, English, history, geography, and civics, but remain weaker on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology. The paper’s contribution is primarily a benchmark and evaluation resource, not an intervention study on learner outcomes.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT performed at a human level in a number of areas, including literature and English, when evaluated on the VNHSGE dataset. The paper reports that it could handle knowledge and comprehension level questions, but it struggled with complex calculations and multi-step reasoning; no sample size, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
findings.measure: Accuracy on VNHSGE subject exams and question types

findings.finding_summary: On the literature dataset, ChatGPT was described as capable of responding to literary queries and generating essays. The paper indicates human-level performance in literature overall, but does not provide quantitative outcomes for reading comprehension or writing measures.
findings.measure: Literature reading comprehension and essay-writing performance
