Because no effect sizes are reported and the evidence is benchmark-style rather than instructional, the impact on learner outcomes is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Students to Question the Machine: An AI Literacy Intervention Improves Students Regulation of LLM Use in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a brief AI literacy workshop can improve middle-school students’ ability to use generative AI effectively in a school-like science task. The central problem is that students may over-trust fluent LLM outputs, accept underspecified prompts, and fail to evaluate or regulate the AI’s responses. The authors ask whether explicit instruction in how LLMs work and how to interact with them can improve students’ regulation of LLM-supported problem solving.

The intervention was a two-hour classroom workshop delivered two days before the test session. It combined conceptual content about LLM strengths and limitations with procedural guidance on how to prompt, monitor, and evaluate AI responses. The control group received no training. The study took place in one French middle school and involved 116 students in grades 8–9 (ages 13–15), who completed six science inquiry exercises using a generative AI chatbot.

Results showed that trained students performed better on final written answers and demonstrated stronger interaction regulation: they rejected underspecified prompts more often, asked follow-up questions when initial answers were insufficient, and judged response correctness more accurately. The intervention’s benefits appeared to come from better strategic regulation rather than better prompt discrimination alone. Self-reported GenAI attitudes/knowledge and metacognitive self-reports did not predict performance, suggesting that behavioral measures are more informative than self-report for assessing effective AI use in this age group. The study concludes that short, scalable AI literacy instruction can improve how middle-school students use generative AI in science tasks, though the findings are limited to one school, one subject area, and immediate post-intervention outcomes.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model chatbot used to generate and evaluate responses and support interactive problem solving.
identified_tools.use_case: Middle-school students used a GenAI chatbot during six science inquiry tasks; the intervention tested whether a short AI literacy workshop improved students' regulation of LLM use compared with no training.

findings.finding_summary: In a controlled classroom study with n=116 grade 8–9 students, the intervention group achieved higher final-answer performance than controls on a 0–20 scale (M=11.38, SD=3.87, n=76 vs. M=10.29, SD=3.04, n=40; Mann–Whitney U=1871, p=.040, r=.19). The paper reports that the advantage was tied to improved strategic use of the GenAI system rather than a large gain in prompt-discrimination ability.
findings.measure: Final written answer quality / exercise score summed across six tasks and converted to a 0–20 scale

findings.finding_summary: Trained students more often rejected underspecified prompts, asked follow-up questions when initial responses were insufficient, and judged AI answer correctness more accurately. The paper reports a significant group difference for accepting underspecified prompts (51.5% vs. 66.7%, p=.044) and a significant interaction for the benefit of follow-up questioning after underspecified prompts (interaction p=.038).
findings.measure: Prompt acceptance/rejection, follow-up questioning, and correctness judgments during LLM-supported science tasks

findings.finding_summary: The workshop did not produce meaningful changes in GenAI self-report scores. A repeated-measures MANOVA in the intervention group found no overall pre–post effect (Pillai’s trace=.116, F(6,62)=1.36, p=.247), with only small non-robust increases for Attitude and Fairness & ethics after FDR correction.
findings.measure: GenAI self-report questionnaire dimensions before and after the workshop

findings.finding_summary: Across all students, GenAI self-report scores were not associated with performance (r=.01, p=.88, R2<.001, n=116). Metacognitive self-report scores likewise did not predict exercise scores (r=.04, p=.65, R2=.002, n=116), and pre–post changes in GenAI self-reports did not predict sensitivity to prompt specificity within the intervention group.
findings.measure: Correlations between self-report measures and task performance

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled classroom study with a comparison group, pre-specified behavioral outcomes, and quantitative analyses, so it meets strong quasi-experimental evidence standards. It is not blue because it is not a fully randomized trial as described and relies on a single-school sample.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main performance effect is modest (r=.19; mean difference about 1.1 points on a 20-point scale). The strongest effects are on interaction regulation behaviors rather than on large gains in academic performance.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report evaluates how several large language models (LLMs) perform on high school mathematics examination questions and discusses their potential educational uses. The core question is not whether LLMs improve student learning directly, but how well they can solve high school science/mathematics items across different question types, difficulty levels, and prompting conditions.

The study uses mathematics college entrance examination papers from 2019 to 2023 as the evaluation set. It tests at least eight LLMs, including GLM-4-Flash, ERNIE-Speed-128K, Spark-lite, Hunyuan-lite, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, gemma-2-9b-it, Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Yi-34B. The report compares single-solution and multi-solution outputs using accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance sensitivity, and creativity-related metrics. Questions are grouped by type (multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, comprehensive) and by difficulty level.

The main findings are that performance varies substantially by model and metric. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and ERNIE-Speed-128K perform best on accuracy for comprehensive questions and multi-solution tasks, while some models are faster but less accurate. Hunyuan-lite performs well in logical guidance tasks, GLM-4-Flash is strongest in creativity/richness but slow, and gemma-2-9b-it is fastest on some tasks. The report concludes that LLMs show promise as educational tools for mathematics problem-solving, but their reasoning quality, consistency, and efficiency still need improvement before broad instructional use.

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba's Qwen family of large language models for general-purpose text generation, question answering, and reasoning.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of eight LLMs on high school mathematics exam questions from 2019-2023, including single-solution and multi-solution prompting, across accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance sensitivity, and creativity.

findings.finding_summary: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct performed strongly on accuracy and efficiency in this mathematics-question evaluation. It had the best single-solution accuracy on fill-in-the-blank questions (0.250, tied) and the best accuracy on intermediate questions (50.00%, tied), and it achieved the top multi-solution accuracy (0.64).
findings.measure: Single-solution accuracy on question types and difficulty levels; multi-solution accuracy

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta's LLaMA family of large language models for instruction-following, dialogue, and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of eight LLMs on high school mathematics exam questions from 2019-2023, with outputs assessed for accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance responsiveness, and creativity.

findings.finding_summary: Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct showed relatively balanced but generally middling performance. It had the shortest response times on multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and several difficulty levels, but its accuracy was lower than the best-performing models and its multi-solution accuracy was the lowest at 0.35 (tied).
findings.measure: Response time; single-solution accuracy; multi-solution accuracy

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic large language model / generative AI chatbot systems used for question answering, reasoning, and text generation without a single named product focus.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated multiple unnamed LLMs as a class on high school mathematics exam questions, comparing performance on accuracy, timing, logic, guidance, and creativity rather than studying a single product.

findings.finding_summary: Across eight LLMs, performance varied by question type and metric. The strongest single-solution accuracy was on comprehensive questions for ERNIE-Speed-128K (0.950) and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (0.850), while the best multi-solution accuracy was Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (0.64) and ERNIE-Speed-128K (0.63).
findings.measure: Single-solution accuracy, multi-solution accuracy, response time, logic, guidance, creativity

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a grey-literature-style evaluation report with unclear methodology, no control group, and no validated causal design. It reports descriptive performance comparisons only, so it does not meet stronger evidence thresholds.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported differences are descriptive and sometimes substantial in raw percentage terms, but there are no effect sizes or causal comparisons to business-as-usual or non-AI supports. The paper therefore suggests potential performance variation rather than demonstrated educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing to Improve Health Literacy and Communication in Pediatric Populations and Beyond
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) can generate health explanations at reading levels that may improve health literacy for children, adolescents, and caregivers. The authors frame health literacy as an important barrier to understanding medical information and suggest that AI tools could help make explanations more accessible.

The study evaluates ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing using 288 pediatric medical conditions and 26 prompt formats. Two basic prompts (“Explain {condition}” and “What is {condition}”) were compared with grade-targeted prompts (“Explain {condition} to a __ grader” and “Explain {condition} at a __-grade reading level”), with readability measured using standard indices and word counts. The work was conducted entirely through prompting the LLMs; no human participants were recruited.

Across models, basic prompts usually produced content at or above high-school reading level, often around college level for ChatGPT models. When prompts specified grade levels, all models showed some ability to adjust readability, but none reliably matched the requested grade, and all struggled to generate outputs below roughly sixth-grade level. ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 showed the widest range and generally better adaptation to lower reading levels than Bing and Bard, but the authors conclude that current LLMs are promising for health communication while still needing validation for accuracy, comprehensibility, and real-world effectiveness.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: A Google large language model chatbot for generating and transforming natural language responses. In this paper, Bard is normalized to Gemini per the required LLM family mapping.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper tested Google Bard on prompts asking it to explain pediatric medical conditions at specific reading-grade levels and compared output readability and word count across prompts and models.

findings.finding_summary: This paper did not measure student literacy gains; it measured the readability of model outputs as a proxy for accessibility. Google Bard produced outputs at roughly the 7th- to 10th-grade reading level when prompted with grade-level constraints, and at about the 9th- to 11th-grade level for some prompt sets; it also failed to generate outputs for some conditions (e.g., 11 and 19 failures for the basic prompts noted in the discussion/results).
findings.measure: Output reading grade level (average of Gunning Fog, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Automated Readability Index, and Coleman-Liau indices) and word count; prompt completion/failure
findings.sample_size: n=288 conditions; subset n=150 for ChatGPT-4, Bard tested on 288 conditions

findings.finding_summary: Across the basic prompts, Bard's outputs were around the 10th- to 11th-grade level, and when prompts specified lower grades, its outputs still generally stayed at high-school level rather than matching the requested grade. The authors interpret this as limited ability to tailor readability below the sixth-grade level.
findings.measure: Output reading grade level and word count by prompt type

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot family for producing natural-language responses to user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper tested ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 on pediatric medical-condition explanation prompts at baseline and at specified reading-grade levels to assess whether outputs could be tailored for health literacy.

findings.finding_summary: For basic prompts ('What is/are' and 'Explain'), ChatGPT outputs were at or above high-school level, with baseline output at approximately college level. For prompts specifying a target grade, ChatGPT-3.5 ranged from the 7th-grade to college-freshman reading level, and ChatGPT-4 ranged from the 6th-grade to college-senior reading level, showing greater flexibility than Bing or Bard.
findings.measure: Output reading grade level (average of four readability indices) and word count
findings.sample_size: n=288 conditions; ChatGPT-4 tested on a random subset n=150 conditions

findings.finding_summary: When asked to explain conditions 'to a __ grader' or 'at a __-grade reading level,' both ChatGPT versions varied output more than Bing and Bard and increased word count for higher-grade prompts. However, the models still struggled to precisely hit the requested grade and could not reliably produce outputs below the sixth-grade reading level.
findings.measure: Output reading grade level, word count, and ability to match requested grade level

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not an intervention study on K-12 reading outcomes; it is a descriptive readability analysis of AI-generated text. There is no experimental comparison with student literacy outcomes or a control group.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report learner outcome effects, only output readability. As such, it provides no direct evidence of impact on K-12 reading or literacy achievement.

paper_profiles.title: Integrating Universal Generative AI Platforms in Educational Labs to Foster Critical Thinking and Digital Literacy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how contemporary generative AI platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and related text/image/video tools can be used in education, not as autonomous tutors, but as objects of critical inquiry. The authors argue that because current GenAI systems can generate plausible but incorrect outputs, educators should design learning experiences that help students evaluate, compare, and question AI-generated content rather than accept it uncritically.

The main intervention proposed is an interdisciplinary laboratory model in which students create prompts on material they already know, submit those prompts to multiple GenAI systems, and then judge the outputs for accuracy, completeness, and conceptual depth. Students use rubrics to distinguish fully correct, partially correct, and incorrect responses. The paper also describes a pilot implementation in a General Astronomy course for non-science majors, where students interacted with text, image, and video GenAI tools to generate and critique content related to astronomy topics.

The population discussed is primarily undergraduate students at Borough of Manhattan Community College, with the pilot focused on non-science majors. The setting is a college classroom/lab environment, and the work was implemented across several cohorts over multiple semesters. The paper concludes that text-based GenAI tools currently have the most educational value for college-level learning because they can produce mostly accurate explanations, while image and video tools are better suited to creative or speculative tasks and are currently unreliable for scientifically precise instruction. Overall, the paper emphasizes critical thinking, digital literacy, and informed AI use rather than direct evidence that GenAI improves literacy or reading outcomes.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General-purpose generative AI / large language model chatbots and multimodal GenAI platforms used to generate text, images, and video content.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper examines student interaction with general-purpose GenAI tools in an astronomy lab and compares outputs across platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, NightCafe, Bing Image Creator, Google ImageFX, Craiyon, InVideo, Kapwing, and Synthesia.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that the GenAI-integrated astronomy lab increased student engagement, initiative, and critical thinking for non-science majors. It notes that multiple student cohorts completed the lab over several semesters, that some students completed all components within the allotted two hours, and that many voluntarily extended work outside class and shared outputs online. No standardized literacy outcome or comparison group is reported.
findings.measure: Student engagement, initiative, critical thinking, voluntary continuation of work, and qualitative pedagogical impact

findings.finding_summary: The paper claims the lab supported digital literacy and GenAI literacy, and that students learned to craft better prompts, check AI answers, and evaluate output quality. These conclusions are based on descriptive observation rather than a controlled literacy assessment, and no reading-specific outcome is reported.
findings.measure: Digital literacy / GenAI literacy / prompt engineering and critical evaluation skills

findings.finding_summary: The paper states that students deepened comprehension of astronomy content and strengthened scientific reasoning by comparing chatbot outputs against known answers and identifying inaccuracies. Text-based GenAI was reported to answer over 90% of undergraduate-textbook-difficulty questions accurately, while image tools reportedly failed on college-level scientific content with error rates approaching 100%; these are descriptive claims without experimental effect estimates.
findings.measure: Accuracy of GenAI responses on course-content questions; conceptual understanding of astronomy/science topics

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive, implementation-oriented paper with no control group, standardized outcome measure, or causal design. The paper itself explicitly notes the absence of rigorous experimental methods, so it does not meet stronger evidence criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports potentially meaningful positive engagement and learning signals, but provides no effect sizes or direct causal evidence. Because the reported impacts are qualitative and unquantified, the strength of impact is unclear rather than demonstrably large.

paper_profiles.title: On the Detectability of ChatGPT Content: Benchmarking, Methodology, and Evaluation through the Lens of Academic Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT-generated text can be reliably detected in academic writing, with a particular focus on paper abstracts. The central question is not educational learning outcomes, but the broader detectability of AI-written content in scholarly contexts, including how well humans and existing detectors can distinguish human-written from ChatGPT-written abstracts.

To study this, the authors construct GPABench2, a large benchmark of more than 2.8 million academic abstracts across computer science, physics, and humanities/social sciences. They generate three kinds of ChatGPT outputs: fully written abstracts, completed abstracts, and polished abstracts, using multiple prompt styles. They then evaluate commercial and open-source detectors, build a new detector called CheckGPT, and run a user study with researchers, faculty, and graduate students to test human judgment.

The participants were drawn from a university and a research organization, primarily involving faculty, researchers, and graduate students. The study finds that humans are close to chance at identifying ChatGPT content, even when given examples for reference, and that commercial detectors perform modestly to poorly, especially on polished text. CheckGPT performs very strongly on the benchmark and transfers well across prompts, disciplines, and several external writing datasets, but the paper does not provide evidence about K-12 reading or literacy outcomes.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model chatbot / text generation system used to compose, complete, and polish text.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate academic abstracts in three modes: fully written from scratch, completed from a partial abstract, and polished from an existing abstract. The paper also evaluates GPT-4 on the same abstract-generation tasks as a new source of generated text for detection tests.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper does not evaluate an educational intervention or learner outcome; it is a technical study of detecting ChatGPT-generated academic writing. There is no causal or correlational evidence about K-12 reading/literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No reading or literacy outcome is measured, so there is no educational impact on K-12 learners to rate. The reported results concern detectability/classification performance, not student learning.

paper_profiles.title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) function as real-time writing support in K-12 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms. The authors focus on a central question in AI-supported literacy instruction: whether step-by-step LLM scaffolding helps students improve writing performance, and how those effects vary across learner proficiency levels in a classroom setting.

To study this, the authors developed WriteAid, a chat-based LLM writing support tool designed to scaffold sentence construction, grammar explanations, and grammar revision rather than simply giving direct answers. The system was deployed in a South Korean public middle school over six weeks with 157 eighth-grade students; 133 consented to share their data. Students used the tool during two in-class writing tasks, and the researchers analyzed 14,863 query-response pairs, observed three class sessions, and later administered a delayed written assessment on the same topic.

The findings suggest that the LLM improved grammatical accuracy during in-class writing, especially for sentence construction, but the benefits were uneven. Higher-performing students tended to use the system for lower-level tasks such as vocabulary translation and validation, while lower-performing students more often relied on it for sentence generation and revision, which sometimes increased dependence and demotivation. In the delayed assessment, many AI-assisted sentences were retained verbatim, but transfer into final essays was much stronger for higher-performing students than for middle- and low-performing students.

The study concludes that LLMs can scale support in real-time classrooms, but step-by-step scaffolding is not uniformly beneficial. The authors argue that classroom AI tools should be proficiency-aware, cross-linguistically informed, and designed to preserve teacher awareness, peer learning, and equitable participation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general large language model-based chatbot or writing support system that provides interactive, context-aware assistance for generating, revising, and explaining language use.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as WriteAid, an LLM-based chat interface for real-time K-12 EFL writing support. Students used it for sentence construction, grammar revision, and vocabulary/grammar explanations during class writing activities.

findings.finding_summary: In the fall-semester deployment, students constructed 632 sentences with LLM assistance; 309 (48.9%) were later incorporated verbatim into final essays, and 82.3% of those incorporated sentences were grammatically correct. The authors conclude that the LLM improved grammatical accuracy during in-class writing, though transfer into final essays varied by proficiency group.
findings.measure: Grammatical correctness of LLM-assisted sentences and verbatim incorporation into final essays

findings.finding_summary: Retention and transfer differed sharply by performance level: high-performing students correctly incorporated 65.8% of LLM-constructed sentences into their final written assessments, compared with 37.8% for middle-performing students and 14.0% for low-performing students. This suggests stronger downstream writing benefit for higher-performing learners, but weaker retention/application for lower-performing learners.
findings.measure: Correct incorporation of LLM-constructed sentences into delayed written assessment

findings.finding_summary: Lower-proficiency students showed signs of demotivation and increased dependence on the system when scaffolding was step-by-step and time-constrained. The paper reports more confusion/annoyance in the middle- and low-performing groups (12.2 and 11.4 instances per session on average, respectively) than in the high-performing group (3.8).
findings.measure: Observed affective responses during LLM interaction (confusion, annoyance, indifference, gratitude)
findings.sample_size: n=15 sampled students for qualitative coding; n=133 consented students overall

findings.finding_summary: The system reduced teacher burden for routine questions: the teacher reported having more time to walk around and check progress because the LLM handled simple spelling and basic grammar questions. At the same time, the paper notes that teacher roles became less clear and that it was harder to identify common student difficulties once questions were split between teacher and AI.
findings.measure: Classroom observation and teacher interview on orchestration workload and monitoring

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a deployment study with qualitative coding, descriptive statistics, and a delayed written assessment, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental efficacy trial. The evidence is informative yet mixed-methods and observational, so it fits a yellow tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive gains in grammatical accuracy and some classroom efficiency, but no effect sizes are reported and benefits are uneven across proficiency groups. The strongest effects are descriptive and appear larger for high-performing students, while lower-proficiency students show mixed or negative experiences.

paper_profiles.title: Generating AI Literacy MCQs: A Multi-Agent LLM Approach
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 56th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V. 2 (SIGCSE TS 2025)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of scalable and reliable assessment materials for AI literacy in K-12 education. The authors ask whether a multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflow can generate high-quality multiple-choice questions (MCQs) aligned with learning objectives, grade levels, and Bloom’s taxonomy levels.

The intervention is a multi-agent MCQ generation system built with LangGraph and OpenAI’s gpt-4o-mini model. It uses a generator agent plus critique agents for language quality and item-writing flaws, with a supervisor agent that approves or revises items iteratively. The system produced 40 AI literacy MCQs for grades 7–9.

The evaluation involved three expert K-12 AI literacy educators reviewing the generated questions with a ten-item rubric covering correctness, readability, alignment to objectives, grade appropriateness, and classroom usability. Results suggested the questions were generally clear, grammatically sound, and relevant to the intended objectives, though experts differed on Bloom’s level and grade-level appropriateness for some items. Overall, the authors conclude that the approach shows strong potential for generating pedagogically useful AI literacy assessment items, but it has not yet been tested in real classrooms or on student learning outcomes.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model system used for generating and critiquing AI literacy multiple-choice questions.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within a multi-agent workflow (via LangGraph) to generate, critique, revise, and approve K-12 AI literacy MCQs aligned to learning objectives, Bloom's levels, and grade level.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a prototype/system description with expert judgment of generated item quality, not an empirical study of student outcomes. It does not test whether the AI tool improves K-12 reading or literacy outcomes versus business-as-usual or non-AI supports.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported results suggest the system can generate pedagogically acceptable AI-literacy MCQs, but there is no measured learner impact. Because no effect on student outcomes is reported, impact on K-12 literacy is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can generate high-quality reading comprehension materials for middle school English learners and whether those materials are suitable for classroom use. The motivating problem is that teachers often rely on outdated or repetitive reading exercises, and creating fresh, personalized passages and multiple-choice questions is labor-intensive.

The intervention is a reading-exercise generation system built around ChatGPT, with zero-shot and one-shot prompting for passage generation and prompt-based generation of multiple-choice questions. The authors also compare against a fine-tuned GPT-2 + PPLM baseline. The study is set in Chinese middle school English education, using reading passages collected from Beijing middle schools and textbook materials. Evaluation is largely human-centered: Chinese college students, native English speakers, and experienced middle school teachers rate generated passages and questions on readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, suitability, and other dimensions.

The main finding is that ChatGPT-generated passages are judged to be higher quality than both the GPT-2 baseline and, in many comparisons, human-written textbook passages. Topic adherence and suitability for middle school use are also rated highly. However, the generated multiple-choice questions are weaker than human-written ones, especially in distractor quality and diversity, so teachers may need to edit or select from generated questions. The paper concludes that ChatGPT shows promise for generating reading materials for Chinese middle school English learners, but question generation remains a key limitation.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used to generate text and answer questions from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate personalized middle-school English reading passages and multiple-choice reading comprehension questions, in zero-shot and one-shot settings, compared against a GPT-2 + PPLM baseline and human-written materials.

findings.finding_summary: Human raters found ChatGPT-generated reading passages to be higher quality than human-written passages across multiple dimensions. In Table 2, experienced Chinese students rated ChatGPT passages above human-written passages on readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, and overall quality; in Table 3, ChatGPT passages were preferred over human-written ones in pairwise comparison (0.87 vs 0.13 in zero-shot; 0.80 vs 0.20 in one-shot).
findings.measure: Human-rated passage quality, pairwise preference, readability/correctness/coherence/engagement/overall quality
findings.sample_size: n=9 Chinese college students; n=364 native English speakers; 10 passages in pairwise comparison; 30 passages in main evaluation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single conference paper with human evaluations of generated materials, not a student outcome trial. The evidence is qualitative/mixed-methods and does not directly test reading achievement gains versus business-as-usual.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows strong acceptability and quality ratings for generated passages, but it does not report learner outcome effect sizes on reading comprehension or literacy achievement. Direct educational impact on K-12 reading outcomes is therefore unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in the EFL Writing Context: Students' Literacy in Perspective
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines EFL learners’ literacy in using generative AI tools for writing support, rather than testing whether AI tools improve writing outcomes through an intervention. The study asks how familiar students are with generative AI for EFL writing, whether that literacy differs by background characteristics, and what students perceive as the main challenges and affordances of such tools.

The study used a descriptive-survey design with a closed-item questionnaire and semi-structured interviews. The sample consisted of 278 undergraduate EFL students from a public higher education institution in Saudi Arabia, specifically from English and translation departments. Quantitative analysis summarized students’ self-reported literacy across tasks such as brainstorming, translation, grammar and spelling help, paraphrasing, vocabulary support, and generating writing prompts, while nonparametric tests examined differences by specialization, GPA, and generative AI mastery level. Twenty students also participated in interviews to elaborate on challenges, affordances, and suggestions.

Findings showed a generally medium level of generative AI literacy overall. The highest-rated uses involved vocabulary learning, improving clarity and concision, punctuation/spelling/capitalization help, and translation. Specialization did not significantly affect responses, but GPA and mastery level did. Interview data suggested that students saw generative AI as easy to use and useful for personalized learning and feedback, while also noting problems with organization, word choice, and prompt-related skills. The paper concludes that students are positively disposed toward generative AI for EFL writing, but further training and support are needed.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools or large language model chatbots used for producing, revising, translating, and giving feedback on text and language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper surveyed EFL undergraduates’ literacy and perceived use of generative AI tools for supporting writing tasks such as translation, brainstorming, drafting, paraphrasing, grammar checking, vocabulary support, and real-time feedback.

findings.finding_summary: This descriptive survey found that EFL undergraduates reported a medium overall level of generative AI tools literacy for writing support (total mean=3.15, SD=1.134; n=278). The strongest self-reported items were help with punctuation/spelling/capitalization (mean=3.42), making writing clearer and more concise (mean=3.42), learning new vocabulary (mean=3.72), and suggesting synonyms or more sophisticated words (mean=3.41).
findings.measure: Questionnaire ratings of generative AI literacy for EFL writing tasks

findings.finding_summary: Responses did not differ significantly by specialization (Translation vs English; Mann-Whitney U, p=.120), but did differ by GPA (Kruskal-Wallis, p=.000) and mastery level of generative AI tools (Kruskal-Wallis, p=.012). Higher GPA students (4-5) had higher mean ranks than lower GPA groups, and the paper reports significant group differences by mastery level, though the direction is described inconsistently in the text.
findings.measure: Group differences in questionnaire total scores by specialization, GPA, and AI mastery level

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper is a descriptive survey with interviews, not an experimental study of tool effects on outcomes. It provides correlational and self-reported evidence about literacy and perceptions, which is useful but not causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No causal effect sizes on reading/literacy achievement are reported, and the study measures perceived literacy rather than learning gains. The practical signal is moderate self-reported readiness/usage, but direct outcome impact is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: The impact of generative AI on academic reading and writing: a synthesis of recent evidence (2023–2025)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly growing literature on generative AI (GAI) in higher education, with a specific focus on reading and writing practices in the social sciences. The authors ask what the recent evidence (2023–2025) shows about how GAI tools, especially ChatGPT and related applications, are being used, what benefits and risks are reported, and which theoretical and methodological trends characterize this emerging field.

The review used a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review and the SALSA framework to search Scopus and Web of Science for open-access English- and Spanish-language journal articles published between January 1, 2023 and March 7, 2025. The final corpus included 136 studies, most of which involved university students, though some also included educators. The reviewed studies covered a wide range of contexts across multiple countries, with especially strong representation from Asia, Europe, and North America.

Overall, the review concludes that GAI is widely perceived as useful for supporting academic writing, idea generation, translation, grammar correction, paraphrasing, and formative feedback. The strongest reported benefits are improvements in text quality, especially coherence, discursive organization, lexical richness, and argumentation, as well as greater student autonomy in self-editing. At the same time, the review highlights important concerns: overreliance on AI, reduced metacognitive engagement, plagiarism and authorship issues, weak detection reliability, bias, and inequitable access. The paper argues that responsible integration depends on critical AI literacy, teacher guidance, transparent use, and redesigned assessment practices.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/model family used for text generation, dialogue, and writing assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the most frequently referenced GAI tool in the reviewed literature, used for academic reading/writing support, idea generation, paraphrasing, and formative feedback in higher education. The review also discusses its use in comparison with peer and teacher feedback and in reading comprehension tasks.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was repeatedly associated with improved text quality in academic writing, especially coherence, discursive organization, lexical richness, and argumentation. The review also reports benefits for narrative fluency, originality, idea generation, paraphrasing, and self-editing autonomy, but notes risks of overreliance and reduced metacognitive engagement.
findings.measure: Text quality; coherence; discursive organization; lexical richness; argumentation; narrative fluency; originality; paraphrasing; self-editing autonomy
findings.sample_size: n=136 (review corpus); underlying study sample sizes not consistently reported

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that ChatGPT-supported formative feedback improved English-as-a-second-language writing skills compared with traditional methods. It also notes that students and teachers often valued ChatGPT feedback as practical, interactive, and adaptive, although responses could be inconsistent and required teacher supervision.
findings.measure: Formative feedback quality; writing skill improvement compared with traditional methods; perceived usefulness of feedback

findings.finding_summary: For reading-related tasks, the review notes a study on reading comprehension and inference using AI-based short-answer grading, and cites findings that students had lower comprehension than ChatGPT in one context. However, the paper does not provide pooled effect sizes or a K-12-specific estimate, and the evidence is not directly about school-age learners.
findings.measure: Reading comprehension; inference skills

identified_tools.name: Grammarly
identified_tools.description: An AI-assisted writing and grammar correction tool that provides feedback on language accuracy, style, and text quality.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed in the review as a commonly studied AI writing support tool and in at least one quasi-experimental study of writing improvement.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that Grammarly had a positive impact on grammatical accuracy and lexical richness in writing in a quasi-experimental study. The paper presents this as evidence that AI writing support can improve surface-level writing quality.
findings.measure: Grammatical accuracy; lexical richness

identified_tools.name: QuillBot
identified_tools.description: An AI paraphrasing and writing-support tool used for rewriting, paraphrasing, and text improvement.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned as one of the AI tools adopted in writing classrooms and as a tool for improving paraphrasing skills.

findings.finding_summary: The review states that QuillBot was used to improve paraphrasing skills and that adoption of QuillBot alongside other tools was associated with improvements in content and organization of texts. No pooled effect size or study-level estimate is provided.
findings.measure: Paraphrasing skills; content and organization of texts

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, not a direct experimental study, so the evidence is synthesized rather than primary causal evidence. The included literature is methodologically mixed and heavily based on surveys and quasi-experiments, which limits certainty for outcome effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports positive associations for writing quality, feedback, and paraphrasing, but no pooled effect sizes or K-12-specific direct estimates are given. The impact appears promising but is mostly modest/unclear because the evidence is indirect and primarily higher-education focused.

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT Pass High School Exams on English Language Comprehension?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI systems can answer high-stakes high school reading comprehension questions at a level comparable to students. Rather than testing an instructional intervention, the study benchmarks ChatGPT against Dutch national English reading comprehension exams to evaluate the model’s raw performance on educational assessment items.

The paper evaluates GPT-3.5 through the ChatGPT web interface and GPT-4 through the OpenAI API on three Dutch VWO English exams from 2022. These exams are mandatory for students in the Preparatory Scientific Education track in the Netherlands, which is the most academically rigorous high-school pathway and is intended for university-bound students. The tasks included multiple-choice, open short-answer, and multi-part reading comprehension questions covering identifying main ideas, inference, vocabulary in context, and related subskills.

Results showed that GPT-3.5 performed about at the average student level, while GPT-4 outperformed the average student on the exam grading scale. GPT-4 was strongest on multiple-choice items and more consistent under automated prompting, though it still made some errors and showed instability on a subset of questions. The author concludes that large language models already pose risks for exam integrity in online assessment contexts while also suggesting potential educational uses such as feedback, summarization, and support for comprehension.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model chatbot, accessed via web interface or API, capable of generating and evaluating text responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to answer Dutch VWO English reading comprehension exam questions (GPT-3.5 via web interface; GPT-4 via API) to assess performance on high school English reading comprehension tasks.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) achieved an overall mean grade of 7.3/10 on three Dutch VWO English reading comprehension exams, compared with the mean student grade of 6.99 on Exam 1. Without re-prompting, its mean grade was 6.5/10. GPT-4-0314 and GPT-4-0613 scored higher overall (8.3 and 8.1/10, respectively), but this paper evaluated exam performance rather than instructional impact on learners.
findings.measure: Performance on Dutch national high school English reading comprehension exams (grades converted from points); comparison to student exam performance on Exam 1
findings.sample_size: n=124 exam questions; student comparison n=35,698 for Exam 1 only

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single benchmark study of an AI model's exam performance, not an educational intervention study. It does not provide direct causal evidence that the tool improves K-12 reading outcomes for learners.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows strong performance on a reading comprehension assessment, with GPT-4 exceeding average student scores, but this is model capability on test items rather than impact on student learning. No learner effect size or instructional outcome is reported.

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Generation and Evaluation of Reading Comprehension Test Items with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically generating and evaluating multiple-choice reading comprehension items, with a focus on whether large language models (LLMs) can produce items of acceptable quality in German. The authors argue that conventional item development is time-consuming and that common automatic evaluation metrics are not well suited to this task, especially because similarity to reference items does not necessarily indicate good comprehension measurement.

To address this, they propose a new evaluation protocol centered on two quantities: answerability (performance with the text) and guessability (performance without the text). Their new metric, text informativity, is defined as the difference between these two measures and is intended to capture how well an item actually depends on reading the source text. They apply the protocol to human-written items and items generated by two instruction-tuned LLMs, Llama 2 Chat and GPT-4, using German texts from Deutsche Welle online language courses at CEFR B1 level.

The study uses both human annotators and LLMs as evaluators. Six native German-speaking university students or recent graduates judged items for answerability, guessability, and quality, and the authors also tested whether GPT-4 or Llama 2 could serve as automatic evaluators. The findings suggest that GPT-4 generates the strongest items overall and most closely matches human judgments, while Llama 2 performs less reliably. However, GPT-4-generated items were also often easier to guess, showing that high quality ratings do not always align with strong comprehension measurement. The paper concludes that zero-shot LLMs are promising for reading-comprehension item generation and that text informativity offers a useful human-centric evaluation method, though it does not capture all aspects of item quality.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: A family of large language models from Meta, including chat/instruction-tuned variants used for text generation and classification/evaluation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used zero-shot to generate German multiple-choice reading comprehension items and to automatically evaluate item answerability/guessability with and without text.

findings.finding_summary: Llama 2 generated reading comprehension items of acceptable overall quality in zero-shot German item generation, but it performed worse than GPT-4. On text informativity, human evaluators rated Llama 2-generated items at 0.160 (95% CI [0.109, 0.213]), and GPT-4 as evaluator rated them at 0.129 (95% CI [0.082, 0.178]), the lowest among generators.
findings.measure: Text informativity of generated multiple-choice reading comprehension items; human quality ratings
findings.confidence_interval: [0.109, 0.213] (human-evaluated text informativity for Llama 2-generated items); [0.082, 0.178] (GPT-4-evaluated text informativity for Llama 2-generated items)
findings.sample_size: 50 texts for automatic evaluation; 10 texts for human evaluation

findings.finding_summary: As an automatic evaluator, Llama 2 was less consistent with humans than GPT-4. Its mean Cohen’s κ with human annotators was 0.051 without text and 0.651 with text, below GPT-4 and below the average human-human agreement with text (0.683).
findings.measure: Inter-annotator agreement (Cohen’s κ) between Llama 2 and human annotators on item responses with and without text
findings.sample_size: 10 texts; 93 binary responses with text; fewer responses without text because each human annotated a third of items

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT family of large language models, including GPT-4, used here for zero-shot generation and automatic evaluation of reading comprehension items.
identified_tools.use_case: Used zero-shot to generate German multiple-choice reading comprehension items and to automatically evaluate item answerability and guessability with and without text.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4 generated the strongest German reading comprehension items in zero-shot prompting. Human evaluators rated GPT-4-generated items highest overall, and GPT-4’s text informativity was 0.267 (95% CI [0.219, 0.316]) by human evaluation and 0.227 (95% CI [0.187, 0.269]) by GPT-4 evaluation.
findings.measure: Text informativity of generated multiple-choice reading comprehension items; human quality ratings
findings.confidence_interval: [0.219, 0.316] (human-evaluated text informativity for GPT-4-generated items); [0.187, 0.269] (GPT-4-evaluated text informativity for GPT-4-generated items)
findings.sample_size: 50 texts for automatic evaluation; 10 texts for human evaluation

findings.finding_summary: As an automatic evaluator, GPT-4 most closely matched human responses. The mean Cohen’s κ between GPT-4 and humans was 0.185 without text and 0.724 with text, and the with-text agreement exceeded the average human-human agreement (0.683).
findings.measure: Inter-annotator agreement (Cohen’s κ) between GPT-4 and human annotators on item responses with and without text
findings.sample_size: 10 texts; 93 binary responses with text; fewer responses without text because each human annotated a third of items

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical methods paper on automatic item generation and evaluation, not a K-12 intervention study. It does not test classroom implementation, learner outcomes, or causal effects on student reading achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct evidence is provided that any AI tool improves K-12 reading or literacy outcomes relative to business-as-usual or non-AI supports. The reported outcomes concern item quality and evaluator agreement, not student learning impact.

paper_profiles.title: Generating Reading Comprehension Exercises with Large Language Models for Educational Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of automatically generating high-quality English reading comprehension exercises for educational use. The authors argue that large language models (LLMs) have strong potential for educational text generation, but that existing work has focused more on teaching support and writing correction than on the generation of assessment content such as reading comprehension items.

To address this gap, the paper proposes Reading Comprehension Exercise Generation (RCEG), a framework that combines supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, PPO-based reinforcement learning, and post-processing control mechanisms. The system uses task-specific datasets built from RACE and Chinese examination sources, then applies controlled decoding and a toxicity-filtering discriminator to produce reading passages, questions, answer options, and explanations that are more coherent, relevant, and pedagogically aligned.

The paper evaluates the framework using automatic text-similarity and reasoning metrics, plus human preference and toxicity-related analyses, rather than learner outcome measures. The only clearly named educational population referenced is Chinese middle school students in a cited prior study, but this paper itself is a model-development and evaluation study on benchmark datasets rather than a classroom intervention. The authors conclude that RCEG improves generated exercise quality and robustness compared with baseline models, but the evidence is about content generation quality, not direct K-12 reading or literacy gains.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A large language model-based educational content generation framework for automatically generating English reading comprehension exercises, including articles, questions, answers, explanations, and controlled candidate selection.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes Reading Comprehension Exercise Generation (RCEG), a framework built on LLMs and evaluated for generating English reading comprehension exercises for educational use.

findings.finding_summary: The framework was evaluated on generated reading comprehension content, not learner achievement. Compared with baseline models, RCEG-SP improved BLEU-4 and ROUGE scores for text similarity; for example, RCEG-SPQwen2.5-3B achieved BLEU-4 = 27.23 and ROUGE-1 = 22.12, outperforming its base model and the GPT2 finetune baseline. The full RCEG pipeline also lowered perplexity on clean and toxic test sets, indicating better fluency and robustness.
findings.measure: BLEU-4, ROUGE-1/2/L, perplexity (SFT-TEST, ToxicRandom, ToxicTop)

findings.finding_summary: On zero-shot reasoning benchmarks used as proxy evaluations, RCEG-SP improved HotpotQA and HellaSwag in several cases but showed mixed effects on ARC and ReClor. For example, Qwen2.5-1.5B improved from 27.02 to 41.39 on HellaSwag and from 89.25 to 95.25 on HotpotQA, while ARC and ReClor declined for that model.
findings.measure: FreeEval benchmark scores on ARC, ReClor, HotpotQA, HellaSwag

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a framework/prototype paper evaluating generated text quality and benchmark proxy metrics, not a student-level intervention study. It does not provide direct K-12 reading or literacy outcome evidence relative to business-as-usual or non-AI supports.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No learner outcome effect size is reported, and the reported improvements are on generation quality and proxy reasoning benchmarks rather than K-12 reading achievement. Therefore there is no direct evidence of educational impact on reading/literacy outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Trust and Reliance on AI in Education: AI Literacy and Need for Cognition as Moderators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students’ trust in an AI assistant relates to their ability to rely on AI output appropriately during educational problem solving. The core question is not whether AI improves learning outcomes directly, but whether higher trust leads students to use AI recommendations more or less selectively, especially when some recommendations are intentionally wrong.

The study used a single-session lab experiment with 432 undergraduate students enrolled in computing-related courses at the University of Florida. Participants solved 14 Python output-prediction problems while interacting with an AI chatbot that provided a mix of correct and misleading recommendations and explanations. The researchers measured appropriate reliance behaviorally as accepting correct recommendations and rejecting incorrect ones, and also collected survey measures of trust, AI literacy, need for cognition, programming self-efficacy, and programming literacy.

Results showed that higher post-task trust was associated with lower appropriate reliance, indicating greater likelihood of accepting AI suggestions without sufficient discrimination between correct and incorrect output. This relationship was non-linear but did not show an optimal mid-range trust pattern. AI literacy and need for cognition significantly moderated the trust–reliance relationship, such that these characteristics were associated with better selective reliance under lower-trust conditions. The authors conclude that instructional and interface supports should prompt verification and reflection when students use AI assistance.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot/model family used for dialogue, recommendations, explanations, and follow-up question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Students interacted with an AI assistant in a Wizard-of-Oz programming task; the platform integrated OpenAI's API (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125) for follow-up interactions, while initial recommendations included both accurate and intentionally misleading suggestions.

findings.finding_summary: In a single-session laboratory experiment with 432 undergraduates completing 14 Python output-prediction problems, higher post-task trust in the AI assistant was associated with lower appropriate reliance. Appropriate reliance averaged 61.77% (SD=10.78), and trust was a strong negative predictor of appropriate reliance (b=-3.65, SE=0.39, t(430)=-9.48, p<.001, R2=.173).
findings.measure: Appropriate reliance on AI recommendations during programming problem-solving

findings.finding_summary: A quadratic model fit slightly better than a linear model for predicting appropriate reliance from trust (R2=.185 vs. .173; 94R2=.012). Both the linear trust term (b=-3.18, SE=0.43, t(429)=-7.45, p<.001) and the squared term (b=0.56, SE=0.22, t(429)=2.55, p=.011) were significant, indicating a steeper decline from low to moderate trust that attenuated at higher trust values without reversing direction.
findings.measure: Nonlinear association between post-task trust and appropriate reliance

findings.finding_summary: Trust was also negatively associated with task accuracy on the programming output-prediction items (r=-.38, p<.001). The paper reports that students frequently followed misleading recommendations (overreliance M=86.03%, SD=25.52) while rejecting correct recommendations was uncommon (underreliance M=2.37%, SD=8.27).
findings.measure: Task accuracy on Python output-prediction problems

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-session observational laboratory experiment with regression analyses, not an RCT or QED evaluating learning gains relative to a comparison group. Evidence is useful for mechanism/trust behavior, but it is correlational with respect to outcome relations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported association with appropriate reliance is moderate in magnitude (e.g., R2=.173; r=-.42), but it is negative and concerns trust/reliance behavior rather than demonstrated improvement in K-12 reading or literacy outcomes. The paper does not provide evidence of beneficial impact on literacy achievement.

paper_profiles.title: An Experiential Approach to AI Literacy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a practical gap in AI literacy: people may hear about AI and understand it in the abstract, yet still struggle to identify where AI fits into their real workflows or how to judge whether it is appropriate for a given task. The authors argue that AI education often creates “knowing” without “doing,” especially for non-technical audiences, and propose an approach that makes AI literacy more grounded, contextual, and useful.

The proposed intervention is an experiential AI literacy model with three phases. First, participants take part in an interactive workshop that introduces high-level concepts of AI, including how it works, what it can and cannot do, and how to evaluate its use. Second, over roughly 2–4 weeks, participants reflect on their daily work experiences and brainstorm potential AI use cases in their own contexts using design tools and short activities. Third, they return for a sharing workshop where they present and refine these use cases through storytelling, including discussion of opportunities, limitations, fairness, privacy, accountability, and workflow integration.

The intended population is stakeholders in diverse workplaces, with examples including nurses in emergency departments, elementary school teachers, and municipal government workers. The paper is not an empirical evaluation; instead, it is a conceptual proposal grounded in prior AI literacy and experiential learning literature. The authors conclude that embedding AI literacy in participants’ own lived and work experiences should support deeper understanding, better participatory design of AI systems, and more practical, stakeholder-centered AI use-case development.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI/LLM chatbot or assistant used for broad AI capability discussion and ideation, without a specific commercial or research product being evaluated.
identified_tools.use_case: This position paper proposes an experiential AI literacy approach that references generic examples of AI such as chatbots, but does not empirically evaluate any specific AI tool in K-12 reading or literacy instruction.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/position paper proposing an experiential AI literacy approach. It does not report an empirical study, comparison group, or outcome data relevant to K-12 reading or literacy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct evidence is presented on learner outcomes, effect sizes, or impacts relative to business-as-usual or non-AI supports.

paper_profiles.title: Areas of Strategic Visibility: Disability Bias in Biometrics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position statement responding to a request for information on biometrics, with a focus on how biometric systems can harm or exclude disabled people. It argues that accessibility problems are not limited to algorithmic accuracy; they also arise from inaccessible interfaces, biased datasets, unsuitable configuration, and systems that encode ableist assumptions. The paper frames disability in terms of systemic barriers and emphasizes that equitable biometric use requires moving beyond narrow notions of fairness or inclusion toward agency, control, and disability justice.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or a learner population. Instead, it synthesizes risks and opportunities across biometric recognition and inference, including identification, access control, diagnosis, public safety, and workplace monitoring. It highlights how disabled people may be misrecognized, excluded, or pathologized by biometric systems, and why data collection, validation, governance, and transparency processes must involve disabled communities from design through deployment.

Its main conclusion is that biometrics should never be treated as sufficient for disability identification or service eligibility, and that stronger regulation, accessible design, participatory development, and interpretability/correctability are required. The authors argue that without these guardrails, biometric technologies can amplify discrimination and produce serious harms, even when framed as fairness-improving or beneficial tools.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI/chatbot systems based on large language models or similar generative methods.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not evaluate a reading or literacy tool; it is a disability-bias position statement about biometrics and AI governance, with only incidental references to AI systems such as HireVue and biometric recognition technologies.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position statement / policy response rather than an empirical study. It contains no direct evaluation of an AI tool on K-12 reading or literacy outcomes, no comparison group, and no effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no reported intervention effect on student outcomes, so impact on reading or literacy cannot be assessed from this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Vocalnayno: Designing a Game-Based Intervention to Support Reading Development in Primary Schools
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 6th European Conference on Games-Based Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting early reading development in primary schools, especially when schools depend on teaching assistants or parent volunteers to provide individualized reading practice and assessment. The author argues that existing paper-based or informal support processes can be inefficient, slow to communicate pupil needs, and limited in the type of feedback they provide to teachers.

To respond to this problem, the paper proposes and sketches a game-based intervention called Vocalnayno. The system is designed as a reading game in which pupils read letters and words aloud to progress, while the software records their performance as an assessment measure. The intended use is on a laptop or tablet, with results stored in a database accessible to parents and teachers so that helpers can receive prompts and teachers can better monitor phonics strengths and weaknesses.

The paper is based on an action-research-inspired design process at a local primary school in the United Kingdom. It describes early prototype development, informal consultation with teaching assistants, parents, and children, and a pilot test involving the author and one pupil. The work is explicitly presented as in progress rather than as an efficacy study. Its main conclusion is that a game-based reading tool may be promising as a more objective and engaging assessment aid, but substantial technical and design challenges remain, including unreliable voice recognition and the need for further development before classroom deployment.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI-enabled reading/game-based assessment concept using speech recognition and an interactive game to capture oral reading performance and provide feedback to teachers and assistants.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and prototypes Vocalnayno, a game that prompts pupils to read letters and words aloud so the system can measure phonics/reading ability and support formative assessment in primary schools.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a design-oriented, work-in-progress paper with a prototype and no classroom deployment or controlled evaluation. It reports no empirical outcome data on reading or literacy improvement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No impact can be established because the paper does not report measured effects on learner outcomes versus business-as-usual or non-AI supports. The text only argues potential usefulness and notes pilot technical issues.

paper_profiles.title: On the Effect of Anticipation on Reading Times
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether readers’ expectations about upcoming words influence reading times beyond the standard surprisal effect. The authors argue that reading is not only responsive to already observed words, but also anticipatory: readers may allocate processing time based on how uncertain they are about future words. They operationalize anticipation using contextual entropy and related Rényi entropy measures.

The study compares entropy- and surprisal-based predictors on four naturalistic reading datasets: two self-paced reading corpora (Brown and Natural Stories) and two eye-tracking corpora (Provo and Dundee). The analysis uses GPT-2 small to estimate word-level surprisal and entropy, then fits linear regression or logistic regression models to predict reading times and word skipping. The participants are adult readers, including undergraduate readers in Brown and adult native English speakers in the other corpora, all reading naturalistic English texts in lab-style reading tasks.

The main finding is that contextual entropy often predicts current-word reading times above and beyond surprisal, especially in Brown, Natural Stories, and Dundee, with Rényi entropy (alpha = 1/2) sometimes outperforming Shannon entropy. However, entropy effects are generally local and do not reliably predict spillover in the way surprisal does. The paper finds some evidence that word skipping is associated with entropy, but weaker evidence that entropy effects on reading times are driven by budgeting or preemptive processing. Overall, the authors conclude that reading behavior reflects both responsive and anticipatory processing, but that anticipation appears to matter most for current-word processing rather than later spillover.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic language model / chatbot-style generative AI system producing word probabilities used to compute surprisal and entropy over text.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper uses GPT-2 small as a language-model estimator to approximate word surprisal and contextual entropy in naturalistic reading corpora; it does not study an educational AI product or K-12 learning intervention.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a psycholinguistics paper about reading-time prediction, not an educational intervention study. It uses a language model as an analytic estimator, but does not evaluate an AI tool for K-12 learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 literacy or instructional impact is measured. The reported results concern model fit to adult reading-time data, not learner achievement or educational effectiveness.

paper_profiles.title: Question Generation for Assessing Early Literacy Reading Comprehension
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of generating reading-comprehension questions for early literacy assessment, especially for K-2 English learners. The authors argue that content-based interactions such as dialogic reading are important for reading acquisition, and propose an automated way to create comprehension questions that can cover source material thoroughly and adjust to learner proficiency.

The intervention presented is YourBench4Edu, a question-generation framework built on the YourBench pipeline. It ingests learning materials in formats such as PDF, HTML, and markdown, summarizes and segments the text, and then uses large language models to generate diverse question-answer pairs across question types such as factual, analytical, true/false, single-shot, and multi-hop questions. The system is designed to be configurable by question type, difficulty, and quantity, and is intended for use in conversational agents and educator preparation of assessment items.

The paper validates the framework on the FairytaleQA validation and test sets, which contain narrative-comprehension questions for kindergarten through eighth-grade level materials, though the paper’s stated educational target is K-2 learners. The evaluation compares several language models, including Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Qwen3-235B-A22B, and QwQ-32B, against prior question-generation methods using MAP@N with Rouge-L F1 and BERTScore F1. The authors conclude that their framework achieves strong results, especially on Rouge-L-based MAP@N, and suggest it could support autonomous AI-driven English instruction.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: A Meta LLaMA-family large language model used for question generation and reading-comprehension assessment in an educational pipeline.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as the underlying language model for YourBench4Edu to generate early-literacy comprehension questions from story text and ground-truth answers for K-2 English learners.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct used within YourBench4Edu achieved competitive question-generation quality on the FairytaleQA validation and test sets. On MAP@N with Rouge-L F1, the model scored 0.515/0.497 at Top 10, 0.508/0.489 at Top 5, 0.500/0.481 at Top 3, and 0.477/0.459 at Top 1; on MAP@N with BERTScore F1 it scored 0.9027/0.8996, 0.9018/0.8987, 0.9006/0.8977, and 0.8971/0.8943, respectively.
