It reports benchmark metrics on generated questions rather than learner-level effects, so it does not meet evidence standards for direct effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are on automated generation metrics (MAP@N with Rouge-L F1/BERTScore F1), not on student reading or literacy outcomes, so educational impact is indirect and unclear. No effect sizes on learner outcomes are provided.

paper_profiles.title: Fostering learners’ self-regulation and collaboration skills and strategies for mobile language learning beyond the classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Routledge Handbook of Language Teaching and Learning beyond the classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter examines how self-regulated learning (SRL) and collaborative learning can be supported in mobile-assisted language learning (MALL) beyond the classroom. The authors argue that language learners need support to manage their own learning processes, collaborate effectively, and make productive use of mobile technologies across settings, especially as learning increasingly happens outside traditional classrooms.

Rather than reporting a single intervention study, the chapter reviews a sample of 20 empirical studies published between 2010 and 2020 on mobile language learning, SRL, and collaboration. The paper highlights mechanisms used in prior work, such as goal-setting support, dashboards, self-monitoring tools, peer feedback structures, and teacher-orchestrated collaborative tasks. It also discusses how learning analytics and artificial intelligence could be used to provide adaptive language learning paths.

The population context spans second/foreign language learners, including older K-12 students, university students, and migrant adult learners, though the chapter is especially attentive to out-of-class mobile learning contexts. The main conclusion is that mobile technologies can help foster SRL and collaboration, but effective design requires clear theoretical grounding, attention to learner support, privacy, and adaptive feedback. The chapter does not evaluate generative AI tools or reading/literacy outcomes directly; instead, it offers a conceptual and design-oriented synthesis for future MALL development.

identified_tools.name: Mobile Learning Apps (General)
identified_tools.description: Mobile-assisted language learning applications and related mobile learning systems used to support language learning outside the classroom, sometimes with adaptive or self-regulation features.
identified_tools.use_case: The chapter reviews empirical studies of mobile-assisted language learning and discusses how mobile apps and related designs can support self-regulation and collaboration in language learning beyond the classroom; it does not evaluate one specific named AI product.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed MALL studies, the chapter reports generally positive associations between mobile technology use and self-regulated learning, and suggests these technologies can support individualized and adaptive language learning paths. However, the chapter is a narrative synthesis of selected studies (20 papers) rather than a direct causal evaluation of a single AI tool.
findings.measure: Narrative synthesis of self-regulated learning and collaborative language learning outcomes in mobile-assisted language learning studies

findings.finding_summary: The chapter states that m-learning enhanced learners' SRL and SRL enhanced m-learning in the reviewed literature (Palalas & Wark, 2020 cited within the chapter, n=38 reviewed studies). It also notes that SRL behavior was the most important factor in predicting linguistic outcomes in one cited study, but the chapter does not provide direct effect sizes for that result.
findings.measure: Association between mobile learning and self-regulated learning; linguistic outcomes in cited studies
findings.sample_size: 38 reviewed studies (as cited in the chapter)

findings.finding_summary: For collaborative mobile language learning, the chapter reports benefits such as increased opportunities for communication, target-language negotiation, peer feedback, and writing quality/quantity, but also emphasizes that gains are hard to attribute directly to collaboration because many interventions mixed individual and collaborative components.
findings.measure: Collaboration-related language learning outcomes (communication, peer feedback, writing, speaking/listening practice) in reviewed studies

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative book chapter synthesizing prior studies rather than reporting a controlled evaluation of one AI tool. The evidence is therefore descriptive and secondary, with no direct effect sizes reported in the chapter text.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter suggests potentially meaningful benefits of mobile and AI-supported language learning designs, but it does not provide quantified impacts on K-12 reading/literacy outcomes relative to business-as-usual or non-AI supports. The strongest claims are qualitative and refer to heterogeneous studies with mixed designs.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks what it means for learning, teaching, and assessment in higher education. The central concern is whether a powerful generative AI chatbot can disrupt traditional assessment practices, particularly written assignments and essays, while also creating new opportunities for instruction and learning support.

The paper is not an intervention study with participants. Instead, it combines a desktop literature review with hands-on experimentation using ChatGPT. The authors situate ChatGPT within the broader history of AI in education and compare it to established AI-powered writing and assessment tools such as Grammarly, Wordtune, automated essay scoring systems, and intelligent tutoring systems. The context is higher education, though the article repeatedly frames its implications for students, teachers, and institutions more broadly.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is impressive but limited. It can generate fluent prose, explain concepts, and support some writing tasks, but it also produces inaccurate, generic, biased, or fabricated content and struggles with higher-order reasoning, citations, and some languages. The authors argue that ChatGPT is unlikely to be a reliable substitute for human judgment or robust assessment, but it will likely force educators and institutions to rethink assessment design, policy, and teaching practices.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational AI chatbot built on GPT-family large language models; designed to generate and answer text in natural language.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviews ChatGPT's functionality and experiments with it for explanations, mathematical problem solving, essay drafting, and Chinese composition, while comparing it conceptually to established AI writing/feedback tools.

findings.finding_summary: Across the paper's literature review and author demonstrations, ChatGPT was described as useful for conceptual explanations and simple question answering, but weak for higher-order academic writing. The paper reports that it produced generic, shallow essays, struggled with accurate citations, had uneven factual accuracy, and performed poorly in Chinese composition; no sample sizes or effect sizes were reported.
findings.measure: Quality of generated explanations, essays, citations, and Chinese composition; functional limitations observed during experimentation

findings.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can save time by generating responses within about 60-120 seconds and could help with brainstorming, drafting, and quick reference use. However, it also notes limitations including network errors, character limits, outdated knowledge after 2021, inability to draw diagrams, and risk of producing bogus references or biased/offensive outputs.
findings.measure: Observed response speed and functional limitations during hands-on testing and literature review

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/review-style article with informal experimentation rather than a controlled empirical study. It provides no rigorous design, no inferential statistics, and no effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful classroom and assessment implications, but it does not quantify impact. Reported effects are mostly qualitative, and several limitations and risks are emphasized alongside the benefits.

paper_profiles.title: A comprehensive AI policy education framework for university teaching and learning
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapid rise of text-generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in higher education and the need for an institutional policy response. The author argues that universities need guidance on academic integrity, privacy, accountability, equity, and pedagogy because generative AI can both support learning and create risks such as cheating, over-reliance, reduced critical thinking, and unclear attribution of AI-assisted work.

The study uses a mixed-methods survey of stakeholders in Hong Kong universities. Data were collected from 457 students and 180 teachers and staff across disciplines through an online questionnaire with closed- and open-ended items. The quantitative component measured experiences and perceptions of generative AI use, while thematic analysis of open-ended responses identified key concerns and policy priorities.

Based on the findings, the paper proposes an AI Ecological Education Policy Framework with three dimensions: Pedagogical, Governance, and Operational. The framework emphasizes responsible use, AI literacy training, transparent governance, equitable access, monitoring and evaluation, assessment redesign, and support for student holistic competencies. The main conclusion is that generative AI should be integrated as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for human teaching, with policy structures to mitigate risks and maximize educational benefits.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based generative AI chatbot/system used for text generation and conversational assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper examines perceptions, risks, and policy implications of using ChatGPT and similar generative AI technologies in university teaching and learning.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods survey of 457 students and 180 teachers/staff in Hong Kong universities, respondents broadly supported institutional planning for generative AI (students mean=4.5, teachers mean=4.54 on the need for a plan to manage risks). At the same time, they expressed concerns about academic misconduct, unequal advantage in assignments, over-reliance, privacy, transparency, accountability, and weakened critical thinking and transferable skills.
findings.measure: Survey ratings and open-ended responses on perceptions of ChatGPT/generative AI, including risk management, academic misconduct, privacy/security, over-reliance, and effects on skills

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative and quantitative mixed-methods survey study, not an experimental evaluation of outcomes. It provides useful stakeholder perceptions and policy implications, but no causal estimate of tool effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial perceived impact on academic integrity, governance, and student skills, but these are attitudes and concerns rather than measured learning effects. No effect size is reported.

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper examines how ChatGPT responds to prompts about science education and what its outputs might mean for educators. The author asks three questions: how ChatGPT answers science-education questions, how it might be used in science pedagogy, and how it can function as a research tool. Rather than evaluating a classroom intervention with participants, the paper uses a self-study methodology to generate and analyze ChatGPT outputs and compare them with established science-education literature.

The paper focuses on generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, and illustrates its use in producing responses about effective science teaching, pedagogical choices, supporting students who are failing, designing a Year 7 science unit using the 5Es model, creating a self-assessment rubric, and generating a quiz. The context is science education broadly, with examples framed for K-12 classroom use, especially Year 7 energy-source lessons. The paper argues that ChatGPT can be useful for brainstorming, drafting, and scaffolding teaching resources, but only as a starting point that requires educator expertise and contextual adaptation.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT’s outputs often align with key themes in the science-education literature, but they are not reliable enough to be used uncritically. The author highlights important limitations and risks, including lack of evidence-based grounding, potential to present itself as an epistemic authority, biased or Western-centered output, false citations, environmental costs, content moderation issues, and copyright concerns. The paper recommends that educators model responsible use, encourage critical thinking, and be transparent about expectations when AI tools are used in teaching or research.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model / generative AI chatbot for generating and revising human-like text and assisting with a range of language and content tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a self-study exploratory paper to answer science-education prompts, generate a Year 7 unit using the 5Es model, draft a self-assessment rubric, generate a quiz with answer key, and assist with editing/rephrasing the manuscript.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT's answers often aligned with key research themes in science education, including inquiry-based learning, real-world connections, differentiation, collaboration, assessment, and supportive responses to students who are failing. However, the author notes that the outputs were generic at times and required refinement, and that alignment did not substitute for evidence-based justification.
findings.measure: Author comparison of ChatGPT outputs with cited science-education literature

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can help educators generate ideas for science units, rubrics, and quizzes, and can support researchers with editing, phrasing, flow, and word choice. The author describes it as a useful starting point that can reduce blank-page barriers and help clarify research narrative, especially for early-career teachers and pre-service teachers.
findings.measure: Author reflections on utility for lesson planning, assessment design, and editing support

findings.finding_summary: The paper warns that ChatGPT can position itself as an epistemic authority despite lacking grounded evidence, may produce false or misleading references, may reflect Western perspectives and bias, and raises ethical concerns including environmental impact, content moderation labor, copyright infringement, and assessment integrity. These risks are presented as limitations and unintended consequences requiring critical educator oversight.
findings.measure: Author analysis of risks and ethical concerns discussed alongside ChatGPT outputs

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory self-study and reflective analysis rather than a controlled evaluation, so it provides useful descriptive insights but not high-causal evidence. The paper includes no effect sizes or comparison groups.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported influence is potentially meaningful for teacher planning and research workflows, but the paper does not quantify educational gains. The strongest claims are about practical usefulness and risk awareness rather than measured outcome impact.

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in higher education: Benefits, challenges, and future research directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the role of ChatGPT in higher education, asking what benefits and challenges generative AI presents for teaching, learning, assessment, and academic work. Framed by constructivist theory of learning, it is a perspective/theoretical article rather than an empirical study. The authors organize the discussion around five benefits and five challenges, and they propose 19 propositions for future research and institutional practice.

The paper argues that ChatGPT could support adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research and writing assistance, administrative automation, and innovative assessment design. It situates these possibilities in higher education contexts where students, academics, and administrative staff may use ChatGPT through direct prompting or integration into learning management systems. The analysis emphasizes that these benefits are most aligned with constructivist principles when ChatGPT is used to scaffold active learning, inquiry, and personalized support rather than replace human instruction.

At the same time, the paper highlights risks and unintended consequences including ethical and equity concerns, academic integrity violations, biased or falsified information, inability to evaluate graduate skill sets, and difficulty assessing learning outcomes. The authors conclude that higher education institutions should prioritize AI literacy, responsible-use education, better assessment design, and safeguards against bias and misconduct. Overall, the article positions ChatGPT as potentially useful but requiring careful governance to avoid superficial learning and compromised educational quality.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot and large language model system for conversational text generation, question answering, and related language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses ChatGPT as a generative AI tool in higher education, focusing on its potential benefits and challenges for learning, feedback, research support, administrative support, and assessment design.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical paper rather than an empirical evaluation, so it does not provide a study design, sample, or measured outcomes. The paper synthesizes arguments and propositions about ChatGPT’s use in higher education.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ChatGPT may improve adaptive learning, feedback, and efficiency, but it does not report quantitative impact estimates or causal evidence. Because it is not an empirical study, impact is best treated as unclear rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that the rapid spread of generative AI in education, especially ChatGPT and other large language models, requires schools to rethink how students and teachers use these tools. The central problem is not whether AI should be present in classrooms, but how institutions can avoid misuse, overreliance, hallucinations, unfair advantages, and loss of independent thinking while still taking advantage of AI’s potential for personalized learning and support.

The article proposes three core competencies for AI-era education: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It draws on a conceptual discussion, informal discussions at a Swiss university of applied sciences, and a narrative literature review, then illustrates the approach through a case study of Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich. The case describes how the institution created AI guidelines for student work, requiring transparency about tools used, how they were used, and how outputs were critically evaluated. The paper also summarizes examples of classroom uses such as AI experiments, case study generation, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive technologies.

The main conclusion is that simple bans or unrestricted permission are both inadequate. Instead, institutions should build an AI culture through workshops, clear guidelines, ongoing staff support, dedicated resources, and deliberate instruction in AI literacy and prompt engineering. The author emphasizes that students should use AI as a sparring partner rather than a ghostwriter, and that critical reflection is essential to reduce risks such as hallucinations, bias, unethical copying, and diminished learning.

identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot for generating and refining text-based responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as one of several AI chatbots/LLMs used by students and lecturers for academic writing, brainstorming, classroom experiments, and prompt-engineering practice; also referenced in the institution's guidelines as an example model.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational large language model chatbot for generating text and other outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned in the institutional guidance as an example of an AI model students might declare using; also referred to via Bard as a comparable chatbot for classroom experimentation.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's conversational large language model chatbot for generating text-based responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Listed in the paper's example disclosure of AI tools that students should document if used in academic work.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbots and related generative models used for text, image, and sound creation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a broad category for AI tools discussed conceptually in higher education and K-12-adjacent classroom practice, including student writing support, case-study generation, curricula support, gamification, immersive/virtual reality, and prompt-engineering pedagogy.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review with a single institutional case example, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool. No controlled study, sample-based outcome data, or tool-specific effect estimates are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for meaningful educational relevance and identifies practical risks and limitations, but it does not report measured impacts or effect sizes. As a framework paper, its influence is conceptual rather than evidence-quantified.

paper_profiles.title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can encode and use clinical knowledge effectively, and how to evaluate their safety and usefulness in medical question answering. The authors argue that existing benchmarks were too narrow and focused mainly on accuracy or automated text metrics, which are insufficient for real-world clinical use. To address this, they introduce MultiMedQA, a benchmark that combines six existing medical question-answering datasets with a newly curated consumer-health dataset, HealthSearchQA.

The study evaluates PaLM, Flan-PaLM, and an instruction prompt-tuned version called Med-PaLM on multiple-choice and long-form medical questions. The paper includes automated evaluation, selective prediction analysis, and human evaluation by clinicians and lay users across dimensions such as scientific consensus, correctness, completeness, harm, bias, helpfulness, and intent alignment. Although Flan-PaLM achieves state-of-the-art performance on several multiple-choice medical benchmarks, human evaluation shows important gaps in factual grounding, harmfulness, and bias. Med-PaLM improves substantially over Flan-PaLM and approaches clinician performance on several axes, but still does not match clinicians overall.

The paper’s context is medical AI rather than K-12 education. No school-based participants, classrooms, teachers, or students were studied. The main conclusion is that LLMs show promise for medical question answering, but reliable deployment requires better grounding, uncertainty handling, fairness evaluation, and safety alignment. The paper also identifies risks such as hallucinated misinformation, outdated consensus, inappropriate content, and demographic bias, and calls for more robust evaluation frameworks and future research.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: A Google large language model / foundation model family for natural language understanding and generation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluates PaLM and its instruction-tuned variant Flan-PaLM, and introduces instruction prompt tuning to create Med-PaLM.

findings.finding_summary: On multiple-choice medical QA benchmarks, Flan-PaLM achieved state-of-the-art performance, including 67.6% accuracy on MedQA (USMLE-style questions), 57.6% on MedMCQA, and 79.0% on PubMedQA. The paper reports that this exceeded prior state of the art by more than 17% on MedQA.
findings.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, and MMLU clinical topics

findings.finding_summary: Human evaluation found major limitations in Flan-PaLM long-form answers: 61.9% were judged aligned with scientific consensus, 16.1% contained inappropriate and/or incorrect content, 47.6% omitted important content, 29.7% were potentially harmful, and 7.9% contained biased information. Med-PaLM improved several of these outcomes, with 92.6% aligned with scientific consensus, 15.3% missing important content, 5.9% potentially harmful, and 0.8% biased, but 18.7% still contained inappropriate and/or incorrect content.
findings.measure: Clinician-rated scientific consensus, incorrect content, missing content, extent of possible harm, and bias on consumer medical questions
findings.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap percentile interval reported, exact values not provided in text

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary empirical study with human evaluation and benchmark testing, but not a randomized or quasi-experimental education study. The evidence is observational/benchmark-based and partly qualitative, so it does not meet higher experimental evidence criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported benchmark gains are substantial on medical QA, but the paper is not about K-12 learning outcomes and does not report a standardized effect size for classroom impact. Human-rated harms and limitations are important, but overall impact on the requested K-12 literacy context is indirect.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in higher education: Considerations for academic integrity and student learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines how ChatGPT was being discussed in news coverage about higher education in early 2023, with a particular focus on academic integrity concerns and the possible educational uses of generative AI. Rather than testing ChatGPT directly in classrooms, the paper asks how public discourse framed the tool’s risks and benefits, including cheating, detection, policy responses, and opportunities for learning.

The study uses content analysis of 100 English-language news articles from Australia, New Zealand, the United States, and the United Kingdom. The context is university teaching and assessment, with articles coded for themes such as university responses, academic integrity, AI output limitations, and student learning opportunities. The analysis also examined whose voices were represented, finding that university staff voices dominated while student voices were comparatively limited.

The paper concludes that public discussion was heavily weighted toward cheating and avoidance, but that articles also recognized legitimate educational uses such as feedback, brainstorming, plain-language explanations, and support for diverse learners. The authors argue that banning ChatGPT is likely impractical and that universities should instead revise assessments, develop clear policies, and involve students more directly in conversations about ethical AI use. They also note that ChatGPT may create both risks and opportunities, especially around equity and inclusion, while its limitations and biases mean its use must be guided carefully.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot that produces text responses from user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper analyzes media coverage of ChatGPT in higher education and discusses its uses, risks, limitations, and policy responses; it does not evaluate ChatGPT directly in K-12 classrooms.

findings.finding_summary: Across 100 news articles, discussion of ChatGPT was mixed: articles emphasized academic integrity concerns (n=88) and avoidance strategies (n=87), while fewer discussed productive teaching uses (n=58) or institutional policy allowing use (n=10). The paper reports no direct effect estimates; instead, it synthesizes reported risks such as cheating, inaccurate outputs, bias, privacy/security concerns, and potential learning benefits such as plain-language explanations and feedback.
findings.measure: Content analysis of news articles; frequencies of themes and reported concerns/benefits

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative content analysis of news articles, not an empirical study of student outcomes. The evidence is useful for mapping reported themes and concerns, but it does not provide causal or performance effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes are reported, so classroom impact cannot be quantified. The paper suggests potentially meaningful risks and opportunities, but the impact level remains unclear from the evidence presented.

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in education: Applications, challenges: insights from a systematic review
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Information Technology Education: Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper conducts a systematic literature review of empirical studies on the use of ChatGPT in school and higher education. The review asks how ChatGPT is being used by teachers and students, what its performance is across subject areas, what limitations and ethical issues arise, and what impact it has on student performance, higher-order thinking, motivation, and related outcomes.

Using PRISMA, the authors searched major academic databases for studies published between January 2023 and January 2024 and screened 1,653 records down to 50 included empirical articles. The review covers preschool, primary, secondary, and higher education, with most evidence coming from higher education and foreign language learning, but with a substantial subset of K-12 studies as well. Reported uses include lesson planning, quiz and assessment creation, personalized materials, dialogue practice, writing support, problem-solving assistance, and grading support.

The review finds that ChatGPT can support cognitive performance, critical thinking, motivation, language learning, and some subject-specific tasks, but its performance is uneven. Limitations and risks include inaccurate or superficial responses, fabricated references, weak deep reasoning, calculation errors in STEM, biased content, privacy concerns, academic integrity violations, copyright issues, overdependence, and potential misuse. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has educational promise, but its integration requires AI literacy, prompt engineering, human oversight, and further empirical research, especially in primary and secondary education.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative conversational AI chatbot / large language model used to generate, revise, explain, and evaluate text and other educational content.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic review examined empirical studies using ChatGPT in school and higher education, including its use by teachers for lesson plans, quizzes, rubrics, assessment tasks, and personalized materials, and by students for language practice, feedback, problem-solving, and writing support.

findings.finding_summary: Across the 50 included empirical studies, ChatGPT was reported to support cognitive performance, critical thinking, motivation, language skills, and AI literacy in many contexts, including K-12 settings. However, the review also identified recurring limitations and risks, especially for K-12 classrooms: inaccurate or superficial responses, fabricated citations, reduced higher-order thinking, academic integrity violations, copyright concerns, bias, privacy issues, dependence, and occasional negative effects on academic achievement, critical reasoning, and motivation in one study.
findings.measure: Systematic review synthesis of reported effects and limitations across included empirical studies

findings.finding_summary: The review reports positive effects on language-related outcomes in school and higher education, including improved essay writing, vocabulary and grammar practice, feedback use, and writing improvement. These benefits were especially visible in foreign language learning contexts such as English, German, and Chinese.
findings.measure: Reported language and writing outcomes across included studies

findings.finding_summary: In STEM-related studies, ChatGPT was reported to help students with conceptual understanding and problem-solving, particularly in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and programming. The review also notes important limitations in complex or numerical calculations, with several studies reporting computational errors.
findings.measure: Reported STEM learning outcomes and problem-solving performance

findings.finding_summary: Several studies in the review reported increased motivation, engagement, persistence, and enjoyment when students used ChatGPT. These outcomes were observed in history, data science, programming, business administration, and English learning contexts.
findings.measure: Motivation, engagement, persistence, and enjoyment reports

findings.finding_summary: The review found repeated reports of improved critical thinking and higher-order thinking when ChatGPT was used in structured ways, including knowledge construction, lesson planning, and writing tasks. At the same time, the paper stresses that the model can be limited in deep, creative, and complex problem-solving and may weaken critical thinking if used dependently.
findings.measure: Critical thinking / higher-order thinking outcomes reported in included studies

findings.finding_summary: The review identifies substantial ethical and institutional concerns: academic integrity violations, copyright infringement, privacy risks, biased content, unequal access, and potential malicious use. It also reports concerns about inaccurate student evaluation and shortcomings in curriculum design when ChatGPT is used for grading or instructional planning.
findings.measure: Reported ethical, privacy, assessment, and curriculum-design concerns

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of empirical studies rather than a single controlled intervention, so the evidence is useful but indirect. The included studies are mostly qualitative, mixed-method, or exploratory, and the paper does not provide pooled effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports many positive educational uses, but the magnitude of effects is not quantified in aggregate and several important risks are emphasized. Because the evidence is synthesis-level and effects are not numerically estimated, impact is best treated as modest/unclear rather than strong.

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review article that surveys the existing literature on artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than evaluating a specific classroom intervention, it synthesizes prior work to describe what AI tools can do in educational settings, including personalized learning, instant feedback, automated assessment, language support, and administrative support for teachers and institutions.

The paper frames ChatGPT as a generative AI system capable of human-like text generation and discusses how it compares conceptually with earlier educational AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics systems, and chatbots used for feedback or tutoring. The discussion is broad and includes potential applications across learners, educators, and administrators, but it does not report a primary empirical sample, grade-level participants, or a specific school implementation.

Its main conclusion is that AI tools such as chatbots and ChatGPT have substantial promise for supporting teaching and learning, especially through personalization and efficiency gains. However, the authors emphasize major limitations and risks, including bias, privacy concerns, deception, accuracy problems, over-reliance, weakened academic integrity, lack of human interaction, and the need for teacher training and ethical oversight. The paper argues that effective and responsible integration of generative AI into education will require careful policy, pedagogical alignment, and further research.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot based on GPT models that generates human-like text responses from natural language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Reviewed as the focal AI tool in education, especially for chat-based assistance, personalized feedback, language support, and classroom use; the paper discusses ChatGPT alongside other AI tools but centers on ChatGPT's transformative potential.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a review article and conceptual overview, not an empirical evaluation of ChatGPT in classrooms. It synthesizes prior literature and discusses opportunities, limitations, and risks without reporting original measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ChatGPT may have substantial educational potential, but it does not provide effect sizes or direct outcome data. Reported impact is therefore suggestive rather than evidenced in this study.

paper_profiles.title: E-EVAL: A Comprehensive Chinese K-12 Education Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces E-EVAL, a benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in the Chinese K-12 education domain. The authors argue that existing Chinese benchmarks emphasize broader or more advanced abilities and do not adequately cover the full K-12 range, especially elementary content. E-EVAL is designed to measure knowledge and reasoning across primary, middle, and high school subjects using multiple-choice questions drawn from homework, practice questions, and mock exams.

The benchmark contains 4,351 questions across 23 subjects, split into arts and science categories. The paper describes the construction pipeline, including PDF/Word parsing, manual formula processing, multiple rounds of human checking, answer balancing, and the creation of development, validation, and test splits. The evaluation compares 15 open-source and proprietary LLMs using zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, and few-shot-chain-of-thought prompting.

Results show that Chinese-dominant models generally outperform English-dominant models on Chinese K-12 tasks, although all models struggle more on science than arts subjects, and especially on mathematics. The paper also reports that few-shot prompting is often helpful, particularly for arts, while chain-of-thought prompting tends to help science but can reduce overall performance, especially in arts. The authors conclude that strong performance on higher-level knowledge does not guarantee mastery of simpler elementary material, highlighting a gap in current models’ educational capabilities.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family conversational large language model system used for dialogue, question answering, and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of 15 LLMs on the E-EVAL Chinese K-12 benchmark under zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, and few-shot-chain-of-thought prompting.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports ChatGPT's overall accuracy on E-EVAL as 54.6% average across prompt settings, with 54.5% zero-shot, 56.9% five-shot-ao, and 52.3% five-shot-cot. It performed better on arts than science overall (61.0 / 63.1 / 57.5 vs. 54.6 / 56.9 / 52.4) and was notably weaker than Chinese-dominant models on this Chinese K-12 benchmark.
findings.measure: accuracy on E-EVAL multiple-choice questions

findings.finding_summary: On the paper's simple primary-school mathematics example, ChatGPT was among the top-3 models that answered incorrectly; the correct answer was B (Qiang Qiang), but the model predicted C (Ming Ming). The authors use this as evidence that even simple elementary-level math can be problematic for LLMs.
findings.measure: accuracy on a primary school math word problem example

identified_tools.name: GPT 4.0
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-4 family conversational large language model system used for dialogue and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as a benchmarked LLM on E-EVAL under zero-shot and few-shot prompting.

findings.finding_summary: GPT 4.0 achieved 70.6% average accuracy on E-EVAL overall, with 70.5% zero-shot, 73.8% five-shot-ao, and 67.4% five-shot-cot. The paper reports that it outperformed ChatGPT but still lagged behind the best Chinese-dominant models on Chinese K-12 questions.
findings.measure: accuracy on E-EVAL multiple-choice questions

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that GPT 4.0 performed poorly on simple primary-school math as part of the top-3 models that answered the race-time question incorrectly, despite succeeding on harder high-school math examples. This is cited as evidence that mastery of more complex knowledge does not guarantee mastery of easier elementary knowledge.
findings.measure: accuracy on math examples at primary and high-school levels

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba's Qwen family of large language models used for dialogue, reasoning, and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated on E-EVAL, including Qwen-72B-Chat and Qwen-7B-Chat, across zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, and few-shot-chain-of-thought prompting.

findings.finding_summary: Qwen-72B-Chat had the highest reported overall E-EVAL accuracy at 88.9% average, with 89.0% zero-shot, 88.7% five-shot-ao, and 88.8% five-shot-cot. The paper highlights it as outperforming GPT 4.0 and most other models on Chinese K-12 tasks.
findings.measure: accuracy on E-EVAL multiple-choice questions

findings.finding_summary: Qwen-72B correctly answered the simple primary-school race-time math example and the harder high-school logarithm comparison example. The authors cite it as an example of strong math performance relative to other models, though they also note broad science weakness across models.
findings.measure: accuracy on selected math examples

identified_tools.name: ERNIE-Bot 4.0
identified_tools.description: Baidu's ERNIE-Bot 4.0 large language model, a knowledge-enhanced conversational model with multimodal capabilities.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of the commercial LLMs on E-EVAL.

findings.finding_summary: ERNIE-Bot 4.0 achieved 85.5% average accuracy on E-EVAL, with 86.7% zero-shot, 85.2% five-shot-ao, and 84.6% five-shot-cot. It ranked second overall and was close to Qwen-72B-Chat, but still below the best Chinese-dominant model.
findings.measure: accuracy on E-EVAL multiple-choice questions

findings.finding_summary: ERNIE-Bot 4.0 was among the top-3 models that answered the simple primary-school race-time question incorrectly, even though it handled the harder logarithm comparison example correctly. The authors argue this suggests poor robustness on elementary numeracy.
findings.measure: accuracy on math examples at primary and high-school levels

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic large language model chatbots and general-purpose generative AI systems without a single named product focus.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper benchmarks multiple LLMs as general-purpose generative AI systems for Chinese K-12 question answering and prompt-based evaluation.

findings.finding_summary: Across all evaluated models, the paper reports a consistent pattern that models performed better on arts than science subjects, and Chinese-dominant models generally outperformed English-dominant models on the Chinese K-12 benchmark. The authors also report that few-shot prompting usually helped modestly, while chain-of-thought prompting often reduced overall performance except in some science subjects.
findings.measure: accuracy across arts/science and prompting conditions

findings.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly notes that nearly all models performed poorly in complex mathematics, and that even very simple primary-school math could be answered incorrectly. It further argues that higher-order knowledge does not imply mastery of lower-order knowledge, indicating a limitation of current LLMs in elementary numeracy.
findings.measure: accuracy on mathematics questions across primary, middle, and high school levels

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark paper evaluating multiple LLMs on a custom K-12 test set, but it is not a randomized intervention study and does not examine classroom implementation. The evidence is therefore useful but methodologically limited for causal claims about educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are accuracy differences rather than intervention effect sizes, and no standardized impact metric is provided. The paper shows substantial performance variation across models and subjects, but the practical classroom impact remains indirect and uncertain.

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models Only Pass Primary School Exams in Indonesia: A Comprehensive Test on IndoMMLU
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents IndoMMLU, a new benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on Indonesian exam questions spanning primary school through university entrance level. The work addresses the gap that most multilingual LLM evaluation has focused on English or translated English benchmarks, which can miss local language, culture, and curriculum-specific content. The authors argue that school exams are useful educational assessments because they are designed by expert teachers and test both language proficiency and higher-order reasoning.

To build the benchmark, seven professional Indonesian teachers collected 14,981 publicly available multiple-choice questions from web sources across 64 tasks and four education levels. The dataset covers STEM, social science, humanities, Indonesian language, and local languages/cultures, with explicit attention to culturally grounded content such as Javanese, Sundanese, Balinese, Minangkabau, and other local languages. The paper then evaluates 24 multilingual LLMs, including GPT-3.5, XGLM, Falcon, BLOOMZ, mT0, LLaMA, and Bactrian-X, using zero-shot and few-shot prompting.

The main finding is that GPT-3.5 performs best overall, but only reaches a level comparable to passing primary school exams in Indonesia, and all models struggle badly on local language and culture questions. Few-shot prompting helps some base models but can hurt instruction-tuned models. The authors also report that negation makes questions harder and examine model confidence calibration. Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs still lack robust Indonesian language and cultural competence, and that education-science-informed benchmarks are important for more meaningful multilingual evaluation.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT family of large language models used for natural language understanding and generation, including ChatGPT-style GPT-3.5/GPT-4 systems.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of several multilingual LLMs on the IndoMMLU benchmark to assess Indonesian language, local culture, and school-exam knowledge across education levels.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-3.5 achieved the highest overall accuracy on IndoMMLU at 53.2% across 64 tasks, but this was still low relative to the paper's 65% passing threshold. It passed the highest primary school level for general subjects, but performance fell below passing for grades 3 and above in Indonesian language and it showed limited knowledge of local languages and culture.
findings.measure: Zero-shot multiple-choice accuracy on IndoMMLU; passing threshold of 65%

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark evaluation study, not an RCT or controlled intervention study. The methodology is systematic and empirical, but the paper reports model benchmarking rather than causal evidence about classroom effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: GPT-3.5 shows moderate benchmark performance on Indonesian primary-school content, but the paper does not report effect sizes and explicitly notes substantial limitations, especially for local language/culture and higher grades. The practical impact is therefore mixed and uncertain for K-12 use.

paper_profiles.title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) function as real-time writing support in K-12 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms, with a focus on whether AI scaffolding helps or harms learning under classroom constraints. The authors ask how students at different proficiency levels interact with LLM-based support, what effects these interactions have on grammar and vocabulary learning, and how classroom dynamics change when AI is introduced as a learning aid.

The intervention was WriteAid, a chat-based LLM writing support tool designed as a technology probe. It provided step-by-step scaffolding for sentence construction, grammar explanations, and grammar checking, rather than direct answers. The system was co-designed with a middle school teacher and deployed in a public South Korean middle school over six weeks, using two writing assignments. The study involved 157 eighth-grade students, with 133 consenting to data analysis, and combined interaction log analysis, qualitative coding of student queries, classroom observation, and follow-up teacher input.

The paper finds that LLM support can improve grammatical correctness and help higher-performing students efficiently delegate lower-level tasks such as vocabulary lookup and validation. However, the same step-by-step scaffolding was often counterproductive for lower-performing students: it could demotivate them, increase dependence on the system, and produce frustration when answers were withheld under time pressure. The authors also report classroom-level risks, including reduced teacher visibility into struggling students, dominant participation by a few extroverted students, and diminished peer learning as students turned to the AI instead of classmates. The paper concludes that LLMs can be useful classroom tools, but only if they are designed for proficiency-aware support, clearer teacher-AI role division, and better mechanisms for monitoring equity and over-reliance.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-family large language model used as an LLM-based writing support system that provides chat-based, step-by-step scaffolding for sentence construction, grammar revision, and vocabulary/grammar explanations.
identified_tools.use_case: Implemented as WriteAid in a real-time K-12 EFL classroom deployment to scaffold eighth-grade students’ English writing over six weeks; the paper also used GPT-4o to analyze extracted sentences and grammar correctness.

findings.finding_summary: In a six-week deployment with 157 eighth-grade students (133 consented for analysis), the LLM-supported writing tool improved grammatical accuracy during in-class writing. Of 632 sentences constructed with LLM assistance, 309 (48.9%) were incorporated verbatim into final essays, and 82.3% of those incorporated sentences were grammatically correct.
findings.measure: Grammatical correctness of LLM-constructed sentences and their incorporation into final essays

findings.finding_summary: The tool’s step-by-step scaffolding benefited higher-proficiency students more than lower-proficiency students. High-performing students correctly incorporated 65.8% of LLM-constructed sentences into final assessments, compared with 37.8% for middle-performing students and 14.0% for low-performing students, suggesting weaker retention/transfer among lower-proficiency learners.
findings.measure: Transfer/recall of LLM-constructed sentences into delayed written assessment

findings.finding_summary: While the system improved baseline sentence accuracy, it also created unintended learning risks for lower-proficiency students. The paper reports that step-by-step guidance could demotivate these students and increase dependence on the system, especially under real-time classroom time constraints.
findings.measure: Observed student dependence, demotivation, and interaction patterns during classroom use

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods deployment study with qualitative coding, descriptive statistics, and classroom observations rather than a randomized or quasi-experimental causal design. The evidence is informative but limited by the single-school setting and lack of a control condition.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful improvements in grammatical accuracy and sentence use, but no effect sizes are provided and the outcomes are mixed across proficiency groups. It also documents notable negative consequences, including demotivation, dependence, and reduced peer interaction, which temper overall impact.

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Large Language Models on K-12 Education in Rural India: A Thematic Analysis of Student Volunteer’s Perspectives
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how student volunteer teachers perceive the potential impact of large language models (LLMs) on K-12 education in rural India. The authors focus on a practical question: whether generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Bard, and Claude can support learning in under-resourced rural classrooms, and what barriers or risks may limit adoption.

The study is based on 23 semi-structured interviews with volunteer educators involved in rural teaching programs in Rajasthan and Delhi. These participants, mostly university-affiliated student volunteers with direct experience teaching in rural schools, discussed AI awareness, classroom infrastructure, teacher preparedness, student learning needs, parental attitudes, and ethical concerns. The analysis used Braun and Clarke’s thematic analysis approach.

Findings suggest that participants saw LLMs as potentially useful for personalized learning, visualization, language support, and reducing teacher workload, but only as complementary tools rather than replacements for human teaching. Major barriers included poor connectivity, lack of devices, low teacher AI literacy, language mismatches, cost, parental skepticism, and fears of over-reliance, reduced creativity, privacy risks, and academic misuse. The paper concludes that LLMs may have value in rural K-12 settings if they are locally adapted, supported by training, and implemented within a hybrid teacher-led model.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot or assistant used for educational support, content generation, tutoring, and feedback-related tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied through 23 semi-structured interviews with student volunteers about the potential use of LLM-based tools in rural K-12 classrooms in Rajasthan and Delhi.

findings.finding_summary: Interview participants viewed GenAI as a complementary tool that could personalize learning, reduce teacher workload, generate visuals/content, and support multilingual explanation. At the same time, they raised concerns about infrastructure barriers, low teacher readiness, parental skepticism, over-reliance, privacy, and misuse in rural K-12 settings; no quantitative effects were reported.
findings.measure: Perceptions of benefits, barriers, ethical concerns, and implementation feasibility from semi-structured interviews

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative thematic analysis based on 23 interviews, which provides grounded perceptions but no causal or quantitative evidence. The study is methodologically clear, but it does not estimate effects of an intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports potentially meaningful educational uses of GenAI, but impact is speculative and not measured with outcomes. Reported benefits and risks are important, yet no effect sizes or student outcome data are provided.

paper_profiles.title: Approaching the Limits to EFL Writing Enhancement with AI-generated Text and Diverse Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Hong Kong secondary school students used AI-generated text while composing an English feature article, and whether particular interaction patterns with generative AI were associated with better writing quality. The study is motivated by a concern that generative AI may change the writing process in EFL classrooms, but that benefits may vary by students’ existing writing competence and AI literacy.

The intervention-like activity was a two-hour school workshop on writing with ChatGPT support, after which 59 secondary students completed a feature-article writing task using their own words plus text from at least one generative AI chatbot. Students could use any chatbot, but had to highlight AI-generated text in their submissions. The researchers analyzed the compositions using content analysis, multiple linear regression, and cluster analysis to examine the relationship between AI/human text use and human-rated scores for content, language, and organization.

The results suggest that overall writing quality was driven mainly by the total number of words in a composition rather than by how AI text was integrated. High-achieving students appeared better able to benefit from AI because they could write independently and use AI strategically, while lower-achieving students relied more heavily on AI-generated text and often did not gain higher scores from more AI use. The paper concludes that generative AI can support EFL writing, but the benefits are uneven and depend on students’ traditional literacy, process-writing skills, and ability to prompt and revise effectively; without careful pedagogy and AI literacy instruction, AI may distort rather than improve some students’ writing development.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system used for text generation and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Students used ChatGPT-like generative AI chatbots to generate and revise text while composing a feature article; the authors also state they used ChatGPT to improve readability and language during manuscript preparation.

findings.finding_summary: In 59 Hong Kong secondary school EFL compositions written with AI-generated text, composition quality was mainly associated with the total number of words rather than how AI text was integrated. Across all submissions, partial correlations between total score and AI words (0.417**) and human words (0.424**) were positive and statistically significant, while chunk-level pattern variables were not significant.
findings.measure: HKDSE-based human-rated composition scores (content, language, organization, total) and word/chunk counts in student compositions

findings.finding_summary: Among high-banding schools (n=37), scores were more strongly associated with the number of AI words (total score partial correlation 0.578**) and human words (0.544**). Short AI chunks showed slight negative associations with scores (#), suggesting some ineffective drafting/revising patterns, but students in this band also appeared capable of writing independently of AI text.
findings.measure: Partial correlations between composition scores and AI/human word and chunk counts, stratified by school band

findings.finding_summary: Among low-banding schools (n=22), more AI words did not help students achieve higher scores; the model p-values were larger than 0.05 and AI-word partial correlations were not statistically significant. Human revision of AI text was negatively associated with content and organization scores, and compositions relying on long AI chunks were more likely to score higher on content and organization, suggesting that revising AI output could lower scores for less competent writers.
findings.measure: Partial correlations between composition scores and AI/human word and chunk counts, stratified by school band

findings.finding_summary: Cluster analysis identified multiple learner profiles: some students achieved high scores with high AI use, some with low AI use, and some scored poorly regardless of AI reliance. The authors conclude that the same interaction pattern with AI-generated text can benefit some students' writing but not others, and that low-banding students relied more heavily on AI-generated text overall.
findings.measure: Cluster profiles based on AI/human word proportions, chunk features, and total scores

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods/correlational study with content analysis, regression, and clustering, not an experimental causal design. The evidence is informative but limited by observational associations and no reported effect sizes or confidence intervals.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are primarily descriptive and correlational, with no standardized effect sizes given. The practical implications are meaningful for classroom writing instruction, but the magnitude of impact on outcomes is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school students regulate inquiry when using ChatGPT for science investigation tasks. The central question is whether students can meaningfully initiate, evaluate, and continue question-asking cycles with a generative AI tool in ways that support learning, or whether they over-rely on the system and terminate inquiry too early.

The study asked 63 French middle school students aged 14–15 to complete six science tasks using ChatGPT 3.5. Students were shown either efficient or inefficient suggested prompts, judged prompt quality, interacted freely with the model, rated every AI response, and then wrote short answers in their own words. The researchers measured prompt discrimination, answer evaluation sensitivity, follow-up questioning, and task success, and related these behaviors to prior knowledge, AI attitudes, and metacognitive skills.

Results showed weak prompt discrimination, poor ability to tell high-quality from low-quality AI answers, and very limited follow-up questioning. Students often accepted vague or low-level answers and frequently ended inquiry prematurely. Positive attitudes toward AI and self-reported prior knowledge were associated with worse interaction quality, while metacognitive regulation and more critical perceptions of AI were associated with better performance. The authors conclude that GenAI can create an “illusion of understanding” in K-12 classrooms and that effective use requires explicit AI literacy and metacognitive-regulation instruction, not just technical familiarity.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used for open-ended question answering and content generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Middle-school students used ChatGPT during six science investigation tasks to initiate question-asking cycles, evaluate AI responses, and decide whether to ask follow-up questions.

findings.finding_summary: Students showed near-chance ability to discriminate efficient from inefficient prompts (mean d'=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08; n=63). They also struggled to judge answer quality, with near-zero sensitivity to expert-rated response quality (mean d'=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65), and only 14 students asked any follow-up questions across six tasks.
findings.measure: Prompt discrimination sensitivity (d'), answer-quality discrimination sensitivity (d'), and follow-up question frequency

findings.finding_summary: Task performance was moderate/low despite unrestricted access to ChatGPT. The average correct solution rate across six problems was Msuccess=0.51 (SD=0.25), and success was predicted by receiving high-level AI answers, sensitivity to answer quality, and asking follow-up questions after low-level answers.
findings.measure: Final written science explanations / correct solution rate

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary empirical study with a clear procedure and defined measures, but it is correlational/observational rather than an experimental RCT. The paper also reports several modeled associations and descriptive outcomes rather than causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are mostly chance-level sensitivities and a moderate success rate (Msuccess=0.51) without a single clear large effect size reported. The practical impact is important for classroom use, but the measurable effects are mixed and often small or null.

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review on Prompt Engineering in Large Language Models for K-12 STEM Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how prompt engineering has been used with large language models (LLMs) in K-12 STEM education. The authors note that although LLMs such as GPT-4 and ChatGPT are increasingly used for tutoring, problem solving, feedback generation, lesson planning, and assessment, there was no comprehensive review focused specifically on prompt engineering in K-12 STEM settings. To address this gap, they conducted a PRISMA-based systematic review of empirical studies published from 2021 through January 25, 2024.

The review screened 2,654 papers and included 30 studies. Across these studies, the authors catalogued prompt strategies such as simple prompting, role-assigned prompting, zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, retrieval-augmented generation, and structured output formatting. The reviewed work covered K-12 STEM subjects including math, physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, and related interdisciplinary areas, with most evidence coming from elementary, middle, and high school contexts.

The paper concludes that advanced prompting strategies often improve LLM performance relative to simple prompting, but gains depend heavily on task, model, and prompt design. GPT-series models dominated the literature, though some smaller fine-tuned models performed better in specific contexts. However, the review finds limited real-world validation, substantial variability in evaluation methods, and major reproducibility issues because many papers do not fully share prompts or implementation details. The authors also emphasize limitations such as prompt sensitivity, poor generalizability across tasks, difficulty handling visual content, and the need for more rigorous classroom-based studies.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model chatbot system used for generating, explaining, evaluating, and interacting with educational content.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper systematically reviewed K-12 STEM studies that used ChatGPT/GPT-series models with prompt engineering for problem solving, lesson planning, feedback generation, grading, tutoring, and chatbot-based student interactions.

findings.finding_summary: Across 30 reviewed studies, GPT-series models (including ChatGPT/GPT-3.5/GPT-4) were the dominant tools used in K-12 STEM prompt-engineering research. The review reports that GPT-4 generally performed strongly, but smaller fine-tuned models sometimes outperformed larger GPT-series models in specific tasks, and real-world validation was limited to only 2 student studies (n=53 and n=70).
findings.measure: Review synthesis of model performance, task outcomes, and real-world validation frequency

findings.finding_summary: The review identifies several limitations for ChatGPT/GPT-series use in K-12 STEM classrooms, including sensitivity to prompt wording, non-deterministic outputs, limited generalizability across tasks, difficulty handling visual content, and a need for substantial human review and iteration. It also notes that many studies lacked accessible prompts and standardized benchmarks, hindering reproducibility and comparability.
findings.measure: Reported limitations, risks, and reproducibility issues across reviewed studies

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta's LLaMA-family large language models, including open-weight and fine-tuned variants used for text generation and educational support.
identified_tools.use_case: The review included studies using LLaMA, LLaMA-2, and fine-tuned derivatives for K-12 STEM tasks such as question answering, physics problem solving, dataset generation, and tutoring-related interactions.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that smaller fine-tuned LLaMA-based models sometimes outperformed larger GPT-series models in specific educational contexts. For example, an EduChat system built from a fine-tuned LLaMA 13B model outperformed other LLaMA 13B variants but was still less effective than GPT-4, while another fine-tuned smaller model reportedly outperformed GPT-3 in teacher-simulation tasks.
findings.measure: Review synthesis of comparative model performance in cited studies

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot systems without a single named product specified.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviewed generic LLM-based systems and prompt-engineering approaches for K-12 STEM classroom uses such as tutoring, feedback, grading, content generation, and student interaction.

findings.finding_summary: The review concludes that LLM prompt engineering can improve educational outputs, especially when using few-shot or chain-of-thought prompting, but empirical validation in authentic K-12 settings remains sparse. Only 2 studies included direct classroom/student validation, and many papers relied on custom indicators or subjective evaluation rather than standardized benchmarks.
findings.measure: Review synthesis of effectiveness and validation practices across included studies

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that limited prompt transparency, inconsistent evaluation methods, and the non-deterministic nature of LLM outputs reduce reproducibility and hinder classroom adoption. It also flags ethical and methodological concerns, including bias, privacy, and the evolving role of educators when integrating AI tools.
findings.measure: Review synthesis of implementation limitations, ethical concerns, and reproducibility issues

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, not a primary causal study. The evidence is useful for mapping tools, uses, and limitations, but the paper aggregates heterogeneous studies with mostly non-randomized or non-classroom evaluations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests meaningful classroom relevance for LLM prompt engineering, but reported effects are not pooled into comparable effect sizes and authentic K-12 validation is limited. Overall impact appears promising but still uncertain.

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Learning Experiences for K-12: Emerging Works, Future Opportunities and a Design Framework
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence literacy has been addressed in K-12 education and what additional design guidance is needed for learning experiences in school contexts. The authors note that most AI literacy work had been developed for general or non-technical audiences, while K-12 classrooms have different constraints such as engagement, developmental appropriateness, limited time, and the need for teacher support.

To address this, the paper conducts an exploratory review of 49 K-12 AI education tools, curricula, and related learning experiences from the literature and recent conference proceedings. The authors adapt Long and Magerko’s AI literacy framework to K-12 settings, coding each work against competencies and design considerations. They also identify nine future opportunities and synthesize eleven additional design guidelines for creating K-12 AI learning experiences.

The paper covers elementary, middle school, and high school contexts, along with some unspecified K-12 work. The review spans tools such as block-based programming environments, conversational agents, robotics activities, data science lessons, and teacher-facing curricula. Rather than evaluating learner outcomes experimentally, the paper organizes and interprets existing work to provide an educator-friendly reference chart and a conceptual framework for researchers, designers, teachers, and parents.

The main conclusion is that K-12 AI education has made progress, but important gaps remain in explaining general vs. narrow AI, clarifying strengths and weaknesses, embedding ethics more broadly, gradually unveiling complexity, supporting parents, and addressing equity and inclusion. The authors argue that future K-12 AI tools should better scaffold novices, use concrete and contextualized data, integrate reflection, and fit within core school curricula.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General computer-assisted instruction / AI education tools and curricula used to teach students about AI and machine learning concepts.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper reviews and synthesizes K-12 AI education literature, including AI literacy curricula and tools, to derive design guidelines and future opportunities for K-12 learning experiences.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory review and conceptual design-framework paper, not an empirical evaluation of a single AI tool or intervention. It synthesizes literature rather than reporting primary outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper proposes design guidelines and identifies gaps with potential relevance to K-12 AI education, but it does not report measured intervention effects. Its impact is conceptual and field-shaping rather than outcome-based.

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Teacher Education in Developing Countries: The Role of Generative AI in Bridging Theory and Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper addresses a structural problem in teacher education in developing countries: programs often emphasize content delivery and standardized assessment while neglecting pedagogical modeling and performance-based assessment. Using Ghana as the main case, the paper argues that these long-standing issues contribute to a gap between theory and classroom practice in initial teacher education, with downstream effects on the readiness of pre-service teachers and eventually K-12 learning outcomes.

The paper does not report an empirical intervention. Instead, it uses a logical deduction approach and reviews recent literature on generative AI (GenAI) in teacher education to argue that tools such as ChatGPT could reduce the time teacher educators spend on content transmission. This, in turn, would allow more attention to pedagogical modeling, authentic assessment, professional development, resource generation, digital literacy, and critical thinking. The paper also notes that GenAI may help teacher educators and pre-service teachers access resources and support lesson planning and other teaching tasks.

The context is Ghanaian initial teacher education, especially four-year college-based programs preparing pre-service teachers for future K-12 classrooms. The paper concludes that GenAI could catalyze broader reform in teacher education if implemented in a scaffolded and responsible way. It warns, however, that misuse of GenAI may undermine critical thinking and creativity, and it recommends GenAI literacy, ethical training, prompt engineering skills, and critical evaluation of AI-generated content.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative artificial intelligence / large language model tools used for content support, drafting, and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: A perspective/theoretical paper arguing that GenAI could support content knowledge acquisition, pedagogical modeling, performance-based assessment, resource acquisition, digital literacy, critical thinking, and teacher professional development in teacher education.

findings.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI could reduce the burden of content delivery in teacher education, freeing time for pedagogical modeling and performance-based assessment, and potentially improving future K-12 learning outcomes. It is presented as a theoretical claim rather than an empirically tested effect; no sample size or effect size is reported.
findings.measure: Theoretical argument about teacher education functions and downstream K-12 learning outcomes

findings.finding_summary: The paper cautions that misuse of GenAI could undermine critical thinking and creativity skills that are currently nurtured through traditional lecture-based teaching and content-based assessments. This is a stated risk in a perspective paper, not an empirically measured outcome.
findings.measure: Potential undermining of critical thinking and creativity
