paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical paper with no empirical evaluation, no study sample, and no measured outcomes. The claims are inferential and supported by cited literature rather than original data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially broad system-level benefits, but these are speculative rather than observed effects. Because no effect sizes or outcome data are reported, impact cannot be quantified and remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: MDK12-Bench: A Comprehensive Evaluation of Multimodal Large Language Models on Multidisciplinary Exams
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to rigorously evaluate multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on educational problem-solving tasks, especially in ways that go beyond static benchmarks. The authors argue that existing multimodal exams are too small, too narrow, and too weakly annotated to reveal how models perform across difficulty levels, changing exam years, and different question formats.

To address this, the paper introduces MDK12-Bench, a large benchmark built from real-world K–12 exams across six disciplines: mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, geography, and information science. The benchmark includes 141K instances, five question formats, difficulty labels, exam-year annotations, a six-layer knowledge taxonomy, and detailed explanations. The authors also propose a dynamic evaluation framework that perturbs visual and textual inputs, and they test knowledge-point reference-augmented generation (KP-RAG) to examine whether explicit knowledge references improve reasoning.

The population represented is K–12 educational content rather than human participants: the benchmark spans elementary, middle school, and high school material, and the data curation process involved researchers and K–12 educators. The context is benchmark development and model evaluation rather than classroom implementation. The main conclusions are that current MLLMs perform better on easier and older items, struggle more with math and physics, are highly sensitive to contextual shifts, and gain only limited benefit from knowledge augmentation on harder reasoning tasks. The paper concludes that more robust, generalizable multimodal models require better reasoning, multimodal fusion, and knowledge integration.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs): AI systems that combine language and visual inputs to solve problems, generate answers, and perform reasoning across text-image tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper benchmarks a range of MLLMs on real-world K–12 multidisciplinary exam questions, including standard, dynamic, and knowledge-point reference-augmented (KP-RAG) evaluation settings. It evaluates proprietary and open-source models rather than a single product.

findings.finding_summary: Across 141,320 K–12 exam instances, current MLLMs showed substantial limitations in multidisciplinary problem solving, especially on harder and newer exams. The paper reports accuracy drops of 8.3% on harder exams, 12.6% on newer exams, and a 13.7% average performance reduction under dynamic perturbations, indicating weak generalization and sensitivity to contextual shifts.
findings.measure: Accuracy on K–12 multidisciplinary exam questions under standard, harder/newer exam, and dynamic evaluation conditions
findings.effect_size: 13.7% performance reduction under dynamic evaluation; 8.3% drop on harder exams; 12.6% drop on newer exams

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark study with systematic evaluation, but it is not a classroom intervention study and does not use an experimental educational design. The evidence is quantitative and comparative, yet centered on model performance rather than learner outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are notable for model robustness and generalization, but they are not direct student-impact estimates. The paper shows meaningful limitations and risks for classroom use, but no direct evidence of academic gains or harms for K-12 students.

paper_profiles.title: MDK12-Bench: A Multi-Discipline Benchmark for Evaluating Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for more robust benchmarks to evaluate the multimodal reasoning abilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The authors argue that existing benchmarks are too narrow in domain coverage, data size, structure, and reasoning depth, making it difficult to diagnose where current models succeed or fail on real-world academic tasks.

To address this, the paper introduces MDK12-Bench, a large-scale benchmark built from K-12 examination questions spanning six disciplines: mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, geography, and information science. The benchmark includes 141,320 questions, both text-only and multimodal, and adds fine-grained annotations such as grade, curriculum, topic, knowledge points, difficulty labels, answer explanations, and cross-year partitions. The dataset was curated with the participation of over 20 researchers and several K-12 educators, using online exam repositories plus GPT-4o-assisted screening and human review.

The paper also proposes a dynamic evaluation framework that bootstraps text and image content to reduce contamination and test model robustness under altered question formats and visual styles. The benchmark is used to evaluate several closed- and open-source MLLMs, showing that current models still struggle with high-order multimodal reasoning and are sensitive to contextual changes and question perturbations. The results suggest that both stronger reasoning models and more resilient evaluation protocols are needed for future progress.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: A Google multimodal large language model family used for image-text reasoning, generation, and question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Benchmarked as one of several closed-source multimodal large language models on MDK12-Bench, including Gemini-2.0-flash-exp and Gemini-2.0-flash-thinking-exp.

findings.finding_summary: Gemini2-thinking achieved the highest overall accuracy on MDK12-mini at 59.4%, and Gemini2-flash followed at 57.2%. On the full benchmark and dynamic evaluation subsets, Gemini models showed substantial performance drops under bootstrapped textual/visual perturbations, indicating sensitivity to contextual shifts and potential contamination issues.
findings.measure: Accuracy on MDK12-Bench / MDK12-mini and accuracy change under dynamic bootstrapped evaluation
findings.sample_size: n=141,320 overall benchmark; n=14,595 MDK12-Mini; dynamic subset n=2,637 multimodal instances

findings.finding_summary: Under dynamic evaluation, Gemini2-thinking dropped from 58.1 to 41.6 on the sampled subset, a 16.5-point decrease overall. The paper reports an even larger decline on easy items for Gemini2-thinking (22.9 points), suggesting high sensitivity to altered context outside the original distribution.
findings.measure: Accuracy difference between original and dynamically bootstrapped queries
findings.effect_size: -16.5 percentage points overall; -22.9 percentage points easy subset
findings.sample_size: n=2,637 multimodal instances for dynamic evaluation

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based multimodal large language model family used for reasoning, question answering, and multimodal understanding.
identified_tools.use_case: Benchmarked as GPT-4o, GPT-o1-mini, and GPT-o3-mini on MDK12-Bench; also used GPT-4o API and GPT-based judging/interpreter steps in data processing and evaluation.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4o reached 50.0% overall accuracy on MDK12-mini, while GPT-o1-mini reached 53.1%. The paper also reports GPT-4o at 51.2% on the original sampled subset before dynamic augmentation. Overall, OpenAI models performed below the best Gemini model and were challenged by dynamic bootstrapping.
findings.measure: Accuracy on MDK12-Bench / MDK12-mini and accuracy under dynamic bootstrapping

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4o dropped from 51.2 to 40.9 on the original versus dynamically bootstrapped subset, a 10.3-point decrease. The paper interprets this as evidence that the model is vulnerable to combined textual and visual perturbations and relies heavily on contextual reasoning.
findings.measure: Accuracy difference between original and dynamically bootstrapped queries
findings.sample_size: n=2,637 multimodal instances for dynamic evaluation

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's Claude model family, a general-purpose multimodal large language model used for reasoning and text-image understanding.
identified_tools.use_case: Benchmarked on MDK12-Bench as Claude-3.7-Sonnet among the closed-source MLLMs.

findings.finding_summary: Claude-3.7 scored 49.8% overall accuracy on MDK12-mini and 46.7% on the sampled original subset. It was outperformed by Gemini models and showed lower performance than the strongest open-source reasoning-oriented models in some settings.
findings.measure: Accuracy on MDK12-Bench / MDK12-mini

findings.finding_summary: On dynamic evaluation, Claude-3.7 dropped from 46.7 to 31.4 overall, a 15.3-point decrease. The paper uses this as evidence that the model is sensitive to combined textual and visual bootstrapping and contextual shifts.
findings.measure: Accuracy difference between original and dynamically bootstrapped queries
findings.sample_size: n=2,637 multimodal instances for dynamic evaluation

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba's Qwen multimodal model family used for vision-language reasoning and question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Benchmarked in multiple variants, including Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen2-VL-7B, and Qwen2-VL-7B-GRPO.

findings.finding_summary: Qwen2.5-VL-72B achieved 51.9% overall accuracy on MDK12-mini, while smaller Qwen variants scored lower (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B at 47.9%, Qwen2-VL-7B at 43.8%, and Qwen2-VL-7B-GRPO at 44.1%). The paper concludes that larger models generally perform better, but all Qwen variants remained sensitive to subject and difficulty variation.
findings.measure: Accuracy on MDK12-Bench / MDK12-mini

findings.finding_summary: Under dynamic evaluation, Qwen2-VL-7B-GRPO dropped from 28.2 to 26.0 overall, and Qwen2-VL-7B dropped from 27.3 to 26.1 overall. The paper also notes that Qwen2-VL-7B showed only a small decline on the hard subset but was still vulnerable to text-format changes and contextual perturbations.
findings.measure: Accuracy difference between original and dynamically bootstrapped queries
findings.sample_size: n=2,637 multimodal instances for dynamic evaluation

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta's LLaMA family of open-weight large language models.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned in related work as part of the broader LLM foundation-model landscape, but not evaluated on MDK12-Bench.

identified_tools.name: DeepSeek
identified_tools.description: DeepSeek family of reasoning-oriented large language models.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned in related work as a reasoning model family (DeepSeek-R1 / DeepSeek-E1 style reasoning) and not evaluated directly in the benchmark results presented here.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / multimodal large language models used for reasoning, text interpretation, and answer generation when no single product is the focus.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper broadly evaluates multiple multimodal large language models as benchmark subjects and uses GPT-based tools for automatic screening, parsing, translation, and answer judging.

findings.finding_summary: Across the benchmark, current MLLMs showed significant limitations in multimodal reasoning, with scores varying widely by discipline and difficulty. The paper emphasizes that more reasoning-trained models performed better, but all systems remained vulnerable to dynamic perturbations and contextual changes.
findings.measure: Benchmark accuracy across six K-12 disciplines and three difficulty levels

findings.finding_summary: The dynamic evaluation framework revealed that combined textual and visual bootstrapping substantially reduced accuracy, especially for easier tasks. The authors interpret this as evidence that MLLMs are highly sensitive to format shifts, text wording changes, and image-style transformations, raising concerns about robustness and contamination in evaluation.
findings.measure: Accuracy under bootstrapped text and image transformations
findings.sample_size: n=2,637 multimodal instances for dynamic evaluation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark paper rather than a K-12 intervention study, RCT, or meta-analysis. It reports empirical model evaluations, but not educational effectiveness evidence in classrooms.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear benchmark performance differences and sensitivity to perturbations, but effect sizes are mostly in percentage-point accuracy changes rather than standardized educational impact metrics. The findings are informative for model robustness, though classroom impact is indirect.

paper_profiles.title: EduEval: A Hierarchical Cognitive Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Chinese Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to evaluate large language models (LLMs) for educational use in a way that reflects authentic K-12 classroom demands rather than relying on narrow benchmark questions. The authors argue that existing evaluation suites for Chinese and general-purpose LLMs overemphasize low-level recall and single-turn prompts, while failing to capture higher-order skills such as application, reasoning, creativity, and ethical judgment that matter in real classrooms.

To address this gap, the paper introduces EduEval, a benchmark built around a new EduAbility Taxonomy that combines Bloom’s Taxonomy and Webb’s Depth of Knowledge. EduEval includes over 11,000 items across 24 task types drawn from real exam archives, classroom transcripts, student essays, and expert-authored prompts. The benchmark covers Chinese K-12 education from primary through high school and evaluates 14 LLMs in zero-shot and few-shot settings, using accuracy, Rouge-L, RMSE, and GPT-based scoring depending on the task.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs perform well on memorization and some comprehension tasks, but struggle on authentic classroom applications such as dialogue classification and show uneven performance on creative generation and complex reasoning. Few-shot prompting helps some task types but can also constrain creativity or reduce performance on reasoning. The paper also reports that domain-specific fine-tuning can improve educational tasks but may narrow broader reasoning ability, and it highlights concerns about privacy, bias, and premature classroom deployment.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Large language models used for educational tasks such as tutoring, automated grading, classroom dialogue analysis, content generation, and ethical reasoning.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper benchmarks 14 LLMs on Chinese K-12 educational tasks to evaluate capabilities across cognitive dimensions, including memory, understanding, application, reasoning, creativity, and ethics.

findings.finding_summary: Across 14 LLMs, models performed well on factual/memory tasks but struggled on classroom dialogue classification and more complex application/reasoning tasks. The paper reports that accuracy can drop below 30% for classroom dialogue classification, while top systems exceeded 90% on some recall tasks; however, no single overall effect size is reported.
findings.measure: Accuracy on benchmark tasks; Rouge-L for some understanding tasks; RMSE for essay scoring

findings.finding_summary: Few-shot prompting did not uniformly improve performance. The paper reports that examples sometimes helped task-specific conventions such as classroom dialogue classification and ethics, but often slightly reduced average performance overall and could constrain creative generation or interfere with reasoning paths.
findings.measure: Zero-shot vs few-shot benchmark performance across cognitive dimensions

findings.finding_summary: Domain-specific fine-tuning improved educationally contextual tasks but could reduce broader abstract reasoning. The education-specialized EduChat-sft-002-13B improved over its Baichuan-13B base model in most authentic educational contexts, especially application and ethics, but showed a slight decrease on abstract reasoning tasks.
findings.measure: Benchmark task performance comparing EduChat-sft-002-13B with Baichuan-13B

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/evaluation paper rather than a controlled intervention study, meta-analysis, or QED. The evidence is descriptive model benchmarking with no causal estimate or experimental comparison against classroom literacy interventions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial performance differences across tasks, including large drops on classroom dialogue classification and notable gains on factual recall, but it does not provide a single effect size tied to an educational outcome intervention. The practical impact is meaningful for tool evaluation, yet the reported findings are not directly intervention-based.

paper_profiles.title: From Model to Classroom: Evaluating Generated MCQs for Portuguese with Narrative and Difficulty Concerns
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI models can produce reading-comprehension multiple-choice questions (MCQs) suitable for Portuguese elementary classrooms, and how those generated items compare with human-authored questions. The authors focus on two practical challenges in educational question generation: controlling narrative alignment (e.g., character, feeling, action, causal relationship) and controlling difficulty levels for young readers. They also explicitly investigate failure cases, because the paper is motivated by concerns that generated items may be unreliable in real classroom use.

The study compares three generation pipelines: GPT-4o in a one-step prompting setup, Gemma-2 in a one-step prompting setup, and a two-step pipeline using a fine-tuned ptt5-v2 model to generate the wh-question followed by Gemma-2 to generate options and difficulty. The content consists of 12 narrative texts recommended for Portuguese elementary education, and the resulting MCQs were evaluated by 18 Portuguese-language experts in education/learning-resource development. The authors then filtered validated items and administered 124 MCQs to 284 students across 14 classes in Portuguese schools to estimate psychometric properties such as difficulty and discrimination.

Overall, the paper concludes that GPT-4o and Gemma-2 generated MCQs of broadly comparable quality to human-authored items in terms of expert acceptance, psychometric difficulty, and discrimination, although human items still had slight advantages in distractor quality and some psychometric measures. The two-step pipeline performed worse, especially on answerability and distractor reliability. Reported limitations and risks include semantic ambiguity, unclear option wording, answerability failures, use of the wrong Portuguese variant (Brazilian instead of European Portuguese), and distractors that are less engaging or less plausible than human-authored ones. The authors argue that generative AI can be useful for MCQ creation, but classroom use requires careful validation and still does not fully match human item construction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based generative AI chatbot/model family used for text generation and instruction-following tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a one-step zero-shot prompting setup to generate Portuguese reading-comprehension MCQs with question, correct answer, distractors, difficulty, and narrative label.

findings.finding_summary: Expert review found GPT-4o-generated MCQs were largely acceptable and comparable to human-authored items. Well-formed wh-questions were 40/45 (88.9%), option clarity was 38/42 (90.5%), answerability was 33/38 (86.8%), and narrative alignment was 42/42 (100%); experts noted some semantic issues and unclear options, but overall quality was close to human-authored MCQs.
findings.measure: Expert ratings of well-formedness, narrative alignment, options clarity, and answerability

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s Gemini family of generative AI models used for text generation and instruction-following tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a one-step zero-shot prompting setup to generate Portuguese reading-comprehension MCQs; the paper refers to Gemma-2-27B as Gemma-2.

findings.finding_summary: Expert review found Gemma-2-generated MCQs were broadly comparable to human-authored MCQs, though with more issues than GPT-4o in several dimensions. Well-formed wh-questions were 33/45 (73.3%), option clarity was 35/41 (85.4%), answerability was 33/35 (94.3%), and narrative alignment was 41/41 (100%); experts reported semantic problems and unclear options, but no statistically significant differences were found in distractor plausibility or difficulty versus other provenances.
findings.measure: Expert ratings of well-formedness, narrative alignment, options clarity, answerability, distractor plausibility, and difficulty

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s Gemini family of generative AI models used for text generation and instruction-following tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a two-step pipeline with ptt5-v2-large to generate the remaining MCQ components after the wh-question was produced.

findings.finding_summary: The two-step ptt5-v2+Gemma-2 approach performed worse on several expert-review measures than the one-step LLM approaches. Well-formed wh-questions were 38/45 (84.4%), option clarity was 37/39 (94.9%), but answerability was only 25/37 (67.6%), and experts noted multiple valid answers, mismatches, and ambiguity; the paper concludes the two-step method may not be effective for MCQ creation.
findings.measure: Expert ratings of well-formedness, options clarity, and answerability

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model systems used for automated text and question generation without a single named product being studied.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies current generative models for producing Portuguese reading-comprehension MCQs and compares them to human-authored items and a fine-tuned encoder-decoder baseline.

findings.finding_summary: Across the study, generated MCQs were often comparable to human-authored ones, but limitations and risks were identified. Reported issues included semantic ambiguity, unclear or nonsensical questions, distractors that were less plausible than human-authored ones, answerability failures, and a recurring tendency to output Brazilian Portuguese instead of the requested European Portuguese; the two-step generation setup performed especially poorly on answerability and reliability.
findings.measure: Expert review and psychometric analysis of generated MCQs versus human-authored MCQs
findings.sample_size: n=238 MCQs for expert review; n=124 validated MCQs for student psychometrics

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study with expert review and student-response psychometrics, but it is not a controlled intervention trial. The evidence is useful and detailed, yet it is observational/measurement-based rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mostly descriptive comparisons and no effect sizes for learning outcomes, so the classroom impact is unclear. It does identify practical risks and quality limitations, but not medium or large instructional gains.

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Large Language Models Creation of Interactive Learning Lessons
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can automatically generate scenario-based interactive lessons for training novice human tutors. The central question is whether an LLM-based, retrieval-augmented workflow can produce tutor-training lessons that are comparable in quality to those written by expert lesson designers, and how the level of prompt decomposition affects output quality.

The intervention studied is a lesson-generation pipeline that combines retrieval-augmented generation with GPT-4o and task decomposition prompting. The authors generated English lessons for three tutor-training topics: encouraging students’ independence, encouraging help-seeking behavior, and turning on cameras. Each lesson followed a five-part structure: title page, scenario 1, instruction, scenario 2, and conclusion. The main experimental factor was how the lesson was split across prompts, ranging from one segment to five segments.

The context is online tutor training for novice human tutors teaching middle school mathematics. Rather than testing student learning directly, the paper evaluated generated lessons with two experienced human raters and then compared the best-performing LLM-generated lessons with human-crafted lessons through feedback from two lesson designers. The study found that a three-segment decomposition performed best overall, outperforming a single-step prompt and slightly outperforming more granular decompositions. Human evaluators and lesson designers saw clear benefits such as time savings, realistic scenario generation, and useful instructional charts, but they also identified recurring problems including generic feedback, unclear learning objectives, logical disconnects in instruction, and unreliable or fabricated references. The authors conclude that LLMs are promising for draft lesson creation, but human review remains necessary to ensure pedagogical quality and citation authenticity.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model system used for generating and evaluating educational text and other content.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) in a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline to automatically generate scenario-based tutor-training lessons for middle school mathematics.

findings.finding_summary: Human evaluators rated the three-segment prompting approach highest for lesson quality (average rating 14.67) compared with one-segment generation (average 10.67). The paper reports that decomposing lesson generation into multiple subtasks improved overall quality of the LLM-generated tutor-training lessons.
findings.measure: Human-coded lesson quality ratings
findings.sample_size: n=3 lessons generated per segmentation approach

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods study with human ratings and designer feedback, not a controlled student-outcome experiment. The methodology is structured, but the evidence is not causal and does not report inferential effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a clear improvement in rubric scores for decomposed prompting, but the effect is not expressed as a standardized effect size and is based on only three lessons per condition. Impact on learner outcomes remains untested, so practical impact is suggestive rather than established.

paper_profiles.title: CAPability: A Comprehensive Visual Caption Benchmark for Evaluating Both Correctness and Thoroughness
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2025 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that existing visual captioning benchmarks no longer adequately evaluate modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The authors argue that traditional caption benchmarks are limited by short ground-truth captions, sentence-level overlap metrics, and narrow evaluation scopes that miss many visual details. In response, they introduce CAPability, a benchmark designed to assess caption quality across multiple views and dimensions rather than by comparing entire sentences alone.

CAPability includes 6 views and 12 dimensions covering object-related, global-related, text-related, camera-related, temporal-related, and knowledge-related aspects. The benchmark uses nearly 11K human-annotated images and videos, with separate data collected for static and dynamic dimensions. The authors evaluate several state-of-the-art open- and closed-source MLLMs using precision, hit, and a derived know-but-cannot-tell (K¯T) metric. They also convert annotations into question-answer pairs to measure whether models can answer correctly when prompted but fail to express the same information in captions.

The paper is methodological rather than a study of students, teachers, or classrooms. Its main conclusions are that current MLLMs often achieve relatively high precision but much lower hit, indicating a gap between accurate descriptions and thorough coverage. Models also struggle especially with object counting, camera angle, camera movement, character identification, action, and some event-related captions. The benchmark is presented as a more reliable and interpretable way to assess detailed visual captioning than traditional metrics such as BLEU, CIDEr, and METEOR.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family multimodal large language models used for visual understanding, caption generation, QA answering, and automated evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated GPT-4o and GPT-4 Turbo as part of its benchmark pipeline: GPT-4o was one of the studied MLLMs for captioning performance, GPT-4 Turbo was used to score generated captions by dimension, and GPT-4o/GPT-4 Turbo were also used in pre-annotation and QA-style evaluation workflows.

findings.finding_summary: On CAPability, GPT-4o (0806) achieved high caption precision (79.2% average) and moderate hit (56.5% average) across 13 dimensions. The paper reports that GPT-4o was the best model on precision among the evaluated systems in the closed-source group and that it excelled in recognizing camera angle, but it still showed low hit on several dimensions such as object number and character identification, indicating incomplete coverage.
findings.measure: Precision and hit on CAPability captioning benchmark

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's Gemini family of multimodal large language models used for visual understanding, caption generation, QA answering, and automated evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated Gemini-1.5-pro and Gemini-2.0-flash as benchmarked MLLMs for image/video captioning, and used Gemini models in the pre-annotation workflow for data preparation.

findings.finding_summary: Gemini-1.5-pro achieved the best overall hit on CAPability among closed-source models (60.4% average) and was reported as especially strong in object counting, including a 10% and 16.3% advantage in hit over the second place on image and video object-counting dimensions, respectively. The paper also notes that Gemini-1.5-pro had the lowest K2 metric (25.2%), suggesting a smaller gap between answering questions correctly and automatically expressing the same information in captions, although it still struggled on some dimensions such as character identification and action.
findings.measure: Precision, hit, QA accuracy, and K2 on CAPability

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba's Qwen-family multimodal large language models used for visual understanding, caption generation, QA answering, and automated evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated multiple Qwen model variants (Qwen2VL, Qwen2.5VL, Qwen-VL-Max, Qwen2.5-Max) as benchmarked MLLMs and also used Qwen models in the pre-annotation/merging pipeline for constructing benchmark annotations.

findings.finding_summary: Among open-source models, Qwen2.5VL achieved the best 72B-model performance on CAPability, with the highest overall hit among the 72B open-source group (53.4%) and strong precision (75.9%). The paper also reports that Qwen2.5VL-7B achieved the best precision (75.5%) and hit (48.1%) among 7B models, but all Qwen variants still showed relatively low hit on object number, character identification, action, camera movement, and event dimensions.
findings.measure: Precision and hit on CAPability captioning benchmark

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative multimodal AI/large language model systems used for image/video captioning and benchmark scoring, without reliance on a single named product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a benchmark/evaluation study of modern multimodal large language models rather than an intervention study. It uses generic MLLMs for caption generation, pre-annotation, and QA conversion, and compares their strengths and weaknesses across caption dimensions.

findings.finding_summary: Across evaluated MLLMs, the paper finds a consistent gap between precision and hit: models often produce accurate captions for what they mention, but omit many annotated visual elements. The authors highlight persistent weaknesses in object number, camera angle, camera movement, character identification, and action recognition, and describe a 'know but cannot tell' phenomenon where models answer related QA correctly yet fail to express the same information automatically in captions.
findings.measure: Benchmark-level comparison of caption correctness, thoroughness, and QA/caption gap

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/evaluation paper rather than a classroom intervention study, and it does not report an empirical K-12 educational effect with a causal design. The evidence concerns model performance on captioning metrics, not educational outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful benchmark differences and identifies practical limitations of multimodal GenAI systems, but it does not quantify educational impact in K-12 classrooms. The effects are descriptive and system-level rather than outcome-based for learners.

paper_profiles.title: PsyDraw: A Multi-Agent Multimodal System for Mental Health Screening in Left-Behind Children
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of early mental health screening for left-behind children in China, a population facing elevated risks of anxiety, depression, suicidal thoughts, and other psychological difficulties due to parental migration and limited access to mental health professionals. The authors focus on the House-Tree-Person (HTP) drawing test, which is engaging for children but traditionally requires expert interpretation, making it difficult to use at scale in resource-limited rural settings.

To address this, the paper proposes PsyDraw, a multi-agent multimodal system built on multimodal large language models. PsyDraw separates the task into feature extraction and report generation, using specialized agents to analyze drawings and produce structured psychological reports, plus a manager agent for handling exceptional cases. The system is designed as an assistive screening tool for mental health professionals rather than a standalone diagnostic system.

The study evaluates PsyDraw on 290 HTP drawings from Chinese primary school students in a rural school context. Psychological teachers reviewed the generated reports and rated consistency against their professional judgments, with 71.03% of cases judged highly consistent and 31.03% flagged as requiring professional attention. The paper concludes that PsyDraw shows promise for preliminary screening in underserved schools, while emphasizing that it should support, not replace, human professionals and that its performance and cultural generalizability still need further validation.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's Claude family of large language models for text generation and multimodal reasoning.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the text-only model in PsyDraw for HTP drawing feature analysis and professional report generation.

findings.finding_summary: PsyDraw used Claude-3.5-sonnet as the text-only model within a multimodal, multi-agent system for mental health screening. The paper reports system-level agreement with psychological teachers rather than a direct Claude-only effect; across 290 HTP drawings, 71.03% of analyses were rated High Consistency, 26.21% Moderate Consistency, and 2.76% Low Consistency.
findings.measure: Teacher-rated consistency of generated HTP analysis reports

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT family of large language models for text and multimodal generation and reasoning.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the multimodal model in PsyDraw for analyzing HTP drawings and generating psychological reports.

findings.finding_summary: PsyDraw used GPT-4o as the multimodal model within a multi-agent pipeline for HTP drawing interpretation. The paper reports that, over 290 primary school students' drawings, 71.03% of generated analyses achieved High Consistency with professional evaluations, 26.21% Moderate Consistency, and 2.76% Low Consistency; 31.03% of cases were classified as requiring professional attention (Warning).
findings.measure: Teacher-rated consistency of generated HTP analysis reports; binary risk classification (Warning vs Observation)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-system empirical study using teacher-rated agreement on generated reports, but it is not a controlled trial and does not isolate the effect of the specific LLMs from the broader PsyDraw system. The design is observational/mixed-methods with no randomized comparison.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported consistency is fairly high (71.03% High Consistency), but no effect size is provided and the outcome is system-level agreement rather than direct learning or clinical impact. The practical impact is promising yet indirect and therefore unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: K12Vista: Exploring the Boundaries of MLLMs in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the limited availability of comprehensive benchmarks for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on K-12 educational tasks, especially in Chinese science subjects. The authors argue that prior benchmarks are too narrow in subject coverage, data scale, question-type diversity, and evaluation methodology, often focusing only on final-answer accuracy rather than the reasoning process.

To address this, the paper introduces K12Vista, a large Chinese multimodal benchmark with 33,660 questions spanning five subjects (mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, and geography) across K-12 grade levels and three question types: multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and free-response. The benchmark includes rich metadata such as grade, knowledge points, difficulty, and reference solution steps. The paper also proposes a process-evaluation pipeline, including K12-PEM-800K for step-level supervision and K12-PEM for judging reasoning quality, along with K12-PEBench for human-annotated evaluation of process assessment.

The context is benchmark development and model evaluation rather than a classroom intervention. The paper evaluates multiple closed- and open-source MLLMs, finding that reasoning-enhanced models such as Gemini2-thinking perform best, while all models struggle more with higher-grade problems, fill-in-blank items, and free-response reasoning. The main conclusion is that current MLLMs have substantial weaknesses in K-12 multimodal reasoning, and that step-by-step evaluation reveals errors and limitations that answer-only scoring misses.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google multimodal large language model family used for reasoning and evaluation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of the expert models for step-wise annotation in K12-PEM-800K construction, as a baseline MLLM on K12Vista, and in examples such as Gemini2-thinking and Gemini2-flash.

findings.finding_summary: On K12Vista, Gemini2-thinking achieved the highest reported overall accuracy among the listed MLLMs. It scored 55.47% on direct inference and 57.36% on step-by-step evaluation across the full benchmark; the paper also reports that reasoning-enhanced models like Gemini2-thinking performed better than most others.
findings.measure: Accuracy on K12Vista direct inference and step-by-step evaluation

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT model family used for multimodal reasoning and evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in the paper as GPT-4o for solution generation, step decomposition, expert panel judging, caption extraction, and direct-inference evaluation.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4o was used as part of the expert panel and as an evaluation model, with the paper reporting a kappa coefficient of 0.91 for direct-score evaluation and 0.73 for step-by-step evaluation against expert averages. In benchmark performance, GPT-4o scored 35.02% overall on direct inference and 35.00% overall on step-by-step evaluation on K12Vista.
findings.measure: Kappa coefficient vs expert evaluations; accuracy on K12Vista
findings.sample_size: n=1,000 sampled for quality assessment; n=33,660 questions for benchmark accuracy

identified_tools.name: Qwen
identified_tools.description: Alibaba Qwen multimodal and language model family used for generation, captioning, evaluation, and process supervision.
identified_tools.use_case: Used for data cleaning, caption generation, direct inference evaluation (Qwen2.5-VL-72B), process evaluation model fine-tuning (K12-PEM based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct), and as a baseline across multiple model sizes.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that Qwen2.5-VL-72B achieved 51.39% direct-inference overall accuracy and 49.93% step-by-step overall accuracy on K12Vista, while Qwen2.5-VL-32B reached 55.42% and 53.35% respectively. For evaluation reliability, Qwen2.5-VL-72B had a kappa of 0.88 on direct-score evaluation and 0.67 on step-by-step evaluation against expert averages.
findings.measure: Accuracy on K12Vista; kappa coefficient vs expert evaluations
findings.sample_size: n=33,660 questions; n=1,000 sampled for quality assessment

identified_tools.name: DeepSeek
identified_tools.description: DeepSeek language model family used in the study as a text-only baseline after image captioning.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as a text-only LLM using captions generated from images and concatenated with questions.

findings.finding_summary: Deepseek-v3 was evaluated in the text-plus-caption setting and achieved 44.97% overall direct-inference accuracy and 47.60% overall step-by-step accuracy on K12Vista. The paper reports that text-only LLMs generally performed worse than top multimodal models, underscoring the importance of visual information.
findings.measure: Accuracy on K12Vista using captions plus text

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an evaluation/benchmark paper rather than an intervention study, and it does not report experimental treatment effects in the K-12 classroom sense. The evidence is useful for model comparison but is not the type of causal educational evidence the tiering system rewards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial differences in benchmark accuracy across models, but these are task-performance metrics rather than educational outcome gains. The findings are informative for model capability assessment, yet classroom impact is indirect and not quantified.

paper_profiles.title: VisScience: An Extensive Benchmark for Evaluating K12 Educational Multi-modal Scientific Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VisScience, a new benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on K-12 scientific reasoning. The authors identify a gap in existing benchmarks, which often emphasize mathematics or general visual understanding while underrepresenting physics and chemistry, and they further note the need for bilingual evaluation across English and Chinese and for natural difficulty progression from elementary through high school content.

VisScience is built from 450,000 K-12 questions with visual information and manually curated down to 3,000 final questions, evenly split across mathematics, physics, and chemistry. The dataset covers 21 subjects and five difficulty levels, and is intended to test both text and image understanding in educational science problems. The paper evaluates 25 representative models, including closed-source and open-source MLLMs, using zero-shot and 2-shot CoT settings with GPT-4o as the judge.

The main findings are that closed-source MLLMs generally outperform open-source ones, with different proprietary models leading in different disciplines. The authors also provide error analysis showing that reasoning errors are the most common, followed by knowledge and vision-recognition errors, especially in physics and chemistry. The work concludes that current MLLMs still struggle with deeper scientific reasoning in multimodal K-12 settings and that benchmarks like VisScience can help identify areas needing improvement.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-family conversational large language model / multimodal assistant used for text and image understanding, generation, and evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of the evaluated models on the VisScience benchmark, and GPT-4o was also used as the judgment model to compare model responses with standard answers.

findings.finding_summary: On the Chinese VisScience benchmark, GPT-4o achieved 31.1% in mathematics, 38.0% in physics, and 39.6% in chemistry in the text-only setting; with image input, it reached 51.7% in mathematics, 38.2% in physics, and 41.6% in chemistry. The paper also reports that GPT-4o’s errors were dominated by reasoning errors (56.5% in mathematics, 50.1% in physics, 40.6% in chemistry), with vision-recognition and knowledge errors also contributing substantially.
findings.measure: Accuracy on VisScience across mathematics, physics, and chemistry; error-type distribution for GPT-4o

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark evaluation paper, but it is not an intervention study and does not report causal effects or randomized comparisons. The methods are systematic, yet the evidence is descriptive performance benchmarking rather than experimental impact estimation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports accuracy levels and error patterns rather than effect sizes, so educational impact cannot be quantified directly. The findings suggest meaningful capability differences, but the classroom impact remains indirect and uncertain.

paper_profiles.title: Interactive Evidence Maps for Visualizing and Understanding Systematic Reviews
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem in research synthesis: systematic reviews and meta-analyses often provide only static tables, figures, and narrative summaries, which can obscure study-level detail, overgeneralize findings, and make it difficult for readers to explore evidence in ways that match their own questions. The authors propose interactive evidence maps as a way to make systematic review data more transparent, explorable, and analytically flexible.

The approach combines large language model-based topic modeling with interactive visualization. Review data that have already been systematically coded are uploaded in structured form, then an LLM (Claude) is prompted to identify topics and subtopics from study titles and abstracts. These topics are linked back to the original coded variables and displayed in an interactive interface built with D3.js and React, allowing filtering by topic and by coded study features such as year, methodology, educational level, and outcome type. The paper is therefore a framework/proof-of-concept rather than a primary intervention study.

To demonstrate the tool, the authors use data from a published scoping review of 112 studies on pedagogical agents in K-12 education. The dataset includes studies involving primary, lower secondary, and upper secondary learners, with topics such as science, mathematics, language, and social skills. The paper concludes that interactive evidence maps can complement traditional review reporting by revealing patterns, research gaps, and temporal shifts that are hard to detect in static summaries, while also improving transparency and supporting exploratory analysis. The authors also note several open concerns, including scalability, reproducibility, probabilistic assignment transparency, and the instability of LLM-generated topic labels.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's large language model / conversational AI assistant used for prompt-based topic extraction and labeling from structured review data.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in the proof-of-concept pipeline to analyze coded study data and identify 6-8 main topics and 2-3 subtopics for each, assigning each study to a topic based on semantic similarity.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a proof-of-concept methods paper about interactive evidence maps, not an empirical evaluation of student outcomes or a controlled study of the AI tool itself. It reports implementation considerations and limitations rather than quantitative effectiveness evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests the tool may improve transparency, exploration, and identification of patterns and gaps in reviews, but it does not report outcome effect sizes on learners or classrooms. The impact is therefore promising but indirect and unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: Headsprout Early Reading for Specific Literacy Difficulty: A Comparison Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the computer-assisted reading program Headsprout Early Reading (HER) produces stronger literacy gains than the supplementary literacy support typically delivered by a school SENCO for children with specific literacy difficulty. The broader problem is the persistent attainment gap for struggling readers and the concern that many school-based interventions are eclectic, inconsistently delivered, and not strongly evidence-based.

The study compared HER, an internet-based, systematically sequenced phonics and early reading program, with treatment as usual (TAU), which consisted of SENCO-delivered instruction such as guided reading, paper-based phonics training, and word-recognition tasks. Participants were primary school children aged 6–9 in a Northern Irish school, all receiving free school meals and supplementary literacy support. Thirty-two pupils were analyzed after random assignment to HER or TAU.

Over approximately 7 months, children in the HER group completed 30-minute sessions five times per week in small groups using laptops and headphones, while the TAU group received daily 1:1 SENCO support. Outcomes were assessed with standardized measures of word/non-word recognition, sentence reading, and sight words, plus a teacher social-validity questionnaire. HER produced significantly greater gains than TAU on all reported reading outcomes, suggesting that systematic computer-assisted instruction can outperform the school’s usual eclectic literacy support. The paper also suggests HER may be more cost-effective and less staff-intensive, while noting that conventional SENCO instruction may not be sufficiently systematic to close the attainment gap.

identified_tools.name: Headsprout Early Reading
identified_tools.description: An internet-based computer-assisted early reading program that delivers systematic, individualized phonics and early literacy instruction with immediate feedback and mastery-based progression.
identified_tools.use_case: Compared against SENCO-delivered supplementary literacy instruction for primary school children with specific literacy difficulty over 7 months.

findings.finding_summary: Children receiving Headsprout Early Reading (HER) gained significantly more than the TAU group on word/non-word recognition over 7 months. Posttest mean scores were 99.41 (SD 7.13) for HER (n=17) versus 78.27 (SD 8.70) for TAU (n=15); the ANOVA reported F(1,30)=55.14, p=0.0001, with Cohen's d=2.65.
findings.measure: Phonics and Early Reading Assessment (PERA) word/non-word recognition

findings.finding_summary: HER produced significantly greater gains than TAU on sentence reading. Posttest mean scores were 97.53 (SD 8.64) for HER versus 88.67 (SD 9.85) for TAU; the ANOVA reported F(1,30)=14.44, p=0.002, with Cohen's d=0.96.
findings.measure: Phonics and Early Reading Assessment (PERA) sentence reading score (SRS)

findings.finding_summary: HER outperformed TAU on sight-word acquisition as measured by the Dolch words assessment. Posttest mean scores were 65.8 (SD 34.6) for HER versus 23.4 (SD 18.5) for TAU; the ANOVA reported F(1,30)=8.26, p=0.0001, with Cohen's d=1.53.
findings.measure: Dolch sight words assessment

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized comparison study with pre/post measures and a concurrent control group, which supports relatively strong causal inference. However, the sample is small and from a single school, and the paper notes limited procedural-integrity documentation and some attrition.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: All reported effects are large by the paper's own Cohen's d values (0.96 to 2.65), indicating strong impact on literacy outcomes. The gains are substantial on multiple reading measures, though generalizability is limited by the study context.

paper_profiles.title: The SAGE framework for developing critical thinking and responsible generative AI use in cybersecurity education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This case study examines how generative AI tools can be integrated into cybersecurity management education in ways that strengthen students’ critical thinking rather than encouraging passive reliance on AI output. The paper addresses the pedagogical problem of balancing the benefits of GenAI for drafting, brainstorming, and scenario analysis with the risks of over-dependence, weak contextual understanding, and incomplete or inaccurate AI-generated content.

To address this, the authors introduce the Structured AI Guided Education (SAGE) framework, a two-stage instructional approach that embeds GenAI first in guided tutorials and then in assessment tasks. Students used tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and later DeepSeek to generate initial cybersecurity policies and strategies, critique them using academic research and industry standards, and refine them to fit regulatory and organisational requirements. The framework was implemented in two cybersecurity management units at Central Queensland University, with undergraduate and postgraduate students working through workshops, written assignments, and presentations over a 12-week semester.

The study draws on student reflections, assignment artefacts, and instructor observations to describe learning outcomes and implementation challenges. Findings suggest that GenAI can improve efficiency and support deeper analysis when used within a structured pedagogical model, but its outputs are often generic, incomplete, or contextually limited. Reported risks included AI dependence, variability in AI literacy, and the need for human oversight. The authors conclude that responsible GenAI use in cybersecurity education requires explicit critique, evidence-based refinement, and alignment with regulatory frameworks, rather than treating AI as a substitute for expert judgment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot for text generation, drafting, question answering, and iterative refinement tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used alongside Gemini, Claude, and later DeepSeek in cybersecurity management tutorials and assessments to draft initial policies, risk assessments, and security strategies for student critique and refinement.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative case study with 105 students across two cybersecurity units, ChatGPT served as a useful starting point for drafting security policies and strategies, which students then refined using research, industry standards, and regulatory frameworks. Students reported that this workflow improved their ability to identify gaps in AI-generated outputs, tailor solutions to context, and focus on compliance and security details rather than initial content creation.
findings.measure: Student reflections, instructor observations, and assessment artefacts examining critical thinking, policy refinement, and contextual alignment

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's generative AI chatbot for text generation and assistance with drafting and synthesis tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used with ChatGPT and Claude for generating cybersecurity policy drafts, risk assessments, and strategy content that students critiqued and refined within tutorials and assessments.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's generative AI chatbot for text generation, drafting, and analytic assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used with ChatGPT and Gemini for generating cybersecurity policy drafts, risk assessments, and strategy content that students critiqued and refined within tutorials and assessments.

identified_tools.name: DeepSeek
identified_tools.description: DeepSeek's generative AI chatbot used for text generation and assistance with analytical drafting tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Introduced later in the semester and used by many students for cybersecurity policy drafting and refinement alongside ChatGPT and other GenAI tools.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative mixed-methods case study based on student reflections, assignment artefacts, and instructor observations rather than a controlled experiment. The evidence is useful for describing implementation experiences and reported limitations, but it does not estimate causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful pedagogical benefits in critical thinking and policy refinement, but no effect sizes or quantitative impact estimates are provided. The influence is therefore suggestive rather than demonstrated at a measured medium or large level.

paper_profiles.title: It’s a Tool Not a Crutch: A Pilot Generative AI Intervention to Enhance Pre-service Teachers’ Self-efficacy and AI Literacy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI-supported scenario-based learning (SBL) intervention can improve pre-service teachers’ self-efficacy and AI literacy. The study is motivated by the rapid uptake of GenAI tools in education and the need to understand both their pedagogical value and their risks, especially in teacher education. The authors frame the work around the question of how GenAI can be integrated into initial teacher education (ITE) in ways that are educationally useful, ethically responsible, and developmentally appropriate.

The intervention used Microsoft CoPilot in two two-hour workshops. In the first workshop, participants completed structured scenario tasks where CoPilot generated classroom vignettes aligned with self-efficacy dimensions such as instructional strategies, classroom management, and student engagement, along with response options and feedback. In the second, participants reflected on a dilemma from school placement and dialogued with CoPilot in a more open-ended way. The study used pre/post survey measures of teacher self-efficacy and AI literacy, plus focus groups with primary pre-service teachers. Participants came from an Irish university context and included 4th-year undergraduate primary pre-service teachers and 2nd-year postgraduate post-primary pre-service teachers.

Findings suggest the intervention increased self-efficacy and AI literacy, especially awareness, usage, and evaluation of AI. Qualitative data showed participants valued the low-stakes scenario practice, immediate feedback, and opportunities for reflection. At the same time, the paper highlights important limitations and risks, including overreliance on AI, the need for critical evaluation of outputs, concerns about trustworthiness, and the importance of scaffolding for early-stage trainees. The authors conclude that GenAI can function as a supportive pedagogical tool in ITE, but only if embedded thoughtfully, with attention to ethics, developmental stage, and long-term impact.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI chatbot/assistant used to generate, adapt, and provide feedback on scenario-based learning prompts and responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as Microsoft CoPilot in a pilot scenario-based learning intervention to generate classroom scenarios, offer multiple response options, provide feedback, and suggest readings for pre-service teachers.

findings.finding_summary: In this pilot mixed-methods study with pre-service teachers (primary n=12; post-primary n=6; total n=18), the GenAI-SBL intervention increased overall teacher self-efficacy from a mean of 74 to 80.35. Subscale means also increased for instructional strategies (25.71 to 27.35), classroom management (24.82 to 27.12), and student engagement (23.47 to 25.88).
findings.measure: Teacher self-efficacy scale (overall and subscales: instructional strategies, classroom management, student engagement)

findings.finding_summary: AI literacy scores improved after the intervention, with overall AI literacy rising from 51.12 to 62.23. Subscale means increased for AI awareness (13.59 to 15.18), AI usage (12.29 to 15.76), AI evaluation (11.88 to 16.88), and AI ethics (13.55 to 14.41).
findings.measure: AI literacy scale (overall and subscales: awareness, usage, evaluation, ethics)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-methods pilot study with a very small sample and no control group, so it provides limited causal evidence. The design is informative but not strong enough for a higher evidence tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are positive but small-scale and descriptive, with no effect sizes reported. Impact is therefore promising but uncertain and not yet established at medium or large magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Understanding PSE students’ reactions to the postplagiarism concept: a quantitative analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how postsecondary education (PSE) students perceive “postplagiarism,” a framework proposed to reconceptualize academic integrity in response to generative AI. The central question is whether students accept the idea that GenAI is becoming a normal part of academic writing and whether they agree with related claims about creativity, attribution, responsibility, and the future of plagiarism definitions.

The study uses a cross-sectional quantitative survey built specifically for this project. Nineteen statements were derived from Eaton’s six tenets of postplagiarism and administered on a 4-point Likert scale to 581 PSE students residing in Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Participants were recruited through Prolific, and most reported regular GenAI use. The instrument showed acceptable overall internal consistency, though several tenet-level subscales were weaker and suggested the need for refinement.

Findings show broad acceptance of hybrid human-AI writing, attribution, and policy adaptation, but also clear resistance around the idea that it is futile to distinguish human from AI-generated text, that AI enhances creativity without threat, and that humans can retain full control over writing in the age of AI. The paper concludes that institutions should not rely only on detection-based approaches; instead, they should develop nuanced policies and pedagogy that support ethical AI integration while preserving agency, creativity, and attribution norms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative artificial intelligence tools used to generate, rewrite, or assist with text production and communication.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper examines PSE students’ perceptions of GenAI in academic writing, including hybrid human-AI writing, attribution, creativity, control, and plagiarism-related policy adaptation. It does not evaluate a specific product.

findings.finding_summary: In a cross-sectional survey of 581 postsecondary students across Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States, 93.1% agreed that hybrid human-AI writing is becoming normal (PPM1), and 91.6% reported regular GenAI use. At the same time, 65.92% disagreed that it is futile to distinguish human- from AI-generated text (PPM3), 60.76% rejected the claim that AI does not threaten human creativity (PPM5), and 32.7% disagreed that humans can retain full control over what they write in the age of AI (PPM11).
findings.measure: Student agreement with 19 postplagiarism Likert-scale statements; survey responses on hybrid writing, creativity, human-AI distinction, and control

findings.finding_summary: The study found strong acceptance of GenAI-related policy adaptation and attribution norms: 95.1% agreed that citing, referencing, and attribution remain important (PPM17), and 90.0% agreed that policy definitions of academic integrity can and must adapt because of AI (PPM19). These results suggest students broadly support institutional adjustment to GenAI, even while expressing concerns about creativity and control.
findings.measure: Agreement with postplagiarism policy/attribution statements

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey study with self-reported attitudes, not an experiment or meta-analysis. The instrument is newly developed and only preliminarily validated, so evidence is informative but not causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes are reported, so impact cannot be quantified. Findings indicate broad acceptance of GenAI normalization and policy adaptation, but the study mainly reports perceptions rather than measured learning or performance impacts.

paper_profiles.title: DeBiasMe: De-biasing Human-AI Interactions with Metacognitive AIED (AI in Education) Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Workshop: AI Augmented Reasoning (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a gap in AI literacy and educational technology research: while generative AI tools are increasingly used in academic work, most existing literacy interventions emphasize technical understanding of AI bias rather than the human cognitive biases that shape how learners prompt and interpret AI outputs. The paper argues that automation bias, confirmation bias, and anchoring can combine with algorithmic and systemic bias to create harmful feedback loops that undermine learning, critical thinking, and appropriate reliance on AI.

To address this, the author proposes DeBiasMe, a metacognitive AIED intervention centered on deliberate friction and bi-directional human-AI interaction. The design includes two main components: a Prompt Refinement Tool that flags possible bias before a prompt is submitted, and a Bias Visualization Map that explains potential biases in AI outputs after generation. The tool is framed as a way to make hidden bias processes visible, support reflection, and strengthen students’ metacognitive knowledge and regulation when using AI.

The work is situated in higher education and is informed by mixed-methods user research with university students, but the paper itself is primarily a conceptual/position paper rather than an outcome study. It surveys existing AI literacy tools and compares them with the proposed approach, emphasizing accessibility, adaptive scaffolding, and trust dynamics. The main conclusion is that AI literacy interventions should move beyond operational and ethical competencies to explicitly support human bias awareness and reflective AI use through metacognitive scaffolding.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General generative AI / LLM chatbot tools used to generate, summarize, and interpret text in educational and knowledge-work contexts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a position/conceptual paper about designing metacognitive AI literacy interventions for students interacting with generative AI, especially LLM text generators such as GPT-4 on Azure, rather than an empirical evaluation of a single commercial product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position/theoretical paper proposing a metacognitive AI literacy intervention and related design framework. It does not report an empirical evaluation with measurable outcomes, sample sizes, or effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No impact can be assigned because the paper does not present outcome data for a studied intervention. The discussion is conceptual and forward-looking rather than evidence of measured effects.

paper_profiles.title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a short AI literacy intervention can reduce students’ tendency to accept incorrect ChatGPT recommendations. The authors frame the problem around over-reliance on large language models in education, noting concerns that students may trust fluent but wrong outputs, which can undermine critical thinking and promote cognitive offloading.

The intervention consisted of a short educational text for 12th-grade students explaining ChatGPT’s working mechanism, prompt design, limitations, risks, and tips for appropriate use, supplemented with screenshots of hallucinations and other errors. The control group read only the introductory, general-information portion of the text. After reading, students completed eight Kangaroo math puzzles with ChatGPT recommendations, half of which were deliberately incorrect. Participants decided whether to follow each recommendation and then solved the puzzle if they chose not to rely on ChatGPT.

The study was conducted online with 36 Estonian high school seniors from 10 schools. The main finding was that over-reliance was widespread: students adopted incorrect ChatGPT recommendations in 52.1% of cases. The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance; instead, it increased under-reliance, meaning students were more likely to ignore correct ChatGPT answers after the AI literacy text. The authors conclude that short-form AI literacy interventions may not be sufficient to counter over-reliance on LLMs in K-12 settings and may inadvertently cause users to distrust correct outputs as well as incorrect ones.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot that generates text-based responses from user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the AI system students consulted to solve math puzzles; the paper tested whether a short AI literacy text reduced over-reliance on ChatGPT's recommendations, especially when recommendations were incorrect.

findings.finding_summary: Among 36 Estonian 12th-grade students, mean over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations was 52.1% (SD = 28.90). The intervention group showed lower over-reliance than the control group (48.68% vs 55.88%), but this difference was not statistically significant, t(28.78) = -0.73, p = .236, d = -0.25.
findings.measure: Over-reliance rate on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations during eight math puzzles

findings.finding_summary: The intervention increased under-reliance on correct ChatGPT recommendations. Under-reliance was higher in the intervention group (M = 36.84, SD = 24.11) than in the control group (M = 19.12, SD = 20.78), t(34) = 2.35, p = .025, d = 0.78, indicating a moderate-to-large effect.
findings.measure: Under-reliance rate on correct ChatGPT recommendations during eight math puzzles

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small randomized experiment with a control group, but the final analyzed sample was only 36 students and the main outcome did not show a significant reduction in over-reliance. The design is empirical, but the small sample and limited scope lower confidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention showed no meaningful improvement on the primary target outcome (over-reliance), and the only significant effect was adverse: increased under-reliance with d = 0.78. That makes the practical impact unclear to negative for classroom use.

paper_profiles.title: Breakable Machine: A K–12 Classroom Game for Transformative AI Literacy Through Spoofing and eXplainable AI (XAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to teach critical, transformative AI literacy in K–12 settings by moving beyond conventional “build an AI model” activities. The authors argue that many AI education tools emphasize model construction and basic functionality, but give less attention to AI failure, brittleness, bias, and the social consequences of misclassification. In response, they propose a classroom game centered on adversarial spoofing and explainable AI as a way to help students interrogate AI systems as sociotechnical artifacts rather than treat them as reliable or neutral decision-makers.

The intervention, Breakable Machine, is a browser-based classroom game in which learners aged 10–15 use a mobile device camera to manipulate their appearance or environment in order to trick an image classifier into making a high-confidence prediction. The game includes a shared teacher dashboard, student devices, a leaderboard, access to the training data, and a heat-map view based on class activation maps to show salient image regions. The paper situates the resource in grade 4–9 classrooms and positions it as a complement to established K–12 AI literacy tools such as Teachable Machine and other model-building activities, while extending them toward critical reflection on failure and bias.

The paper is non-empirical and does not report a formal evaluation of learning outcomes. Instead, it presents the design rationale, intended learning outcomes, and classroom use scenarios. The authors conclude that spoofing-based play can support students’ understanding of confidence versus correctness, adversarial attacks, feature sensitivity, brittleness, and the real-world consequences of misclassification. They argue that this kind of activity can foster skepticism, ethical awareness, collaborative sensemaking, and transformative agency in AI education.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system is a digital educational system that adapts instruction, feedback, or task difficulty based on learner input and performance.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not evaluate an ITS directly; it references established AI education tools and contrasts the Breakable Machine game with tools that focus on training models rather than interrogating system failures.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical, non-empirical design paper. It describes the Breakable Machine classroom game and its pedagogical rationale, but explicitly states that empirical evaluation of learning outcomes is future work.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The proposed resource is potentially important for K-12 AI literacy, but the paper reports no measured outcomes, so there is no empirical impact to assess. The likely educational relevance is clear, but evidence of effect is absent.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Students to Question the Machine: An AI Literacy Intervention Improves Students Regulation of LLM Use in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a brief AI literacy workshop can improve middle-school students’ use of generative AI in science problem solving. The authors focus on a central challenge in K-12 GenAI use: students may over-trust fluent LLM outputs, accept incorrect answers too quickly, and fail to regulate their interaction with the system. The study asks whether explicit instruction in how LLMs work and fail, together with practical heuristics for prompting and checking answers, can improve both interaction quality and final task performance.

The intervention was a two-hour classroom-feasible workshop that combined conceptual content (e.g., hallucinations, bias, sycophancy, how LLMs are trained) with procedural guidance (e.g., specifying context, asking follow-up questions, evaluating plausibility, and reformulating prompts). Students then completed six science inquiry tasks with access to a GenAI chatbot. The sample was drawn from one French middle school and included 116 students in grades 8–9 (ages 13–15). A control group received no training, while the intervention group attended the workshop two days before the task session.

The study found that trained students performed better on the final science answers and showed stronger regulation of LLM interaction: they rejected underspecified prompts more often, asked more follow-up questions when needed, and judged AI answers more accurately. The authors conclude that even a short, scalable AI literacy intervention can improve how adolescents use generative AI in school-like tasks. At the same time, the effects were modest, performance remained limited overall, and the authors caution that the results are short-term and based on one school context.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model chatbot/system used for generative text, question answering, and response evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: Students used GPT-4o mini via DuckDuckAI for science problem solving; when unavailable, some used other public chatbot interfaces running GPT-4o, GPT-4.1-nano, or GPT-3.5-turbo. GPT-4o was also used as an LLM-as-judge to validate prompt manipulation and score student answers.

findings.finding_summary: In a controlled classroom study with grade 89 students, access to ChatGPT-family chatbots supported science task completion, but a brief AI literacy workshop improved how students used the tool. Intervention students achieved higher final-answer scores than controls (M=11.38, SD=3.87, n=76 vs. M=10.29, SD=3.04, n=40; MannWhitney U=1871, p=.040, r=.19), indicating modest gains in performance during LLM-supported problem solving.
findings.measure: Final-answer performance / exercise scores on six science tasks (020 scale)

findings.finding_summary: The workshop improved interaction regulation with ChatGPT-family systems.
