Trained students accepted fewer suggested prompts overall (p=.018) and were less likely to accept underspecified prompts than controls (51.5% vs. 66.7%, p=.044), while rejecting well-specified prompts reduced performance only in controls, not in the intervention group.
findings.measure: Prompt acceptance / rejection behavior

findings.finding_summary: Trained students judged AI response correctness more accurately, especially when prompts were well-specified; the group �d7 prompt specificity interaction was significant (p=.012). They were also more likely to ask follow-up questions after accepted underspecified prompts (59.2% vs. 27.9%, p<.001), and in the intervention group this behavior was associated with higher-quality answers (approximately +5 points out of 20; interaction p=.038).
findings.measure: Correctness judgments and follow-up questioning during LLM interaction
findings.effect_size: approximately +5 points out of 20 for the follow-up-questioning benefit

findings.finding_summary: Self-reported GenAI attitudes/knowledge did not predict task performance. Across all students, GenAI self-report scores were not correlated with performance (r=0.01, p=.88, R2<.001, n=116), and metacognitive self-report scores were also unrelated to exercise scores (r=0.04, p=.65, R2=.002, n=116).
findings.measure: GenAI self-report and Jr. MAI metacognitive self-report versus performance

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled classroom study with a comparison group and pre/post intervention elements, providing relatively strong evidence. However, the sample comes from one school, the intervention was short-term, and some measures were secondary or self-report, which leaves a few design and generalizability concerns.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed effects are modest in size overall (e.g., r=.19 and approximately +5 points out of 20 on one outcome). The workshop meaningfully improved regulation behaviors, but the absolute performance gains were not large and the study does not show long-term impact.

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy, Safety Awareness, and STEM Career Aspirations of Australian Secondary Students: Evaluating the Impact of Workshop Interventions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a short, workshop-based AI literacy intervention can improve secondary students’ understanding of artificial intelligence, awareness of synthetic media risks, and interest in STEM careers. The authors focus on a practical problem in K-12 education: adolescents are already encountering and sometimes sharing deepfakes and other AI-mediated content, but schools have limited evidence on how to teach AI literacy in ways that connect to students’ everyday digital lives.

The intervention was Day of AI Australia’s curriculum-aligned workshop sequence, which covered foundational AI concepts, ethics, safety, misinformation, privacy, and AI in careers. The study used pre- and post-intervention surveys plus open-ended reflections to measure changes in self-reported AI knowledge, confidence, conceptual understanding, tool recognition, and STEM career aspirations. Because the surveys were anonymous and not linkable at the individual level, the analysis compared pre- and post-samples rather than tracking within-student change. The sample came from three New South Wales government secondary schools and included students in Years 7–10.

Findings suggest that the workshops produced clear short-term gains in self-reported AI knowledge, confidence, and understanding of AI training, bias, privacy, and data consent. Students also became better at identifying AI in everyday platforms such as Netflix, Spotify, TikTok, and Face Unlock, indicating that the intervention helped them move beyond a narrow view of AI as only chatbots or generative tools. However, effects on STEM career aspirations were small, suggesting that one-off workshops may spark interest but are unlikely to shift long-term trajectories on their own. The authors conclude that scalable AI literacy programs should pair foundational AI concepts with explicit attention to safety, ethics, and synthetic media, and they emphasize the need for sustained curriculum integration rather than isolated sessions.

identified_tools.name: Day of AI Australia
identified_tools.description: A curriculum-aligned AI literacy program offering workshop-based lessons on how AI works, AI ethics, safety, privacy, misinformation, and AI in careers.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the workshop intervention delivered to Years 7–10 students in three New South Wales government secondary schools to improve AI literacy, safety awareness, and STEM career aspirations.

findings.finding_summary: In pre/post mixed-methods survey data (N=205 pre; n=163 post), students reported higher AI knowledge and confidence after the workshop, with significant increases in knowledge about AI (r=.445), confidence in AI tools (r=.279), understanding AI training (r=.399), and understanding AI bias/errors (r=.302). The paper interprets these as short-term gains in conceptual AI literacy from the Day of AI Australia workshops.
findings.measure: Self-reported AI knowledge, AI confidence, understanding AI training, understanding AI bias/errors

findings.finding_summary: The intervention improved students' ability to identify AI in everyday platforms and recommendation systems. Significant post-workshop increases were reported for Netflix (+27.1%, p<.001), Spotify (+16.2%, p<.001), TikTok (+12.8%, p<.001), and Face Unlock (+11.2%, p=.013), suggesting the workshops reduced the misconception that algorithms are separate from AI.
findings.measure: Proportion identifying specific tools as using AI
findings.sample_size: N=368 total responses (N=205 pre + n=163 post)

findings.finding_summary: Students reported increased interest in AI, Computer Science, and Engineering careers after the workshop, but the effects were small (AI r=.189; Computer Science r=.115; Engineering r=.119). The authors conclude the one-day intervention may spark interest but is unlikely to shift longer-term career trajectories on its own.
findings.measure: STEM career interest (AI, Computer Science, Engineering)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods pre/post intervention study rather than a randomized trial. It provides useful empirical evidence, but the pre/post samples were not individually paired and outcomes were self-reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced medium effects for AI knowledge and some related constructs (e.g., r=.445, r=.399, r=.302), indicating meaningful short-term gains. However, some outcomes were small, especially STEM career interest, so the overall impact is modest rather than large.

paper_profiles.title: The Agency Gap: How Generative AI Literacy Shapes Independent Writing after AI Support
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether students’ generative AI (GenAI) literacy predicts how well they can write independently after AI assistance is removed, and whether that relationship depends on the style of AI interaction. The authors frame this as an “agency gap”: the extent to which learners can transfer support gained from GenAI tools into later independent performance when external scaffolding is no longer available.

To test this, the study compared two GenAI chatbot designs in a multimodal academic writing task based on visual data from a healthcare simulation. One chatbot was reactive, responding only to learner queries; the other was proactive, actively scaffolding the task through structured questions and iterative feedback. Seventy-nine participants, all current students or graduates from medical or nursing programs, were randomly assigned to one of the two conditions, completed the AI-supported writing task, and then completed a parallel writing task without AI support. The study measured GenAI literacy, visualization literacy, and writing quality across insightfulness, visual data integration, organization and coherence, linguistic quality, and critical thinking.

The main findings were that GenAI literacy predicted stronger independent writing performance after AI removal, but primarily in the reactive condition. In that condition, higher GenAI literacy was associated with better performance on several writing dimensions; in the proactive condition, GenAI literacy did not significantly relate to performance. Visualization literacy did not significantly predict writing outcomes. The authors conclude that GenAI literacy is a meaningful transferable competence, but that proactive scaffolding can reduce dependence on that literacy by equalizing outcomes across learners. They argue that designers should both cultivate GenAI literacy and use proactive AI support to mitigate inequities in AI-supported learning.

Because the study was conducted in a controlled online experiment with a relatively small sample of medical/nursing students, the authors’ claims are best read as evidence about short-term transfer in a specific multimodal writing context rather than broad classroom generalizations.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI chatbot system that can answer questions, generate or scaffold content, and provide feedback during writing tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Students used a custom-built GenAI chatbot for multimodal academic writing support in two interaction modes: reactive (responds only to learner queries) and proactive (actively scaffolds with structured questions and feedback). The underlying model is described as multimodal GPT-4o, but the paper studies the general GenAI chatbot system rather than a specific commercial product.

findings.finding_summary: In the reactive condition (n=39), higher GenAI literacy was positively associated with independent writing performance after AI support was removed. Significant correlations were reported for insightfulness (rs=.41, p=.010), visual data integration (rs=.40, p=.013), organisation and coherence (rs=.44, p=.005), linguistic quality (rs=.32, p=.045), critical thinking (rs=.37, p=.019), and composite score (rs=.44, p=.005).
findings.measure: Independent multimodal academic writing rubric scores at AI-removal stage

findings.finding_summary: In the proactive condition (n=40), GenAI literacy was not significantly correlated with writing performance at either AI-support or AI-removal stages. The paper reports no significant associations in this condition, suggesting proactive scaffolding reduced dependence on learners' GenAI literacy.
findings.measure: Independent multimodal academic writing rubric scores at AI-support and AI-removal stages

findings.finding_summary: Ordinal logistic regression showed that higher GenAI literacy significantly predicted stronger independent writing after AI support was withdrawn for visual data integration (b=0.13, SE=0.06, z=2.07, p=.039, OR=1.14), critical thinking (b=0.14, SE=0.07, z=2.18, p=.029, OR=1.15), and composite score (b=0.10, SE=0.05, z=2.15, p=.032, OR=1.11). GenAI literacy did not significantly predict insightfulness, organisation and coherence, or linguistic quality.
findings.measure: Ordinal logistic regression of AI-removal writing rubric outcomes

findings.finding_summary: Mediation analyses found no significant indirect effect of GenAI literacy on independent writing through AI-supported performance in either condition. In the reactive condition, the indirect effect was 0.032 with 95% CI [-0.022, 0.108]; in the proactive condition, the indirect effect was 0.022 with 95% CI [-0.055, 0.102].
findings.measure: Indirect effect from GenAI literacy  AI-support writing  AI-removal writing

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-method experimental study with quantitative analyses, but the evidence is not randomized across a broad educational setting and the main inferences are correlational/associational rather than causal for the literacy-performance link. The paper still provides reasonably detailed measurement and analysis, but the study context is narrow and uses a custom platform.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported associations are modest to moderate, with several correlations around rs=.32-.44 and odds ratios around 1.11-1.15. The practical implication is meaningful but not large: GenAI literacy appears to matter more when support is reactive and less when proactive scaffolding is provided.

paper_profiles.title: Preliminary Study of the Impact of AI-Based Interventions on Health and Behavioral Outcomes in Maternal Health Programs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-scheduled outreach interventions in a maternal mobile health program can improve not only engagement with automated health messages, but also mothers’ knowledge and self-reported health-related behaviors. The core question is whether an AI system that allocates limited live service calls can translate increased listenership into better behavioral and health outcomes.

The intervention is studied in ARMMAN’s mMitra program in India, which sends weekly automated voice messages to pregnant and postpartum women. A decision-focused learning restless multi-armed bandit algorithm schedules live calls from health workers for a subset of beneficiaries, while a control group does not receive those calls. The study follows three enrollment cohorts totaling 60,464 beneficiaries, and then administers a health survey to a high-risk subset; survey responses are matched across intervention and control groups to compare outcomes.

Results show a statistically significant increase in listenership after AI-scheduled interventions. The authors also report generally better survey performance among intervention beneficiaries, with some statistically significant differences on individual questions, especially among those whose listenership improved the most. However, the overall behavioral/health outcome differences are not consistently statistically significant because of small effective sample sizes, noisy survey responses, and selection issues in who completed the survey. The paper concludes that AI-scheduled intervention allocation can improve engagement and may help improve downstream maternal health knowledge, but larger follow-up studies are needed to establish the effect more firmly.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring / adaptive intervention system that allocates instructional or support actions using algorithmic decision-making.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies AI-scheduled live service calls in the mMitra maternal health program, where a DFL-RMAB algorithm selects beneficiaries for intervention to increase listenership of automated health messages.

findings.finding_summary: The AI-scheduled intervention increased beneficiary listenership relative to control. The paper reports an average increase of 7.43 seconds per call over the 12 automated voice calls following the intervention, with a summed additional listenership of 89.16 seconds over the next 12 calls; the 95% CI was [45.516, 132.936] and p=6.4656 × 10−5.
findings.measure: Listenership over the 12 automated voice calls following intervention
findings.effect_size: 7.43 seconds per call; 89.16 seconds summed additional listenership

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports generally better survey-based behavioral and health knowledge outcomes for beneficiaries who gained in listenership after AI-scheduled interventions, but the overall summed score difference was not statistically significant (p=0.13). Two questions showed statistically significant differences: single-choice question 5 and multiple-choice question 3 (p=0.0021 for the latter).
findings.measure: Survey scores on engagement, knowledge, breastfeeding practices, communication, and supplements

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary field study / randomized controlled trial with matching and subgroup analysis, but the paper itself notes small sample sizes, noise in responses, and residual confounding from survey nonresponse. Those concerns prevent a blue-tier rating.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported listenership effect is statistically significant but modest in magnitude (7.43 seconds per call). The broader behavioral/health outcomes are positive but mixed and often not statistically significant, so the overall practical impact appears modest.

paper_profiles.title: Fake News Mitigation via Point Process Based Intervention
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of mitigating the spread of fake news in social networks. The authors ask how to optimally allocate intervention resources so that users exposed to fake news are also exposed to real news, reducing the likelihood that fake news will persuade them. Rather than focusing on content classification or manual fact-checking, the paper frames fake news mitigation as a sequential control problem over a network.

The proposed approach models fake news and mitigation activities as competing multivariate Hawkes point processes. Interventions are implemented by increasing the exogenous intensity of selected campaigner nodes over multiple stages under budget constraints, and the optimal policy is learned with a reinforcement-learning style least-squares temporal difference (LSTD) policy-iteration method. The paper defines reward functions based on either correlation maximization between fake and real news exposures or minimization of their difference, and derives first- and second-order statistics needed for policy evaluation.

The empirical context is not K-12 education but social media, including synthetic Twitter-like networks and a real-time experiment using Twitter accounts discussing machine learning topics. The main conclusion is that the proposed LSTD intervention method outperforms several baselines, including open-loop optimization, certainly equivalence control, centrality-based heuristics, and random allocation, in both synthetic and real-time experiments. The authors also note several limitations of their evaluation, including the content-neutral nature of the real-world experiment, imperfect measurement of exposure, and the fact that the method optimizes conditional intensity rather than exact intervention times.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI system or method category; in this paper, the relevant AI method is a point-process-based reinforcement learning intervention framework for social network activity, not a named commercial product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and evaluates a point process intervention framework using reinforcement learning and LSTD to optimize mitigation activity against fake news propagation in a network.

findings.finding_summary: The proposed point-process-based intervention framework outperformed baseline mitigation strategies in synthetic and real-time Twitter experiments. In the real-time experiment, the authors report that their method outperformed three baselines (CEC, EXP, and RND) by a reasonable margin; the paper notes roughly a 5-point increase for the correlation maximization objective and around a 7-point result for the difference minimization objective, but does not report standardized effect sizes.
findings.measure: Total reward; average correlation; average difference in exposure; rank correlation for prediction
findings.sample_size: synthetic: n=300 nodes; real-time: 1894 users and 23407 directed edges

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/methodological paper with synthetic and real-world proof-of-concept experiments rather than a randomized or quasi-experimental education study. The evidence is therefore useful but indirect for K-12 classroom applications.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are described in relative terms and appear practically meaningful in the paper’s network-intervention context, but no standardized effect size is provided. Because the work is not an education intervention study, its classroom impact remains uncertain and indirect.

paper_profiles.title: Integration of AI in STEM Education – Addressing Ethical Challenges in K-12 Settings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the ethical and pedagogical challenges of integrating artificial intelligence into K-12 STEM education, with a particular focus on bias, privacy, surveillance, and equity. Rather than evaluating a specific AI product through an empirical study, it synthesizes recent literature to ask how AI tools can be introduced in ways that support personalized learning and efficiency without undermining student agency, fairness, or human judgment.

The paper discusses several AI applications commonly used or proposed for classrooms, including intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment tools, predictive analytics, and surveillance technologies such as facial recognition and behavior tracking. It contrasts their claimed benefits—such as real-time feedback, adaptive instruction, and reduced teacher workload—with risks including algorithmic bias, opaque decision-making, data privacy violations, reduced pedagogical flexibility, and potential harm to marginalized or neurodiverse learners.

The intended context is K-12 STEM schooling, especially classrooms and school systems considering AI adoption. The authors propose a three-phased implementation roadmap and a four-phase professional development model grounded in TPACK and critical algorithmic literacy. Their conclusion is that responsible AI integration requires teacher preparation, equity-centered design, low-resource adaptations, and policy-level governance so that AI complements rather than replaces human-centered education.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: Intelligent Tutoring Systems are adaptive AI systems that personalize instruction, feedback, pacing, and support based on learner responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a major AI application in K-12 STEM education, including benefits, limitations, and ethical risks; no single ITS product was empirically tested in this paper.

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: AI systems that automatically evaluate learner work and provide immediate, tailored feedback or scoring.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as AI-powered automated assessment tools in STEM classrooms, including automated essay/scoring and diagnostic feedback; no specific product was evaluated.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer-assisted instruction systems that include AI-enabled classroom monitoring, surveillance, assessment, and adaptive learning functions.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed broadly through AI surveillance technologies such as facial recognition, emotion detection, behavior tracking, and predictive analytics in K-12 STEM settings; no named product was studied.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a critical conceptual review and synthesis, not an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. It provides thematic claims and recommendations drawn from prior literature rather than new study data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that AI tools may improve personalization and efficiency but also introduces substantial risks; however, it does not report original effect sizes or direct intervention outcomes. The impact is therefore framed as potentially meaningful but not empirically demonstrated in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: ActiveAI: Enabling K-12 AI Literacy Education & Analytics at Scale
paper_profiles.venue: Companion Proceedings 15th International Conference on Learning Analytics & Knowledge (LAK25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the shortage of large-scale, reusable data and scalable classroom materials for K-12 AI literacy education. The authors argue that although AI literacy initiatives and summer programs have expanded, the field still lacks broad learning datasets that would support replication, secondary analysis, and more generalizable findings.

To address this gap, the paper presents ActiveAI, a web-based learning platform built with Next.js and OpenAI APIs. The platform includes AI literacy modules, isomorphic pre/post assessments, interactive activities with an AI agent in simulated scenarios, and role-based access for students, teachers, and researchers. It was designed using backward design and aligned with AI literacy standards and partner-school priorities, including topics such as identifying LLM hallucinations.

The platform was deployed across 12 secondary schools in North America, Asia, and Australia, engaging over 1,000 learners, with 426 completing all components. The paper reports preliminary analyses showing learning gains in some objectives, stronger gains for interactive activities than passive reading, and gender differences on one module. The authors conclude that the platform can support scalable AI literacy instruction and produce valuable learning analytics data for future research and classroom use.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / LLM-based assistant used within an online K-12 AI literacy learning platform for interactive activities, including simulated scenarios and feedback-enabled scaffolding.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as an AI agent in interactive learning modules to help students practice AI literacy tasks such as identifying LLM hallucinations in news summaries and completing scaffolded activities.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports preliminary learning gains on 4 of 7 learning objectives across 4 modules, based on Wilcoxon tests of pre- and post-test scores. The platform engaged over 1,000 unique learners, with 426 completing all components; objectives with significant gains were associated with interactive activities, while smaller gains were linked to passive reading.
findings.measure: Pre-test/post-test learning gains on AI literacy learning objectives
findings.sample_size: n=426 completed all components; over 1,000 unique learners used the platform

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preliminary mixed-methods / observational report from a platform deployment, not a controlled experiment. The paper reports descriptive and nonparametric pre-post comparisons, but no randomized design or full effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports significant gains on some objectives, but no effect sizes are provided, so the magnitude of impact is unclear. The evidence suggests modest learning benefit at the activity level, but not enough to classify as clearly moderate or large.

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Detection: Rethinking Education in the Age of AI-writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI is changing writing instruction and assessment, especially in secondary education. Its central question is not whether AI can write, but what is lost when students use AI to bypass the writing process, and how educators should respond in ways that preserve learning rather than merely police cheating. The authors argue that writing is a cognitive activity through which students develop thinking, memory, reflection, and intellectual independence.

Rather than presenting a new empirical intervention, the paper synthesizes cognitive psychology, educational theory, and classroom examples to propose pedagogical responses to AI writing tools such as ChatGPT. It reviews limitations of AI-text detection and watermarking, then discusses classroom practices including AI-assisted outlining, image generation from student writing, revision reflections, tightly constrained assignments, in-class freewriting, progress-based grading, and prompts that exploit recent events or contextual knowledge AI may not know.

The population and context are secondary school writing classrooms, with references to both school teachers and university professors, but the concrete classroom examples are mainly from high school settings. The paper concludes that banning AI is counterproductive and that educators should instead redesign assignments to make authentic writing more meaningful and harder to fake. It also argues that recognizing AI-generated text should become a core literacy skill for students and teachers, especially as synthetic text becomes harder to detect reliably.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based conversational AI chatbot used for generating and transforming text.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as the generative AI tool entering classrooms and as the exemplar of AI-assisted writing in secondary school contexts; also referenced in relation to students using it for essays and teachers using it to teach writing.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic’s conversational AI language model family for generating text.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned only as one of the models experienced human annotators could robustly identify as AI-generated text sources.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper grounded in cited literature and examples, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention or tool. It does not report original study design, participant data, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that generative AI may undermine writing, memory, and critical thinking and that detection/banning has limits, but it does not present original effect estimates. Its impact is therefore important conceptually but not empirically quantified in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Navigating the State of Cognitive Flow: Context-Aware AI Interventions for Effective Reasoning Support
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a design problem in AI-augmented reasoning: how to provide cognitive support without interrupting or degrading a person’s engagement while they are thinking through a task. The authors argue that many current AI reasoning assistants use static, one-size-fits-all interventions that can be poorly timed, overly intrusive, or mismatched to the user’s needs, thereby breaking focus and reducing the quality of reasoning.

To address this, the paper proposes a context-aware cognitive augmentation framework grounded in Flow Theory and extends it to what the authors call cognitive flow. The framework emphasizes adapting the type, timing, and scale of interventions based on real-time multimodal cues such as gaze behavior, typing hesitation, interaction speed, gestures, and other engagement signals. The aim is to infer when a user is overloaded, stuck, or under-challenged and then provide support that is minimally disruptive and personalized.

The paper does not report an empirical study with a defined participant population; instead, it presents a conceptual and theoretical call to action for future AI systems. The main conclusion is that effective reasoning support should be evaluated not only by task performance or engagement metrics, but also by how well it maintains cognitive flow, supports autonomy, and preserves a sense that the user arrived at the conclusion through their own reasoning. The authors recommend mixed-method evaluation in future work, combining behavioral analytics with subjective feedback.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI reasoning-support or cognitive-augmentation system that delivers adaptive interventions, feedback, questions, or prompts based on user context and behavior.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a theoretical proposal about context-aware AI interventions for reasoning support, describing how generative AI systems should adapt the type, timing, and scale of interventions using multimodal behavioral cues.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper proposing a framework for context-aware cognitive augmentation, not an empirical evaluation of a tool. It reports no study design, sample, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially meaningful design improvements in AI reasoning support, but it provides no empirical evidence of impact. Because no effects are measured, impact remains speculative and unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Competing Visions of Ethical AI: A Case Study of OpenAI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how OpenAI publicly frames AI ethics over time, asking how the company has used terms such as “ethics,” “safety,” “alignment,” and related concepts in its public communications and what those choices signal about ethics in practice. The central concern is not classroom intervention, but the discursive construction of AI ethics by a leading developer during a period of rapid generative AI growth.

The study uses a mixed-methods case study design with a large corpus of OpenAI-authored public materials from December 2015 through July 2025. The authors analyze 424 website articles and 30 publications using keyword frequency analysis, topic modeling, clustering, and qualitative content analysis. They distinguish between public-facing web articles and more academic/publication-oriented materials, including arXiv papers and site-hosted reports.

The paper finds that OpenAI overwhelmingly emphasizes safety, risk, responsibility, and alignment, while explicit references to ethics are rare and often superficial. Ethics appears more often in academic or collaborative publications than in web articles, but still usually in peripheral locations such as headers, footnotes, or policy language. The authors conclude that OpenAI’s discourse reflects ethics-washing and a narrowing of AI governance toward technical safety and compliance, with justice-oriented and broader social concerns receiving much less attention.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's family of GPT-based large language models and ChatGPT interface.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a case study of OpenAI and its public discourse about AI ethics, safety, alignment, and related concepts; it does not evaluate educational use of the model.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative and computational discourse analysis case study of OpenAI's public communications, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool in classrooms or learning settings.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no educational intervention outcomes, student learning measures, or classroom impact estimates; it analyzes rhetoric and framing rather than impact.

paper_profiles.title: Stacking interventions for equitable outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of updating predictive risk scores when the scores themselves influence behavior and interventions. The author argues that in many domains, including health care, a risk model can become biased after it is used to trigger actions, because those actions change the outcomes that later model versions are trained on. The paper proposes an alternative updating strategy called "stacked interventions," designed to preserve calibration while avoiding the paradox of performative prediction.

The method repeatedly releases a sequence of risk scores, each intended to be interpreted by expert agents as the expected risk after successive interventions. Rather than trying to identify the exact causal effect of each intervention, the algorithm only assumes that interventions are generally well-intentioned and move risk toward an acceptable level. The framework is presented for both deterministic and probabilistic interventions, and the paper proves convergence-style results under assumptions of no drift, oracle risk estimation, and later relaxed settings with estimation error and drift.

No human participants, classrooms, or K-12 settings are studied empirically. The paper is theoretical, with supporting simulation examples and illustrative applications to existing health risk scores such as QRISK and SPARRA. The main conclusion is that stacked interventions can, under stated assumptions, lead to equitable distribution of outcome risk and safer model updating without requiring explicit identification of intervention effects. The author also notes practical drawbacks, including the need to distribute multiple scores and retrain users to apply them in sequence.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic predictive risk-score updating and intervention-stacking algorithm, not a generative AI product. It uses a sequence of risk scores to guide expert interventions over time in order to adjust outcome risk toward an acceptable level.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and analyzes this algorithm theoretically, then illustrates it via simulation and discusses potential implementations for updating clinical risk scores such as QRISK and SPARRA.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/method paper with simulations, not an empirical evaluation of an AI tool in classrooms or any K-12 setting. It does not report a study design, sample, or outcome effects for a tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear methodological relevance for predictive-risk systems, but it is not a classroom intervention study and reports no effect sizes on educational outcomes. Impact on K-12 literacy practice is therefore indirect and unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper examines how ChatGPT responds to prompts related to science education and what its outputs suggest for teaching, learning, and research. The central problem is not an instructional intervention in a classroom, but rather whether a generative AI tool can provide useful, pedagogically relevant, and evidence-aligned responses for science education purposes.

The study uses a self-study methodology in which the author queries ChatGPT with prompts about effective science teaching, pedagogical choices such as chalk-and-talk versus student-centred instruction, responses to students failing in science, and examples of classroom resource design. The paper also examines ChatGPT as a research tool, with the author using it for editing and experimenting with clearer phrasing. Although some prompts are framed around Year 7 science resources, the paper does not report actual classroom implementation with K-12 participants; the discussion is primarily analytic and reflective.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can generate plausible, often broadly aligned pedagogical advice and can be useful for drafting units, rubrics, and quizzes, but its outputs are frequently generic and insufficiently grounded in evidence. The author emphasizes that ChatGPT should be treated as a starting point rather than an authority, and that educators must critically evaluate AI-generated materials in light of context, student needs, curriculum demands, and ethical concerns such as bias, copyright, and transparency in research use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot for generating and revising text, answering questions, and drafting structured content.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a self-study exploratory paper to answer science-education prompts and to generate/edit teaching resources (a 5Es unit, a rubric, and a quiz); also used as a research-writing aid for editing and rewriting sentences.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory self-study and reflective analysis of ChatGPT outputs, not a controlled empirical evaluation with comparison groups or outcome testing. No K-12 student learning outcomes are measured.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical utility for educators in drafting units, rubrics, quizzes, and revising text, but it provides no quantitative evidence of impact on student outcomes. Any impact is therefore speculative and context-dependent.

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports an exploratory investigation of an early, text-only version of GPT-4 and argues that it exhibits broad capabilities that may place it on a path toward artificial general intelligence. The authors focus on demonstrating general competence across many domains rather than evaluating a specific educational intervention. They present qualitative examples in language generation, coding, mathematics, vision-related tasks, tool use, interaction with the world, theory of mind, explainability, and discrimination/fact-checking, often contrasting GPT-4’s outputs with ChatGPT.

The approach is not a controlled empirical study but a set of hand-crafted prompts and demonstrations intended to probe capabilities and limitations. The paper emphasizes interdisciplinary composition, such as producing Shakespeare-style proofs, code for graphics, and support letters in stylized voices, as well as reasoning tasks and common-sense judgments. It also includes examples illustrating shortcomings like hallucinations, arithmetic mistakes, and lack of planning.

No student population or educational setting is studied. The context is a research demonstration using prompts to an early version of GPT-4 during development at Microsoft Research/OpenAI. The main conclusion is that GPT-4 shows strikingly general and sometimes human-level performance across diverse tasks, but still has important limitations and is not yet a complete AGI system.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model chatbot/system for natural-language generation and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a direct comparison model against GPT-4 in tasks involving poem-style proof writing, Plato-style dialogue generation, teacher-like comparison of outputs, common-sense reasoning, and hallucination checking.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive, exploratory paper about GPT-4 capabilities rather than a controlled K-12 study. No empirical evaluation of student-facing reading/literacy instruction or elementary-grade outcomes is reported for ChatGPT in the provided text.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no literacy learning effect sizes or student outcome evidence for the tool in the K-12 context. Its comparisons are illustrative demonstrations of language generation quality, not instructional impact.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in Teaching Physics Hands-On Experiments in Primary School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the potential role of ChatGPT in primary school physics instruction, focusing on hands-on experiments and interactive learning. The central problem addressed is how generative AI might help make abstract physics concepts more concrete and engaging for young learners, especially in primary grades where concepts such as force, motion, energy, and matter can be difficult to teach through lecture alone.

Rather than reporting a controlled empirical study, the paper presents a conceptual discussion supported by examples and references to prior literature. It describes how ChatGPT could be used to generate simulations, provide instant feedback, offer tailored explanations, assist with experiment design, and support inquiry-driven learning during hands-on physics activities. The intended users are primary school students and their educators, in classroom-based science instruction in Greece as the author is affiliated with a Greek university, though the paper does not describe a specific participant sample or site.

The paper concludes that thoughtful integration of ChatGPT may improve student engagement, curiosity, comprehension, and problem-solving in primary physics education. It also argues that AI use should be monitored ethically, with attention to privacy, bias, and the continued importance of teacher judgment. The paper ends by calling for ongoing evaluation and future research on long-term effects and educational effectiveness.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot that can answer questions, generate text, provide explanations, and offer interactive support.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a student-facing AI assistant for primary school physics hands-on experiments, including simulations, real-time feedback, tailored explanations, and support for designing experiments.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper is a conceptual/discussion article about using ChatGPT in primary physics instruction. It does not report a clear empirical study design, comparison group, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper claims potentially beneficial effects such as improved engagement and understanding, but these are not supported by reported quantitative effect sizes or direct comparative evidence in the text provided.

paper_profiles.title: E-EVAL: A Comprehensive Chinese K-12 Education Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces E-EVAL, a new benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in Chinese K-12 education. The authors argue that existing benchmarks do not adequately cover the elementary, middle, and high school levels in China, especially with respect to culturally specific content and the often-overlooked primary school domain. The central problem is not intervention effectiveness in a classroom, but the lack of a comprehensive evaluation suite for educational LLM capability in Chinese K-12 settings.

E-EVAL contains 4,351 multiple-choice questions across 23 subjects spanning primary school, middle school, and high school, with subjects grouped into arts and science. The benchmark was built from homework, practice questions, and mock exams collected from regional sources in PDFs and Word documents, then manually cleaned and checked for accuracy, formula correctness, and answer balance. The paper evaluates 15 LLMs, including open-source and commercial systems, under zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, and few-shot-chain-of-thought prompts.

The evaluation is conducted on Chinese K-12 content, with results reported separately for arts and science and for primary, middle, and high school levels. The authors find that Chinese-dominant models generally outperform English-dominant models on this benchmark, but still struggle on complex science and mathematics questions. They also report that models tend to do better on arts than science, and that performance on primary school items is sometimes worse than on middle school items, suggesting weaknesses in simple foundational knowledge. The paper concludes that E-EVAL can serve as a useful tool for tracking progress in LLMs for Chinese K-12 educational applications.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model product used for dialogue-based text generation and question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of 15 LLMs on the E-EVAL Chinese K-12 benchmark across zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, and few-shot-chain-of-thought prompting.

findings.finding_summary: On E-EVAL, ChatGPT achieved 54.6% average accuracy overall. It scored 60.5% on arts and 46.8% on science, and its results varied by prompt setting (54.5% zero-shot, 56.9% five-shot-ao, 52.3% five-shot-cot).

findings.sample_size: n=4351 (benchmark total); model evaluation across 23 subjects

The paper also reports that few-shot prompting usually helped, while chain-of-thought prompting often reduced overall performance except on more complex science questions.

paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported accuracy differences are substantial for model benchmarking, but they do not translate into directly measured student learning impact. The paper’s educational relevance is important, yet the evidence is about evaluation performance rather than instructional effect.

paper_profiles.title: Can Large Language Models Make the Grade? An Empirical Study Evaluating LLMs Ability to Mark Short Answer Questions in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs), especially GPT-4, can accurately grade short-answer responses in K-12 educational settings. The central question is whether LLMs can approximate expert human raters when marking open-ended student answers, and whether performance is stable across different subjects, grade levels, and question difficulty.

The authors built a dataset of 1,710 student responses from the Carousel online quizzing platform, covering Science and History questions across UK Key Stages 2, 3, and 4 (ages 5–16). Student responses were previously marked by qualified teachers, and the study compared model predictions against these human labels. The evaluation tested GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 under zero-shot and few-shot prompting conditions, using a simple API-based workflow and fixed temperature settings.

Results showed that GPT-4 with few-shot prompting performed best, reaching Cohen’s kappa of 0.70, close to human interrater agreement of 0.75. Performance varied only modestly by subject, grade level, and question difficulty. The paper concludes that LLMs may be useful for low-stakes formative assessment in K-12 contexts, potentially saving teachers substantial time while maintaining near-human scoring quality.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT family of large language models used for text generation and evaluation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used via the OpenAI API to automatically mark short open-ended student responses as correct or incorrect, comparing model judgments against expert human raters across Science and History questions for grades spanning ages 5-16.

findings.finding_summary: On 1,710 student responses, GPT-4 with few-shot prompting achieved the best agreement with human raters, reaching Cohen’s kappa = 0.70 versus human rater agreement kappa = 0.75. The paper reports this as close to human-level performance and notes that performance was consistent across subjects, key stages, and question difficulty.
findings.measure: Agreement with expert human ground truth on binary short-answer scoring

findings.finding_summary: The authors estimate that marking the 1,700 responses manually would have taken teachers at least 11 hours, whereas using GPT-4 with a generic script took approximately 2 hours. This was presented as a substantial time saving for low-stakes formative assessment tasks.

findings.effect_size: time saving from ~11 hours to ~2 hours

Performance improved substantially with GPT-4, but the GPT-3.5 results were still above chance and were described as lower than human performance.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study using a real student-response dataset and direct comparison to human raters, but it is not an experimental study of learning effects and does not test instructional outcomes. The evidence is therefore useful but methodologically limited for claims about educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported agreement with human grading is moderately strong (kappa up to 0.70) and the paper also reports substantial time savings for teachers. However, the outcomes are assessment accuracy and efficiency rather than student learning gains, so the impact is modest rather than large.

paper_profiles.title: LitLinker: Supporting the Ideation of Interdisciplinary Contexts with Large Language Models for Teaching Literature in Elementary Schools
paper_profiles.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping elementary school literature teachers design interdisciplinary contexts for reading instruction. The authors argue that creating such contexts requires substantial search, interpretation, and alignment work across disciplines, which is difficult for teachers to do efficiently and in ways that fit classroom practice.

To support this task, they develop LitLinker, a human-AI collaborative web system powered by the GLM-4 large language model. LitLinker uses multiple LLM-based roles to recommend interdisciplinary contexts, analyze the relationships between contexts and reading materials, support question asking and editing, and generate structured lesson plans with course outlines, introductions, and activity suggestions. The system is grounded in a context database, prompt templates, and iterative design with teachers.

The paper reports two empirical studies in mainland China. Experiment I is a within-subject study with 16 participants, described as novices of Chinese literature teaching / teacher trainees from university programs, who compared LitLinker against a baseline LLM web app while completing lesson-planning tasks using elementary Chinese reading materials. Experiment II consists of expert interviews with elementary Chinese language teachers. Results suggest that LitLinker improves the depth of interdisciplinary integration in lesson plans, reduces workload, and is viewed positively for supporting ideation, although teachers raise concerns about content quality and reliability in purely generated material.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A large language model (LLM)-powered interactive system for generating, analyzing, and organizing interdisciplinary literature-teaching contexts and lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: LitLinker was studied as an LLM-powered support tool for elementary Chinese language teachers to ideate interdisciplinary contexts, analyze reading materials, and generate structured lesson plans; the baseline was a generic LLM web application using the same model.

findings.finding_summary: In a within-subjects study (n=16), LitLinker outperformed a baseline LLM web application on outcome lesson-plan quality. Specifically, the paper reports significantly deeper integration of different subjects in the generated lesson plans, and significantly higher satisfaction and efficiency, with reduced task workload.
findings.measure: Lesson plan quality ratings based on Content Alignment, Alignment with Educational Objectives, and Depth of Integration; task workload (NASA-TLX); usability (SUS); creativity support (CSI)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods within-subject study with qualitative follow-up and without reported effect sizes in the provided text. The design is empirical, but the evidence strength is limited relative to a full RCT or meta-analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant improvements, but no effect sizes are provided in the excerpt, so the practical magnitude cannot be verified. The impact appears promising but remains unclear from the reported data.

paper_profiles.title: Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can estimate the difficulty of assessment items using only item content and metadata, rather than requiring time-consuming field testing with students. The authors frame item difficulty estimation as a practical problem in educational assessment, especially for K-5 mathematics and reading items where calibration is needed for adaptive testing and item development.

The study evaluates two GPT-4o-based approaches on 5,170 vertically scaled K-5 math and reading items from Edmentum’s Exact Path Diagnostic. In the first approach, GPT-4o directly predicts a difficulty rating for each item in a zero-shot prompt and those estimates are then aligned to Rasch difficulty values. In the second approach, GPT-4o is used to extract cognitively and linguistically grounded features, which are then entered into random forest and gradient boosting models alongside item metadata. The authors compare both approaches against grade-level dummy regressors, TF-IDF baselines, and metadata-only models.

The findings suggest that direct LLM judgments can moderately approximate item difficulty, but performance is uneven across grades and is weaker for some early-grade items. The feature-based pipeline performs better overall, especially for reading, and generally outperforms the non-AI baselines. The paper concludes that LLMs may help streamline item development and pre-screening, but structured feature extraction is more effective than asking the model for a single holistic difficulty judgment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT family large language model used for zero-shot analysis, feature extraction, and text generation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-4o to estimate the difficulty of K-5 math and reading assessment items directly from item content and to extract structured item features for downstream predictive models.

findings.finding_summary: Using direct GPT-based estimation, the model predicted Rasch item difficulty for K-5 math and reading items better than a grade-specific dummy regressor overall. For math, holdout performance was RMSE=0.91 and MAE=0.72 versus benchmarks of 1.01 and 0.81, with r=.83 across grades; for reading, RMSE=0.86 and MAE=0.69 versus 1.04 and 0.84, with r=.81.
findings.measure: Holdout-set item difficulty prediction error and Pearson correlation against Rasch-calibrated difficulty

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single observational model-evaluation study using precalibrated assessment items, not an experimental design with student outcomes. Evidence is useful but limited to correlational prediction of item difficulty.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported correlations are strong and error reductions are modest but meaningful versus baselines, especially on reading and upper grades. However, the outcome is item-difficulty estimation rather than direct instructional impact.

paper_profiles.title: Classroom AI: Large Language Models as Grade-Specific Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that large language models (LLMs) often generate educational explanations at reading levels that are too advanced for their intended student audience, even when explicitly prompted to simplify. The authors argue that this is especially limiting for direct student-facing use in classrooms, where students need answers they can actually understand and use.

To solve this, the paper proposes a grade-specific fine-tuning framework that adapts LLM responses to six educational levels: lower elementary, middle elementary, upper elementary, middle school, high school, and college/adult. The method uses synthetic question-answer data generated across eight curriculum fields and classifies outputs with an integrated readability metric built from seven established readability formulas. The paper fine-tunes GPT4o-mini on the resulting grade-labeled corpus to produce separate grade-targeted models.

The study evaluates the approach on multiple datasets, including ScienceQA, ELI5-Category, Natural Questions, and synthetic GPT4o-generated questions, with compatibility and accuracy assessed through automated metrics and human surveys. Results show that the finetuned models substantially improve grade-level alignment compared with prompt-based baselines while maintaining factual accuracy. Human participants and GPT4o both judged the grade-specific outputs as matching intended comprehension levels, suggesting the framework can support more age-appropriate AI-assisted learning.
paper_profiles.study_country: Republic of Korea, United States, England, and online participants via Amazon Mechanical Turk

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used for question generation, answer generation, and evaluation/judging of survey responses in educational text generation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate sample questions, generate synthetic questions for training data, produce answers in the survey evaluation, and act as a judge for survey responses; also referenced as GPT-4o/GPT4o-mini in the experiments.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that finetuned GPT4o-mini models substantially improved grade-level alignment compared with prompt-based methods while maintaining response accuracy. Across four datasets, the average target-grade success rate improved by 35.64 percentage points over the prompt-based baseline, and human surveys with 208 participants found strong alignment between intended and perceived difficulty (Kendall's c4=0.76 across 108 participants for Type 1 questions).
findings.measure: Grade-level alignment / compatibility; human perception of answer difficulty and comprehensibility; accuracy retention
findings.sample_size: n=208 (overall evaluation); n=108 (Survey 1 Type 1); n=120 (Survey 2 Type 2)

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google large language model used here as a source model for generating educational questions and few-shot demonstrations in the data construction pipeline.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate questions across subjects and grade levels as part of the question-generation stage for finetuning data.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA

identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate questions, create grade-specific answers, and serve as the base architecture for finetuning grade-specific models and layer-level analysis.

The evidence is mainly about text-grade alignment and perceived comprehensibility rather than student achievement.

paper_profiles.title: Empowering the Deaf and Hard of Hearing Community: Enhancing Video Captions Using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Software Development and Technologies for Enhancing Accessibility and Fighting Info-exclusion (DSAI ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of inaccurate automatic captions for Deaf and Hard of Hearing (DHH) users, focusing on how large language models (LLMs) can be used to correct and improve captions generated by automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. The authors argue that ASR captions often contain errors such as typos, grammatical mistakes, homophone confusions, missed words, and poor handling of domain-specific terminology, which can reduce accessibility and comprehension in video-based content.

The proposed approach is a caption-correction pipeline in which YouTube’s ASR-generated captions are used as input and an LLM is prompted, in zero-shot mode, to correct the caption while preserving the original word order. The paper compares multiple models in a selection process, including GPT-2, T5, Llama2-13B, and GPT-3.5, and then evaluates the strongest candidates on a curated dataset of 52 short YouTube videos drawn from education, cooking, travel and tourism, entertainment, and news. Ground-truth captions were manually created for comparison.

The study reports that ChatGPT-3.5 performs best overall, substantially reducing word error rate and improving BLEU and ROUGE scores relative to the original ASR captions. Llama2-13B also improves some captions but is less faithful to the exact wording, which can hurt synchronization and word-level accuracy. Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs can meaningfully improve caption quality for accessibility, though they may still struggle with nuance, idioms, and culturally specific language.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI GPT-family large language model chatbot used for text generation and correction tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to correct ASR-generated YouTube video captions under zero-shot prompting, comparing corrected captions against manually created ground truth captions. It was also compared with Llama2-13B and the original YouTube ASR captions.

findings.finding_summary: On the 52-video dataset, ChatGPT-3.5 reduced caption error relative to the original YouTube ASR captions. The paper reports WER of 9.75% for ChatGPT-3.5 versus 23.07% for the original YouTube-ASR-Caption system, along with higher BLEU (0.85 vs 0.67) and slightly higher ROUGE-2 (0.97 vs 0.96).
findings.measure: Caption correction accuracy against manually created ground truth captions, using WER, BLEU, and ROUGE

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: A Meta large language model family used here as a text-correction model for caption post-processing.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to correct ASR-generated YouTube video captions under zero-shot prompting and compared against ChatGPT-3.5 and the original YouTube ASR captions.

findings.finding_summary: Llama2-13B improved some caption outputs and corrected homophones/inaccurate words, but it did not outperform the original YouTube-ASR-Caption system on WER. The paper reports WER of 24.42% for Llama2-13B versus 23.07% for YouTube ASR, while BLEU was slightly higher (0.68 vs 0.67) and ROUGE was lower (ROUGE-1: 0.90 vs 0.98; ROUGE-2: 0.82 vs 0.96; ROUGE-L: 0.88 vs 0.98).
findings.measure: Caption correction accuracy against manually created ground truth captions, using WER, BLEU, and ROUGE

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical system comparison, but it is a small caption-correction study rather than a K-12 educational intervention study. It is also outside the requested student-facing reading/literacy use case and does not evaluate learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported caption-quality improvement for ChatGPT is substantial in WER terms, but the outcome is accessibility/caption accuracy rather than student learning. Because the paper does not study K-12 literacy instruction or direct educational impact, the educational impact tier is unclear overall.

paper_profiles.title: Data Augmentation using Large Language Models: Data Perspectives, Learning Paradigms and Challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of data augmentation methods using large language models (LLMs). It focuses on how LLMs are changing data augmentation from both a data-centric perspective and a learning-paradigm perspective, rather than evaluating a specific educational intervention or user study. The paper organizes the literature into categories such as data creation, data labeling, data reformation, and co-annotation, and then further distinguishes generative learning and discriminative learning settings.

The central question is how LLMs can be used to create, label, transform, or score data in ways that improve downstream machine learning performance. The survey discusses examples across NLP and some multimodal tasks, including instruction tuning, in-context learning, alignment learning, classification, regression, and counterfactual generation. It also reviews major concerns such as contamination, controllability, cultural bias, multimodal complexity, and privacy risks.

The paper does not study a student population, classroom use, or any K-12 literacy intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior computational research and proposes a taxonomy and future directions for LLM-based data augmentation. Its main conclusion is that LLMs substantially expand the possibilities for synthetic data generation and annotation, but careful handling is needed to address quality, contamination, bias, and privacy issues.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic large language model-based generative AI used for data augmentation, annotation, rephrasing, instruction generation, and evaluation tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: This is a survey of large language model (LLM)-based data augmentation methods. It reviews how generic LLMs are used to create synthetic data, label datasets, reformulate text, and provide annotations or scores across NLP and other domains.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a survey/review paper with no original empirical evaluation of a student-facing AI tool. It summarizes prior work on LLM-based data augmentation rather than reporting a controlled study or meta-analytic estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not test an intervention in K-12 reading or literacy instruction and reports no outcome effects. Its relevance is conceptual only for the stated education research topic.

paper_profiles.title: ERRORRADAR: Benchmarking Complex Mathematical Reasoning of Multimodal Large Language Models via Error Detection
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces ERRORRADAR, a new benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on mathematical error detection rather than standard problem solving. The authors argue that existing math benchmarks mostly assess whether models can solve problems correctly, but educational use cases require a more student-centered capability: identifying the first incorrect step in a solution and classifying the type of error made.

The benchmark consists of 2,500 multimodal K-12 mathematics problems collected from a global educational organization’s question bank and enriched with real student incorrect answers and step-by-step annotations. The data were manually annotated by professional educational experts to label the first erroneous step and one of five error categories: visual perception, calculation, reasoning, knowledge, and misinterpretation. The paper evaluates a range of open-source and closed-source MLLMs, along with human educators as a comparison standard, using the benchmark’s error-step identification and error-categorization tasks.

The population represented in the benchmark is K-12 students, though the paper does not specify grade-level breakdowns within K-12. The user roles present are students, whose incorrect work supplies the core data, and educators, who annotate and evaluate the responses. The paper is not an intervention study in a classroom setting; it is a benchmark and model-evaluation paper.

The main conclusion is that current MLLMs still struggle substantially with complex mathematical error detection. Closed-source models, especially GPT-4o, outperform open-source systems, but even the best models remain below human educator performance. The authors also find that identifying the erroneous step is easier than categorizing the error, calculation errors are easiest while knowledge errors are hardest, and model performance improves with scale mainly for step identification rather than error categorization.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family multimodal large language model/chatbot used for general-purpose reasoning, text generation, and visual-language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of several closed-source multimodal large language models on the ERRORRADAR benchmark for mathematical error detection in K-12 multimodal problems.

findings.finding_summary: GPT-4o was the strongest-performing model overall on ERRORRADAR, achieving 55.1% accuracy on error-step identification (STEP) and 53.1% on error categorization (CATE). It also obtained the highest category scores among MLLMs for visual perception (46.3%), reasoning (64.9%), and misinterpretation (46.3%).
findings.measure: Accuracy on error-step identification, error categorization, and per-error-category classification

findings.measure: Accuracy on error-step identification, error categorization, and per-error-category classification

The paper reports strong category-specific differences across these LLaMA-based multimodal models, with especially low performance on KNOW for CogVLM2-LLaMA3 (0.7%).
