paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark paper, not a controlled intervention study in K-12 instruction. It reports model accuracies on a custom dataset, but does not evaluate educational outcomes from classroom use or compare to a non-AI instructional condition.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The work has clear technical relevance for educational AI evaluation and uses real K-12 student data, but it measures benchmark performance rather than instructional impact. The reported gains are model-accuracy differences without an educational treatment effect size.

paper_profiles.title: Meta-Cognitive Analysis: Evaluating Declarative and Procedural Knowledge in Datasets and Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how two kinds of knowledge from metacognitive theory—declarative knowledge (“knowing that”) and procedural knowledge (“knowing how”)—affect the performance of large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that prior work lacked a systematic way to compare these knowledge types in datasets and models because they are difficult to define, separate, and measure directly.

To study the question, the paper introduces an in-context knowledge injection method. Using GPT-4 as a decomposer, the authors split question-answer reasoning into declarative hints, procedural hints, or a combination of both, and then evaluate 32 open LLMs on 13 datasets spanning arithmetic, commonsense reasoning, and broader knowledge tasks. The setup is not a human-subject or educational intervention; it is a model-analysis experiment using benchmark datasets and LLMs.

The main conclusion is that declarative knowledge usually provides larger gains than procedural knowledge across most tasks, while procedural knowledge helps more in simpler reasoning tasks such as elementary arithmetic and basic commonsense. The paper also finds that larger models and models with more pre-training steps are better at using both kinds of hints, especially declarative hints. The authors present these results as guidance for evaluating and improving LLM reasoning and knowledge use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model / chatbot used for generation and in-context reasoning.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-4 to decompose original reasoning into declarative and procedural knowledge, and as GPT-3.5 API among the evaluated LLMs; the paper also cites GPT-4 in the decomposition workflow.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta LLaMA-family open-weight large language model.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as one of the 32 open LLMs on in-context knowledge injection tasks across multiple datasets.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic large language model / generative AI system with no single named product focus.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies in-context knowledge injection into multiple LLMs rather than a single instructional product; the broader method and conclusions are about LLMs generally.

findings.finding_summary: Across 13 benchmark datasets and 32 open LLMs, the paper reports that declarative hints usually improve performance more than procedural hints, with procedural hints outperforming declarative hints only on simpler reasoning tasks. The authors summarize this as a general pattern in how LLMs utilize injected knowledge, but they do not report a single aggregate effect size or confidence interval.
findings.measure: Relative performance improvement from declarative hints, procedural hints, and combined hints versus no hint

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a methodological paper about analyzing LLM knowledge types, not an education study or an evaluation of a K-12 instructional AI tool. It does not present a pedagogical intervention, randomization, or student outcome evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 reading/literacy outcome is measured, and no effect size for instructional impact is reported. The paper’s results are about benchmark task performance of LLMs, not educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: Build-a-Bot: Teaching Conversational AI Using a Transformer-Based Intent Recognition and Question Answering Architecture
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for more adaptable and flexible AI education tools that let students learn AI by building systems, rather than only learning terminology, use cases, or ethics. The authors argue that existing AI education resources often treat AI systems as black boxes or focus on rule-based chatbot activities, leaving a gap for tools that teach the supervised learning process in an intuitive way.

To address this, the paper proposes Build-a-Bot, an open-source tool that lets students and teachers create customizable conversational AI systems from their own curricular materials. The pipeline includes student data collection and labeling, data augmentation via backtranslation, keyword-based policy filtering, BERT-based intent recognition, and question answering with DistilBERT or T5. The design is presented as a middle-school-appropriate, no-code interface intended for classroom use, with instructors defining intents and contexts and students interacting with each step of the pipeline.

The paper is framed around K-12 AI literacy, especially elementary and middle school contexts, and it draws on constructivist and active learning principles. It includes a sample fifth-grade science testing suite and a machine learning concept suite, but it does not report an actual classroom trial or comparative outcome study. The main conclusion is that Build-a-Bot may help educators of varying technical backgrounds support AI literacy by enabling students to tinker with and understand conversational AI systems, though the authors note that classroom piloting and efficacy testing remain future work.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general conversational AI/chatbot pipeline that uses transformer-based intent recognition and question answering to generate responses to user questions.
identified_tools.use_case: Proposed and prototyped as Build-a-Bot, an open-source classroom tool for students to create custom chatbots from their own course materials and learn AI concepts through the model-building process.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a proposal/prototype paper describing Build-a-Bot and its architecture, not an empirical evaluation of student outcomes. The paper explicitly notes that further work is needed to provide the tool to schools and seek student and teacher evaluations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No outcome data are reported, so there is no measurable demonstrated impact on student learning or instructional efficiency. The paper does suggest potential classroom utility, but that remains untested in the text provided.

paper_profiles.title: CelloAI: Leveraging Large Language Models for HPC Software Development in High Energy Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of using large language models (LLMs) to assist with software development in high-performance computing (HPC) environments for high energy physics (HEP). The authors argue that generic coding assistants are inadequate for scientific codebases because of privacy constraints, large repositories, sparse documentation, reproducibility requirements, and the need to understand complex dependencies and performance-portability issues.

To address this, they introduce CelloAI, a locally hosted coding assistant that combines retrieval-augmented generation with separate code/text vector collections, syntax-aware Tree-sitter chunking, pattern matching, and callgraph-based prompt enhancement. The system is designed for documentation generation, code comprehension, code generation, and code translation across HEP applications.

The evaluation uses real HEP software from ATLAS, CMS, and DUNE, including FastCaloSim, P2R, Patatrack, and WireCell. The results show that retrieval and callgraph augmentation improve kernel recall, documentation quality, and porting coverage for several open-weight models, although harder porting tasks still fail mainly because of memory-mapping and directive-selection errors. The paper concludes that transparent, on-premise, retrieval-centered LLM workflows can improve productivity for scientific programming, but robust correctness for complex GPU porting remains an open challenge.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google Gemini is a family of large language models and AI assistants for general-purpose text generation, code assistance, and multimodal reasoning.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of the commercial AI assistants compared against CelloAI for identifying GPU kernels in scientific code repositories; also referenced as Gemini-cli / Gemini-2.5-Pro in the comparison.

findings.finding_summary: In the kernel-identification prompt, Gemini-cli sometimes exceeded the token limit by attempting to read and concatenate the entire repository. The paper reports that Gemini-cli either looped through files or concatenated the whole codebase before collecting patterns, causing a token-count error on large repositories such as Patatrack.

Overall, the authors conclude that none of the commercial tools sustained high recall once the search space exceeded a few hundred symbols.
findings.measure: Kernel recall / completeness of retrieved GPU kernels

This is supported by the comparative kernel-recall and porting tasks where baseline tools often missed many kernels or produced compilationally incorrect code.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not an education-study RCT or meta-analysis; it is an applied systems paper in scientific computing. Evidence is based on benchmark-style comparisons and qualitative interpretation rather than controlled K-12 instructional research.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported outcomes concern HPC code retrieval and porting, not student learning, literacy instruction, or educational impact. No K-12 academic effect size is reported.

paper_profiles.title: SAISA: Towards Multimodal Large Language Models with Both Training and Inference Efficiency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of improving the training and inference efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The authors analyze two mainstream MLLM alignment strategies: embedding-space alignment, which is relatively cheap to train but costly at inference because it concatenates many visual tokens, and cross-attention-space alignment, which is more efficient at inference but requires many new parameters and substantial training data. The central question is how to build MLLMs that are efficient in both stages without sacrificing performance.

To solve this, the paper proposes NAAViT (No Attention Among Visual Tokens), a self-attention variant that removes attention among visual tokens, and SAISA (Self-Attention Input Space Alignment), an architecture that aligns visual features directly with the input spaces of self-attention blocks. SAISA also avoids applying feed-forward networks to visual tokens, further reducing computation. The paper validates the design through pilot experiments, ablation studies, and benchmark comparisons against LLaVA-1.5 and other MLLMs, using Vicuna-7B and CLIP-ViT-L/14-336 as the main configuration.

The work is not an education study: it does not involve students, teachers, schools, or any K-12 population. Instead, it evaluates general-purpose multimodal benchmarks such as MMMU, MMBench, POPE, GQA, ScienceQA IMG, OK-VQA, and vision-centric benchmarks. The main conclusion is that attention among visual tokens is highly redundant in these MLLMs, and SAISA can substantially reduce FLOPs and latency while matching or exceeding baseline performance under the tested settings.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: A family of large language models used as the backbone for multimodal large language models (MLLMs).
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of the LLM backbones in the SAISA experiments and ablations (e.g., Llama 2, Llama 3 variants normalized to LLaMA).

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that SAISA outperformed LLaVA-1.5 when using LLaMA-family backbones in ablation experiments. With Llama3-8B and CLIP, SAISA improved benchmark scores across several multimodal benchmarks while reducing inference TFLOPs from 9.17 to 2.10.
findings.measure: Benchmark performance on MMMU, MMBench, POPE, GQA, ScienceQA IMG, and OK-VQA; inference TFLOPs

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that SAISA with LLaMA-family backbones achieved better performance and much lower computational cost than the LLaVA-1.5 baseline. The results are reported as benchmark score gains and FLOPs reductions rather than statistical effect sizes.
findings.measure: Inference latency and benchmark performance in multimodal evaluation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a computer vision / multimodal model architecture paper, not an education study, and it does not use a rigorous causal or educational research design. The paper is empirical, but the evidence is outside the K-12 literacy domain and lacks the study design criteria relevant for high-tier educational evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 reading or literacy outcomes are studied, and no educational intervention effects are reported. The reported performance gains are on general multimodal benchmarks and compute efficiency, so there is no direct instructional impact for the target topic.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Financial Reasoning: A CFA-Based Benchmark Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates how well recent large language models can answer domain-specific multiple-choice questions drawn from official CFA mock exams. The central problem is whether state-of-the-art LLMs can perform the kind of long-context, quantitative, and conceptually integrated reasoning required for professional financial certification, and whether retrieval augmentation can improve performance over zero-shot prompting.

The study compares GPT-4o, GPT-o1, and o3-mini on 1,560 CFA mock questions spanning Levels I–III, using two approaches: zero-shot answering and a domain-reasoning Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline. The RAG system retrieves relevant passages from the official CFA curriculum using generated summaries and keywords, then supplies the retrieved context to the model for answering. The paper also analyzes error types, readability, and question types (conceptual vs. calculation).

The population is not a human learner sample but the set of CFA exam questions, which represent adult professional financial certification content. The context is professional finance rather than schooling, and the task is benchmarking model performance on authentic exam materials. The main conclusion is that GPT-o1 performs best overall, RAG generally improves accuracy especially on more complex levels and knowledge-intensive topics, and most failures are due to missing domain knowledge rather than readability or simple arithmetic alone.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language models used for question answering, reasoning, and retrieval-augmented generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Benchmarked as zero-shot and RAG-enhanced models on CFA multiple-choice exam questions; the paper evaluates GPT-4o, GPT-o1, and o3-mini under the normalized ChatGPT family.

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,560 CFA mock questions, ChatGPT-family models showed strong financial reasoning performance, with GPT-o1 achieving the highest zero-shot accuracies at 94.78% (Level I), 89.32% (Level II), and 79.09% (Level III). RAG further improved performance at higher levels, with GPT-o1 rising to 91.36% on Level II and 87.73% on Level III.
findings.measure: Accuracy on CFA mock exam multiple-choice questions

findings.finding_summary: RAG improved performance most at higher difficulty levels, especially for GPT-o1 (+2.05 percentage points at Level II and +8.64 at Level III) and o3-mini (+4.55 at Level II and +5.45 at Level III). The paper reports minimal RAG gains at Level I, suggesting retrieval was more useful for complex, context-heavy questions.
findings.measure: Accuracy improvement from zero-shot to RAG across CFA levels

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark study of LLM performance on CFA exam questions, not a K-12 instructional intervention, and it does not evaluate a student-facing educational tool. The paper is empirical, but its relevance to the requested K-12 literacy topic is indirect.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 reading/literacy outcome is measured, and no direct student impact is reported. The findings concern finance-domain exam accuracy rather than educational effectiveness in elementary literacy instruction.

paper_profiles.title: Automated Assessment of Encouragement and Warmth in Classrooms Leveraging Multimodal Emotional Features and ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automating classroom observation scores for the Encouragement and Warmth (EW) component of the Global Teaching Insights (GTI) protocol. The authors argue that manual coding of classroom videos is time-consuming, expensive, and often inconsistent across raters, and they ask whether multimodal machine learning and large language models can approximate human judgments of EW from lesson recordings and transcripts.

The study compares three approaches: a supervised multimodal model using explicit interpretable features from video (facial emotion recognition for smiling), audio (speech emotion recognition for laughter), and transcripts (sentiment analysis for positive comments); zero-shot ChatGPT scoring of whole transcript segments; and an ensemble that combines both sources of prediction. The data come from authentic German math lessons in the GTI dataset, segmented into 16-minute units and double-rated by human coders using a 1-4 scale. Models were evaluated with lesson-independent 5-fold cross-validation and compared against average human ratings.

The context is K-12 classroom instruction in Germany, specifically middle and upper primary/secondary mathematics lessons are not individually specified, so the paper only clearly supports the broader K-12 category. The paper reports that the best supervised model achieved a Pearson correlation of .441 with human ratings, GPT-4 reached .341 in zero-shot mode, and the weighted ensemble matched human inter-rater reliability at .513. The authors conclude that explicit multimodal features are useful, text sentiment is the strongest predictor, and GPT-4 can provide concrete reasoning useful for teacher feedback. The work is framed as a post hoc classroom-observation tool rather than a real-time classroom intervention.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational large language model system used for zero-shot text understanding, generation, and annotation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to score classroom Encouragement and Warmth from German lesson transcripts in a zero-shot prompt, with reasoning requested; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were compared, and GPT-4 was also combined in an ensemble with the supervised model.

findings.finding_summary: On 367 16-minute classroom segments from 92 authentic lesson recordings, ChatGPT zero-shot transcript scoring correlated weakly to moderately with human ratings depending on the model version. GPT-3.5 showed no significant correlation (r=.027), while GPT-4 reached r=.341; the weighted ensemble of GPT-4 with the best supervised model reached r=.513, matching human inter-rater reliability.
findings.measure: Pearson correlation between model estimates and mean human ratings of Encouragement and Warmth
findings.effect_size: r=.027 (GPT-3.5); r=.341 (GPT-4); r=.513 (weighted ensemble with MLP regressor)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study with a correlational evaluation design rather than an RCT or QED. It provides direct comparative evidence against human ratings, but the outcome is model agreement with human coding rather than learner achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: GPT-4’s direct transcript scoring showed a modest-to-medium association with human ratings (r=.341), and the ensemble reached human-level agreement (r=.513). That indicates meaningful potential for classroom feedback workflows, though the study does not measure student learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities, risks, and implementation challenges of large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 and ChatGPT in education. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, it synthesizes early research and offers a conceptual discussion of how LLMs may support learning, teaching, assessment, content creation, and educational technology design.

The paper discusses potential learner-facing uses across educational levels, including elementary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning. For elementary students, it highlights possible support for reading and writing development, such as grammar correction, question generation, and reading comprehension support through summaries and explanations of complex texts. It also describes teacher-facing uses such as personalized feedback, lesson planning, language support, assessment assistance, and generation of exercises and learning materials.

The paper's main contribution is a balanced analysis of benefits and risks. It argues that LLMs can enhance engagement, personalization, and efficiency, but only if deployed with strong human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, privacy protections, bias mitigation, and responsible governance. The authors conclude that LLMs are promising educational tools, but their adoption should be cautious, ethical, and accompanied by further research on best practices.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model/chatbot system used for generating, answering, and assisting with text-based tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a position paper discussing ChatGPT/GPT-3-family large language models in education, including potential uses for reading comprehension, question generation, summaries, and personalized feedback; it does not report an empirical evaluation.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and literature discussion, not an empirical study with a clear comparison group or measured outcomes. It offers conceptual claims and examples rather than evaluative evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ChatGPT may support reading and literacy-related tasks, but it does not present outcome data or effect sizes. Impact is therefore plausible but unmeasured in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) has been studied and applied in higher education, where the research is coming from, and whether authors critically discuss ethical challenges and risks. Rather than testing a single intervention, it systematically reviews peer-reviewed journal articles published from 2007 to November 2018 and synthesizes the scope of AI uses in higher education.

The review screened 2,656 records and included 146 articles. The paper organizes AI applications into four main areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. The studies span both student-facing and institution-facing uses, such as dropout prediction, automated grading, feedback systems, adaptive learning environments, and tutoring systems. Most studies were quantitative and drawn heavily from computer science and STEM fields; only a small minority came from education departments.

The population focus was predominantly undergraduate students, with a smaller number of postgraduate studies. The context was higher education institutions across many countries, with the largest share of studies coming from the United States, China, Taiwan, and Turkey. The review concludes that AI research in higher education is expanding, but the literature shows limited explicit definitions of AI, very little critical reflection on privacy, ethics, and cost, and a weak connection to pedagogical theory. It calls for more educator involvement and more attention to ethical and educational perspectives.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: Intelligent tutoring systems are AI-based educational systems that simulate aspects of one-to-one tutoring by adapting instruction, providing hints or feedback, diagnosing learner needs, and sometimes supporting collaboration or teacher workflows.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of higher-education AI research; ITS is one of the four main application categories synthesized from the included studies, with subtypes such as teaching content, automated feedback, curating materials, and facilitating collaboration.

findings.finding_summary: Across the 29 ITS studies included in the review, most implementations reported positive or satisfactory preliminary results, though the authors note that these were typically short-term studies and did not account for novelty effects. The review also cites an earlier meta-analysis of 39 ITS studies by Steenbergen-Hu and Cooper (2014), which found a moderate effect on learning, that ITS were less effective than human tutoring, but outperformed traditional classroom instruction, reading printed or digital text, or homework assignments.
findings.measure: Review synthesis of ITS study outcomes; prior meta-analysis of learning outcomes
findings.effect_size: moderate effect (meta-analysis cited in review); exact pooled effect size not reported in this paper
findings.sample_size: n=29 ITS studies in this review; meta-analysis of n=39 studies cited

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, but it synthesizes heterogeneous ITS studies rather than evaluating a single intervention with experimental controls. The paper also reports limited critical appraisal and mostly short-term evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports generally positive preliminary effects for ITS and cites a moderate meta-analytic impact, but exact effect sizes are not provided in this paper and the evidence is indirect for any single tool. The overall impact therefore appears modest to unclear at the review level.

paper_profiles.title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines university students’ perceptions of generative AI (GenAI), especially tools such as ChatGPT, in higher education. The authors aim to understand how familiar students are with GenAI, what benefits and risks they associate with it, and how they think it should be integrated into teaching and learning. The study is motivated by the rapid rise of GenAI and the lack of direct evidence on student perceptions of these tools specifically.

The study used an online survey with both closed-ended and open-ended questions. A total of 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students from six universities in Hong Kong participated. The survey measured knowledge of GenAI, willingness to use it, concerns about its use, and qualitative explanations of perceived benefits and challenges. The context was higher education rather than K-12, and the participants came from a range of disciplines, including STEM and non-STEM fields.

Findings showed generally positive attitudes toward GenAI, with students seeing value in personalized learning support, writing and brainstorming help, research assistance, multimedia creation, and administrative efficiency. At the same time, students expressed concerns about accuracy, transparency, privacy, plagiarism, over-reliance, effects on critical thinking and creativity, career prospects, human values, and unclear policy guidance. The authors conclude that GenAI should be integrated cautiously and responsibly, with attention to AI literacy, ethical use, institutional policy, and support for higher-order skills.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI conversational large language model chatbot that generates human-like text responses and can assist with writing, brainstorming, question answering, summarization, and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the primary example of generative AI technology in a survey of university students’ familiarity, willingness to use, perceived benefits, and concerns about GenAI in higher education.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey with open-ended responses, so it provides perception data but not causal evidence of learning effects. The study is methodologically clear, but it is not an intervention or comparative effectiveness design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceptions and perceived utility rather than measured learning outcomes. No effect sizes are reported, and the evidence supports possible usefulness but not demonstrated impact on achievement.

paper_profiles.title: A vaccine chatbot intervention for parents to improve HPV vaccination uptake among middle school girls: a cluster randomized trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether a conversational AI chatbot can improve HPV vaccination uptake among parents of adolescent girls. The study asks whether providing parents with an AI-powered, vaccine-focused consultation tool can increase vaccine initiation and improve vaccine-related knowledge, confidence, and willingness compared with usual care.

The intervention was a bespoke chatbot built with GPT-4 plus retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering, drawing on verified public-health information from Chinese health authorities. It offered two interaction styles, an expert persona and a nurse persona, and was delivered through WeChat and web browsers. Parents in the intervention arm were reminded to use the chatbot over a two-week period, while control participants received usual local HPV vaccination promotion without the chatbot.

The trial took place in ten middle schools across Shanghai and Anhui Province, China, and enrolled parents of female middle school students in grades 6–9, typically aged 12–15 years. Participants were clustered by class and randomly assigned to chatbot or usual-care conditions. The main outcome was whether daughters received or scheduled HPV vaccination within two weeks; secondary outcomes included consultation with health professionals and changes in HPV literacy, knowledge, rumor discernment, willingness, and vaccine confidence.

The study found that the chatbot group had substantially higher HPV vaccination initiation than usual care, along with more consultations with health professionals and improved HPV-related literacy, knowledge, and rumor screening. The intervention did not significantly change willingness or vaccine confidence over the short study window. The authors conclude that AI chatbots may be a promising scalable tool for improving vaccine communication and uptake, especially where cost and misinformation are barriers.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI GPT-family large language model chatbot used for conversational question answering and information retrieval via a tailored, retrieval-augmented setup.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied a bespoke AI-powered vaccine chatbot for parents of middle school girls in China; it used GPT-4 with retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering, delivered via WeChat and web browser, with expert and nurse personas.

findings.finding_summary: In a school-based cluster randomized trial (n=2,671 parents; 180 classes), the chatbot increased HPV vaccine receipt or scheduled appointment for daughters over 2 weeks: 7.1% (92/1,294) in the chatbot group versus 1.8% (25/1,377) in usual care. The adjusted relative risk was 3.85 (95% CI 2.48–5.97; P<0.001).
findings.measure: Receipt of or scheduled appointment for HPV vaccine among female middle school students over a two-week intervention period

findings.finding_summary: The chatbot also increased HPV vaccination-specific consultations with health professionals: 49.1% (635/1,294) in the chatbot group versus 17.6% (242/1,377) in usual care. The adjusted relative risk was 2.73 (95% CI 2.41–3.09; P<0.001).
findings.measure: HPV vaccination-specific consultation with health professionals

findings.finding_summary: Parental willingness to vaccinate their daughter declined slightly in both groups and the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Post–pre change was -3.4 percentage points in the chatbot group and -4.1 percentage points in usual care; adjusted RR was 1.02 (95% CI 0.98–1.07; P=0.325).
findings.measure: Parental willingness to vaccinate their daughter against HPV

findings.finding_summary: High vaccine confidence increased slightly in both groups, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant. Post–pre change was 5.1 percentage points in the chatbot group and 2.5 percentage points in usual care; adjusted RR was 1.02 (95% CI 0.97–1.08; P=0.375).
findings.measure: High HPV vaccine confidence

findings.finding_summary: HPV-related literacy improved in the chatbot group relative to usual care. Mean literacy scores increased from 6.3 to 7.1 in the chatbot group versus 6.1 to 6.2 in usual care, with an adjusted between-group coefficient of 0.70 (95% CI 0.52–0.88; P<0.001).
findings.measure: HPV-related literacy score

findings.finding_summary: HPV-related knowledge improved significantly. Scores rose from 3.9 to 4.3 out of 6 in the chatbot group compared with 3.7 to 3.8 in usual care; the reported adjusted coefficient was 0.38 (95% CI 0.26–0.50; P<0.001).
findings.measure: HPV-related knowledge score

findings.finding_summary: Rumor screening/identification improved significantly. Scores increased from 2.5 to 2.7 out of 4 in the chatbot group versus 2.4 to 2.4 in usual care; the reported adjusted coefficient was 0.32 (95% CI 0.21–0.43; P<0.001).
findings.measure: HPV-related rumor screening / rumor identification score

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cluster randomized trial with a non-AI comparator, clear allocation by class, intention-to-treat analysis, and reported adjusted effects with confidence intervals. The design and reporting support high causal credibility, though it is a single study and the intervention is short-term.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The primary behavioral outcome shows a large effect (adjusted RR=3.85) and the consultation outcome is also sizable (adjusted RR=2.73). The literacy outcomes are also statistically significant with moderate coefficients, indicating meaningful practical impact.

paper_profiles.title: The application of chatbot as an L2 writing practice tool
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a chatbot-based writing practice tool can improve second-language (L2) writing performance for young learners and how students perceive using such a tool. The study responds to a gap in prior chatbot research by testing direct comparative evidence against a non-AI instructional comparator in an elementary school context, rather than only describing feasibility or user attitudes.

The intervention was a chatbot built with Google Dialogflow and manually encoded with expressions from a Grade 5 Korean English textbook. It was designed as a conversational partner for controlled, scenario-based writing practice tied to classroom lessons. The comparison condition received traditional teacher-led writing instruction and textbook-based sentence completion/writing activities. Both groups were taught by the same teacher and used the same textbook over a 15-week period, but only the experimental group used the chatbot for individual writing practice at the end of lessons.

Participants were 75 fifth-grade elementary school students in South Korea, randomly assigned to control and experimental groups. Outcomes included pretest and posttest writing scores, rated holistically by trained raters, plus a survey of experimental-group students’ perceptions of the chatbot. The authors found no significant baseline difference between groups, but the chatbot group performed significantly better on the posttest, even after controlling for pretest scores with ANCOVA. Survey results suggested that students generally found the chatbot useful for reviewing what they learned and felt relatively comfortable using it, although perceptions of its human-likeness and effectiveness were moderate rather than strong.

The study concludes that chatbot-mediated writing practice can support young L2 learners’ writing performance and reduce anxiety by providing a less face-threatening environment than teacher-led practice. The paper also notes that the controlled, textbook-based design may be especially suitable for elementary EFL contexts where learners have limited exposure to English and limited opportunities for individualized practice.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A chatbot-based AI writing practice tool built with Google Dialogflow and scenario-based dialogue, used as an L2 language-learning conversational partner.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by Korean fifth-grade elementary students for individual English writing practice over 15 weeks, compared against traditional teacher-led writing instruction.

findings.finding_summary: In the posttest, the experimental group using the chatbot scored significantly higher than the control group receiving traditional writing instruction. The paper reports a posttest mean of 2.11 for the experimental group versus 1.74 for the control group (n=37 vs. n=38), with Mann-Whitney U = 876.50, p < .05; ANCOVA also found a significant treatment effect controlling for pretest scores (F=7.014, p=0.010).
findings.measure: Holistic English writing test scores (pretest and posttest); ANCOVA-adjusted posttest scores

findings.finding_summary: The experimental group reported generally favorable perceptions of the chatbot as a writing practice tool. Mean ratings indicated it was helpful for reviewing what was learned at school (M=3.54, n=37) and that students generally did not feel nervous when using it (M=2.14 for the nervousness item, where lower scores indicate disagreement).
findings.measure: Perception survey on chatbot usefulness, comfort, anxiety, and perceived improvement

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized two-group intervention with pretest-posttest comparison and ANCOVA, providing reasonably strong causal evidence for a specific educational chatbot. Some concerns remain because the posttest prompt differed from the pretest and the outcome was a short holistic writing score rather than a standardized measure.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported treatment effect on posttest writing performance is statistically significant, and the adjusted mean difference is moderate in practical terms (2.13 vs. 1.72 on a 0-3 scale). However, the paper does not report a standardized effect size, so the magnitude is best characterized as modest to moderate.

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that "AI literacy" has become a widely used but inconsistently defined term, especially after the public emergence of generative AI. The authors ask how researchers conceptualize AI literacy in K-12 and higher education and what new trends have emerged in the wake of generative AI. To answer this, they conduct an integrative review of empirical and theoretical studies on AI literacy published from 2020 through July 2024, ultimately synthesizing 124 studies.

The paper is not an intervention study itself; instead, it reviews and categorizes AI literacy work using a conceptual framework based on two dimensions: how AI is conceptualized (technical details, tools, sociocultural impact) and how literacy is conceptualized (functional, critical, indirectly beneficial). The review includes K-12 and post-secondary studies across a range of topics, from machine learning curricula and AI ethics activities to newly emerging generative-AI-focused work such as teaching ChatGPT use and prompt engineering. Elementary, middle school, high school, and undergraduate contexts are all represented in the reviewed corpus.

The main conclusion is that AI literacy discourse is fragmented but increasingly shaped by generative AI. Before generative AI, most K-12 work emphasized technical AI knowledge, often paired with critical or ethical understanding. After generative AI, there is a sharp rise in tool-focused literacy, especially in higher education, including studies on effective use of ChatGPT and prompt engineering. The review argues that AI literacy should be described with more precise terms than a single umbrella label, because different studies target very different goals, technologies, and pedagogical approaches.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general category of generative AI/large language model chatbots and tools used for natural-language interaction, prompting, and content generation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is an integrative review of AI literacy studies and discusses generative AI tools conceptually; it does not evaluate a single AI product as an intervention in the paper itself.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an integrative review and conceptual framework paper rather than a primary evaluation of an AI intervention. It synthesizes prior literature instead of reporting a single study design with direct causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has high conceptual relevance for AI literacy research, but it does not measure student outcomes for a specific tool. Its impact is therefore indirect rather than an effect on learner performance or behavior.

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceived a generative AI-powered tool designed to support creative mathematical writing. The authors focus on a classroom implementation of a GenAI system that helped students create and revise math stories, with the broader goal of understanding what benefits and challenges arise when AI is used as a writing and problem-solving scaffold in K-12 mathematics instruction.

The intervention used a three-step instructional sequence: Ask, Represent, and Transform. In the Ask phase, students analyzed provided math stories; in the Represent phase, they modeled their understanding visually; and in the Transform phase, they entered story goals, characters, settings, and events, after which GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 generated story drafts and images. Students then evaluated the AI-generated stories using a checklist. The study was conducted in six fifth-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools, involving 79 students and six teachers. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations.

Using thematic analysis, the authors found that participants perceived several benefits of GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing: fostering creativity, improving mathematical understanding, promoting AI literacy, and supporting affective outcomes such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. They also identified challenges, including students' limited critical evaluation of AI output, difficulty generating coherent stories, the AI system being perceived as too perfect, insufficient pedagogical feedback, reduced opportunities for autonomous work, limited social interaction, and a lack of multiple communication modes. The paper concludes that GenAI can support creative and mathematical learning, but its educational value depends on deliberate instructional and interface design that preserves room for student thinking, feedback, collaboration, and accessibility.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model family used for generating and revising text content, here in a multimodal form paired with image generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within the [ANONYMOUS] classroom platform to generate draft math stories from student inputs; the paper explicitly states it leveraged OpenAI's GPT-4 for story generation.

identified_tools.name: DALL·E 3
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's text-to-image generation model for creating images from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within the classroom platform to generate corresponding images for the student-authored math stories.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative classroom study with interviews, surveys, and observations, not an experimental comparison or causal design. It provides useful descriptive evidence about perceptions, but not effectiveness evidence with quantified outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived benefits and challenges rather than measured academic impact, and no effect sizes are provided. The evidence suggests potential instructional value, but the magnitude of impact is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Learning Experiences for K-12: Emerging Works, Future Opportunities and a Design Framework
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2020 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '20)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing need for K-12-specific guidance on designing AI learning experiences. The authors note that although AI literacy is increasingly important, most prior AI literacy frameworks and learning tools were developed for general or older audiences and do not sufficiently account for the pedagogical, developmental, and practical constraints of school settings.

The paper does not test a new intervention. Instead, it conducts an exploratory review of 49 K-12 AI education works and tools, using Long and Magerko’s AI literacy framework as an analytic lens and extending it for K-12 contexts. The review covers AI curricula, classroom activities, tools, and learning experiences spanning elementary through high school, with some materials also involving teachers and parents. The authors code each work against AI literacy competencies and design considerations, then synthesize the findings into an educator-friendly reference chart and an extended design framework.

The main conclusions are that existing K-12 AI learning experiences often emphasize explainability, transparency, programming opportunities, and data contextualization, but under-address areas such as general-vs-narrow AI, interdisciplinarity, ethical reflection across all AI topics, gradual unveiling of complexity, identity and values, and parent support. The paper argues for more comprehensive AI literacy goals, built-in scaffolding, stronger engagement strategies, greater teacher and parent involvement, and deeper integration of AI into other school subjects.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / conversational AI systems used by students, with no specific commercial product named.
identified_tools.use_case: Not directly evaluated in this paper. The paper is a conceptual/design-focused review of K-12 AI learning experiences and mentions generative AI only as one type of AI system in the literature.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory review and design-framework paper, not an empirical evaluation of a student-facing AI tool. It synthesizes prior K-12 AI education literature rather than reporting primary outcome data from a controlled study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct tool impact is measured in this paper, so there is no empirical effect to score. The paper offers conceptual guidance and future opportunities, but not outcome evidence.

paper_profiles.title: Can Large Language Models Make the Grade? An Empirical Study Evaluating LLMs Ability to Mark Short Answer Questions in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can accurately score open-ended short answer responses in K-12 education. The motivating problem is that formative assessment is valuable for learning but expensive and time-consuming to grade at scale, especially when responses require human judgment rather than simple right/wrong matching. The authors ask whether modern LLMs, especially GPT-4, can approximate expert human raters on authentic student responses.

To study this, the authors built a dataset of 1,710 student short-answer responses from the UK-based Carousel platform. The responses came from open-response questions in Science and History across three Key Stages corresponding to ages 5-16, and were initially rated by qualified teachers. When two human raters disagreed, a third expert teacher resolved the disagreement to establish ground truth. The models were then evaluated on the same binary grading task using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 in zero-shot and few-shot settings, with the question, exemplar answer, and candidate answer provided in the prompt.

The results showed that GPT-4 performed best, with few-shot prompting reaching Cohen's kappa of 0.70, close to the human interrater benchmark of 0.75. Performance was relatively stable across subject, grade level, and question difficulty, suggesting that LLMs may be useful for low-stakes formative assessment across different K-12 contexts. The paper concludes that LLMs could substantially reduce teacher grading time while maintaining near-human agreement, though the authors caution that more research is needed across broader datasets and task types, including those outside the studied subjects and grades.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model system used for text generation, classification, and evaluation tasks via prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to mark open-text student responses to short answer questions as correct or incorrect, using GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 and GPT-4-0125-preview with zero-shot and few-shot prompting through the OpenAI API.

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,710 student responses, GPT-4 with few-shot prompting achieved the strongest agreement with expert human raters for correctness classification (Cohen's kappa = 0.70), compared with human rater agreement of 0.75. The paper reports that this performance was close to human level and substantially better than GPT-3.5.
findings.measure: Agreement with expert human ratings on correct/incorrect classification of short-answer responses

findings.finding_summary: The authors estimate that marking the 1,710 responses manually would have taken teachers at least 11 hours, whereas using GPT-4 with a generic script took approximately 2 hours. The paper presents this as a substantial time saving for low-stakes formative assessment tasks.
findings.measure: Estimated grading time for 1,710 short-answer responses

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical comparative study using real student responses, but it is not an RCT or QED and does not evaluate student learning outcomes. The evidence is observational/benchmark-style and focused on model-rater agreement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported agreement with human raters is substantial (kappa = 0.70) and the estimated grading-time savings are meaningful. However, the paper measures assessment automation performance rather than direct instructional impact on students.

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Chemistry Learning with ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Bard, and Claude as Agents-to-Think-With: A Comparative Case Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether four generative AI chatbots—ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Bard, and Claude—can support Chemistry learning when used as “agents-to-think-with.” The author frames the work within constructivist and constructionist perspectives and focuses on how these tools might promote critical thinking, problem-solving, comprehension, creativity, and more personalized learning through Socratic-style dialogue.

The study uses a single-case study approach. Rather than involving real classroom participants, the researcher acted as a simulated student persona in four interaction sessions, one with each chatbot. The prompts centered on common Chemistry learning difficulties such as balancing chemical equations, understanding chemical reactions, combustion, graphing reaction changes over time, and distinguishing atoms, molecules, and moles. Interaction logs and reflective journals were analyzed using content analysis, with categories including instructional strategies, engagement and interactivity, analogies, reinforcement and feedback, depth of explanation, personalization, and meta-discussion.

The paper concludes that all four GenAI tools showed educational promise, especially for prompting reflection and giving examples or analogies. ChatGPT was judged to perform best overall, particularly in contextual comprehension and depth, with Bing Chat, Bard, and Claude also offering useful but somewhat less effective responses. The author emphasizes that prompt crafting matters greatly and argues that educators will need training to use these tools well in educational settings.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational AI chatbot / GPT-based assistant used for generating text and multimodal responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of four generative AI chatbots in a single-case comparative study of chemistry learning dialogue, with GPT-4 and Advanced Data Analysis mode mentioned in the session.

findings.finding_summary: In the authors' qualitative comparison, ChatGPT was judged to be the strongest performer overall across the simulated chemistry-learning dialogue. The paper says it 'stood out, decisively surpassing Bing Chat's performance,' with more in-depth, precise, and nuanced understanding.
findings.measure: Qualitative assessment of response quality in simulated student dialogue

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT was described as especially effective for engagement, analogical explanation, and instructional support. The paper notes its use of questions, real-world analogies, and a graph in response to the student's request, which the author interpreted as stronger instructional depth and interactivity than the other tools.
findings.measure: Qualitative coding of interaction logs and reflective journals

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational AI chatbot family (formerly Bard/PaLM-based), used for generative dialogue and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as one of four chatbot tools in simulated chemistry-learning sessions; the paper refers to Bard, which maps to Gemini under normalization.

findings.finding_summary: Bard/Gemini was viewed as capable of supportive explanations and analogies, but it was judged less effective than ChatGPT overall. The author also noted a mismatch in one graph-related response, where Bard returned a graph of water phase changes rather than the requested time-based reaction illustration.
findings.measure: Qualitative assessment of response relevance, personalization, and instructional fit

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic’s conversational AI assistant used for generating explanations and dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as one of four generative AI chatbots in simulated chemistry learning conversations with a simulated student persona.

findings.finding_summary: Claude was assessed as generally helpful and conversational, with step-by-step explanations and invitations for clarification. However, the paper judged its graph output inferior and potentially confusing, weakening its instructional usefulness in that task.
findings.measure: Qualitative assessment of dialogue quality and generated visual explanation

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational AI chatbot / GPT-based assistant used for generating text and multimodal responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper also describes ChatGPT's Advanced Data Analysis mode as the mode used to generate a graph for one chemistry explanation task.

findings.finding_summary: When the student requested a visual representation of reaction changes over time, ChatGPT in Advanced Data Analysis mode was judged to provide a graph that directly addressed the question and clearly showed reactant decline and product increase. The author described this as demonstrating excellence in instructional strategy and detail depth.
findings.measure: Qualitative evaluation of generated graph and explanatory response

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational AI chatbot family (formerly Bard/PaLM-based), used for generative dialogue and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reports Bard/Google results for graphs and explanatory support in simulated chemistry instruction.

findings.finding_summary: For the student's request for a graph of gases turning into water over time, Bard did not produce a directly relevant graph; instead, it surfaced a graph of water phase changes. The author treated this as a failure of personalization and instructional alignment for the specific prompt.
findings.measure: Qualitative assessment of relevance to student prompt

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative single-case comparative study with a simulated student rather than real K-12 learners. It provides useful descriptive comparison, but the evidence base is small and non-experimental.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear qualitative differences in response quality, but no effect sizes or student outcome data are provided. Claimed impact is therefore plausible but unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Act II: Test Time Scaling Drives Cognition Engineering
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual and technical position paper about a new paradigm the authors call “cognition engineering.” It argues that first-generation large language models mainly excel at knowledge retrieval and prompt-based interaction, but remain limited by shallow reasoning, knowledge latency, and weak deliberation. The paper’s central question is how generative AI can move beyond static knowledge generation toward deeper, more human-like cognitive processes.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or any participant population. Instead, it synthesizes prior work on test-time scaling and related training strategies, including parallel sampling, tree search, multi-turn correction, long chain-of-thought reasoning, reinforcement learning, and self-training. It frames these methods as mechanisms for allocating more computation at inference time and for shaping models to reason more deliberately.

The authors position cognition engineering as a systematic methodology for constructing AI systems that can think, reason, and problem-solve more deeply. They conclude that test-time scaling is the most immediate practical bridge from current LLMs to this new paradigm, and they outline a roadmap for applying these methods across domains. The paper is theoretical and tutorial-oriented rather than empirical, and it does not involve K-12 learners, teachers, or classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general large language model / generative AI chatbot capable of conversation, content generation, reasoning, and related language-based tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a conceptual/theoretical overview of cognition engineering and test-time scaling in generative AI; it does not evaluate a specific product in a K-12 reading or literacy intervention.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/framework paper about cognition engineering and test-time scaling, not an empirical study with student outcomes or a controlled design. No K-12 intervention, comparator, or measurable literacy outcome is reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct educational impact is measured or demonstrated in the paper. The text discusses potential applications of generative AI broadly, but provides no effect on reading, literacy, or student performance.

paper_profiles.title: Self-Regulated Reading with AI Support: An Eight-Week Study with Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how college students use generative AI chatbots to support self-regulated academic reading, and how those interaction patterns relate to cognitive engagement over time. The authors note that while AI tools are increasingly used for reading support, there has been little granular evidence about what students actually do during AI-supported reading sessions, especially across multiple weeks.

The study followed 15 undergraduate students in an introductory AI course at a large public university in the United States over eight weeks. Students completed AI-supported reading logs for their assigned readings, producing 239 reading sessions and 838 prompts. The researchers coded prompts into four cognitive themes — Decoding, Comprehension, Reasoning, and Metacognition — and also conducted interviews with five students plus thematic analysis of optional reflections. There was no non-AI comparison group; instead, the paper focused on characterizing AI use and students’ own perceptions of it.

The findings show that students used AI mostly for comprehension support, especially summaries and explanations, with reasoning prompts less common and metacognitive prompts rare. Most sessions consisted only of the minimum required number of prompts, and prompt engineering techniques were seldom used even after instruction. Cognitive engagement shifted within sessions from comprehension toward reasoning, but overall patterns stayed stable across the eight weeks, with strong individual differences. Qualitative results suggest that efficiency was the main driver of AI use, and that students often used AI summaries to triage what to read more deeply, effectively reading through AI rather than with it. The authors conclude that AI reading systems should better scaffold deeper engagement and caution that instruction alone may be insufficient to change students’ habits without stronger system support.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI chatbot/assistant used for conversational support over text, including summarization, explanation, questioning, and follow-up dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: Students used AI chatbots of their choice to support self-regulated reading of course assigned texts, asking for summaries, explanations, definitions, implications, comparisons, and other forms of reading support over an eight-week period.

findings.finding_summary: In an eight-week longitudinal study of 15 undergraduates across 239 reading sessions and 838 prompts, students used the AI primarily for comprehension support (59.6% of coded prompts), followed by reasoning (29.8%), metacognition (8.5%), and decoding (2.1%). The paper reports qualitative and descriptive evidence that AI use often improved efficiency and access to understanding, but also encouraged shallow processing, reduced deep engagement, and strategic triage of reading through AI-generated summaries rather than with the original text.
findings.measure: Prompt coding distribution; reading-session logs; interviews and optional reflections

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods longitudinal study with descriptive coding and interviews rather than an experimental comparison. It provides useful evidence about usage patterns, but not causal estimates of learning effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports important behavioral patterns and perceived benefits/costs, but it does not provide measurable learning gains or effect sizes. The impact on literacy learning is therefore suggestive but unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Text Summarization Using Large Language Models: A Comparative Study of MPT-7b-instruct, Falcon-7b-instruct, and OpenAI Chat-GPT Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates the comparative performance of several large language models for text summarization. The central question is how different instruction-tuned LLMs perform on summarization tasks when evaluated with standard automatic metrics such as BLEU, ROUGE, and BERTScore.

The study compares MPT-7b-instruct, Falcon-7b-instruct, and OpenAI text-davinci-003 on two news summarization datasets: CNN/Daily Mail 3.0.0 and XSum. The authors vary some generation hyperparameters, including temperature and maximum token length, and generate summaries for 25 test samples from each dataset. The work is implemented using LangChain and Hugging Face pipelines on Google Cloud virtual machines with NVIDIA T4 GPUs.

The paper does not involve human participants, educational settings, or K-12 learners; it is a machine learning benchmark study in NLP. Results show that text-davinci-003 consistently outperforms the two open-source 7B models across both datasets, while MPT-7b-instruct performs slightly better than Falcon-7b-instruct. The authors conclude that larger, more capable models can produce higher-quality summaries and suggest that future work could extend to larger models and more varied datasets.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model/chatbot used for generating and summarizing text.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of the compared LLMs for text summarization on CNN/Daily Mail and XSum datasets; the paper specifically evaluates the text-davinci-003 model under the OpenAI/ChatGPT family.

findings.finding_summary: On the CNN/Daily Mail dataset (n=25), text-davinci-003 achieved ROUGE-1=0.272, ROUGE-2=0.096, ROUGE-L=0.255, and BERTScore F1=0.868. On XSum (n=25), it achieved ROUGE-1=0.206, ROUGE-2=0.053, ROUGE-L=0.173, and BERTScore F1=0.868; the authors report it outperformed MPT-7b-instruct and Falcon-7b-instruct on both datasets.
findings.measure: ROUGE-1/2/L and BERTScore on generated summaries

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a comparative NLP benchmarking paper rather than an education study, and it does not use a randomized or quasi-experimental design in K-12 learning. The methodology is a model comparison on summarization datasets, so evidence quality for the requested education context is not established.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact on K-12 reading or literacy outcomes is measured. The reported metrics are NLP summarization scores, not learner outcomes, so there is no direct instructional impact to assess.

paper_profiles.title: Comparing Software Developers with ChatGPT: An Empirical Investigation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can match or outperform human software developers on coding tasks, with a specific focus on objective technical outcomes such as runtime performance and memory efficiency. The authors position the study within broader debates about AI-assisted software engineering and argue that empirical comparisons with human solutions are needed to understand when automated code generation is useful.

The intervention studied is ChatGPT-4 used to generate solutions for LeetCode programming problems. The authors selected one recent LeetCode contest containing four problems of varying difficulty, prompted ChatGPT with the original problem statements, and then submitted the generated code to LeetCode to obtain runtime and memory metrics. They compared these results against solutions previously submitted by 42 human programmers, split into experienced contest programmers and novice/non-contest programmers based on contest rank and participation history.

The study found mixed results. ChatGPT outperformed novice programmers on performance for easy and medium problems, and showed better memory efficiency on one medium problem. However, it did not outperform experienced contest programmers on performance, and it did not consistently beat them on memory efficiency. The authors conclude that AI and human programmers have complementary strengths, and that task allocation in software engineering should depend on developer expertise and task requirements.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI system for generating and evaluating text and code from natural language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate code solutions for LeetCode coding problems and to compare those outputs against solutions produced by human programmers.

findings.finding_summary: In a controlled experiment, ChatGPT-4-generated code was compared with solutions from experienced contest programmers and novice/non-contest programmers on LeetCode problems. The paper reports that ChatGPT outperformed novice programmers on easy and medium problems for performance, and outperformed both experienced and novice programmers on memory efficiency for one medium problem, but did not outperform experienced programmers on performance and did not show superior memory efficiency on easy or hard problems.
findings.measure: LeetCode runtime performance and memory usage / memory efficiency for coding solutions
findings.sample_size: n=42 programmers; ChatGPT outputs for 4 contest problems

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical controlled experiment with explicit comparator groups and quantitative metrics, but it is not a randomized K-12 education study and the paper’s methodology is specific to software engineering rather than classroom instruction. The evidence is internally structured and comparative, but generalizability to education is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are task-specific and mixed, with some comparative advantages and some null results, and no standardized effect sizes are reported. Overall impact is unclear to modest rather than clearly medium or large.

paper_profiles.title: Simulation Streams: A Programming Paradigm for Controlling Large Language Models and Building Complex Systems with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to use large language models (LLMs) to drive long, complex simulations without losing consistency, violating rules, or drifting out of context over many iterations. The authors argue that ordinary prompt-based simulation breaks down because LLMs can become inconsistent in format, fail to track state, and ignore or hallucinate constraints in extended trajectories.

To address this, the paper proposes Simulation Streams, a programming paradigm for controlling LLM behavior through a state-based architecture. Programs are expressed as sequences of operators that update state variables, generate structured output rows, and selectively invoke the LLM only when needed. The framework also supports substreams for context management and an Entity-Component-System (ECS) organization for modular simulation programs. The implementation is described as a Python codebase with a Flask-based editor and supporting utilities.

The paper is not an education study. Its examples are illustrative simulations, including a grid-world cheese-finding task, reinforcement-learning benchmark tasks, a social simulation with three characters, and a market economy simulation. The paper compares model behavior within these simulations and argues that newer Gemini models, especially Gemini-2.0-Flash variants, are well suited to the framework because they maintain format consistency and simulation state more reliably.

Overall, the main conclusion is that Simulation Streams offers a flexible and minimally interfering way to structure LLM-driven simulations, enabling consistent long-running trajectories and easier comparison across models and workflows.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s family of large language models used for generative AI, including Flash, Pro, and Thinking variants.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and evaluates the Simulation Streams framework using several Gemini model variants (e.g., Gemini-1.5-Pro-002, Gemini-1.5-Flash-002, Gemini-2.0-Flash-Exp, Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking-Exp-01-21) as the language model component for simulation generation and control.

findings.finding_summary: Across the social simulation, Gemini-2.0-Flash-Exp maintained complete consistency across each character’s 250 decisions, and Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking-Exp made only a handful of mistakes. The paper also reports that Gemini-2.0-Flash-Exp generated exactly one additional simulation row in the correct format, reducing excess tokens and resampling needs.
findings.measure: Simulation consistency across multi-agent social simulation decisions; adherence to exact output format

findings.finding_summary: In the RL benchmark suite, Gemini-1.5-Pro-002 consistently outperformed Gemini-1.5-Flash-002 across all six tasks, while Gemini-1.5-Flash-002 outperformed Gemini-1.0-Pro in five of six tasks. Gemini-2.0-Flash-Exp outperformed Gemini-1.5-Flash-002 in 4 of 6 tasks, and Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking-Exp-01-21 was reported as the best performer on windy gridworld and the only model performing truly well on temperature control.
findings.measure: Performance on six classical RL benchmark tasks (Windy Gridworld, Key-Chest, Maze navigation, Mountain Car, Temperature Control, Robot Cleaning)
findings.sample_size: 10 independent runs x 25 steps x 6 tasks

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/framework paper introducing Simulation Streams, not a K-12 intervention study, RCT, or meta-analysis. The reported experiments are illustrative benchmark and simulation comparisons rather than education research with student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 reading or literacy outcome is reported, and no direct student-facing instructional effect is measured. The paper’s results concern simulation consistency and RL benchmark performance, so educational impact on the requested domain is not demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: CryptoEL: A Novel Experiential Learning Tool for Enhancing K-12 Cryptography Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 56th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V. 1 (SIGCSE 2025)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of age-appropriate, engaging K-12 resources for teaching modern cryptography. The authors argue that cryptography is important for students’ digital security, but is often absent from school curricula and is typically taught through advanced mathematical or programming-heavy materials that are not well suited to younger learners.

To address this gap, the paper presents CryptoEL, a web-based educational tool built around Kolb’s Experiential Learning cycle. The tool teaches three core topics—hashing, symmetric cryptography, and asymmetric cryptography—through realistic scenarios such as a university application portal, a chat application, and a login interface. Students interact with ideal and attacker simulations, reflect with AI-based conversation agents (“CryptoCoach”), watch explanatory videos, and complete simplified Python terminal exercises. The system was designed for independent learning with minimal instructor involvement and was open-sourced for classroom use.

The evaluation involved 51 middle and high school students in a 4-hour online workshop. Students completed pre- and post-surveys, concept quizzes, and Likert-scale feedback measures. Results showed high comprehension scores across all three cryptography topics and statistically significant gains from pre- to post-survey. Students also reported that the tool was engaging and beneficial, especially the visualizations, AI reflections, and hands-on terminal activities. The paper concludes that CryptoEL can effectively support early cryptography education, though some usability issues such as fast animations and lengthy AI responses were noted.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot system used for natural-language interaction and customized conversational assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as customized AI-based conversation agents ('CryptoCoach') for reflective observation in the cryptography learning tool, with separate models tailored to hashing, symmetric cryptography, and asymmetric cryptography.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that the AI reflection stage using CryptoCoach was positively received by students as part of the overall tool. In the user study with n=51 middle and high school students, 73% of middle school students and 86% of high school students said they benefited from the AI-driven reflection stage.
findings.measure: Student-reported benefit from the AI-driven reflection stage

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single preliminary user study with pre/post surveys and satisfaction feedback, not a controlled comparison. The evidence is mixed-methods and observational rather than a rigorous experimental design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported outcomes are positive and fairly high in absolute terms, but no effect size is given and the study lacks a non-AI comparator for the AI component. Impact is therefore promising but unclear.

paper_profiles.title: WavLLM: Towards Robust and Adaptive Speech Large Language Model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents WavLLM, a speech large language model designed to improve robust speech understanding, instruction following, and generalization across diverse speech tasks. The central problem addressed is that prior speech LLMs struggle with unseen or complex prompts and lack effective chain-of-thought-style decomposition for multi-step speech tasks.

The proposed system combines two frozen speech encoders, Whisper for semantic content and WavLM for acoustic/speaker information, with a LLaMA-2-7B-chat language model.
