The authors introduce a two-stage curriculum learning strategy: first, mixed single-task training on ASR, speech translation, speaker verification, emotion recognition, and speech question answering; second, advanced multi-task training on composite prompts that require completing multiple tasks sequentially. A prompt-aware LoRA adapter is added in the second stage to adapt the LoRA scaling to different instructions.

The evaluation uses speech benchmarks and in-house multi-task datasets, including spoken query answering, zero-shot English listening comprehension, independent multi-task instructions, and chain-of-thought tasks. Across these benchmarks, WavLLM is reported to outperform open-source baselines such as SALMONN and Qwen-Audio-Chat on many tasks, with especially strong gains in multi-task instruction following and CoT-style speech processing. The paper concludes that curriculum learning plus prompt-adaptive LoRA improves robustness and generalization for speech LLMs.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: A family of large language models from Meta, used here as the LLaMA-2-7B-chat backbone for speech-language instruction following.
identified_tools.use_case: Served as the core LLM backbone in WavLLM, with LoRA-based adaptation for speech understanding, instruction following, and multi-task dialogue.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that WavLLM, built on LLaMA-2-7B-chat, outperformed baseline speech-LLM systems on several speech understanding and instruction-following tasks. For zero-shot English listening comprehension (SQA), it achieved 67.55% accuracy versus 25.50%-59.30% for baselines; for multi-task instruction following (II-tasks), it achieved 62.44% accuracy and 92.50% IFR.
findings.measure: SQA accuracy; II-task accuracy and instruction-following rate (IFR)

findings.finding_summary: The advanced multi-task training stage improved performance over mixed single-task training. On II-tasks, accuracy increased from 22.92 to 62.44 and IFR from 26.25 to 92.50; on CoT-based Gigaword summarization/translation, R-1 improved from 14.7 to 16.5 and BERTScore from 69.71 to 70.60.
findings.measure: II-task accuracy/IFR; CoT summarization metrics (R-1, R-2, R-L, BERTScore)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical model paper, but the requested K-12 reading/literacy evidence is not the paper's focus; it evaluates a speech LLM on benchmark speech and dialogue tasks rather than an education intervention study. No randomized or quasi-experimental classroom design is reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are large on the paper's own benchmark tasks, but they are not education outcomes for K-12 literacy instruction and do not include effect sizes, sample sizes, or direct student learning measures. Impact for the requested topic is therefore unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Effects of Generative AI-Assisted Media Literacy Instruction on Learning Achievement and Cognitive Load among Elementary School Students
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Information and Education Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI chatbot can improve elementary students’ media literacy learning, specifically their ability to detect fake news, while also reducing cognitive load and improving technology acceptance. The authors frame the study around a practical problem: upper elementary students often struggle with online information evaluation because of limited reading comprehension and search skills, which can make traditional fact-checking instruction cognitively demanding.

The intervention embedded Microsoft Copilot into media literacy instruction as a student-facing learning support tool. In the experimental condition, students used natural-language interaction with the chatbot to verify news content, whereas the control group used the Taiwan FactCheck Center website plus conventional Google search strategies. The study used a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design with 56 fifth- and sixth-grade students from one elementary school in Pingtung County, Taiwan, and the same teacher taught both groups. Instruction lasted 120 minutes and focused on fake news detection.

Results showed that the AI-supported group significantly outperformed the control group on the posttest for fake news recognition, even after controlling for pretest scores. The experimental group also reported slightly lower cognitive load, but the differences were not statistically significant. Students reported high perceived usefulness and ease of use for the chatbot. The authors conclude that generative AI chatbots can be effective and acceptable supports for elementary media literacy instruction, while noting that stronger scaffolding and longer-term studies are needed to determine whether the benefits extend beyond novelty effects and short-term gains.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot system used for natural-language question answering and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a generative AI chatbot learning support tool during upper-elementary media literacy instruction for fake news verification, in contrast to traditional web search and fact-checking websites.

findings.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study with 56 upper elementary students (n=28 experimental, n=28 control), the group using Microsoft Copilot significantly improved fake-news recognition from pretest to posttest (M=55.00 to 87.50, t(27)=6.53, p<0.001). After controlling for prior knowledge, the experimental group outperformed the control group on posttest achievement (adjusted M=87.661 vs. 65.196, F(1,53)=29.933, p<0.001).
findings.measure: Fake news recognition test / learning achievement posttest

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI chatbot used for conversational, language-based assistance and response generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a student-facing generative AI chatbot in elementary media literacy instruction, with Microsoft Copilot named as the specific implementation in the paper text.

findings.finding_summary: The experimental group using the generative AI chatbot showed significantly higher fake-news detection learning outcomes than the control group using the Taiwan FactCheck Center website and Google search. Posttest performance was higher after adjusting for pretest scores (adjusted M=87.661 vs. 65.196; F(1,53)=29.933, p<0.001), while the control group's gain was not statistically significant (t(27)=0.983, p=0.334).
findings.measure: Fake news recognition / learning achievement

findings.finding_summary: Perceived cognitive load was not significantly different between groups. For mental load, the experimental group had M=2.76 and the control group M=3.00, t(54)=-0.523, p=0.603; for mental effort, the experimental group had M=2.80 and the control group M=3.40, t(54)=-1.263, p=0.212.
findings.measure: Cognitive load questionnaire (mental load, mental effort)

findings.finding_summary: Students in the experimental group reported favorable acceptance of the generative AI chatbot. Mean ratings were 4.16 for perceived usefulness and 4.23 for perceived ease of use on a five-point Likert scale, indicating generally positive user perceptions.
findings.measure: Technology acceptance questionnaire (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study with a non-AI control group and clear outcome measures, but it is not a randomized controlled trial and uses a relatively small sample from one school. The design is credible but has moderate risk of bias and limited generalizability.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main academic outcome shows a large and statistically significant advantage for the AI-assisted group, with a substantial posttest gap after covariate adjustment. Although effect sizes were not reported, the reported F statistic and mean difference indicate medium-to-large practical impact.

paper_profiles.title: Improving students’ reading, comprehension, and reading motivation through texts generated from their prompts using ChatGPT-4: a mixed-method study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether student-generated prompts, when used with ChatGPT-4 to create reading texts, questions, and visuals, can improve elementary students’ reading performance, comprehension, and motivation. The study is motivated by the need to strengthen literacy in the elementary years and by interest in whether generative AI can support reading instruction in ways that remain aligned with traditional teaching practices.

The intervention was a ChatGPT-4-supported literacy program in which 4th-grade students proposed prompts, the model generated texts and related activities, and students then read and discussed the materials in class. The quantitative component used a Solomon four-group experimental design, while the qualitative component used a case study approach based on student interviews. The study took place in two public primary schools in Bursa, Türkiye, with 106 students in the quantitative sample and 20 students in the qualitative follow-up.

Results indicated that the experimental groups outperformed the control groups on reading errors, comprehension, and reading motivation, with statistically significant differences and large effect sizes. Qualitative feedback suggested that students found the AI-generated materials engaging and motivating, and that the prompt-based process helped them feel active in text creation. The author concludes that ChatGPT-4 can be integrated into primary reading instruction as a supportive tool, particularly for generating texts that match student interests and support comprehension practice.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/large language model system that produces text in response to prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used with 4th-grade students to generate reading texts, comprehension questions, and visuals from students' own prompts for reading instruction and activities.

findings.finding_summary: In the Solomon four-group experiment with 4th-grade students (n=105), the experimental groups outperformed the control groups on post-test reading errors. The paper reports statistically significant differences favoring the experimental groups and an effect size of η²=0.289 for reading error count.
findings.measure: Post-test reading error count from the Error Analysis Inventory

findings.finding_summary: In the same study (n=105), the experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control groups on post-test reading comprehension. The paper reports a large effect size of η²=0.399 for comprehension score.
findings.measure: Post-test comprehension score from open-ended questions in the Error Analysis Inventory

findings.finding_summary: The experimental groups also showed statistically significant gains over the control groups in post-test reading motivation. The paper reports an effect size of η²=0.16, which is interpreted in the article as a large/meaningful effect.
findings.measure: Post-test Reading Motivation Scale score

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-method study with a Solomon four-group experimental component and qualitative interviews, but it is not presented as a fully controlled RCT with all credibility criteria documented in the excerpt. The overall design supports causal inference better than purely correlational work, but the mixed-method nature and some reporting limitations keep it in the yellow tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are large for reading error count (η²=0.289) and comprehension (η²=0.399), and the motivation effect is also substantial at η²=0.16. These are well above the blue-tier threshold for medium/large impact.

paper_profiles.title: The Use of Prompt Engineering in ChatGPT to Improve the Ability to Write Ethnoliteracy-Based Fiction Stories in Elementary Schools: A Quasi-Experimental Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether prompt engineering with ChatGPT can improve fifth-grade elementary students’ ability to write ethnoliteracy-based fiction stories. The study is motivated by persistent weaknesses in elementary students’ narrative writing, especially in structuring stories, developing characters and settings, and integrating local cultural values into writing. The authors argue that conventional instruction is often too generic and insufficiently engaging, while an ethnoliteracy approach may better connect writing tasks to students’ cultural identities.

The intervention combined generative AI with culturally grounded writing instruction. In the experimental condition, students used ChatGPT with structured prompts designed to support fiction writing around folklore and local cultural values; the control group received conventional fiction-writing instruction without AI assistance. The study used a quasi-experimental nonequivalent control group design with pretests and posttests. Participants were 50 fifth-grade students at Cimahi Mandiri 3 Public Elementary School in Cimahi City, West Java, Indonesia.

Results showed improvement in both groups, but the experimental group generally performed better on key indicators such as story structure, plot cohesion, setting, and incorporation of local cultural context. However, the reported N-gain scores were low in both groups, suggesting that overall gains were modest and that creative literacy development still requires sustained support. The authors conclude that ChatGPT-assisted prompt engineering, when paired with ethnoliteracy, can be a useful pedagogical strategy for elementary writing instruction, though it should be implemented thoughtfully and as part of ongoing guided practice.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT-family large language models, used for interactive text generation and task support.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a quasi-experimental intervention with structured prompt engineering to support 5th-grade elementary students in writing ethnoliteracy-based fiction stories, compared against conventional instruction without AI.

findings.finding_summary: The experimental group improved more than the control group on several fiction-writing indicators after ChatGPT-assisted prompt engineering, especially story structure, plot cohesion, setting, and integration of local cultural values. However, the reported N-gain was low in both groups (experimental=0.069; control=0.062), and the paper also reports a non-significant one-tailed t-test result, so overall impact is mixed/unclear despite descriptive gains.
findings.measure: Ethnoliteracy-based fiction story writing test scores; indicator-based rubric scores; N-gain; t-test

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental nonequivalent control group study with pretest/posttest and a non-AI comparator, which provides moderate causal evidence. However, the design is nonrandomized and the reported results are internally mixed, with low N-gain and a non-significant t-test reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports some meaningful descriptive improvements on specific writing indicators, but the aggregate gain is low and overall statistical evidence is unclear/mixed. That places the impact in the modest/unclear range rather than clearly positive medium or large impact.

paper_profiles.title: A cross-sectional look at teacher reactions, worries, and professional development needs related to generative AI in an urban school district
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in a large urban school district reacted to the rapid emergence of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, with a focus on their concerns, perceived benefits, and professional development needs. The authors ask whether teachers’ views differ by grade level, subject area, and years of teaching experience, and whether those characteristics shape willingness to allow student use of AI for different academic tasks.

The study uses a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey of 1,454 certificated educators in one large urban district on the U.S. West Coast. Teachers reported on prior chatbot use, allowability of several AI uses (idea generation, paper editing/completion, full paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation), open-ended concerns and benefits for teachers versus students, and desired professional learning topics. Quantitative analyses included logistic regression and chi-square tests, while open-ended responses were coded thematically.

Findings show a strong grade-level pattern: teachers in higher grades were less willing to allow AI chatbot use than elementary teachers, with high school teachers especially focused on guarding against misuse. More experienced teachers were generally more restrictive, particularly in humanities. Across the sample, teachers worried more about student overreliance and plagiarism than about their own use, while perceived benefits also differed by whether AI was being considered for teachers or students. Professional development needs varied by grade level: elementary and middle school teachers wanted basic AI literacy, whereas high school teachers emphasized guidance on student use and detecting AI-generated work. The authors conclude that AI professional development and policy should be targeted by grade level and teaching context rather than treated as one-size-fits-all.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbot technology used for conversational text generation and related academic tasks; the paper references tools such as ChatGPT but does not evaluate a different named product beyond that example.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers were surveyed about their reactions, concerns, allowability policies, benefits, and professional development needs regarding generative AI chatbots in K-12 schools, with ChatGPT used as the exemplar in survey wording.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods survey of 1,454 teachers in a large urban district, teachers in higher grade levels were less willing to allow student use of generative AI chatbots. The paper reports decreasing likelihood of allowability from elementary to middle to high school across idea generation, paper editing, full-paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation (e.g., marginal effects of about -0.121 to -0.150 across outcomes).
findings.measure: Teacher allowability/policy responses for five chatbot uses

findings.finding_summary: For elementary teachers, those with more than 10 years of experience were substantially less likely to allow student use for writing support tasks. The reported marginal effects were -0.489 for generating ideas, -0.502 for editing a paper, and -0.587 for writing an entire paper (all p<0.05), indicating stronger resistance among more experienced elementary teachers.
findings.measure: Teacher allowability for writing-support uses of AI chatbots by experience level
findings.sample_size: n=113 to n=115 depending on outcome

findings.finding_summary: Among high school teachers, more experienced humanities and STEM teachers were more likely to disallow AI chatbot use for writing support, with significant negative marginal effects for idea generation and paper editing. For example, more experienced humanities teachers had dy/dx=-0.329 for idea generation and -0.378 for paper editing, while more experienced STEM teachers had dy/dx=-0.404 for paper editing; the paper notes no significant model result for code generation at alpha=0.05.
findings.measure: Teacher allowability for AI chatbot writing-support uses by grade level, subject, and experience
findings.sample_size: n=69 to n=97 depending on outcome

findings.finding_summary: Teachers’ concerns and perceived benefits differed significantly when considering AI use by teachers versus students. For concerns, overreliance was most frequently cited for students (29.52%) and teachers (18.21%), plagiarism/misuse was much more common as a student concern (26.35%) than a teacher concern (3.35%), and misinformation was more often a concern for teachers (13.58%) than students (3.17%).
findings.measure: Open-ended concern codes for teacher vs student AI use
findings.sample_size: n=668 to n=669 depending on question

findings.finding_summary: Teachers also viewed benefits differently for themselves and students. For teachers, the most common benefits were insufficient personal knowledge about AI (22.16%), lesson planning/materials (21.41%), and increased efficiency (13.62%); for students, the most common benefit was information retrieval (20.33%), followed by other uncoded benefits (22.57%) and insufficient personal knowledge about AI (22.42%).
findings.measure: Open-ended benefit codes for teacher vs student AI use
findings.sample_size: n=626 to n=630 depending on question

findings.finding_summary: Professional development needs varied significantly by grade level (chi-square p<0.001) but not by subject or experience level. Elementary and middle school teachers more often wanted basic AI introductions, while high school teachers more often wanted training on how to instruct/manage student AI use and how to detect AI-generated work.
findings.measure: Professional development needs from open-ended survey responses

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-district mixed-methods survey study with descriptive coding and regression analyses, not an experimental evaluation. It provides useful correlational evidence about teacher perceptions and setting-specific variation, but causal inference is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports substantial differences in teacher allowability and PD needs across grade levels and experience groups, but it does not estimate student learning gains or other direct outcome effects. Reported effects are mostly marginal effects in policy/attitude models rather than educational impact on achievement.

paper_profiles.title: The great detectives: humans versus AI detectors in catching large language model-generated medical writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-generated academic writing can be detected reliably by commercial AI detectors and by human reviewers, especially after the text has been paraphrased. The authors focus on the growing concern that large language models such as ChatGPT may be used in academic publishing and that existing detection tools may fail when the text is reworded.

To test this, the study used 50 published rehabilitation-related journal articles from high-impact medical journals and fabricated 50 parallel articles with ChatGPT. The fabricated articles were then paraphrased with Wordtune to make them harder to identify. Six AI content detectors were applied to the original, ChatGPT-generated, and rephrased texts, and four blinded human reviewers (two students and two professorial reviewers) assessed original versus AI-rephrased papers. The study was conducted in the context of medical/rehabilitation publishing, not in a K-12 educational setting.

Results showed that Originality.ai and ZeroGPT were the most effective detectors, with Originality.ai identifying all AI-generated texts and ZeroGPT performing very well overall. Turnitin accurately recognized human-written texts but struggled more with AI-rephrased articles. The more experienced human reviewers generally detected rephrased AI text accurately, but student reviewers were less accurate. The paper concludes that some detectors and experienced reviewers can identify AI-generated writing even after paraphrasing, but AI tools remain imperfect and should be used alongside peer review rather than as a standalone gatekeeping mechanism.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used to generate and rewrite text.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to fabricate the introduction, discussion, and conclusion sections of 50 rehabilitation-related academic articles based on original titles, methods, and results.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5-Turbo) was used as the text-generation tool, and the study evaluated whether its generated articles could be detected by AI detectors and human reviewers. The paper reports that ChatGPT-generated articles were detected with high accuracy by some detectors, but the model itself was not evaluated on learning or academic outcomes.
findings.measure: AI detector classification of ChatGPT-generated academic articles; human reviewer classification of AI-rephrased articles

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model chatbot without a specific named product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI more broadly as a source of AI-generated academic writing and as a target for detection tools, beyond the specific ChatGPT product used in the study.

findings.finding_summary: The paper concludes that generative AI can produce plausible academic text, but that current versions are inadequate for generating rigorous scientific articles and may fabricate data or misuse abbreviations. It also notes that AI-rephrasing can reduce detectability by some tools, while some detectors and experienced reviewers can still identify such text accurately.
findings.measure: Accuracy of AI content detectors and human reviewers in identifying AI-generated or AI-rephrased text
findings.sample_size: n=150 articles total (50 original, 50 ChatGPT-generated, 50 AI-rephrased)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single cross-sectional detection study rather than an educational intervention trial, and it does not test student learning outcomes. The paper provides empirical evidence about AI text detection, but the evidence base is not about K-12 literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study has practical relevance for academic integrity and AI screening, but it does not demonstrate direct impact on literacy achievement or instruction. Any impact on K-12 literacy is indirect and not measured in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching with ChatGPT as a Linguistically Responsive Tool for Multilingual Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how K–12 teachers in U.S. public schools are using ChatGPT and related AI tools to support multilingual learners’ language and literacy development. The paper is motivated by concerns that traditional literacy instruction often reflects monolingual and deficit-based assumptions that fail to recognize multilingual learners’ full communicative repertoires. Using a translanguaging lens, the author asks how teachers are incorporating ChatGPT into instruction and whether those uses align with linguistically responsive pedagogy.

The study is situated within a professional development initiative for in-service teachers focused on culturally and linguistically responsive pedagogy. Data came from classroom observations and post-observation interviews with 42 teachers across pre-K through grade 12 in DC public schools and public charter schools. The sample included teachers in general education, Spanish immersion, ESL, dual-language bilingual education, special education, science, math, and ELA, but only eight observations documented actual uses of ChatGPT.

Findings show that teachers primarily used ChatGPT to facilitate communication, such as translating text, transcribing student speech, generating subtitles, and differentiating content by adjusting reading levels or producing exemplar texts. In a smaller number of secondary classrooms, teachers also used ChatGPT to scaffold students’ prompting and to support multimodal literacy through image generation activities. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support translanguaging-related affordances, production, and co-labor, but that assessment and reflection were notably absent. The author argues that more critical, explicit, and pedagogically intentional use of AI is needed to ensure it supports multilingual learners’ agency rather than reinforcing standard language norms.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on large language models, able to generate, transform, translate, and discuss text and other outputs in response to prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by in-service K-12 teachers of multilingual learners to translate texts, transcribe and translate student speech, differentiate reading content, create exemplar disciplinary texts, scaffold student prompting, and support multimodal literacy experimentation.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative study of 42 observed K12 teachers of multilingual learners, ChatGPT was used across 8 observed instances to facilitate communication, differentiate content, scaffold prompting, and support multimodal literacy experimentation. The paper reports that these uses appeared to support multilingual learners' comprehension, access, participation, and agency, but it does not provide quantitative effect sizes or experimental estimates.
findings.measure: Observed instructional practices and post-observation interview reports about ChatGPT use in literacy/content instruction
findings.sample_size: n=42 observed teachers; 8 observations with ChatGPT use

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, observational study with classroom observations and interviews rather than an experimental design. It provides descriptive evidence about how ChatGPT was used, but no causal estimates or quantitative effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful instructional benefits for multilingual learners, but it does not report effect sizes or outcome measures that would support a medium or large impact classification. The impact is therefore promising but unclear from the evidence presented.

paper_profiles.title: Seeing Multilingual Learners through Media and AI: Pre-Service Teachers’ Perceptions in an ESOL Course
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Interdisciplinary Research in Artificial Intelligence and Society
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how pre-service teachers in an ESOL Foundations course understood the influence of media and generative AI on perceptions of multilingual learners, and how they translated those understandings into possible classroom practices. The authors frame the problem as a teacher-preparation challenge: future K–12 teachers increasingly encounter algorithmically curated media and AI-generated content that may shape deficit-oriented beliefs about immigrant and multilingual communities, yet preparation programs often emphasize technical digital skills more than critical evaluation.

The study used an exploratory instrumental case study design centered on one upper-level undergraduate ESOL course at a university in Southwest Florida during Spring 2024. The course included a teacher-attitudes module with assigned readings and a structured class discussion/activity focused on media representation, credibility, and AI-enabled misinformation. Data came from two coursework artifacts: a reading reflection paper and written responses to the class discussion/activity. Thirty-eight undergraduate pre-service teachers participated, mostly women, and the cohort included both monolingual English speakers and bilingual students.

Analysis of the written artifacts produced five themes: media as a curriculum for bias, uncertainty about authenticity and AI-generated content, a perceived gap between computer use and critical media reasoning, movement from diagnosis to classroom design, and links between media/AI literacy and equity-oriented teaching commitments. Overall, participants saw media literacy and foundational AI literacy as important for challenging biased narratives and for supporting more equitable instruction for multilingual learners. The authors argue that critical media literacy and AI literacy should be treated as core professional competencies in teacher education, especially in courses preparing teachers for multilingual classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI systems that can produce or manipulate text, images, or audio content.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discussed generative AI as part of the contemporary information environment shaping pre-service teachers’ perceptions of multilingual learners, and used an AI-generated image in a class activity to prompt verification and provenance reasoning.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative instrumental case study rather than an intervention or causal impact study. It provides useful descriptive evidence about perceptions and proposed practices, but does not test an AI tool’s effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful implications for teacher preparation and critical AI/media literacy, but it reports no outcome effects on student learning or teacher performance and includes no quantitative impact estimates.

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in higher education: Benefits, challenges, and future research directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the prospective role of ChatGPT in higher education, asking what benefits and challenges generative AI may create for teaching, learning, assessment, research, and administration. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, it develops a conceptual perspective grounded in constructivist theory of learning.

The paper positions ChatGPT as a generative AI / large language model that could support adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research and writing assistance, automated administrative support, and innovative assessment design. It also argues that these same affordances create major risks, including academic integrity violations, bias and hallucinations, inequitable access, weakened development of graduate skills, and difficulty assessing authentic learning outcomes.

The population and context are higher education users, especially students, educators, and administrators in tertiary institutions. The authors discuss ChatGPT use in institutional learning systems, feedback processes, research tasks, administrative workflows, and assessment design, but no empirical sample, intervention, or country-specific study is reported. The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can enhance higher education if used cautiously, ethically, and in ways that preserve active, collaborative, constructivist learning while addressing bias, integrity, and equity concerns.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model system for conversational text generation, question answering, feedback, and other language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a perspective/theoretical discussion of ChatGPT's role in higher education, using it as the focal example of generative AI for adaptive learning, personalised feedback, research support, administrative support, and assessment design.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical paper rather than an empirical study, review, or meta-analysis. It proposes benefits, challenges, and propositions about ChatGPT but reports no measured outcomes, sample, or effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No empirical effects are reported, so there is no measurable impact estimate to classify. The paper is conceptual and does not demonstrate observed academic or operational impact.

paper_profiles.title: Generative artificial intelligence: a systematic review and applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a systematic review of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) research, focusing on recent advancements, model variants, and application areas. The authors aim to synthesize the state of the art across major generative paradigms, including GANs, transformers, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models, and to discuss how these methods have evolved over time. The review also emphasizes responsible AI considerations, including ethical issues and sustainability concerns.

The paper is not an intervention study with human participants. Instead, it surveys peer-reviewed literature from 2012–2023, primarily sourced through Google Scholar, and organizes the findings by application domain. These domains include image translation, video synthesis and generation, natural language processing, and several specialized uses such as synthetic data generation and molecule generation. Within each domain, the paper summarizes representative methods, benchmark datasets, and evaluation metrics used in prior work.

The review concludes that GenAI has achieved major progress in language generation, image translation, and other interdisciplinary applications, with transformers and large language models driving particularly strong advances in text-related tasks. It also highlights that unpaired image translation, video generation, and multilingual NLP are active areas of development, but that challenges remain around training stability, performance evaluation, and ethical deployment. Because the paper is a broad technical review rather than a study of K-12 learners or classroom implementation, it does not report participant populations, user roles, or educational intervention outcomes.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based large language model chatbot/system for generating and understanding text.
identified_tools.use_case: Cited as one of the models evaluated in the paper’s discussion of summarization on QMSUM and as a generative AI system in educational contexts; also mentioned in the paper’s broader review of NLP applications.

findings.finding_summary: On QMSUM, ChatGPT achieved the best ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 scores among the compared summarization systems, but not the best ROUGE-L. The paper reports ROUGE-1 = 36.83, ROUGE-2 = 12.78, and ROUGE-L = 24.23 for ChatGPT on QMSUM, compared with HMNet’s higher ROUGE-L of 31.27.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review paper, not a primary educational intervention study. The reported evidence is secondary synthesis and includes benchmark comparisons rather than a controlled study design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports performance metrics from summarization benchmarks, but no effect sizes or K-12 learning outcomes are provided. The impact on education is indirect and not specific to subgroup or instructional settings.

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly emerging debate around ChatGPT and generative AI in education, asking what future educational possibilities and risks these tools may create. Rather than testing an intervention empirically, the authors use speculative methodology and collective writing to generate fictional future narratives that explore both positive and negative educational scenarios.

The article draws on a globally diverse group of educational scholars who each wrote speculative narratives from different contexts and perspectives. The narratives imagine AI supporting personalized learning, translation and language development, accessibility for students with disabilities, assessment support, and communication across languages and distances. They also imagine risks such as plagiarism, dependence on AI, privacy and ethics concerns, algorithmic bias, inequity in access, and possible erosion of human agency and teacher roles.

The paper is not a study of a single student population or school setting; instead, it is a reflective theoretical piece aimed at the broader educational landscape. Its main conclusion is that generative AI in education is context-dependent and full of both promise and risk, and that educators and policymakers need to develop new literacies, rethink assessment, and keep human agency central when adopting AI technologies.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI / large language model chatbot used for text generation, question answering, summarization, translation, feedback, and other language-based tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a speculative/future-oriented reflection centered on ChatGPT and similar generative AI tools in education; it also includes fictional narratives generated by ChatGPT and discusses potential educational uses and risks.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a speculative and theoretical collective reflection, not an empirical evaluation of ChatGPT or any other AI tool. It provides no study design, measures, or outcomes that would support causal or correlational evidence grading beyond opinion/speculation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ChatGPT could have broad educational usefulness, but these are prospective claims rather than measured impacts. Because no effect sizes or outcome data are reported, impact cannot be established empirically.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Applications of ChatGPT to English Language Teaching: Opportunities, Challenges, and Recommendations
paper_profiles.venue: TESL-EJ (The Electronic Journal for English as a Second Language)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how ChatGPT might be used in English language teaching (ELT), focusing on both its pedagogical opportunities and its risks. The authors ask what ChatGPT can contribute to language instruction, what concerns it raises around academic integrity, bias, and learning, and how educators should respond as generative AI becomes more accessible.

Rather than testing a formal intervention, the paper synthesizes emerging scholarship on ChatGPT and combines it with the authors’ own classroom experimentation at Northeastern University. The instructional examples involved undergraduate public speaking students and graduate students in an academic listening and speaking course for international students in a pathways program. In these classes, ChatGPT was used for activities such as generating debate arguments and supporting presentation-skills reflection, with students comparing AI output to their own knowledge, revising prompts, and discussing accuracy and usefulness.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support ELT as a tool for prompting discussion, encouraging critical thinking, and generating language-learning materials, but only when used with human guidance. The authors emphasize that educators should collaborate, reflect with students on appropriate AI use, and redesign learning activities to focus more on process, evaluation, and creativity. They argue that ChatGPT should complement, not replace, teachers, and that critical digital literacy is increasingly important in AI-mediated learning environments.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/large language model interface that generates human-like text responses to prompts and can support conversational interaction, writing, feedback, summarization, and other language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses ChatGPT as the focal generative AI tool in English language teaching and reports the authors' classroom experiments using ChatGPT in undergraduate public speaking and graduate academic listening/speaking activities. It is also used illustratively to describe potential ELT applications and concerns.

findings.finding_summary: This is not an empirical evaluation of ChatGPT; it is a conceptual/review article that synthesizes literature and the authors' classroom observations. The paper reports perceived opportunities (e.g., engagement, critical analysis, support for writing, vocabulary, and assessment) alongside concerns (e.g., academic integrity, bias, false information, and equity), but provides no effect sizes or controlled outcome data.
findings.measure: Literature synthesis and classroom observations/student comments

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper is a conceptual/review-style article with illustrative classroom examples and student comments, not a controlled empirical study. It does not report rigorous causal evidence or quantitative outcomes for ChatGPT.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful classroom benefits such as engagement and supportive use for language tasks, but these are anecdotal and not quantified. With no effect sizes or experimental evidence, impact remains uncertain and best treated as hypothesis-generating.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching with ChatGPT as a Linguistically Responsive Tool for Multilingual Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers of K–12 multilingual learners in U.S. public schools are using ChatGPT and related AI tools to support language and literacy instruction. The study is motivated by concerns that multilingual learners are often taught through monolingual, deficit-oriented practices, and asks whether generative AI can be used in more linguistically responsive ways.

The author analyzes classroom observations and post-observation interviews from 42 in-service teachers participating in a professional development course focused on culturally and linguistically responsive pedagogy. The teachers worked across pre-K through 12th grade in multiple contexts, including general education, ESL, dual-language bilingual education, Spanish immersion, special education, science, math, and ELA. Instances of ChatGPT use were identified in 8 observations.

The findings show that teachers mainly used ChatGPT to facilitate communication (for example, translating text, transcribing student speech, and generating subtitles) and to differentiate content (for example, adjusting reading levels or creating exemplar texts). In some secondary classrooms, teachers also scaffolded students’ prompting skills and used ChatGPT’s image-generation capabilities for multimodal literacy activities. The author concludes that these uses align most clearly with the affordances, production, and co-labor dimensions of translanguaging pedagogy, but that assessment and reflection were notably absent. The paper argues that generative AI has promise for supporting multilingual learners’ access and agency, while also calling for more critical, explicit, and ethical guidance around its use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot and LLM-based assistant for text generation, translation, prompting, and other language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a linguistically responsive tool used by K-12 teachers of multilingual learners to facilitate communication, differentiate content, support prompting, and enable multimodal literacy experimentation.

findings.finding_summary: Across observations and interviews with 42 in-service teachers, ChatGPT was used to translate texts, transcribe student speech, create subtitles, differentiate reading levels, and generate exemplar texts for multilingual learners. The study reports these practices as supporting comprehension, access to content, writing support, and multilingual/multimodal participation, but it does not report quantitative effect sizes.
findings.measure: Classroom instructional uses observed in field notes and post-observation interviews; qualitative evidence of support for comprehension, access, and participation
findings.sample_size: n=42 teachers observed; ChatGPT documented in 8 observations

findings.finding_summary: Teachers used ChatGPT to facilitate communication across languages by translating vocabulary and passages, translating/transcribing student oral language, and helping students draft or revise prompts and writing in preferred languages. The paper characterizes these uses as improving access to language and content for multilingual learners, but no numerical effects are reported.
findings.measure: Observed teacher practices related to translation, transcription, and language support
findings.sample_size: n=42 teachers observed; ChatGPT documented in 8 observations

findings.finding_summary: The paper finds that ChatGPT aligned with translanguaging dimensions of affordances, production, and co-labor, but not assessment or reflection. It also notes limitations such as lack of resources to verify translation quality and concerns about overreliance, bias, and standard-language norms.
findings.measure: Qualitative alignment with translanguaging framework dimensions; documented limitations and gaps
findings.sample_size: n=42 teachers observed; ChatGPT documented in 8 observations

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods classroom observation and interview study, so it does not meet blue/green experimental evidence standards. The paper provides structured empirical documentation of use cases, but no causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports potentially meaningful instructional benefits for multilingual learners, but those benefits are described qualitatively without effect sizes or outcome measures. Impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Improving Writing Feedback for Struggling Writers: Generative AI to the Rescue?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can support writing instruction by producing feedback and instructional suggestions for struggling writers. The authors focus on the practical question of how two versions of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) respond to student essays when prompted in different ways, and how those responses compare with teacher-generated rubric scores and instructional decisions.

The study used 34 persuasive essays written by students in grades 3–7 who were struggling writers, including students with high-incidence disabilities and English language learners. The essays came from an existing technology-based writing intervention that used a graphic organizer and embedded supports (WEGO/TBGO). The authors imported the essays into ChatGPT and ran four prompt types: a specific analytic rubric, a generic 0–4 rating, a request to identify one area of need without a rubric, and a general feedback prompt with no student context.

Across the generated responses, GPT-4 generally produced more specific and individualized feedback than GPT-3.5, while GPT-3.5 more often gave broad, misaligned, or repetitive feedback. Neither version reliably adapted feedback to student grade, disability status, or ELL status, and neither consistently produced instructional suggestions tailored to those characteristics. When compared with teacher judgments using the rubric, ChatGPT’s identification of the main area of need matched teacher decisions only modestly, though GPT-4 aligned better than GPT-3.5. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may be useful as a starting point for feedback generation, but teacher review and judgment remain essential.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model chatbot used to generate and score writing feedback from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Two versions of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5/free and GPT-4/subscription) were used to evaluate 34 student persuasive essays, generate formative feedback, identify areas of need, and suggest instructional responses under four prompt conditions.

findings.finding_summary: Using inductive thematic analysis of 34 persuasive essays, the study found that ChatGPT could generate rubric-based feedback and instructional suggestions, but output quality varied by version and prompt. GPT-4 was generally more specific and individualized than GPT-3.5, yet both versions produced excessive feedback, and neither consistently aligned suggestions with student characteristics such as grade, disability, or ELL status.
findings.measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of AI-generated writing feedback and instructional suggestions

findings.finding_summary: Compared with teacher data-based decision making, GPT-3.5 matched the teacher-identified area of writing need 17.6% of the time and GPT-4 matched 23.5% of the time. For instructional decisions, GPT-3.5 yielded 26.5% partial matches and GPT-4 yielded 47.1% partial matches, indicating limited agreement and substantial need for teacher vetting before classroom use.
findings.measure: Agreement between teacher rubric-based decisions and ChatGPT-generated area-of-need labels and instructional suggestions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an original mixed-methods/qualitative secondary analysis of student writing and AI-generated feedback, not an RCT or meta-analysis. The study is useful for exploratory evidence but does not provide causal impact estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports practical promise, but the main quantitative agreement results are low-to-moderate and no effect sizes are reported. The findings suggest limited current classroom impact without teacher mediation.

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can serve as an effective alternative to human feedback for student writing and whether students prefer it. The authors focus on a practical educational question: can GPT-4-generated corrective feedback on writing support English as a new language (ENL) learners without harming learning outcomes, and how do students perceive such feedback compared with feedback from a human tutor?

The study reports on two linked investigations conducted at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region during Spring 2023. In Study 1, 48 university ENL learners completed six weeks of writing tasks in a quasi-experimental repeated-measures design, with one group receiving feedback from a human tutor and the other receiving individualized feedback generated by GPT-4. Student writing was measured through pre- and posttests rated with an analytic rubric. In Study 2, a different group of 43 ENL learners received both AI and human feedback and completed weekly surveys plus open-ended responses about their preferences.

Results from Study 1 showed no significant difference in writing gains between the AI-feedback group and the human-feedback group, suggesting GPT-4 feedback was not superior but also did not disadvantage learners. Results from Study 2 showed a near-even split in preference between AI and human feedback. Students who preferred human feedback valued face-to-face interaction, engagement, and the ability to ask questions, whereas those who preferred AI feedback emphasized clarity, specificity, and availability. The authors conclude that a blended approach combining human and AI feedback may be most beneficial, especially for language education contexts where efficiency and personalization are important.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s chatbot interface for GPT models, used for generating and interacting with large language model outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-4 via ChatGPT to generate corrective writing feedback for ENL students’ paragraphs in two studies: one compared AI-generated feedback with human tutor feedback on writing outcomes, and the other compared student preferences for AI versus human feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1 (n=48 ENL students), AI-generated feedback from GPT-4 did not produce significantly different writing gains than human tutor feedback over six weeks. The mixed 2x2 RM-ANOVA found no significant group x time interaction (F=3.094, p=0.085, partial eta squared=0.063), and no significant between-group effect on posttest scores (F=0.241, p=0.626).
findings.measure: Pretest/posttest academic writing rubric scores (content, coherence, language use, sources and evidence)
findings.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.063 for time x group; partial eta squared=0.005 for group

findings.finding_summary: In Study 2 (n=43 ENL students), preference for AI-generated feedback versus human tutor feedback was approximately evenly split across six weeks. Quantitative survey means were very close for human and AI feedback, and qualitative responses indicated advantages for both modalities (human interaction/engagement versus AI clarity/specificity).
findings.measure: Weekly preference survey items and open-ended responses on feedback satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall preference

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental mixed-methods study with pre/post comparison and a separate preference survey, but it is not a randomized controlled trial. The design is fairly structured and includes rubric-based scoring and inter-rater reliability, though causal claims are limited by the quasi-experimental setup.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main achievement outcome showed no significant difference between AI and human feedback, with only a small interaction effect (partial eta squared=0.063) that was not significant. Student preference was split and therefore does not indicate a strong impact in either direction.

paper_profiles.title: Reading differently with ChatGPT: EFL learners’ use of Question-Answer Relationship strategy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines how university EFL learners’ reading comprehension developed when they used ChatGPT together with the Question-Answer Relationship (QAR) strategy. The paper is motivated by the need for more individualized reading support in EFL contexts, where learners often struggle with vocabulary, sentence complexity, synthesis across text, and inferencing. The authors ask how learners’ comprehension changes when ChatGPT is used not as a simple answer engine, but as a dialogic reading partner within a structured comprehension framework.

The intervention/approach consisted of five guided reading sessions over five weeks with GPT-4o mini, combined with QAR-based questioning and follow-up reflection. Participants first read TOEFL-style texts and answered comprehension questions, then created their own QAR-type questions, and then interacted with ChatGPT by generating, comparing, and refining questions and answers. The study used three rounds of semi-structured interviews with 35 first-year undergraduate students at a university in northern China; the analysis was thematic and focused on learners’ experiences across different QAR levels (Right There, Think and Search, Author and You).

Findings suggest a developmental progression in comprehension. At the most basic level, ChatGPT helped learners identify explicit information, vocabulary, and sentence-level meaning. As they moved to Think and Search questions, they began synthesizing across text segments, summarizing main ideas, and tracking logical relationships. At the highest level, Author and You questions supported inferencing, interpretation of tone and intent, and critical engagement with authorial choices. The study concludes that ChatGPT can support EFL reading when paired with explicit strategy instruction, but its value depends on learners’ critical use and awareness of limitations such as vague definitions, imperfect sentence parsing, overly literal summaries, and unreliable inferential explanations.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot based on GPT models, capable of generating, explaining, and adapting language in dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a dialogic reading partner alongside the Question-Answer Relationship (QAR) strategy in guided EFL reading sessions; students asked it to generate questions, explain vocabulary and sentences, and support comprehension and inference.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative study with 35 first-year university EFL learners over five weeks, participants reported that ChatGPT helped them progress from locating explicit information to synthesizing across texts and making inferences. The paper reports developmental gains in reading comprehension strategies, but no effect sizes were reported.
findings.measure: Semi-structured interview reports of reading comprehension development using QAR categories (Right There, Think and Search, Author and You)

findings.finding_summary: Participants said ChatGPT supported vocabulary clarification, sentence breakdown, summarization, and interpretation of tone/author intent during reading. Learners also noted limitations such as vague definitions, unclear parsing of long sentences, copied text in summaries, and occasional inferential inaccuracies.
findings.measure: Semi-structured interview reports of reading support across vocabulary, syntax, summarization, and inferential reading

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study with 35 participants, so it provides rich descriptive evidence but not causal or quantitative impact estimates. The methodology is transparent and systematic, but the evidence level is below experimental designs.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful positive experiences and strategy development, but it does not provide effect sizes or standardized outcome gains. The impact is therefore promising yet unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Comparison of generative AI performance on undergraduate and postgraduate written assessments in the biomedical sciences
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether three generative AI tools can produce essays that meet the standards expected in undergraduate and postgraduate biomedical science assessments. The study is motivated by concerns that students may use large language models to draft academic writing, alongside the need for educators to understand what these systems can and cannot do in higher education assessment contexts.

The author prompted ChatGPT 3.5, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing with essay questions taken from four University College London biomedical science courses spanning UK FHEQ levels 4, 5, 6, and 7. The questions covered topics such as glomerular filtration rate, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bioinformatics in biomedical research, and the MHC II antigen processing pathway. Each AI-generated essay was anonymized and independently marked by four assessors using criteria aligned to scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, deviation from topic, context, and coherence. Scores were mapped onto FHEQ level descriptors, and inter-rater reliability was calculated with Kendall’s coefficient of concordance.

Across all levels, ChatGPT generally performed best, followed by Bard and then Bing. The tools were more consistent at postgraduate level than at undergraduate level, but none of them consistently produced strong literature-based examples or reliable references. ChatGPT tended to generate the most coherent, contextually appropriate essays, while Bing was weakest overall, especially in scientific accuracy and narrative quality. The paper concludes that generative AI can produce plausible academic text in biomedical sciences, but it still falls short on depth, precision, and evidentiary support, which limits its suitability as a substitute for student writing and suggests educators should teach students about both the capabilities and limitations of these tools.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model chatbot used to generate text from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate 1000-word university-level essay responses to biomedical science questions at UK FHEQ levels 4, 5, 6, and 7, and to attempt reference generation for the level 7 prompt.

findings.finding_summary: Across all four FHEQ levels, ChatGPT scored highest of the three tools on scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, context, coherence, and total score. Reported total scores were 70.7% (level 4), 70.4% (level 5), 71.85% (level 6), and 69.75% (level 7), with generally high marker agreement on the undergraduate questions.
findings.measure: Marker-rated essay quality across scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, deviation, context, coherence, and total percentage score

findings.finding_summary: When asked to provide four references for the level 7 response, ChatGPT did not generate direct references and instead stated it could not access external sources and recommended consulting databases or textbooks. The paper reports that none of the models provided appropriate scientific references.
findings.measure: Ability to generate appropriate references on follow-up prompt

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s conversational large language model chatbot; the paper refers to Bard, which is Google’s prior product name for Gemini.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate 1000-word university-level essay responses to biomedical science questions at UK FHEQ levels 4, 5, 6, and 7, and to attempt reference generation for the level 7 prompt.

findings.finding_summary: Bard/Gemini ranked second overall behind ChatGPT but ahead of Bing across all four FHEQ levels. Total scores were 65.85% (level 4), 64.35% (level 5), 62.05% (level 6), and 66.9% (level 7); the paper characterizes its writing as plausible and coherent but often repetitive and less detailed.
findings.measure: Marker-rated essay quality across scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, deviation, context, coherence, and total percentage score

findings.finding_summary: On the level 7 follow-up prompt for references, Bard/Gemini returned websites including Wikipedia and other online resources rather than appropriate scientific literature. The paper states that none of the AI models generated appropriate references.
findings.measure: Ability to generate appropriate references on follow-up prompt

identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model chatbot used to generate text from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate 1000-word university-level essay responses to biomedical science questions at UK FHEQ levels 4, 5, 6, and 7, and to attempt reference generation for the level 7 prompt.

findings.finding_summary: Across all four FHEQ levels, ChatGPT scored highest of the three tools on scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, context, coherence, and total score. Reported total scores were 70.7% (level 4), 70.4% (level 5), 71.85% (level 6), and 69.75% (level 7), with generally high marker agreement on the undergraduate questions.

findings.finding_summary: When asked to provide four references for the level 7 response, ChatGPT did not generate direct references and instead stated it could not access external sources and recommended consulting databases or textbooks. The paper reports that none of the models provided appropriate scientific references.
findings.measure: Ability to generate appropriate references on follow-up prompt

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot category with no single named product specified.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI tools in general as text-generating systems for higher-education essay writing, but its empirical comparison is limited to ChatGPT, Bard/Gemini, and Bing.

findings.finding_summary: The paper concludes that generative AI tools can produce coherent, human-like essay text and often achieve reasonable scientific accuracy, but they are inconsistent in mechanistic detail, context, and reference quality. It also reports that performance differed by model and by FHEQ level, with ChatGPT strongest overall.
findings.measure: Qualitative comparative assessment of generative AI essay output

identified_tools.name: Bing
identified_tools.description: Microsoft’s search-integrated generative AI chatbot, leveraging OpenAI GPT-4 according to the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate 1000-word university-level essay responses to biomedical science questions at UK FHEQ levels 4, 5, 6, and 7, and to attempt reference generation for the level 7 prompt.

findings.finding_summary: Bing consistently scored lowest or near-lowest across the four levels, with total scores of 55.75% (level 4), 52.8% (level 5), 55.25% (level 6), and 64.0% (level 7). The paper notes weaker scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, context, and coherence at UG level, although level 7 performance improved somewhat.
findings.measure: Marker-rated essay quality across scientific accuracy, mechanistic detail, deviation, context, coherence, and total percentage score

findings.finding_summary: On the level 7 follow-up prompt for references, Bing produced entirely fictitious references despite formatting them in conventional citation style. The paper explicitly states that Bing falsified references.
findings.measure: Ability to generate appropriate references on follow-up prompt

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single comparative assessment of AI-generated essay output, not a controlled educational intervention study. It provides descriptive ratings and no causal design, and the evidence is limited to higher-education biomedical science rather than K-12 literacy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests moderate-to-strong differences in output quality across tools, especially for ChatGPT versus Bing, but it reports no effect sizes and no direct student learning outcomes. The practical impact is mainly on assessment design and AI text quality, not demonstrated educational gain.

paper_profiles.title: Breakable Machine: A K–12 Classroom Game for Transformative AI Literacy Through Spoofing and eXplainable AI (XAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for K–12 AI literacy experiences that go beyond teaching students how to build or use AI systems and instead help them critically interrogate how AI works, where it fails, and why those failures matter socially. The authors argue that many existing tools emphasize model training and functional success, but fewer resources help learners examine brittleness, bias, adversarial vulnerability, and the sociotechnical nature of AI.

To meet this need, the paper presents “Breakable Machine,” a browser-based classroom game in which students try to spoof an image classifier by changing their appearance or surroundings to trigger high-confidence misclassifications. The game includes an eXplainable AI heat-map view, a shared leaderboard, and access to training data so students can compare strategies, infer what features the model uses, and reflect on why outputs change. The approach is designed for learners aged 10–15 and is intended for use in classroom settings with mobile devices and internet or local network connectivity.

The paper is a non-empirical design and theory paper rather than an evaluation study. It positions the resource as especially suitable for grades 4–9 and for projects that already introduce basic image classification concepts. The authors conclude that spoofing and failure-based activities can support critical and transformative AI literacy by fostering conceptual understanding, ethical awareness, data agency, and collective sensemaking about AI as a fallible sociotechnical system.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring or instructional AI system that provides adaptive guidance, feedback, or scaffolded learning support.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper describes a browser-based K–12 classroom game, Breakable Machine, designed to teach AI literacy by having students spoof an image classifier and inspect XAI heat maps. It does not evaluate a tutoring system, but it does discuss teaching students about AI systems generally.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a non-empirical design/resource paper. It proposes a classroom game and pedagogical rationale but reports no study, no sample, and no measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No impact data are reported, so there is no measurable evidence of learning gains or other effects.

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (arXiv preprint)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to teach K-12 students how to use generative AI responsibly and effectively for learning, with a specific focus on prompting literacy. The authors argue that as AI chatbots become more available in school contexts, students need explicit instruction on how to craft prompts, when to use AI, and how to interpret AI responses in learning situations.

To address this, the paper presents a web-based AI literacy module built around scenario-based prompting practice. Students interact with a chatbot in three hypothetical secondary-school learning scenarios (biology, geography, and math), write prompts, receive responses, and then get immediate automated feedback from an LLM-based auto-grader on prompt quality. The intervention was iteratively refined across two classroom deployments.

The study was conducted in 11 authentic secondary education classrooms in East Asia, with Study 1 involving 111 students and Study 2 using a similar population to evaluate revised assessment items. The work combines quantitative analyses of auto-grading accuracy, pre/post survey and test outcomes, item difficulty/discrimination, and qualitative thematic analysis of student reflections. The main findings are that the auto-grader performed well overall, students improved in some prompting skills such as adding background/context, confidence in using AI for learning increased, and revised True/False and open-ended assessments measured prompting literacy better than multiple-choice questions.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model chatbot system used for generating responses and automated grading/feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the LLM in the interactive K-12 prompting literacy module; the paper states the auto-grader used OpenAI GPT-4o, and students interacted with an AI chatbot in scenario-based prompt-writing activities.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1, the GPT-4o-based auto-grader achieved an average accuracy of 0.92 when assessing 483 unique student-written prompts, and provided high-quality, detailed feedback. Dimension-level pass/fail accuracy was highest for Relevance (0.98) and Background (0.96), with lower accuracy for Purpose (0.85) and No Direct Answer (0.88).
findings.measure: Auto-grading accuracy for student-written prompts across rubric dimensions

findings.finding_summary: After the learning activity, students’ self-reported confidence in using AI for learning increased by 10.4% on average (SD = 0.92), and the Wilcoxon test indicated this increase was significant (p < .001). The paper reports a significant rightward shift in confidence scores after practice with the GPT-4o-supported module.
findings.measure: 5-point Likert confidence item on ability to use AI to help learning

findings.finding_summary: Students improved in the Background/context dimension of prompt writing across practice tasks; the proportion of students scoring correctly on Background was significantly higher in Q3 than in Q1 (p = .039). The paper also reports that prior AI usage frequency was positively correlated with first-task prompt quality (r = 0.27, p = .017).
findings.measure: Prompt-writing rubric performance and self-reported AI use frequency

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary classroom study with mixed-methods and quasi-experimental pre/post elements, but not a randomized controlled trial. The evidence is useful but limited by a small, context-specific sample and several outcomes are descriptive or correlational.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects include a measurable auto-grader accuracy of 0.92 and a statistically significant confidence increase, suggesting modest practical impact. However, the learning gains are narrow and the paper reports limited improvement on the post-test overall, so the broader impact is still uncertain.

paper_profiles.title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: CHI ’26 Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether and how large language models (LLMs) can effectively support K-12 English-as-a-Foreign-Language (EFL) writing in real-time classroom settings. The authors focus on a tension in educational AI: while LLMs can provide immediate, scalable scaffolding, that same step-by-step support may backfire for some learners, especially under classroom time constraints and varying proficiency levels.

To study this, the authors designed and deployed WriteAid, a chat-based LLM writing support tool, in a South Korean middle school English class. The system offered scaffolded support for sentence construction, vocabulary and grammar questions, and grammar revision, and was co-designed with a teacher to fit the curriculum. The deployment lasted six weeks and involved 157 eighth-grade students, with 133 consenting to data analysis. The study combined system logs, qualitative coding of student interactions, naturalistic classroom observation, a follow-up teacher interview, and a delayed written assessment to examine both immediate interaction patterns and learning transfer.

The findings show that LLM support improved grammatical accuracy during class, but effects varied by proficiency. Higher-performing students tended to use the system for lower-level tasks such as vocabulary translation and checking correctness, while lower-performing students more often outsourced core sentence generation and became demotivated or dependent on the system. Classroom observations also showed that LLMs changed teacher-student dynamics: some students redirected routine questions to the AI, introverted students asked the teacher less, and teachers found it harder to detect common struggles. Overall, the paper concludes that LLM scaffolding can be useful in real-time K-12 writing instruction, but only if systems are made proficiency-aware, teacher-facing, and designed to preserve equity and peer learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI GPT-family large language model system used for interactive text generation, explanation, and feedback in natural language.
