identified_tools.use_case: Used as the underlying LLM in the WriteAid system to provide real-time step-by-step writing scaffolding for K-12 EFL students, including sentence construction, vocabulary/grammar explanations, and grammar revision.

findings.finding_summary: In a six-week deployment with 157 eighth-grade students (133 consented for analysis), the LLM-supported sentence construction feature produced 632 sentences in the fall semester; 309 of those sentences (48.9%) were later incorporated verbatim into students' final essays, and 82.3% of the incorporated sentences were grammatically correct. The paper reports that these sentence-level interactions improved grammatical accuracy during in-class writing, although transfer into final essays varied by proficiency group.
findings.measure: Sentence incorporation into final essays; grammatical correctness of constructed sentences

findings.finding_summary: Higher-performing students more efficiently used the LLM for lower-order tasks such as vocabulary translation and validation, whereas lower-performing students more often used it for sentence and paragraph revision or full sentence generation. The study also found that lower-proficiency students could be demotivated by step-by-step scaffolding and become more dependent on the system, especially under time constraints.
findings.measure: Interaction patterns by proficiency level; affective responses during writing sessions; retention/application of grammar and vocabulary in later writing
findings.sample_size: n=15 sampled for qualitative coding; n=133 consented overall

findings.finding_summary: Classroom observations showed that the LLM reduced teacher burden for repetitive questions and allowed more time to monitor the class, but it also made it harder for the teacher to identify common student difficulties because questions were redirected away from the teacher. The presence of the LLM also shifted peer and teacher-student interaction patterns, with introverted students asking fewer questions aloud and some active students dominating teacher attention.
findings.measure: Classroom observation notes and teacher interview on teacher workload, participation, and equity
findings.sample_size: 3 observed class sessions; n=26 average per class

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-site mixed-methods deployment study with qualitative coding and descriptive/inferential analyses, not a controlled trial or meta-analysis. The evidence is informative but has important limitations in generalizability and causal attribution.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful classroom-process effects and some positive literacy-related outcomes, but effect sizes are not reported and the strongest conclusions are qualitative or mixed. The overall impact appears modest and context-dependent, with notable negative effects for lower-proficiency students under time pressure.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Students to Question the Machine: An AI Literacy Intervention Improves Students Regulation of LLM Use in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether middle-school students need explicit instruction to use large language models (LLMs) effectively in school tasks. The authors focus on a core problem in generative AI use in education: students may over-trust fluent AI outputs, accept weak or underspecified prompts, and fail to monitor or regulate their interactions with the system. The study asks whether a brief AI literacy workshop can improve students’ ability to judge prompt quality, evaluate AI responses, and use follow-up questioning strategically.

The intervention was a two-hour classroom-feasible workshop that combined conceptual instruction about how LLMs work and fail with procedural guidance for interacting with them, such as specifying context, asking follow-up questions, and checking answers for plausibility and consistency. After the workshop, students completed six science inquiry tasks with access to a generative AI system. The comparison group completed the same tasks without prior training. The sample included 116 French students in grades 8–9 (ages 13–15) from one middle school. Outcomes were behavioral and performance-based, including prompt acceptance, follow-up questioning, correctness judgments, and final answer quality.

The main finding is that brief AI literacy instruction improved both how students interacted with the LLM and how well they performed on the science tasks. Trained students more often rejected underspecified prompts, asked more follow-up questions when needed, judged AI responses more accurately, and achieved higher final-answer scores. The intervention did not change students’ self-reported AI literacy or metacognitive scores, and those self-reports did not predict performance. The authors conclude that effective GenAI use in school depends more on explicit training in interaction regulation than on students’ self-perceptions of their AI skills.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI / large language model chatbot system used for interactive question answering, response generation, and iterative problem solving.
identified_tools.use_case: Students used a GenAI chatbot during six middle-school science inquiry tasks; the paper also used GPT-4o as an LLM-as-judge for prompt validation and scoring. The intervention taught students how to regulate interactions with the chatbot rather than how to use a specific branded product.

findings.finding_summary: In a controlled classroom study with N=116 grade 8-9 students, the intervention group achieved higher final-answer performance than controls on a 020 scale (M=11.38, SD=3.87, n=76 vs. M=10.29, SD=3.04, n=40; MannWhitney U=1871, p=.040, r=.19). The authors interpret this as improved performance in LLM-supported science problem solving after a brief AI literacy workshop.
findings.measure: Final written answer validity / exercise score (0-20 scale)

findings.finding_summary: Trained students showed stronger interaction regulation: they accepted fewer suggested prompts overall (p=.018), were less likely to accept underspecified prompts (51.5% vs. 66.7%, p=.044), judged AI answer correctness more accurately, and asked more follow-up questions when initial accepted prompts were underspecified (59.2% vs. 27.9%, p<0.001). The paper reports that these process changes were associated with better outcomes, including approximately +5 points out of 20 for follow-up behavior in the intervention group.
findings.measure: Prompt acceptance, correctness judgments, and follow-up questioning during six science tasks

findings.finding_summary: Self-reported GenAI attitudes/knowledge did not predict performance: overall GenAI self-report scores were not correlated with performance (r=0.01, p=.88, R2<.001, n=116), and pre-post changes in GenAI self-reports did not predict prompt discrimination sensitivity within the intervention group. The workshop also produced no overall pre-post change in GenAI self-report dimensions (repeated-measures MANOVA p=.247).
findings.measure: GenAI self-report questionnaires and pre-post changes

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled classroom study with an intervention and comparison group, but it is not a randomized trial as reported and includes some analytic limitations (single school, no demographic subgroup data). The design is stronger than correlational work, yet some credibility concerns keep it below blue.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main performance effect is modest (r=.19; mean difference about 1.1 points on a 20-point scale) but reliable and accompanied by meaningful process gains in regulation behaviors. This suggests a modest practical impact rather than a large one.

paper_profiles.title: The Agency Gap: How Generative AI Literacy Shapes Independent Writing after AI Support
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether students’ generative AI (GenAI) literacy predicts how well they can write independently after AI support is removed. The authors frame this as an “agency gap”: the extent to which GenAI literacy matters when learners must self-initiate and regulate their own use of AI support. The study asks whether this relationship differs by chatbot interaction style and whether performance during AI-supported writing mediates later independent writing performance.

The intervention compared two GenAI chatbot designs: a reactive chatbot that only responded to student queries, and a proactive chatbot that actively scaffolded learners through structured questioning and iterative feedback. Participants first completed a multimodal academic writing task using visual data with chatbot support, then completed a parallel task without AI support. Writing was scored on insightfulness, visual data integration, organisation and coherence, linguistic quality, critical thinking, and an overall composite score. GenAI literacy was measured with the GLAT, and visualisation literacy was measured as task-related domain knowledge.

The sample consisted of 79 higher-education students or recent graduates from medical and nursing programs recruited online via Prolific. The task context was multimodal academic writing based on visuals derived from healthcare simulation data. Results showed that GenAI literacy predicted independent writing performance mainly in the reactive condition, especially for visual data integration, critical thinking, and overall composite quality, even after controlling for visualisation literacy. In the proactive condition, GenAI literacy was not associated with later independent performance. The findings suggest that proactive scaffolding can reduce dependence on learners’ GenAI literacy, while reactive support makes GenAI literacy more consequential for subsequent independent work.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI chatbot system that can respond to prompts, provide scaffolding, and generate or refine writing support; the paper contrasts reactive and proactive interaction styles rather than naming a specific commercial product.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a chat-based support tool during multimodal academic writing tasks. Participants received either reactive support (responding only to user queries) or proactive support (actively scaffolding with structured questions and iterative feedback), followed by a parallel writing task without AI support.

findings.finding_summary: In the reactive chatbot condition (n=39), GenAI literacy was positively associated with independent writing performance after AI support was removed. Significant correlations were reported for insightfulness (rs=.41, p=.010), visual data integration (rs=.40, p=.013), organisation and coherence (rs=.44, p=.005), linguistic quality (rs=.32, p=.045), critical thinking (rs=.37, p=.019), and composite score (rs=.44, p=.005). These associations remained significant after controlling for visualisation literacy.
findings.measure: Independent multimodal academic writing performance at the AI-removal stage; rubric dimensions and composite score
findings.effect_size: rs=.32 to .44; partial rs=.35 to .45; OR=1.11 to 1.15 in regression

findings.finding_summary: In the reactive condition, high GenAI literacy students outperformed low GenAI literacy students at the AI-removal stage on insightfulness (U=99.00, p=.021, rrb=.34), visual data integration (U=87.50, p=.012, rrb=.36), organisation and coherence (U=67.50, p=.002, rrb=.46), and composite score (U=83.50, p=.009, rrb=.41). At the AI-support stage, only linguistic quality differed significantly (U=120.50, p=.038, rrb=.28). No significant low/high GenAI literacy differences were found in the proactive condition.
findings.measure: Low vs high GenAI literacy group differences in writing rubric scores at AI-support and AI-removal stages

findings.finding_summary: Ordinal logistic regression showed that higher GenAI literacy significantly predicted better independent writing after AI support was withdrawn for visual data integration (b=0.13, SE=0.06, z=2.07, p=.039, OR=1.14), critical thinking (b=0.14, SE=0.07, z=2.18, p=.029, OR=1.15), and composite score (b=0.10, SE=0.05, z=2.15, p=.032, OR=1.11). GenAI literacy did not significantly predict insightfulness, organisation and coherence, or linguistic quality, and chatbot type and visualisation literacy were not significant predictors.
findings.measure: Independent writing performance at AI-removal stage from ordinal logistic regression

findings.finding_summary: Bootstrapped mediation analyses did not support an indirect pathway from GenAI literacy to independent writing through AI-supported performance in either condition. The indirect effects were small and non-significant in both the reactive condition (indirect effect=0.032, 95% CI [-0.022, 0.108]) and proactive condition (indirect effect=0.022, 95% CI [-0.055, 0.102]).
findings.measure: Mediation of AI-support writing performance between GenAI literacy and AI-removal writing performance

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical mixed-method experiment with 79 higher-education participants, but the evidence is correlational/associational within experimental conditions rather than a clean K-12 causal trial. The paper reports multiple analyses with acceptable statistical detail, yet the study design and population limit causal certainty for the requested K-12 evidence context.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects are modest to moderate in size (e.g., rs around .32-.44, rrb up to .46, ORs around 1.11-1.15). The strongest findings suggest meaningful but not large differences in independent writing performance after AI support is removed.

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter presents a conceptual overview of modern generative AI as it relates to information access systems. Rather than reporting an empirical study, it explains how large language models and other generative models change the design space for information retrieval and information synthesis. The paper frames two major paradigms: information generation, where models create tailored outputs directly from user prompts, and information synthesis, where models combine retrieved external information to produce grounded responses.

The chapter first reviews foundational technical components of generative AI, including transformer architectures, scaling laws, training stages such as pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback, as well as prompt optimization. It then discusses multimodal understanding and generation, including how language models support image and video tasks.

A substantial portion of the chapter focuses on retrieval-augmented generation and related information synthesis methods, such as naive and modular RAG, optimization of retrieval and generation, retrieval planning for composite information needs, generative retrieval, and domain-specific modeling. The discussion is broad and theoretical, aimed at explaining opportunities, tradeoffs, and open problems rather than evaluating a specific intervention with a learner population. The main conclusion is that generative AI can improve information access both by directly generating content and by synthesizing external knowledge, but many challenges remain around hallucination, controllability, retrieval integration, and domain adaptation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI / large language model systems that create text, images, or other outputs from prompts, and can also synthesize external information via retrieval-augmented methods.
identified_tools.use_case: The chapter discusses generative AI at a foundational level, focusing on information generation and information synthesis in information access systems, including ChatGPT, Bing with RAG, Midjourney, and related LLM-based methods.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical chapter about generative AI foundations and information access, not an empirical study of a K-12 educational tool or intervention. No research design, sample, or outcome data are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter has broad conceptual relevance to generative AI systems, but it reports no measured educational outcomes, so there is no direct evidence of impact in K-12 literacy or related settings.

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a definitional and conceptual problem in the rapidly growing field of AI literacy in education. The authors argue that, especially after the public introduction of generative AI, studies labeled as "AI literacy" have become highly diverse in their goals, content, and assumptions, making it difficult for researchers and practitioners to compare interventions or use the term consistently. To address this, they conduct an integrative review of empirical and theoretical AI literacy studies published from 2020 through July 2024.

The paper is not an intervention study of a single curriculum; rather, it synthesizes 124 studies to identify how AI literacy is conceptualized across K-12 and higher education. The review analyzes how studies define AI, how they define literacy, what learning goals they pursue, and whether they emphasize technical details of AI, AI as a tool, or AI as a sociocultural system. It also distinguishes functional, critical, and indirectly beneficial literacy perspectives. The resulting framework helps organize the field into combinations of AI and literacy perspectives and highlights emerging generative-AI-related trends, such as increased emphasis on tool use and prompt engineering.

The reviewed literature spans K-12 and post-secondary settings, with a broad range of learner ages and contexts, but the paper itself does not study a specific participant sample. The authors report that K-12 technical and ethics-oriented AI literacy curricula are common, while post-secondary AI literacy research has expanded rapidly in the wake of generative AI, especially around effective use of tools like ChatGPT. They conclude that the field needs more precise terminology and more work on critical and sociocultural approaches to generative AI literacy, especially in settings where students are learning not just to use AI, but to understand and evaluate it critically.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / large language model chatbot or tool used for natural-language interaction, prompting, content generation, and related educational tasks without a single named commercial product specified across the review.
identified_tools.use_case: This integrative review synthesizes K-12 and higher education AI literacy studies in the wake of generative AI, including studies that discuss ChatGPT and other generative AI tools as examples of AI tools used for literacy instruction and prompt engineering.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an integrative review and conceptual framework paper, not an empirical evaluation of a single AI tool or intervention. It synthesizes prior studies rather than reporting primary outcome data suitable for effect estimation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper is conceptually influential and maps emerging AI literacy trends, but it does not report direct outcome impacts from a studied tool. Its impact is on framing and field organization rather than measured learner effects.

paper_profiles.title: What is prompt literacy? An exploratory study of language learners’ development of new literacy skill using generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a new AI-era literacy skill, which the authors call "prompt literacy," emerges when learners use generative AI for a language-learning task. Prompt literacy is defined as the ability to craft precise prompts for AI systems, interpret the outputs, and iteratively refine prompts to obtain desired results. The study asks how this skill develops and whether engaging in prompt-based work affects vocabulary learning and students’ perceptions of generative AI.

The intervention was an AI-powered vocabulary-image creation project. Thirty EFL undergraduate students in a university course in South Korea read about the historical and sociocultural meanings of English words, then used ChatGPT and Bing Image Creator to generate images representing those meanings. Students repeatedly drafted, revised, and re-entered prompts until the generated images matched their intended interpretations. The researchers analyzed the resulting images and prompt revisions, a post-project survey about vocabulary-learning strategies, and written reflections on prompt literacy.

Findings suggest that students developed prompt literacy through iterative prompt refinement, especially by specifying contextual details and character/object actions to better represent word meanings. Survey responses indicated high self-perceived gains in vocabulary-learning strategies such as visual encoding, understanding hidden meanings, contextual use, and imagining word use in situations. Reflection data showed that students viewed prompt literacy as enjoyable, useful for communication and problem-solving beyond the task itself, and important for collaborating effectively with generative AI. The paper concludes that prompt literacy is an emerging literacy relevant to AI-mediated learning, particularly for vocabulary learning in L2 contexts.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot for text-based prompting, question answering, and iterative refinement of outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by 30 EFL college students to confirm word meanings, gather additional information, and support iterative prompt drafting/refinement for vocabulary-image creation.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative/mixed-methods study of 30 EFL students, ChatGPT was used to explore word meanings and origins before students generated images in Bing Image Creator. The paper reports that ChatGPT-supported inquiry helped students develop prompt literacy and self-perceived vocabulary learning strategies, but it does not report inferential effect sizes or a comparison condition.
findings.measure: Students' reflections, prompt revisions, and self-reported vocabulary learning strategy ratings

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools that create outputs such as images from text prompts; in this paper, the named image generator is not uniquely treated as the sole evaluated product in the findings beyond being part of the broader generative-AI workflow.
identified_tools.use_case: The study examined an AI-powered vocabulary-image creation project in which students iteratively drafted, evaluated, and revised prompts to generate images representing English word meanings.

findings.finding_summary: Across 30 EFL students, the paper describes the emergence of 'prompt literacy' as learners refined prompts to better align AI-generated images with intended meanings and contexts. Students reported perceived improvement in vocabulary learning strategies, with high mean ratings on the survey (e.g., hidden meaning M=6.47, use in situation M=6.43), but the study is exploratory and does not report causal effect sizes.
findings.measure: Prompt literacy development, reflection themes, and 7-point Likert self-ratings of vocabulary learning strategies

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative/mixed-methods study with descriptive survey data, not an experimental or quasi-experimental design. It provides useful observational evidence, but no causal inference or effect sizes are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful gains in prompt literacy and self-reported vocabulary learning strategy use, but the evidence is descriptive and not quantified with effect sizes. Impact is therefore plausible but remains unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Situationally-Induced Impairments and Disabilities Research
paper_profiles.venue: CHI’19 Workshop: Addressing the Challenges of Situationally-Induced Impairments and Disabilities in Mobile Interaction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses the problem of how to systematically understand the effects of situationally-induced impairments and disabilities (SIIDs) on mobile interaction. The authors argue that while many environmental and contextual factors can temporarily impair smartphone use, the literature has largely studied these effects in an ad hoc manner, making it difficult to compare impairments or build general sensing, modelling, and adaptation techniques.

The paper does not present a new intervention or a single empirical study. Instead, it synthesizes the authors’ prior work on situational factors such as cold environments, ambient noise, and stress, and proposes a systematic research agenda. The authors emphasize using consistent tasks such as target acquisition, visual search, and text entry, along with baseline conditions and participant training, so that effects of different impairments can be compared fairly.

The context is mobile interaction research with adult participants in prior studies, but this paper itself is a workshop position paper rather than a direct study of a school, classroom, or educational population. The main conclusion is that understanding the magnitude and nature of SIIDs is foundational for later work on sensing, modelling, and adaptive interfaces, and that future research should examine combined situational impairments and more complex tasks.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model chatbot system without a specific branded product named.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied in this paper. The paper is a position paper about situationally-induced impairments and disabilities in mobile interaction, not an AI tool evaluation.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/position paper about situational impairments in mobile interaction, not an empirical study of an AI tool. It does not evaluate a K-12 AI system or report educational outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational AI intervention, effect, or learner outcome is reported, so there is no measurable K-12 impact to rate.

paper_profiles.title: “From Unseen Needs to Classroom Solutions”: Exploring AI Literacy Challenges & Opportunities with Project-Based Learning Toolkit in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the challenges and opportunities of teaching AI literacy in K-12 settings using a project-based learning (PBL) toolkit. The authors ask how teachers understand AI literacy, how they design lessons with a modular toolkit, and how teacher and student background differences shape perceptions of AI tools and classroom use. The core problem is that many educators want to teach AI beyond computer science, but lack resources, confidence, and adaptable materials.

The intervention/approach is a PBL AI literacy toolkit containing three demo tools: AI Art Lab, AI Music Studio, and AI Chatbot. Teachers watched a short demo, explored the toolkit, and then participated in semi-structured interviews and co-design discussions about possible lesson plans. The toolkit was intended to support interdisciplinary AI literacy instruction and to make AI concepts accessible without requiring deep technical expertise.

The study involved 13 middle- and high-school teachers from North America and East Asia, teaching a range of subjects in public, private, and charter schools. Teachers designed example activities for subjects such as science, math, Chinese, IT, English, media arts, and social studies. The paper concludes that the toolkit can support creativity, critical thinking, self-directed learning, and ethical discussion, while also helping teachers address resource constraints and student skill gaps. However, teachers worried about accuracy, trustworthiness, copyright, onboarding burden, and uneven student/teacher AI proficiency. The authors argue that adaptable AI literacy tools and stronger teacher support are needed for scalable K-12 AI education.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / LLM chatbot used for conversational assistance, prompt evaluation, and generating text, images, music, and instructional support. In this paper it appears as part of a PBL AI literacy toolkit alongside AI Art Lab and AI Music Studio.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers explored and designed lessons using the toolkit's AI Chatbot for AI Q&A, concept reinforcement, question prompting, guided inquiry, homework support, and prompt evaluation; the paper also describes generative AI capabilities for text, image, and music generation within the toolkit.

findings.finding_summary: This was a formative qualitative/mixed-methods study of 13 middle and high school teachers, so it did not report student outcome effects for the chatbot. Teachers generally viewed the AI chatbot as useful for self-study, concept clarification, and reducing teacher workload, but also raised concerns about accuracy, trustworthiness, misuse, and uneven student/teacher AI skill levels.
findings.measure: Teacher interviews and thematic analysis of toolkit use, course design, and perceived affordances/barriers

findings.finding_summary: Teachers said the AI chatbot could help students review notes, ask questions outside class, and receive support when teachers could not attend to every student. Several comments framed it as a 24/7 tutor and as a way to save teacher time by answering routine questions or reviewing work.
findings.measure: Teacher-perceived classroom support and workload reduction

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general AI image-generation tool within the toolkit, allowing students to create images from prompts and datasets for instructional projects.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers used the AI Art Lab for design projects, poster/logo creation, image generation activities, and to help students explore AI image generation in subject-specific lessons.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers appreciated the AI Art Lab for creative, hands-on learning and for exposing students to how AI generates images, but some felt it did not fit language-learning contexts well. Teachers also requested more scaffolding and adaptation for different student proficiency levels.
findings.measure: Teacher interviews on fit, usability, and adaptability of AI Art Lab

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general AI music-generation tool within the toolkit, allowing students to generate songs and audio based on teacher-provided rubrics and prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers used the AI Music Studio for vocabulary songs, concept-memorization songs, and creative interdisciplinary activities (e.g., geometry, Chinese vocabulary, science concepts).

findings.finding_summary: Teachers described the AI Music Studio as useful for memorizing concepts and vocabulary through songs and for making learning more engaging. The paper reports teacher-designed activities such as Chinese vocabulary songs and geometry songs, but no student achievement data or effect sizes.
findings.measure: Teacher-designed lesson activities and perceived engagement/memorization support

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods formative study based on interviews with 13 teachers and no experimental student outcome evaluation. The evidence is useful for identifying affordances and implementation barriers, but it does not establish causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful classroom utility for supporting creativity, self-study, and teacher efficiency, but it provides no quantitative effect sizes or student outcome evidence. The reported impact is therefore promising but unclear.

paper_profiles.title: ActiveAI: Enabling K-12 AI Literacy Education & Analytics at Scale
paper_profiles.venue: Companion Proceedings 15th International Conference on Learning Analytics & Knowledge (LAK25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for larger-scale, more replicable evidence in K-12 AI literacy education, an area where the authors note that learning materials and summer programs have grown faster than available data. The main goal is to create an online platform that can support classroom AI literacy instruction while also generating standardized log data for secondary analysis by researchers.

The intervention is ActiveAI, a web-based learning platform built with Next.js and OpenAI APIs. It includes AI literacy modules, surveys, pre-tests, learning activities with an AI agent, and post-tests. The learning experiences are designed using backward design and aligned with AI literacy standards and school priorities, such as identifying LLM hallucinations. The platform serves three user roles: students, teachers, and researchers. Teachers can view aggregated class data, while researchers can download de-identified logs compatible with educational data repositories.

The reported data come from 1,000+ users across 12 secondary schools in North America, Asia, and Australia, with 426 learners completing full pre-test, module, and post-test sequences. The paper reports preliminary analyses of learning gains, gender differences on one module, and variation across educational contexts. Qualitative teacher interviews and student cognitive task analysis were used alongside quantitative performance data, making this a mixed-methods preliminary report rather than a controlled evaluation. The authors conclude that interactive activities are associated with stronger learning gains than passive reading and that the platform can support scalable AI literacy research and practice.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system or interactive learning platform that delivers guided instruction, activities, and feedback to learners.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a K-12 AI literacy learning platform with modules, assessments, and interactive activities involving an AI agent in simulated scenarios; the paper also describes it as an interactive tutoring system in related prior work.

findings.finding_summary: Across 7 learning objectives in 4 modules, the authors report significant learning gains in 4 objectives based on Wilcoxon tests comparing pre- and post-test scores. They do not report effect sizes for these gains in this paper.
findings.measure: Pre-test and post-test scores on AI literacy learning objectives
findings.sample_size: n=426 completed all components; over 1,000 total users

findings.finding_summary: For module 4 (Identify LLM Hallucinations), non-male students achieved significantly higher assessment scores than male students on both the pre-test and post-test, with slightly higher learning gains. The paper reports one-way ANOVA results of f=6.97 (p<0.01) on the pre-test and f=6.80 (p=0.01) on the post-test.
findings.measure: Gender differences in pre-test and post-test assessment scores

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods/conference proceeding paper with preliminary analyses, not a controlled trial or meta-analysis. The evidence is observational and descriptive, with statistical comparisons but limited methodological detail.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports significant gains and subgroup differences, but no standardized effect sizes are provided and the study is preliminary. The practical impact appears promising yet remains unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Digital Literacy and Reading Habits of the Central University of Tamil Nadu Students: A Survey Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines university students’ digital literacy skills and reading habits, with particular attention to whether students prefer print or digital reading materials and how they use various digital tools. The authors ask what students know and can do with digital technologies, how often they use specific digital environments and applications, and what formats they prefer for reading in different situations.

The study uses a quantitative survey design with a structured questionnaire administered to 135 students and research scholars at the Central University of Tamil Nadu in India. Participants included undergraduate, postgraduate, integrated UG/PG students, and research scholars. The survey collected self-reported data on typing, web searching, computer and internet literacy, use of digital environments (email, web, text chat, video conferencing, language apps), digital application skills, and reading preferences for print versus electronic formats.

Findings suggest that respondents generally rated themselves as good or very good in several digital literacy dimensions and frequently used common digital tools, especially email, text chatting, and the web. At the same time, print remained the preferred format for many reading purposes, such as reading in bed, reading for pleasure, and reading with children, while electronic formats were preferred for travel, sharing, and quick access to new material. The authors conclude that students are comfortable with digital media and value digital literacy, but still rely on print for many reading activities.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic category of generative AI / LLM chatbot tools used for producing and interacting with text, language, and information in conversational form.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper does not study a generative AI tool. It is a survey of students' digital literacy, digital device use, and reading habits, with one item mentioning mobile apps for language learning but no named AI system.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper is a cross-sectional survey about digital literacy and reading habits, not an evaluation of an AI tool. It reports descriptive frequencies and self-ratings, with no experimental or quasi-experimental design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI intervention or outcome effect is measured, so there is no evidence of impact attributable to a tool.

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy, Safety Awareness, and STEM Career Aspirations of Australian Secondary Students: Evaluating the Impact of Workshop Interventions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a short AI literacy workshop can improve Australian secondary students’ understanding of AI, safety awareness around synthetic media, and interest in STEM careers. The authors focus on a practical problem: adolescents are exposed to AI-enabled systems and deepfakes in daily life, but schools have limited evidence on how to build foundational AI literacy and ethical awareness in context.

The intervention was the Day of AI Australia workshop program, delivered in three New South Wales government secondary schools. Students in Years 7–10 completed anonymous pre- and post-intervention surveys, with quantitative items measuring AI knowledge, confidence, conceptual understanding, privacy and bias awareness, tool recognition, deepfake experiences, and STEM career aspirations. Open-ended post-survey responses were also thematically analysed to capture what students found useful and how the workshops could be improved. Because surveys were anonymous, pre/post responses were not paired at the individual level.

Results showed that students improved in self-reported AI knowledge and confidence, and became better at recognizing AI in common platforms such as Netflix, Spotify, and TikTok. The intervention also increased interest in AI, computer science, and engineering careers, though the effects on career aspirations were small. Students especially valued interactive, hands-on activities. The authors conclude that one-off workshops can produce short-term gains in AI literacy and safety awareness, but sustained curricular integration is likely needed to influence longer-term outcomes.

identified_tools.name: Day of AI Australia
identified_tools.description: A curriculum-aligned AI literacy program providing workshop-based lessons on foundational AI concepts, ethics, safety, misinformation, and careers for school students.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the workshop intervention delivered to Australian secondary students in Years 7–10 across three government schools.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods pre/post study, the workshop intervention was associated with significant increases in self-reported AI knowledge and confidence among Australian secondary students. The paper reports AI knowledge (r=.445, p<.001) and AI confidence (r=.279, p<.001), with n=205 pre and n=163 post.
findings.measure: Self-reported AI knowledge and confidence (Likert-scale survey items)

findings.finding_summary: Students improved in understanding of AI training and AI bias/errors after the intervention. The reported effects were medium in size for understanding AI training (r=.399, p<.001) and understanding AI bias/errors (r=.302, p<.001).
findings.measure: Self-reported understanding of AI training and AI bias/errors
findings.sample_size: n=201 pre/160 post for training; n=200 pre/160 post for bias/errors

findings.finding_summary: The intervention increased students' ability to identify AI in everyday platforms and systems, including Spotify (+16.2%), TikTok (+12.8%), Netflix (+27.1%), Google (+6.9%), and Face Unlock (+11.2%). Recognition of ChatGPT remained high with no meaningful change (-0.9%).
findings.measure: Proportion identifying tools/platforms as using AI

findings.finding_summary: Career interest in AI, computer science, and engineering increased after the workshop, but the effects were small. The paper reports significant post-intervention shifts for AI career interest (r=.189, p<.001), computer science (r=.115, p=.005), and engineering (r=.119, p=.029).
findings.measure: Self-reported interest in AI, computer science, and engineering careers

findings.finding_summary: Students reported greater privacy skills related to social media and schoolwork, and greater importance placed on data consent after the intervention. Reported effects were small-to-moderate: privacy skills (social media) r=.245, privacy skills (school work) r=.218, and importance of data consent r=.175, all p<.001.
findings.measure: Self-reported privacy skills and data-consent attitudes

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods pre/post intervention study with anonymous, non-paired survey data and some attrition between waves. It provides direct empirical evidence, but the design is not randomized and relies heavily on self-report.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Several outcomes show medium effects, especially AI knowledge (r=.445) and understanding AI training (r=.399), which clears the modest-impact threshold. Other outcomes are small, but the overall intervention effect on literacy is meaningful.

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty‑first century skills in the post‑pandemic world
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual paper examines what digital competencies teachers need to effectively use artificial intelligence (AI) in education, especially in the post-pandemic context where online and blended learning increased the use of AI-enabled tools. The authors argue that AI in education has shifted from student-facing tools such as intelligent tutoring systems toward also including teacher-facing tools for planning, assessment, grading, feedback, and learning analytics, but that teachers often lack the knowledge and preparedness to use these systems well.

The paper does not test an intervention with participants. Instead, it synthesizes literature on AI in education and teacher competency, and adapts two established frameworks—the European DigCompEdu framework and the P21 framework for twenty-first century learning—to propose a revised framework for teachers’ AI digital competency. The authors organize teacher competence into areas such as professional engagement, digital resources, teaching and learning, assessment, empowering learners, and facilitating learners’ own AI competencies.

The context is broad and conceptual rather than a specific school, grade level, or country sample. The paper concludes that teachers need not only technical skills but also pedagogical, ethical, collaborative, and life/career-related competencies to use AI responsibly and effectively. It emphasizes that AI should support, not replace, teachers, and that professional development and updated educational standards are needed to prepare educators and students for AI-rich learning environments.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A class of intelligent tutoring systems that provide automated instructional support, personalized guidance, and progress tracking for learners.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses intelligent tutoring systems as examples of AI technologies that automate personalized learning, support learner progress, and provide just-in-time guidance; it does not evaluate a specific system.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper that synthesizes frameworks and examples rather than reporting an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. It does not present a clear study design, sample, or outcome analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No causal impact on literacy or other student outcomes is estimated in the paper. The article proposes competency frameworks and discusses potential uses of AI tools, but reports no measured effects.

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews empirical research on how artificial intelligence (AI) has been used with and for teachers in K-12 and teacher-education contexts. The authors focus on what kinds of data are collected from teachers, what roles teachers play in AI research and development, what benefits AI may offer teachers, what challenges arise in implementation, and which AI methods are most common.

The review searched Web of Science for English-language journal articles published over the prior 20 years and identified 44 empirical studies relevant to teachers’ use of AI or teacher data used to train/analyze AI systems. The included studies covered in-service and pre-service teachers in elementary, middle, high school, and mixed K-12 settings, with particular attention to classroom-based uses such as monitoring, prediction, automated scoring, and adaptive feedback. The review is not a single intervention study; rather, it synthesizes patterns across diverse AI applications and methods.

The authors conclude that AI can support teacher planning, implementation, and assessment by providing information on students’ needs, timely monitoring, immediate feedback, and automated scoring. They also find that teachers often serve as data sources, algorithm trainers, and validators of AI systems. However, the literature is still limited by reliance on self-reported and observational data, limited multimodal/physiological data, technical constraints, context dependence, and sparse involvement of pre-service teachers. The paper argues for more pedagogically grounded, teacher-inclusive, and multimodal AI development in education.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring or adaptive instructional system that uses AI or machine learning to support instruction, monitoring, feedback, or assessment.
identified_tools.use_case: Systematic review of empirical studies on teachers’ use of AI-based systems in K-12 and teacher education, including tutoring-like, feedback, and automated assessment applications rather than any single named product.

findings.finding_summary: Across 44 empirical studies, the review reports that AI-based systems could help teachers with planning, implementation, and assessment. Reported benefits included timely monitoring, immediate feedback, adaptive intervention, reduced workload, and automated essay scoring, but the paper does not synthesize effect sizes or causal estimates.
findings.measure: Reported advantages of AI for teachers across reviewed studies

findings.finding_summary: The review found several challenges that limit teachers’ effective use of AI, including limited reliability, limited technical capacity, limited infrastructure, context dependence, slow feedback, and insufficient teacher technological knowledge. These are synthesis findings from the reviewed literature rather than pooled causal effects.
findings.measure: Reported challenges in AI use by teachers

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of heterogeneous empirical studies, not a single causal study or meta-analysis. The evidence is useful for mapping the field, but it does not provide pooled effect estimates or strong causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports practical benefits for teacher planning, implementation, and assessment, but no quantitative impact estimates are pooled. Reported effects are suggestive rather than clearly measurable at the paper level.

paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 education should be designed when artificial intelligence is introduced as a collaborative learning agent rather than only as a tool. The authors focus on student-AI collaboration (SAC) and ask what curriculum, interaction supports, learning environments, and developmental stages are needed for students to work productively with AI in learning.

The study uses a qualitative design based on in-depth semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AI in education, including both primary and secondary school teachers. Participants were drawn from schools involved in Korea’s software education and AI pilot initiatives, and interviews explored teachers’ views on learning goals, content, assessment, student-AI interaction, and environmental supports for SAC.

Findings suggest that SAC should aim at capacity building, subject-matter understanding, interdisciplinary and authentic tasks, creative work, process-oriented and collaboration-based assessment, and supports such as AI principles, data literacy, error analysis, AI ethics, and intuitive interfaces. Teachers also emphasized flexible spaces, robust digital infrastructure, strong institutional policy, and a collaborative, safe-to-fail culture. They expected SAC to evolve through three stages: learn about AI, learn from AI, and learn together. The paper concludes with a conceptual and design-oriented framework for supporting student-AI collaboration in K-12 schools.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI/GenAI tutoring or collaborative learning agent that can provide instructional scaffolding, personalized feedback, content support, and adaptive interaction in learning tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a qualitative study of K-12 teachers’ perspectives on designing student-AI collaboration, including how AI should support learning goals, interaction, assessment, and environment. It does not evaluate a specific commercial product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study focused on teachers’ perspectives and a conceptual student-AI collaboration model, not an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. No causal design, effect estimates, or outcome measures are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear conceptual relevance for K-12 AI design and literacy-adjacent learning practices, but it reports no measured impact on student outcomes. As a result, impact on literacy outcomes is theoretical and unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in higher education: Considerations for academic integrity and student learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines how ChatGPT was being discussed in news coverage about higher education in the early months after its release. Rather than evaluating a direct educational intervention, it investigates the public framing of generative AI in relation to academic integrity, assessment, and student learning. The authors ask whether media discussion portrayed ChatGPT primarily as a cheating risk or as a tool that could support learning and inclusion.

The study uses content analysis of 100 English-language news articles published between 2020 and February 2023 from Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The corpus included newspaper and online news sources, and articles were coded for themes such as academic integrity concerns, university responses, policy positions, avoidance/adaptation strategies, and opportunities for embracing ChatGPT in teaching and learning. The paper also coded whose voices were represented, including university staff, students, and ChatGPT/openAI outputs.

The findings show that media discourse was dominated by academic integrity concerns, with frequent discussion of cheating, detection, and assessment redesign. Articles also described ways universities might discourage misuse, while fewer pieces discussed productive educational uses such as feedback, brainstorming, drafting support, or accessibility benefits. Student voices were largely absent. The authors conclude that universities and academics should move beyond a narrow cheating narrative, involve students more directly, and develop clearer, ethically grounded guidance for using generative AI to support learning and participation.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on a large language model, able to generate text responses from user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviews media and public discussion of ChatGPT in higher education, including how it is framed as a tool for academic integrity risk, student learning, and assessment redesign.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a content analysis of news articles, not an empirical evaluation of ChatGPT on student outcomes. It reports discourse patterns and themes rather than causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests possible implications for student learning, integrity, and policy, but does not measure an outcome effect size. Impact is therefore indirect and unclear rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review that maps and synthesizes evidence syntheses on artificial intelligence in higher education. The authors ask what kinds of AI evidence syntheses have been conducted, where they are published, who is doing the work, what methods and technologies are used, how high the review quality is, and what AI application areas and findings dominate the literature. The motivation is to provide a more rigorous, field-level picture of AI in education at a time of rapid growth and increasing public attention to generative AI.

The review searched major bibliographic databases and additional sources for English-language journal articles and conference papers published from January 2018 to July 2023 that were secondary studies on AI in formal higher or continuing education and had a method section. From 5,609 records, 66 reviews focused solely on higher education and were included for synthesis. The corpus spans a range of review types, but systematic literature reviews were most common. Most reviews addressed general AI in higher education, with substantial attention also given to profiling and prediction and adaptive systems/personalisation; fewer focused specifically on assessment/evaluation or intelligent tutoring systems.

The paper concludes that AIHEd evidence synthesis has grown quickly but is uneven in quality and reporting transparency. Common shortcomings included incomplete reporting of search methods, inter-rater reliability, coding schemes, and quality appraisal. The review also found that AI applications in higher education are most often discussed in relation to teaching and learning support, especially adaptive systems, chatbots, personalised content, and predictive uses, with comparatively less attention to administrative applications. The authors call for greater ethical scrutiny, stronger methodological rigour, and more interdisciplinary and context-sensitive research in future primary and secondary studies.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A general category of intelligent tutoring systems and related AI instructional support tools that provide adaptive instruction, diagnosis, and automated feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a tertiary review of AI in higher education and uses ITS as one of Zawacki-Richter et al.'s thematic categories for classifying reviewed evidence syntheses; it does not evaluate a single ITS product.

findings.finding_summary: Across the higher-education review corpus, only 21.2% (n=14) of evidence syntheses discussed intelligent tutoring systems. The paper characterizes ITS as AI that teaches course content, diagnoses strengths and weaknesses, offers automated personalised feedback, curates learning materials, and supports collaboration, but it does not report a pooled causal effect for literacy or any other outcome.
findings.measure: Frequency and thematic characterization of ITS-focused evidence syntheses within the review corpus

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic category for generative AI chatbots and text-generation tools without a named product specified.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper mentions generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, DALL-E, Bard, and LLaMA in the introduction and explicitly excludes generative AI/ChatGPT-focused reviews from the included corpus; no empirical evaluation of a specific generative AI tool is conducted.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-systematic review of secondary studies rather than a direct empirical evaluation of an AI tool. It provides descriptive synthesis of review characteristics and themes, not a causal study of a named product or intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has field-level relevance because it maps AI application areas and evidence quality, but it does not estimate an intervention effect on student outcomes. Any impact is indirect and interpretive rather than measured as an effect size.

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in higher education: Benefits, challenges, and future research directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the potential benefits and challenges of using ChatGPT in higher education, framed by constructivist theory of learning. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention, it offers a perspective on how generative AI may reshape teaching, learning, assessment, and academic support in tertiary settings. The authors organize the discussion around five perceived benefits and five major challenges, then propose 19 propositions for future research and institutional practice.

The paper treats ChatGPT as a general-purpose generative AI tool that can support adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research and writing assistance, automated administrative services, and innovative assessment design. In contrast, it identifies risks related to ethics and equity, academic integrity, bias and falsified information, limitations in assessing or reinforcing graduate skills, and difficulties in evaluating student learning outcomes. These issues are discussed in relation to constructivist ideas such as active learning, scaffolding, authentic assessment, and social interaction.

The population and context are higher education users, specifically students, academics/educators, and administrative staff in tertiary institutions. The paper does not study a specific intervention, sample, or outcome; instead, it argues that AI use should be paired with responsible-use education, redesigned assessments, and attention to fairness and reliability. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT can enhance learning experiences in higher education, but only if institutions balance innovation with ethical safeguards and preservation of meaningful learning processes.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT/LLM technology that can generate text, answer questions, provide feedback, and support personalized interactions.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a generative AI tool in higher education, with proposed uses for adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research/writing support, automated administrative support, and innovative assessment activities; no empirical classroom study was reported.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical article rather than an empirical study. It proposes benefits, challenges, and propositions about ChatGPT but does not report a causal design, sample, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ChatGPT may support learning, feedback, and assessment, but it provides no effect sizes or outcome data. Impact is therefore speculative and based on conceptual discussion rather than demonstrated effects.

paper_profiles.title: Evolution and Revolution in Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a historical and forward-looking position piece on the field of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED), rather than an empirical study of a specific intervention. The authors ask what the field’s strengths have been over the previous 25 years and what directions it should take to remain relevant as education changes.

To answer this, the paper analyzes 47 papers published in the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education across three benchmark years (1994, 2004, and 2014). The analysis codes papers by type, domain, breadth, interaction style, collaborative structure, technology, setting, and learning goals, with a particular focus on how AIED has emphasized student use of computers in formal school settings, often in STEM, step-based problem-solving contexts.

The paper argues that AIED has made strong progress in improving tutoring systems and evaluation rigor, but also that the field remains too narrow. It proposes two parallel directions: an evolutionary path that refines existing classroom-centered work in collaboration with teachers, and a revolutionary path that embeds intelligent learning environments into learners’ everyday lives, supports broader skills and contexts, and expands beyond stand-alone computer-based tutoring. The paper concludes that future AIED research should diversify technologies, domains, settings, and stakeholders, including stronger integration with classroom practice, culture, informal learning, and teacher collaboration.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system is an adaptive educational software environment that provides individualized instruction, hints, feedback, and support based on learner responses and models of learner knowledge.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a historical/review analysis of AI in education papers and discusses ITS/ILE research trends rather than evaluating a single system; it references intelligent tutoring systems broadly as the dominant class of tools in the field.

findings.finding_summary: Across 47 IJAIED papers from 1994, 2004, and 2014, the authors report a shift toward more empirical work, greater breadth of topics, more collaboration support, and stronger learning goals beyond domain knowledge. They characterize this as evidence that ITS/ILE research has become more rigorous and more classroom-relevant over time, but no single causal effect size is reported because this is a review synthesis.
findings.measure: Review coding of 47 papers by empirical status, domain, interaction style, collaborative structure, and learning goals

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative historical review of IJAIED papers, not a primary evaluation of one tool with causal identification. The paper synthesizes trends descriptively and does not report experimental estimates for a specific system.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ITS/ILE research is becoming more rigorous and broader in scope, which is potentially important at the field level. However, it does not provide a measurable effect estimate for a tool, so impact on student outcomes cannot be quantified from this paper.

paper_profiles.title: The Potential Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Equity and Inclusion in Education
paper_profiles.venue: OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers / OECD Education Working Papers Series
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This OECD working paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) may affect equity and inclusion in education, with a particular focus on school education. It is not an empirical intervention study; rather, it develops a conceptual framework for thinking about AI tools in education and their potential benefits and risks for different learners and educational actors. The paper organizes the field using a taxonomy of AI tools based on their primary beneficiary and purpose.

The paper distinguishes among three categories of AI tools: learner-centred tools, teacher-led tools, and other institutional tools. Learner-centred tools include intelligent tutoring systems, AI-enabled simulations, tools supporting students with special education needs, and chatbots that inform or advise students. Teacher-led tools include systems that support assessment, classroom management, curation of learning materials, and continuing professional learning. Institutional tools include smart admissions systems, tools for identifying at-risk students, and data-based decision supports.

The working paper discusses how these tools may promote equity and inclusion through adaptive learning, richer content, accessibility supports, and improved institutional decision-making, while also warning about access disparities, techno-ableism, bias, privacy, and over-commercialisation. The authors emphasize that evidence for many AI tools remains limited and that many claims about benefits are still hypothetical rather than based on robust evaluation. The paper concludes by calling for more systematic research, stronger policy guidance, and careful implementation to ensure AI supports rather than undermines equitable and inclusive education.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI / large language model chatbots used to generate text, answer questions, and support tutoring or writing. In this paper, these are discussed as part of the broader category of learner-centred AI tools, with examples including chatbots and text-rewriting tools.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI as a learner-centred tool for tutoring, writing support, information retrieval, and simulation, including references to ChatGPT as an example of a chatbot used in education, but it does not evaluate a specific product empirically.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a policy/review-style working paper that synthesises concepts, examples, opportunities, and challenges rather than reporting an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. It provides no clear study design, counterfactual, or causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No tool-level outcomes or effect sizes are reported. The paper is descriptive and conceptual, so impact on literacy or other outcomes cannot be quantified from the text.

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review of AI, VR, and LLM applications in special education: Opportunities, challenges, and future directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and large language models (LLMs) in special education, with a focus on opportunities, challenges, and future directions. The review asks how these technologies are being used for students with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), how they may be combined, what special education methodologies support their adoption, and what barriers remain for implementation and inclusion.

The authors conducted a systematic review and deductive thematic analysis of 139 studies retrieved from ArXiv and ScienceDirect. The paper synthesizes literature on VR/AR interventions, AI/LLM-based tools, teacher attitudes toward inclusion and technology, and syndrome-specific assistive applications spanning autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disabilities, down syndrome, visual and hearing impairments, learning disabilities, motor disabilities, speech impairments, and emotional/psychological disorders. The context is broad special education practice rather than a single intervention site, and the review considers both student-facing and teacher-facing uses of these technologies.

The main conclusion is that VR, AR, AI, and LLMs each show promise for personalized learning, engagement, communication, and accessibility, but evidence remains fragmented and largely theoretical with limited integrated frameworks for special education. The paper emphasizes unresolved issues including accessibility, bias, cybersecurity, privacy, cost, teacher preparedness, and the need for clearer policies and professional development. It concludes that future work should develop robust implementation frameworks and cross-sector collaboration to support equitable and effective use of these technologies in special education.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic large language model / generative AI chatbot or assistant used for language generation, question answering, feedback, personalization, and related educational support.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic review synthesizes literature on LLMs and other AI/immersive technologies in special education, including uses such as tutoring, feedback, lesson-planning support, content generation, and adaptive communication. It does not evaluate one specific named product as the sole focus; instead it discusses heterogeneous LLM-based systems and applications.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that LLMs and AI can support literacy-related tasks in special education, including simplifying complex texts into Easy-to-Read formats and supporting literacy learning through personalized, multimodal interaction. It also notes that some VR-based interventions were effective in literacy and language learning for students with ADHD, but the paper does not provide pooled effect sizes or controlled-study estimates.
findings.measure: Literacy and language learning outcomes; text simplification/accessibility for cognitive impairments

findings.finding_summary: The review concludes that AI/LLMs may enhance personalized learning, accessibility, inclusion, and teacher support in special education, but emphasizes major concerns about bias, safety, hallucinations/false information, privacy, and lack of validated frameworks. It highlights that teacher-AI collaboration may assist grading, progress tracking, content generation, and personalized feedback, while human oversight remains necessary.
findings.measure: Reported opportunities and challenges for AI/LLM use in special education

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review synthesizing heterogeneous prior studies rather than a primary experimental evaluation. The evidence base is broad, but the paper reports thematic synthesis without pooled quantitative estimates for a single tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for literacy support and personalized learning, but the reported outcomes are qualitative and mixed, with no effect sizes or causal estimates. The practical impact is therefore promising but not quantifiable from this review.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in undergraduate medical education: an updated scoping review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI), especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, has been used in undergraduate medical education (UGME) and how the literature changed after the public release of generative AI tools in late 2022. The authors aimed to map the evolving landscape of AI-related publications, identify major application areas, summarize perceptions of AI among students and faculty, and clarify what competencies, teaching methods, and ethical considerations are being proposed for medical curricula.

The study is a scoping review conducted with Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards. The authors searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, Google Scholar, and Unika for English- and Spanish-language publications from January 2020 to April 2024. After screening 3,238 records, they included 310 publications covering medical students, faculty, and UGME-related AI applications. The review synthesized studies on autonomous tutoring, personalized learning, simulation, assessment generation and grading, feedback tools, and LLM performance on exams and educational tasks.

The review found rapid growth in AI-related UGME literature after ChatGPT’s release, with most studies reporting positive attitudes toward AI but also concerns about accuracy, bias, plagiarism, and overreliance. The authors conclude that evidence remains early and fragmented, with many studies small, single-site, and focused on perceptions or short-term outcomes rather than robust learning effects. They argue for clearer AI competencies, longitudinal curricular integration, faculty development, and stronger evaluation of impacts on critical thinking, clinical reasoning, ethics, and assessment practices.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system used for conversational text generation, question answering, tutoring-style support, and content creation.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied across multiple UGME uses including personalized learning, exam preparation, generating learning content and exam questions, self-assessment, case-based learning support, and feedback/assessment tasks; also discussed as the most frequently mentioned LLM-based tool in the review.

findings.finding_summary: Across the included UGME literature, ChatGPT was reported as helpful for exam preparation, clarifying complex physiological processes, creating mnemonics, explaining clinical vignettes, and generating learning content. It was also found useful for medical terminology learning and case-based learning support, though the review notes content-quality and accuracy concerns and emphasizes the need for human oversight.
findings.measure: Reported usefulness, posttest scores, and qualitative evaluations of learning support and content accuracy across included studies

findings.finding_summary: The review summarized several studies in which ChatGPT performed at or near passing levels on USMLE exams and was compared with other tools for question answering. However, other included studies reported it was unreliable for some self-assessment tasks and that outputs sometimes contained inaccuracies, especially when used to generate exam questions or answer long-form questions.
findings.measure: Exam performance, self-assessment performance, and accuracy on generated/answered questions

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's generative AI chatbot/LLM system, including Bard/Gemini-family tools, used for conversational assistance and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned in a comparison study summarized in the review as being used alongside ChatGPT for answering multiple-choice and long-answer medical questions.

findings.finding_summary: In the review’s summary of included studies, Bard (normalized here to Gemini) was compared with ChatGPT on medical question answering. ChatGPT was slightly superior on endocrinology and diabetes MCQs, while both models lacked up-to-date information; another study found ChatGPT-3.5 and Bard unreliable as self-assessment tools for medical studies.
findings.measure: Multiple-choice question answering and self-assessment reliability

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a scoping review synthesizing heterogeneous studies rather than a single controlled experiment or meta-analysis. The evidence is broad but mostly descriptive, with many included studies being surveys, perspectives, or small interventions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports potentially meaningful educational uses of ChatGPT and Gemini-family tools, but the effect magnitude is largely not reported and many findings are qualitative or mixed. Reported impacts appear promising but remain uncertain and context-dependent.

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of ChatGPT as a Brainstorming Tool on Gifted Students’ Persuasive Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT 3.5 can function as a prewriting brainstorming tool to improve persuasive writing quality. The authors focus on a narrowly defined use of generative AI: not as a teacher-facing planning or feedback system, but as a student-facing ideation aid used before drafting. The study is motivated by concerns that gifted writers may experience perfectionism, difficulty generating ideas, and pressure from expectations, which can hinder writing performance.

The intervention was tested with five gifted senior students majoring in Arabic in the College of Education at Kuwait University. The researchers used an integrated single-subject design with multiple probes across multiple baselines, with students writing persuasive essays across baseline, intervention, and maintenance phases. During intervention, students received explicit instruction and practice on using ChatGPT 3.5 for brainstorming, then used it for 20 minutes before writing each essay. Quantitative outcomes were rated with an adapted persuasive essay rubric, and qualitative social-validity data were collected through a focus group interview.
