Results showed that all participants improved from baseline to intervention, with gains especially strong in rhetorical dimensions such as argumentation, supporting evidence, opposing viewpoints, and voice/tone. Most students maintained gains three weeks later, though one twice-exceptional student showed no maintenance increase. In focus group data, students reported that ChatGPT was efficient, generated abundant ideas, and was helpful for difficult or socially sensitive topics, but they also noted limitations such as repetition, outdated information, and the need to verify AI-generated ideas. The authors conclude that ChatGPT 3.5 can complement traditional brainstorming, while emphasizing careful, critical use rather than dependency.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot for interactive dialogue and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a prewriting brainstorming tool (ChatGPT 3.5) to help gifted Arabic-speaking senior students generate ideas before writing persuasive essays.

findings.finding_summary: In a single-subject multiple-baseline study with five gifted students, persuasive writing quality increased for all participants after ChatGPT 3.5 was introduced as a brainstorming tool. Mean essay scores rose from baseline to intervention for each student, and the authors reported PND = 100% for all five participants, indicating a strong functional relation between the intervention and writing performance.
findings.measure: Overall quality of persuasive essays (Persuasive Essay Rubric; 0-48)

findings.finding_summary: Detailed rubric scores showed large gains in persuasive-writing-specific components after ChatGPT 3.5 brainstorming, especially argument, supporting evidence, opposing viewpoints, and voice/tone. General writing components such as organization, word choice, sentence fluency, and conventions changed little by comparison.
findings.measure: Persuasive Essay Rubric subscales

findings.finding_summary: Effects generally persisted at maintenance 3 weeks later. Four of five students showed continued improvement or retention of gains; one twice-exceptional student showed no additional gain from intervention to maintenance (maintenance mean remained 36).
findings.measure: Maintenance phase persuasive essay scores

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small single-subject intervention study with repeated measures and staggered baselines, which provides causal evidence but not the breadth or randomization of a blue-tier design. The sample is very small (n=5), limiting generalizability.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Reported gains were large in the primary outcome, with PND reported as 100% and clear score increases for all participants. The study attributes substantial improvement in persuasive writing quality to the ChatGPT brainstorming intervention.

paper_profiles.title: Adaptive Artificial Intelligence for Students with Specific Learning Disabilities in Reading Science Content
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the challenges that students with reading-related learning disabilities, especially dyslexia, face when using mainstream generative AI tools for science learning. The authors argue that current text-based large language models are insufficiently adaptive, lack multimodal supports, and do not provide the real-time individualized scaffolding needed by neurodiverse learners. The paper frames these limitations as a barrier to accessible science instruction and learning.

To address this problem, the paper proposes an adaptive AI approach that uses functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) signals and a convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify cognitive demand while students read science texts. The system then adjusts text complexity, reading level, and lexical density in near real time. Although the paper presents laboratory data with 100 students, including 50 students diagnosed with dyslexia and 50 neurotypical students, the main contribution is a proposed neuroadaptive model rather than a classroom intervention focused on teacher-facing planning or feedback tools.

The study context is a controlled laboratory setting with elementary-aged students from schools in a county in the southeastern United States. The authors report that the CNN achieved 0.86 accuracy in classifying cognitive demand and that adaptive text adjustments were associated with improved reading comprehension and test performance, especially for students with dyslexia. The paper concludes that brain-computer-interface-informed adaptive AI could improve accessibility in science learning, but it also acknowledges the need for multimodal supports, longer-term evaluation, and broader implementation research.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model / generative AI chatbot that produces text-based explanations and can be used to generate or adapt educational content.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generic LLM-based tools such as ChatGPT and describes generating science texts with a public-access LLM for adaptive reading tasks; the study itself evaluates an fNIRS-driven text-adaptation pipeline rather than a specific commercial tutoring product.

findings.finding_summary: In the adaptive text condition, students with dyslexia showed improved reading comprehension, with average scores increasing from 55% to 75%. The paper reports that adaptive text adjustments based on fNIRS-classified cognitive demand significantly improved reading comprehension, F(1,48)=35.67, p<.001.
findings.measure: Reading comprehension / content assessment scores

findings.finding_summary: Adaptive text adjustments also improved test performance for students with dyslexia, with average scores increasing from 60% to 78%. The paper reports a significant effect of adaptive text adjustments on test performance, F(1,48)=29.45, p<.001.
findings.measure: Content test performance

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical / method-development paper with an internally described experimental procedure, but the reporting is not sufficient for a clear, well-validated causal study in the usual evidence-framework sense. The text contains strong claims and methodological ambiguities, so the overall evidence quality is low.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports relatively large pre-post percentage gains for dyslexic students in comprehension and test performance, which would indicate medium-to-large impact if valid. However, because the design and reporting are not robustly established, the impact tier should be interpreted cautiously.

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review of AI in second language acquisition using the expanded SAMR model (2015–2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether AI applications in second language acquisition (SLA) primarily enhance existing language-learning tasks or truly transform them. To answer this, the authors systematically reviewed empirical journal articles on AI in SLA published between 2015 and 2024, using the expanded SAMR model to classify each study according to whether technology use left the product and process unchanged, redesigned one of them, or redesigned both.

The review screened Web of Science and Scopus and included 281 studies after full-text assessment. Because this was a review rather than a single classroom intervention, it did not focus on one learner cohort or one instructional setting; instead, it synthesized studies spanning multiple language skills, tools, and contexts. The paper also coded whether studies used generative AI and examined how SAMR levels varied by skill area and year.

The main conclusion is that most AI-in-SLA work still sits at the augmentation level, meaning AI mainly speeds up feedback or makes existing routines more efficient. About 35% of studies reached modification or redefinition, with GenAI appearing more often in later years and especially in transformation-level designs, but not serving as a guarantee of transformation. Writing and speaking dominated the corpus and mostly remained enhancement-oriented, while reading, listening, and vocabulary more often reached higher levels of redesign. The review ends by proposing a GenAI-driven three-stage framework for pre-class, in-class, and post-class use, and argues that deeper transformation requires pedagogical redesign, not just better tools.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot systems used for text generation, dialogic support, and feedback in educational settings.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of AI in second language acquisition; it codes empirical studies across SAMR levels and discusses GenAI as an enabler of transformation in literacy-related language tasks, without focusing on a single named product.

findings.finding_summary: Across 281 empirical AI-in-SLA studies (20152024), 35% reached Modification or Redefinition and 63% remained at Augmentation. The review states that GenAI appeared in roughly 47% of transformation-stage investigations (33/71) across 20232024, but a 2�d72 chi-square test found no significant association between GenAI use and transformation stage (M/R) versus enhancement stage (S/A), c7�b2(1, N=212)�02  p .96.
findings.measure: SAMR-coded transformation vs enhancement across reviewed studies; chi-square test of GenAI use by SAMR stage

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review with transparent search, screening, and coding procedures, but it synthesizes heterogeneous studies rather than reporting a single causal effect estimate. The evidence is observational/descriptive, so it supports mapping and synthesis more than causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests GenAI can enable transformation in some literacy-related designs, but the reported statistical test found no significant overall association between GenAI use and higher SAMR levels. With no effect size and mixed direction, the impact is plausible but unclear.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT-like systems, for education. The central question is how these models might be used to support learning and teaching while also introducing risks related to bias, privacy, integrity, overreliance, and unequal access.

The paper is not an intervention study. Instead, it synthesizes emerging applications and proposes a conceptual discussion of use cases such as generating educational content, providing personalized feedback, supporting language learning, aiding assessment, and assisting teachers with lesson planning and professional development. It also highlights broader educational technology opportunities, including use in immersive AR/VR environments and multilingual access.

The intended populations are broad and include learners from elementary school through higher education, as well as teachers and educational institutions. The paper specifically mentions support for learners with disabilities and multilingual access, but it does not report an empirical sample or subgroup analysis. Its main conclusion is that large language models have substantial educational promise, but responsible adoption requires strong human oversight, ethical safeguards, curriculum integration, and attention to fairness, privacy, and sustainability.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Large language models / generative AI chatbots that can generate text, answer questions, provide feedback, summarize content, and personalize learning or teaching supports.
identified_tools.use_case: Position paper discussing opportunities and challenges of large language models in education, with examples including GPT-3, ChatGPT, and BLOOM; no single system is empirically evaluated.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and literature discussion rather than an empirical study. It does not report a study design, sample, or outcomes from a controlled evaluation of a specific tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that large language models may improve reading, writing, feedback, personalization, and access, but these are proposed opportunities rather than measured effects. Because no effect sizes or empirical impacts are reported, the impact remains unquantified and only cautiously suggestive.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT and large language models in academia: opportunities and challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial examines the emergence of ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs) and argues that they represent a major shift in how text can be generated, edited, and used in academic work. The paper focuses on opportunities and risks rather than reporting an empirical study. It discusses how LLMs may support academic writing, education, programming, grant writing, and peer review, while also raising concerns about hallucinations, plagiarism, bias, access, and environmental cost.

In education, the authors emphasize possible uses of ChatGPT as a classroom aid, interactive study guide, writing assistant, and feedback tool. They suggest it may be especially helpful for non-native English speakers as a writing and editing support, and they also describe how educators might adapt assignments and assessments in response to student use of LLMs. The paper is framed around students and educators across K-12 and higher education, but it does not present data from a specific school, grade level, or instructional setting.

The authors conclude that LLMs should be embraced as useful tools, but only with careful attention to bias, accuracy, disclosure, and ethical use. They argue that LLM outputs should be checked, that bias metrics are needed, and that LLM-generated text should not automatically be treated as plagiarism. Overall, the paper is a position piece that outlines likely educational applications and cautions, rather than testing effects on learning outcomes.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot for generating and revising text, answering questions, and supporting interactive dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a general-purpose generative AI chatbot for academic writing, education, programming, and as an example of LLM use in K-12 and higher education contexts; no empirical evaluation of K-12 literacy outcomes in this paper.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an editorial/opinion piece rather than an empirical study. It discusses ChatGPT's potential uses and risks, but does not report original data, a study design, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No impact effect can be estimated because the paper provides no outcome data or effect sizes. The discussion is conceptual only.

paper_profiles.title: A Prompt Pattern Catalog to Enhance Prompt Engineering with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to engineer prompts more effectively for conversational large language models such as ChatGPT. Rather than studying an educational intervention or learner outcome, it proposes a structured catalog of prompt patterns that can be used to improve the clarity, control, and usefulness of LLM outputs and interactions.

The approach is a framework paper that documents 16 prompt patterns, including Meta Language Creation, Output Automater, Flipped Interaction, Persona, Question Refinement, Alternative Approaches, Cognitive Verifier, and Fact Check List. These patterns are presented in a common pattern form with intent, motivation, structure, example implementation, and consequences. The paper’s examples are mostly drawn from software development and general LLM use, not K-12 education.

No educational population is studied, and there is no intervention, sample, or outcome analysis involving students, teachers, or schools. The main conclusion is that prompt patterns provide reusable, domain-adaptable ways to structure prompts and interactions with LLMs, and that they can help users elicit better outputs, reduce ambiguity, and improve workflow automation. The paper also argues that prompts should often be treated as a form of programming and documented in a way that supports reuse and transferability.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used for prompt-based text generation and interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper presents and tests a catalog of prompt patterns using ChatGPT as the LLM for all examples and demonstrations.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/framework paper about prompt patterns, not an empirical study evaluating learning outcomes. It does not report a research design, sample, or measured effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational outcome or impact on K-12 learners is measured. The paper proposes prompt-engineering patterns for ChatGPT rather than demonstrating impact in literacy or any other domain.

paper_profiles.title: A Multitask, Multilingual, Multimodal Evaluation of ChatGPT on Reasoning, Hallucination, and Interactivity
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 13th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 3rd Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a broad benchmark framework for evaluating ChatGPT across multiple NLP capabilities, including summarization, machine translation, sentiment analysis, question answering, task-oriented dialogue, open-domain knowledge-grounded dialogue, misinformation detection, reasoning, hallucination, and multimodal generation. The authors aim to move beyond anecdotal reports by systematically testing the model’s strengths and weaknesses using publicly available datasets and manually checked outputs.

The approach is not an educational intervention but a large-scale model evaluation. It examines ChatGPT in zero-shot settings on 21–23 datasets, with additional experiments on multilingual performance, multi-turn interaction, and code-mediated multimodal generation. The evaluation includes languages spanning high-, medium-, low-, and extremely low-resource categories, and it assesses reasoning across deductive, inductive, abductive, mathematical, temporal, spatial, commonsense, causal, multi-hop, and analogical categories.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT performs strongly on many tasks in zero-shot settings and can sometimes match or exceed fine-tuned models, but it remains unreliable in reasoning, weak in low-resource and non-Latin-script languages, and prone to hallucination. Multi-turn interaction can improve outputs in summarization, translation, and image-generation-by-code tasks, but the authors emphasize that ChatGPT’s capabilities are inconsistent and far from comprehensive.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI system based on a GPT-family large language model, fine-tuned for dialogue and interactive text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper benchmarks ChatGPT on multitask NLP, multilingual understanding and translation, multimodal code-based image generation, reasoning, factuality/hallucination, and multi-turn interactivity.

findings.finding_summary: On 9/13 NLP datasets with reported zero-shot LLM baselines, ChatGPT outperformed previous zero-shot LLMs. The paper also reports that it outperformed fully fine-tuned task-specific models on 4 tasks, though it lagged behind task-specific fully fine-tuned models in most settings.
findings.measure: Task performance across summarization, translation, sentiment analysis, QA, misinformation detection, dialogue, and knowledge-grounded dialogue
findings.sample_size: subsets of 30 to 200 samples per task

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed stronger performance on high-resource languages and weaker performance on low-resource and extremely low-resource languages. For sentiment analysis and language identification, it achieved 84% accuracy on English, 80% on Indonesian, 78% on Javanese, and 56% on Buginese; for language identification the corresponding accuracies were 100%, 100%, 0%, and 12%.
findings.measure: Accuracy on sentiment analysis and language identification
findings.sample_size: 4 languages; n not clearly reported in the table excerpt

findings.finding_summary: In machine translation, performance was substantially better for high-resource languages than for low-resource languages. The paper reports 24/30 and 29/30 correct XXXEng translations for Chinese and French, versus 7/30 and 9/30 for Javanese and Sundanese; for EngXXX translation, the low-resource languages again performed poorly (6/30 and 0/30).
findings.measure: Manual correctness of translation outputs

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT's reasoning performance was uneven: it was stronger on deduction than induction, weaker on mathematical and spatial reasoning, and relatively strong on commonsense and temporal reasoning. For example, it scored 23.33% (7/30) on MATH, 26/30 on timedial, and 43.33% and 43.75% on StepGame and SpartQA respectively.
findings.measure: Accuracy on reasoning benchmarks
findings.sample_size: Multiple benchmarks; typically n=30 per task, MATH n not explicitly stated in excerpt

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT suffered from hallucination across tasks, especially extrinsic hallucinations in generation settings. The paper states that hallucination was observed in machine translation and QA, while intrinsic hallucinations were rare in summarization and knowledge-grounded open-domain dialogue.
findings.measure: Qualitative hallucination inspection across tasks

findings.finding_summary: Interactive multi-turn prompting improved performance. The paper reports gains of 7.99 ROUGE-1 and 1.64 ROUGE-2 on summarization, and 2% ChrF++ on low-resource machine translation, with 34% of samples improving from turn 1 to 2 and 36% from turn 2 to 3 in the flag-drawing task.
findings.measure: ROUGE-1/ROUGE-2, ChrF++, and flag-drawing error grades across turns
findings.sample_size: 50 SAMSum documents; 50 national flags; MT sample size adapted from translation subset

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark-style empirical paper, but it is not a controlled educational study and does not evaluate K-12 learners or instructional outcomes. The evidence is useful for understanding model capabilities, yet the methodology is heterogeneous and not designed for causal inference in education.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful performance differences on several NLP tasks, including clear weaknesses on low-resource languages and gains from interactivity. However, it does not provide educational effect sizes for K-12 literacy outcomes, so direct instructional impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a systematic review of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education from 2016 through 2022. The authors sought to update prior reviews and answer three questions: where the research was conducted, what academic levels and subject domains were studied, and who the intended users were, as well as how AI was being used in higher education settings.

The review included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles identified through database and hand searches, screened using PRISMA procedures. The studies covered six continents, with the largest share from Asia, especially China and Taiwan, and most first authors were affiliated with colleges of education or computer science. Undergraduate students were the dominant population, while graduate students appeared much less often. Common subject domains included language learning, computer science, and engineering, and intended users were mostly students, followed by instructors and managers.

Through grounded coding, the authors identified five major usage categories: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. Across the literature, AI was commonly used for automated assessment and feedback, prediction of academic performance and dropout risk, and adaptive support through chatbots or tutoring systems. The review concludes that AI in higher education is growing rapidly, with new trends emerging after 2020, but that research remains concentrated in high-income countries, undergraduate contexts, and traditional efficiency-oriented uses rather than more transformative applications.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic artificial intelligence applications in higher education, including assessment, prediction, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and student learning management.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper systematically reviewed 138 higher-education studies using AI from 2016 to 2022 and coded how AI was used across studies, without focusing on one named product.

findings.finding_summary: Across 138 studies, AI in higher education was most often used for assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistant functions, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The review reports that AI was used to support writing, feedback, prediction of academic performance, personalized assistance, and learning analytics, but it does not provide pooled effect sizes.
findings.measure: Systematic review coding of AI use cases in higher education studies

findings.finding_summary: In the language-learning subset of studies, AI was commonly used for writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition. The review notes examples of automated feedback for writing and AI translation support, but no quantitative subgroup effects are reported for literacy outcomes.
findings.measure: Systematic review coding of language learning studies and literacy-related applications

findings.finding_summary: The review found that 72% of studies focused on students, 17% on instructors, and 11% on managers, and it identified managerial uses such as learning analytics, curriculum sequencing, instructional design, and clustering students. These are descriptive findings only, with no pooled estimate of impact.
findings.measure: Systematic review coding of intended users and management-oriented AI uses

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review with transparent PRISMA methods and dual coding, but it synthesizes heterogeneous studies descriptively rather than estimating effects. The evidence is therefore strong for mapping the field, but not for causal impact on outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports important descriptive trends and use cases, but it does not provide effect sizes or outcome magnitudes. As a result, the practical impact is promising but unclear from the evidence reported.

paper_profiles.title: Gender bias and stereotypes in Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether contemporary large language models (LLMs) reproduce and amplify gender stereotypes when resolving pronouns in ambiguous sentences. The authors focus on a simple experimental paradigm built from pairs of occupations that are stereotypically male or female, paired with masculine or feminine pronouns, in order to test whether models systematically favor stereotype-consistent interpretations.

The approach is not an educational intervention; it is an evaluation of four publicly available 2023 LLMs using automatically prompted sentence-comprehension items. The models were asked to choose the referent of a pronoun in ambiguous sentences and then, in a follow-up, to indicate whether the other noun could also be a referent. The paper also includes a baseline with names added to disambiguate the pronoun and compares model choices against both human stereotype ratings and U.S. labor statistics.

The study does not involve human participants, students, teachers, or a school setting. It finds that the models strongly align pronoun resolution with gender stereotypes, often fail to acknowledge ambiguity unless explicitly asked, and provide explanations that can be factually inaccurate or rationalize biased choices. The authors conclude that LLMs reflect and sometimes amplify societal gender bias, and argue that such systems should be carefully evaluated for harms before deployment in high-impact domains, including education.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Large language models / generative AI chatbots that produce and interpret natural language text.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluates four publicly available LLMs on gender bias in pronoun resolution and on how they explain their choices.

findings.finding_summary: Across four LLMs, the models showed strong gender-stereotyped pronoun resolution: stereotypically female occupations were chosen more often with feminine pronouns and stereotypically male occupations with masculine pronouns. The paper reports that models were on average 6.8 times more likely to choose a stereotypically female occupation when a female pronoun was present and 3.4 times more likely to choose a stereotypically male occupation when a male pronoun was present; the sentences were noted as ambiguous only 5% of the time.
findings.measure: Occupation choice in ambiguous pronoun-resolution prompts; ambiguity acknowledgement

findings.finding_summary: When explicit gendered names were added to disambiguate the sentences, the models largely resolved the pronouns correctly even when this contradicted gender stereotypes. Accuracy on these baseline items was very high across models: 98%, 99%, 97%, and 99% respectively, indicating the models could use explicit information to override stereotypical expectations.
findings.measure: Accuracy on gendered-name baseline items

findings.finding_summary: The models’ occupation choices tracked perceived gender stereotypes more closely than labor-market ground truth. Reported Kendall’s τ correlations were τ=0.67 vs τ=0.5 for human ratings vs BLS statistics for the masculine pronoun, and τ=0.49 vs τ=0.46 for the feminine pronoun; all p-values were < 0.001. The paper also reports that stereotypes about women were amplified more than those about men.
findings.measure: Kendall’s tau correlation between model choices and perceived occupation gender association vs BLS statistics

findings.finding_summary: Three of the four models usually acknowledged ambiguity only when explicitly asked, while initially giving categorical answers. On the follow-up question about whether the other noun could also be the referent, the models answered yes at rates of 64%, 82%, 26%, and 85% respectively, but one model mostly insisted its original answer was the only possible one.
findings.measure: Explicit acknowledgment that sentence was ambiguous

findings.finding_summary: The paper finds that the models often produced explanations that were factually inaccurate or rationalized biased choices after the fact. Grammar-based explanations accounted for over 20% of explanations, and explicitly gender-biased explanations were given about 5-15% of the time; however, the study does not report a single pooled numerical effect size beyond these proportions.
findings.measure: Type and frequency of generated explanations

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small, original correlational evaluation of four LLMs with manually coded outputs rather than an experiment on learners. The methodology is clear, but it does not test educational outcomes and provides no causal evidence for K-12 literacy effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s findings concern bias, ambiguity handling, and explanation quality in LLMs, not student learning gains or losses. It is relevant to downstream educational use, but the direct instructional impact is unclear and not quantified for K-12 literacy.

paper_profiles.title: The shaky foundations of large language models and foundation models for electronic health records
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the rapidly growing literature on foundation models for electronic health records (EHRs) and argues that the field’s evaluation practices are not well aligned with the clinical value these models are often claimed to provide. The authors review 84 clinical foundation models, dividing them into clinical language models (CLaMs) and foundation models for EMRs (FEMRs), and analyze their training data, public availability, and evaluation tasks.

Rather than studying an educational intervention or participant outcomes, the paper proposes a taxonomy and critique of existing model-development practices. It highlights that most CLaMs are trained on a narrow set of corpora such as MIMIC-III and PubMed, while most FEMRs rely on structured codes from small public datasets or private health-system data. The review also notes that many models are evaluated on conventional benchmark tasks that mainly measure predictive accuracy.

The main conclusion is that current benchmarks provide limited evidence of real-world usefulness, safety, fairness, or deployment value in healthcare. The authors recommend more clinically grounded evaluation metrics and tasks, including ranking-based measures, subgroup calibration, multimodal reasoning, sample-efficiency analyses, and human evaluation for more qualitative model behaviors.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model chatbot/system for generating and understanding text through conversational prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: This review uses ChatGPT and related GPT-family models as examples of general-purpose foundation models and mentions their application to medical and clinical tasks; it does not evaluate ChatGPT in K-12 literacy.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review in digital medicine, not an empirical education study. It does not present K-12 literacy evidence or a controlled evaluation of the tool in an educational setting.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational outcome, subgroup effect, or implementation impact is reported for K-12 literacy. The paper is outside the scope of the requested evidence base and provides no measurable impact for that domain.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can generate high-quality reading comprehension exercises for middle school English learners, addressing a practical problem faced by teachers: the difficulty of producing updated, engaging, and appropriately leveled reading materials and multiple-choice questions at scale. The authors frame generative AI as a way to reduce teacher workload while improving personalization and freshness of practice materials.

The intervention is a reading-exercise generation system built around ChatGPT. The system uses prompt engineering to generate passages in zero-shot and one-shot settings, and to generate multiple-choice comprehension questions and answers from either model-produced or user-provided passages. A GPT-2 + PPLM baseline is built for comparison. The work also includes a toxicity screen and a graphical interface intended for middle school teachers and students. The data used to develop and test the system come from Beijing middle schools, with reading passages spanning Grades 7 to 9.

Evaluation combines automatic metrics, human ratings from 9 Chinese college students and 364 native English speakers, pairwise comparison studies with additional student evaluators, and first-hand feedback from 3 experienced middle school teachers in Beijing after using the system for a week. The findings suggest that ChatGPT-generated passages are often judged as better than both human-written textbook passages and the GPT-2 baseline, and are seen as suitable for middle school use. However, question generation is weaker than passage generation, especially for distractor quality and variety. Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT has strong promise for generating reading materials in real educational settings, while more work is needed to improve multiple-choice question quality.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s LLM-based chatbot / generative AI assistant used for interactive text generation and instruction following.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate middle-school English reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice exercise questions in zero-shot and one-shot settings, with prompts specifying topic, length, genre, difficulty, and question type; also evaluated as a baseline against fine-tuned GPT-2 + PPLM.

findings.finding_summary: In human evaluation of reading passages, ChatGPT-generated passages were rated higher than human-written passages on multiple dimensions by 9 Chinese college students and 364 native English speakers. For Chinese students, ChatGPT scored 4.61 readability, 4.60 correctness, 4.65 coherence, 4.37 engagement, and 4.46 overall quality versus 4.52, 4.32, 4.39, 4.07, and 4.18 for human-written passages; for native speakers, the corresponding overall quality scores were 4.06 for ChatGPT versus 3.89 for human-written passages.
findings.measure: Human ratings of reading passage quality (readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, overall quality)
findings.sample_size: n=9 Chinese college students; n=364 native English speakers

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise comparisons of passage quality, ChatGPT outperformed human-written passages and the GPT-2 + PPLM baseline. Human-written versus ChatGPT (zero-shot) was 0.13 vs 0.87 for relative quality; ChatGPT one-shot was 0.20 vs 0.80, indicating evaluators preferred ChatGPT passages over human-written ones in most comparisons.
findings.measure: Pairwise relative quality score for reading passages

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT passages were judged to follow prompt constraints very well. In topic coherence scoring, ChatGPT achieved 0.97 in both zero-shot and one-shot settings, compared with 0.40 for the GPT-2 + PPLM baseline on generated passages.
findings.measure: Topic coherence / prompt adherence score for passages

findings.finding_summary: For suitability as middle-school reading materials, ChatGPT scored 0.77 in both zero-shot and one-shot settings, compared with 0.37 for the GPT-2 + PPLM baseline. The authors conclude the generated passages were largely suitable for middle-school English learners in China and in some cases better than textbook passages.
findings.measure: Suitability score for middle-school English learners

findings.finding_summary: For generated multiple-choice reading questions, human-written questions outperformed ChatGPT-generated questions on most human-rated dimensions. Generated questions scored 4.38 for match, 3.25 for usefulness, and 3.48 for suitability, versus 4.58, 3.93, and 3.92 for human-written questions; however, generated questions were perceived as more likely to be model-generated (0.67 vs 0.27).
findings.measure: Human ratings of multiple-choice question quality (match, usefulness, suitability, perceived model-generatedness)

findings.finding_summary: Experienced middle-school teachers reported that the system could reduce cost and time while providing more diverse and personalized learning materials. The paper reports three teachers in Beijing used the system for one week and gave highly positive qualitative feedback.
findings.measure: Teacher feedback on usefulness, ease of use, and overall system quality

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical paper with human evaluation, not a randomized trial or meta-analysis. The evidence is informative but based on small teacher samples for some outcomes and qualitative feedback for system use.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported passage-quality outcomes for ChatGPT are generally large and favorable, especially on human ratings and prompt adherence. However, the exercise-question results are more mixed, so overall impact is modest-to-moderate rather than uniformly strong.

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can be used as a feedback tool to improve foreign language writing for students with a migrant/refugee background in a multilingual and multicultural classroom. The authors focus on vocabulary and grammar in L2 writing, motivated by the need for additional support for socially vulnerable learners who may face extra language barriers.

The intervention was a short classroom-based pilot in a junior high school in Patras, Greece. Eight 15-year-old students enrolled in third-grade German as a foreign language participated. Students first wrote a personal email, then ChatGPT was used to revise the text for vocabulary and grammar, and students reviewed the improved version before writing a second, related email on a similar topic.

Results were reported through text metrics such as total words, unique words, and average words per sentence. The revised writing showed increases on these measures for most students, suggesting that ChatGPT may support L2 writing development and create a more supportive learning environment. The authors conclude that the findings are promising but preliminary, and they call for studies in larger and more diverse settings.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI language model/chatbot based on GPT architecture, capable of generating and revising text in response to prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a feedback tool to improve students' foreign language writing by correcting and enhancing vocabulary and grammar in a multilingual junior high school classroom.

findings.finding_summary: In this pilot study with 8 migrant/refugee-background junior high school students (age 15), ChatGPT-based feedback was followed by increases in writing productivity and complexity on a second, similar writing task. The authors report increases in total words, unique words, and average words per sentence in the improved version of students' work; for example, mean total-word increase was 38%, and mean average words per sentence increased by approximately 42%.
findings.measure: Foreign language writing output characteristics: total words, unique words, average words per sentence

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot classroom study with no control group and no inferential statistics or effect sizes reported. The design is exploratory and descriptive rather than a well-controlled trial.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported changes are directionally positive and sometimes substantial in percentage terms, but the evidence is from a very small sample and limited setting. Without effect sizes or comparison conditions, the magnitude and generalizability remain unclear.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the emerging role of large language models, especially ChatGPT and related systems, in education. The authors ask what opportunities these models create for learning and teaching, and what risks and implementation challenges they introduce. Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, the paper synthesizes early research and offers a conceptual overview of uses, risks, and mitigation strategies.

The paper discusses potential educational applications across multiple contexts, including elementary, middle, and high school, university, professional training, remote learning, and group work. It highlights possible benefits for students such as support for reading, writing, language learning, comprehension, problem solving, and personalized practice; and for teachers such as lesson planning, feedback, assessment support, and content generation. It also notes potential uses for learners with disabilities, including support through speech-to-text and text-to-speech tools, and discusses multilingual access concerns.

The authors conclude that large language models could substantially enhance education if used responsibly, but they emphasize the need for human oversight, critical thinking, fact checking, bias mitigation, privacy protections, and clear institutional strategies. They argue that equitable access, multilingual support, and careful pedagogical integration are essential to prevent widening educational divides and to ensure the technology benefits diverse learners.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational large language model system used for generating, answering, and transforming text across tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: This position paper discusses ChatGPT and related GPT-family large language models as educational tools for content creation, personalized feedback, tutoring, assessment support, and language learning.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper and conceptual review, not an empirical study. It offers no primary data, experimental design, or pooled effect estimates to assess evidence quality.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ChatGPT/GPT-family models have broad potential for education, including literacy support, but it does not report measured impacts. The likely educational relevance is substantial, yet the paper provides no quantitative evidence of effect.

paper_profiles.title: Integrating Generative AI in Knowledge Building
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can be integrated into K-12 learning to support knowledge building and develop students’ AI literacy. The authors are interested in students’ nuanced processes of using GenAI for learning, rather than only whether the tool improves performance. They ask how students incorporate ChatGPT into their knowledge-building work and what kinds of AI literacy emerge through that process.

The study took place in a high school World Religions course guided by Knowledge Building pedagogy. One teacher and 10 consenting students participated, with the course running in English for native Spanish-speaking students in a major South American city. ChatGPT was introduced through teacher-designed activities across two phases: first, students used ChatGPT to generate ideas and questions for critique and selection; later, they used a steering prompt to have ChatGPT answer their questions, provide nuanced viewpoints, and generate follow-up questions, followed by fact-checking, peer discussion, and reflective writing.

Findings from interviews and classroom artifacts show that students used ChatGPT as an information-search tool, a source of alternative ideas, and a way to speed up mundane tasks such as outlining and summarizing. They also described challenges such as inaccurate outputs, prompt engineering difficulties, and uncertainty about citation and verification. The paper concludes that with deliberate pedagogical scaffolding, ChatGPT can support collaborative knowledge building while also helping students develop emerging AI literacy, including understanding of AI strengths, weaknesses, risks, and human-AI relationships.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative AI chatbot/LLM system used for conversational question-answering, text generation, and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by high school students in a World Religions course to support knowledge building: generating essays, questions, summaries, explanations, and conversational responses; also used for prompt engineering and fact-checking within class activities.

findings.finding_summary: In interviews with 10 high school students, ChatGPT was reported as useful for information search, generating ideas, supporting collaboration, and completing mundane learning tasks. Students also described gaining emerging AI literacy through using the tool, including a basic understanding of how it works, its strengths and weaknesses, risks, and societal implications; however, the study is qualitative and does not report quantitative effects.
findings.measure: Semi-structured student interviews; student writing/artifacts and teacher notes used for triangulation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample qualitative/mixed-methods study based primarily on interviews, with triangulation from artifacts and teacher notes. It provides useful descriptive evidence but no experimental design or causal estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful perceived benefits for learning processes and AI literacy, but it does not provide effect sizes or direct achievement outcomes. Impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceived a generative AI-powered learning activity for creative mathematical writing. The authors were interested in both the educational benefits and the challenges of using GenAI to help students create, revise, and reflect on story-based math problems.

The intervention involved a custom GenAI learning platform that supported students through three steps: Ask, Represent, and Transform. In Ask, students analyzed and discussed math stories; in Represent, they visually modeled ideas; and in Transform, they prompted GenAI to co-generate culturally relevant math stories using text and images (GPT-4 and DALL·E 3). Students then evaluated the AI-generated stories and revised their own work. The study was implemented in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. elementary schools, involving 79 students and six teachers. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations, and were analyzed thematically.

The study found that participants perceived several benefits: GenAI supported divergent and convergent thinking, helped students understand mathematical concepts and represent knowledge, promoted AI literacy through prompt refinement, and increased interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning. At the same time, students and teachers identified challenges, including weak critical evaluation of AI outputs, difficulty generating coherent prompts and stories, AI being perceived as too perfect, lack of adaptive pedagogical feedback, limited autonomy, weak social connection features, and insufficient accessibility options such as speech-to-text. The authors conclude that GenAI can support creative mathematical writing in elementary classrooms, but only when paired with deliberate instructional and interface design that preserves opportunities for human learning and interaction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-based generative AI system used for text generation and related conversational assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within the developed GenAI-powered learning technology to generate draft mathematical stories from student input; the paper states the system integrated OpenAI’s GPT-4 and DALL·E 3.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative classroom study with 79 5th-grade students and 6 teachers, participants perceived the GPT-4/DALL�b7E 3-based system as supporting creative mathematical writing, including divergent and convergent thinking, originality, flexible thinking, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and interest/ownership in learning. The paper reports themes from interviews, open-ended surveys, and observations rather than quantitative effects.
findings.measure: Students' and teachers' perceptions from semi-structured interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative artificial intelligence system that can generate text and images and support content creation, drafting, and feedback-like interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a GenAI-powered classroom technology for creative mathematical writing; students used it to draft, modify, and create culturally relevant math stories and to evaluate AI-generated stories.

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported that GenAI supported creative mathematical writing by fostering creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and affective engagement. Reported benefits included story generation, visual representation, prompt iteration, and increased interest, curiosity, and ownership, but the study was qualitative and did not estimate causal effects.
findings.measure: Perceived benefits and challenges in interview themes and observation notes

findings.finding_summary: Participants also reported several challenges: students often did not critically evaluate AI-generated content, had difficulty generating coherent prompts/stories, and felt the AI was too perfect. Teachers and students wanted more adaptive feedback, autonomy, social interaction, and multiple communication modes such as speech-to-text.
findings.measure: Perceived barriers and design needs from interviews and triangulated qualitative data

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative mixed-methods classroom study with interviews, surveys, and observations. It provides useful classroom evidence, but there is no experimental comparison or quantitative effect estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived impacts on engagement, creativity, and mathematical understanding, but these are qualitative and not quantified. Because no effect size is reported, the impact tier is best treated as modest/unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to teach K-12 students how to use generative AI responsibly for learning, with a focus on prompting literacy: knowing when AI is useful, how to ask effective questions, and how to avoid relying on AI for direct answers. The authors argue that although AI chatbots are increasingly present in school contexts, there are few instructional interventions that explicitly teach students responsible, learning-oriented use of these tools.

To address this gap, the paper presents a web-based AI literacy module built around scenario-based practice with an LLM chatbot and immediate automated feedback. Students wrote prompts for three hypothetical secondary-school learning scenarios in biology, geography, and math, and an AI auto-grader evaluated their prompts using rubric-based dimensions such as relevance, purpose, conciseness, context, elaboration, and avoiding direct-answer seeking. Two classroom deployment iterations were conducted in 11 authentic secondary classrooms in East Asia. Study 1 used multiple-choice pre/post assessments and collected student prompts and reflections; Study 2 revised the assessment to include true/false and open-ended items to better measure prompting literacy.

The findings suggest that the auto-grader could evaluate student prompts with high accuracy in most dimensions, and that the module helped students improve especially in adding background/context to prompts and increased their confidence about using AI for learning. Students generally understood prompt basics but still varied in their ability to produce strong prompts, and qualitative feedback indicated both enthusiasm for the AI interaction and challenges related to typing, platform usability, and limited scenario variety. The revised assessment in Study 2 showed better difficulty and discrimination characteristics than the original multiple-choice version, though reliability remained only moderate. Overall, the paper concludes that prompt-writing instruction for K-12 is feasible and promising, but larger-scale studies and further assessment refinement are needed.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model family used as a general-purpose AI chatbot and for AI-based automatic grading/feedback generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the LLM chatbot in the prompting-literacy module and as the AI auto-grader for student-written prompts; the paper specifies OpenAI GPT-4o.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1, the AI auto-grader based on GPT-4o achieved an average accuracy of 0.92 when assessing 483 unique student-written prompts. The paper reports high grading accuracy in most rubric dimensions and notes that the system generated high-quality, detailed feedback.
findings.measure: Grading accuracy of AI auto-grader on student-written prompts

findings.finding_summary: Student self-reported confidence in using AI to help learning increased by 10.4% on average after the activity (SD = 0.92), with a significant Wilcoxon test result (p < .001). The study also reports improved prompting practice, especially for embedding background/context in prompts.
findings.measure: Self-reported confidence in using AI for learning; prompting dimension performance
findings.sample_size: n=111 students (Study 1); n=98 pre/post complete for test score comparison

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom-based mixed-methods study with human grading, surveys, and thematic analysis rather than a randomized or quasi-experimental design. It provides useful descriptive evidence, but causal claims are limited and subgroup analysis is absent.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported outcomes are promising, including 0.92 auto-grader accuracy and a 10.4% confidence increase, but the paper does not report standardized effect sizes for learning gains. The evidence suggests modest instructional impact, but the magnitude for student achievement is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether a brief AI literacy intervention can reduce high school students’ tendency to over-rely on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations. The authors focus on the problem of students accepting misleading large language model outputs without verification, which is especially relevant as schools increasingly consider using generative AI in secondary education.

The intervention consisted of a short educational text about ChatGPT’s working mechanism, limitations, risks, and appropriate use, with screenshots illustrating hallucinations and other failures. A control group received only the introductory portion of the text about ChatGPT. After reading their assigned text, 12th-grade Estonian students completed math puzzles while viewing ChatGPT recommendations that were correct in half of the cases. Participants indicated whether they would use ChatGPT’s recommendation, allowing the researchers to measure over-reliance on incorrect advice and under-reliance on correct advice.

The sample included 36 final participants from Estonian high schools, and the study used a randomized two-group experimental design delivered online. Results showed widespread over-reliance overall: students adopted incorrect ChatGPT suggestions in about half of the instances. The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance; instead, it increased under-reliance, meaning students were more likely to ignore correct recommendations after the text. The authors conclude that a short AI literacy text alone is not sufficient to curb over-reliance on ChatGPT and that future interventions may need to address both critical evaluation and appropriate trust calibration.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot that generates text responses and can assist with a wide range of language and reasoning tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the AI system under study. High school seniors read an intervention text about ChatGPT and then solved math puzzles with ChatGPT's recommendations; the study measured whether students adopted correct or incorrect recommendations.

findings.finding_summary: Among 36 12th-grade students (19 intervention, 17 control), mean over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations was 52.1%. Over-reliance was lower in the intervention group (M=48.68, SD=24.26) than in control (M=55.88, SD=33.69), but the difference was not statistically significant, Welch's t(28.78)=-0.73, p=.236, d=-0.25. The intervention increased under-reliance on correct recommendations (M=36.84 vs 19.12), t(34)=2.35, p=.025, d=0.78.
findings.measure: Over-reliance and under-reliance on ChatGPT recommendations during math puzzle solving

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small randomized experiment with a control group and clear outcome measures, which is stronger than correlational evidence. However, the sample is small and the paper reports only one subgroup (12th-grade Estonian high school seniors), limiting robustness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention had no significant reduction in over-reliance and showed a statistically significant increase in under-reliance, with a medium-to-large effect (d=0.78) for that negative outcome. Overall impact on the intended literacy outcome is limited and mixed.

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school students regulate inquiry when using ChatGPT for science investigation tasks. The central question is whether students can meaningfully initiate, evaluate, and continue question-asking cycles with a generative AI system in ways that support learning, or whether they instead over-rely on the tool and terminate inquiry too early.

The study used six science tasks built around age-appropriate curricular content. Students were given either efficient or inefficient suggested prompts, could accept the suggestion or write their own prompt, and then interacted with ChatGPT 3.5 during a one-hour session. After each AI response, they had to judge its usefulness, and they could ask follow-up questions until they felt ready to answer the task in their own words. The sample was 63 French middle school students aged 14–15 from four institutions in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, France.

Results showed that students performed near chance when discriminating between efficient and inefficient prompts, and they were also near chance at distinguishing high- versus low-quality AI responses. Follow-up questioning was rare, indicating weak regulatory behavior and premature ending of inquiry cycles. Positive attitudes toward AI and higher self-reported prior knowledge were associated with worse regulation, whereas metacognitive regulation and more critical perceptions of AI were associated with better performance. The authors conclude that AI literacy instruction should go beyond technical familiarity and explicitly teach metacognitive regulation and critical, friction-aware inquiry strategies.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used for generating responses to user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Middle-school students used pre-loaded ChatGPT 3.5 during six science investigation tasks to formulate prompts, evaluate responses, and decide whether to ask follow-up questions.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of n=63 middle-school students (ages 14-15), prompt discrimination was at chance level (mean d'=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08), indicating students struggled to reliably distinguish efficient from inefficient prompts. Students also showed near-zero sensitivity when evaluating ChatGPT answers (mean d'=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65), and only 14 students asked any follow-up questions across six tasks.
findings.measure: Prompt discrimination sensitivity, answer-quality sensitivity, and follow-up-question frequency during science inquiry tasks

findings.finding_summary: Task success averaged 0.51 (SD=0.25) across six problems per student, despite unrestricted ChatGPT access. Final success rate was predicted by the frequency of high-level AI answers, sensitivity to AI answer quality, and follow-up-question behavior, suggesting that weak regulation of ChatGPT interactions was associated with poorer conceptual explanations.
findings.measure: Binary-coded final written explanations of scientific concepts

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's large language model chatbot.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned only in the manuscript's declaration of AI-assisted writing as a proofreading tool used by the first author.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's large language model chatbot.
identified_tools.use_case: Mentioned only in the manuscript's declaration of AI-assisted writing as a proofreading tool used by the first author.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study with a correlational/path-analytic design rather than an experiment, and it focuses on interaction quality rather than intervention effects. The evidence is informative but limited by the small sample (n=63) and the lack of randomized comparison of AI use conditions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects include chance-level performance and associations with interaction quality, but the study does not provide a single causal effect size showing a clear medium or large impact of ChatGPT on learning. Overall impact is important conceptually, yet the measured effects are mostly modest, negative, or unclear.

paper_profiles.title: How Motivation Relates to Generative AI Use: A Large-Scale Survey of Mexican High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how high school students’ motivational profiles relate to their use of generative AI tools for learning. Rather than testing an AI intervention, the study examines whether students with different beliefs about their own competence and the value of a subject use generative AI in different ways.

The authors surveyed 7,739 public high school students in Chihuahua, Mexico, and analyzed a final sample of 6,793 students who reported prior experience with generative AI. Students completed Spanish-language survey measures of self-concept and perceived subject value in two domains, math and writing, and reported how often they used AI for specific tasks in each domain. The analysis used K-means clustering to identify motivational profiles separately for math and writing.

Three profiles emerged in both subjects: Aspirational, Confident, and Disengaged. In math, Aspirational students used AI mainly for step-by-step guidance and interpreting problems, Confident students used it more selectively for refinement and exploration, and Disengaged students showed more shortcut-seeking behavior, including the highest direct answer copying. In writing, Aspirational students mainly used AI for brainstorming and outlining, Confident students used it more for grammar, language improvement, and feedback, and Disengaged students used AI least overall. The paper concludes that generative AI use is domain-specific and differs systematically by student motivation, suggesting that AI integration should be tailored to learners’ motivational profiles rather than treated as one-size-fits-all.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools or chatbots used for answering questions, generating content, giving explanations, and providing feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Students reported their use of generative AI tools in math and writing tasks; the paper did not specify any named product.

findings.finding_summary: In a survey of 6,793 Mexican high school students, AI use differed by motivational profile and by domain. In math, the Aspirational group reported the highest use of AI for step-by-step guides (M=2.81) and problem interpretation (M=2.59), the Confident group used AI more selectively, and the Disengaged group showed the highest direct answer copying (M=2.69), exceeding Aspirational (M=2.53, p<.001) and Confident students (M=2.18, p<.001).
findings.measure: Self-reported frequency of generative AI use for math tasks (formula retrieval, direct answer copying, problem interpretation, step-by-step guides, solution verification, practice problem generation)

findings.finding_summary: In writing, the Aspirational group (n=3,191) most often used AI for brainstorming ideas (M=2.83) and outlines (M=2.72), while the Confident group (n=1,915) most often used AI for language/grammar improvement (M=2.79) and writing feedback (M=2.67). The Disengaged group (n=1,687) reported the lowest overall AI usage across most writing tasks.
findings.measure: Self-reported frequency of generative AI use for writing tasks (idea brainstorming, outline production, supporting evidence, language/grammar improvement, writing feedback, requirement adaptation)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational survey study using self-reported usage patterns and K-means clustering, not an experimental evaluation of an AI tool. The methodology is clear and the sample is large, but causal claims are not supported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful subgroup differences in how students use generative AI, but it does not estimate intervention effects or outcome gains. No effect sizes for learning outcomes are reported, so impact on achievement is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Students to Question the Machine: An AI Literacy Intervention Improves Students Regulation of LLM Use in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a brief AI literacy workshop can improve middle-school students’ ability to use generative AI effectively during a science problem-solving task. The authors focus on a key educational concern: students may over-trust large language model (LLM) outputs, accept them uncritically, and fail to regulate their interaction with the system.

The intervention was a two-hour classroom-feasible workshop delivered two days before the task. It combined conceptual instruction about how LLMs work and fail with procedural guidance on prompting, checking answers, asking follow-up questions, and revising or rejecting prompts. Students then completed six science inquiry exercises using a GenAI chatbot. The study compared an intervention group and a control group in a French middle school. The main outcomes were behavioral measures of interaction regulation and final answer quality, rather than only self-reported AI literacy.

Results showed that trained students performed better on the science tasks and used the chatbot more strategically: they rejected underspecified prompts more often, asked more follow-up questions when needed, and judged AI response correctness more accurately. The intervention appeared to improve not just discrimination of good versus bad prompts, but also the ability to respond appropriately once a problem was detected. Self-reported GenAI attitudes/knowledge and metacognitive self-reports did not predict performance. Overall, the paper concludes that short, scalable AI literacy instruction can meaningfully improve middle-school students’ regulation of LLM-supported learning activities in school-like contexts.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI family large language model chatbot used for general-purpose conversational generation and evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the generative AI system in middle-school science inquiry tasks; GPT-4o mini via DuckDuckAI was the primary interface, with GPT-4o, GPT-4.1-nano, and GPT-3.5-turbo used when needed. GPT-4o was also used as an LLM-as-judge for prompt validation and scoring student answers.

findings.finding_summary: In a controlled classroom study with n=116 grade 8–9 students, the intervention group achieved higher final-answer scores than controls on the 0–20 performance scale (M=11.38, SD=3.87, n=76 vs. M=10.29, SD=3.04, n=40; Mann–Whitney U=1871, p=.040, r=.19). The paper reports that performance differences were explained by improved interaction regulation rather than by the LLM itself.
findings.measure: Final written answer quality / task performance on six science inquiry tasks (0–20 scale)

findings.finding_summary: Trained students were less likely to accept underspecified prompts than controls (51.5% vs. 66.7%, p=.044), and they were more accurate at judging whether AI responses were correct, with a larger benefit for well-specified prompts than underspecified prompts (condition × validity interaction p=.012). They were also more likely to ask follow-up questions after accepted underspecified prompts (59.2% vs. 27.9%, p<.001), and this behavior translated into higher-quality answers in the intervention group (interaction p=.038).
findings.measure: Prompt acceptance, correctness judgments, follow-up questioning, and resulting answer quality during LLM-supported science tasks

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled classroom study with an intervention and comparison group, but it is not a randomized trial as described and was conducted in a single school with limited demographic data. The design is stronger than correlational work, yet some generalizability and implementation concerns remain.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported performance gain is modest (r=.19; difference of about 1.1 points on a 0–20 scale), but the intervention also produced meaningful process improvements in prompt regulation and answer evaluation. Overall impact is modest rather than large.

paper_profiles.title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) function as real-time writing support in K-12 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms, focusing on whether step-by-step scaffolding actually helps students during in-class writing. The authors ask how students with different proficiency levels interact with an LLM, how those interaction patterns relate to learning and retention, and how introducing the tool changes classroom dynamics and teacher roles.

The intervention was WriteAid, a chat-based LLM writing assistant designed to provide scaffolded help rather than direct answers. It supported sentence construction, vocabulary and grammar explanations, and grammar revision through tabs, and was used during two classroom writing exercises over six weeks. The study was conducted in a public middle school in South Korea with 157 eighth-grade students; 133 consented for analysis. The researchers combined system-log analysis, qualitative coding of interaction data, a naturalistic observation study, and analysis of a delayed written assessment.

Findings showed that the LLM improved grammatical accuracy and helped students complete writing tasks, but its step-by-step support had mixed effects. Higher-proficiency students used the tool more efficiently and often for lower-level tasks such as vocabulary translation and validation, while lower-proficiency students more often relied on it for sentence and paragraph generation, became more dependent on the system, and sometimes felt demotivated or frustrated by the scaffolded interaction. The classroom observations also showed that the tool shifted teacher attention patterns, reduced some routine question handling, and created new equity concerns because introverted or struggling students sometimes became less visible to the teacher. The authors conclude that LLM scaffolding in real-time K-12 classrooms needs to be proficiency-aware, cross-lingually informed, and better integrated with teacher oversight and classroom orchestration.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model chatbot used for interactive text generation, explanation, and feedback in writing tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Deployed as the underlying LLM in WriteAid to provide step-by-step writing support, sentence construction, grammar revision, and vocabulary/grammar explanations in real-time K-12 EFL classrooms.

findings.finding_summary: In a six-week deployment with 133 consenting eighth-grade students (157 total in the classes), LLM-supported sentence construction improved grammatical accuracy during in-class writing. Of 632 sentences constructed with the LLM in the fall semester, 309 (48.9%) were incorporated verbatim into students' final essays, and 82.3% of those incorporated sentences were grammatically correct.
findings.measure: Grammatical correctness of LLM-constructed sentences and whether those sentences were transferred into final essays

findings.finding_summary: Effects differed by performance group. High-performing students correctly incorporated 65.8% of LLM-constructed sentences into their final written assessments, whereas middle- and low-performing students did so only 37.8% and 14.0% of the time, respectively. The paper reports that lower-proficiency students were more likely to become demotivated and dependent on the system under step-by-step scaffolding.
findings.measure: Rate of correct incorporation of LLM-constructed sentences into final written assessment, by performance group

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative analysis found that lower-proficiency students often became overwhelmed, annoyed, or confused by step-by-step LLM feedback, especially later in the interaction. The paper reports that negative affective behaviors occurred on average 12.2 times per session for the middle-performing group and 11.4 times for the low-performing group, compared with 3.8 times for the high-performing group.
findings.measure: Affective responses during interaction (gratitude, annoyance, confusion, indifference)

findings.finding_summary: The LLM reduced teacher workload by handling simple questions and allowing the teacher to spend more time circulating in class.
