In the follow-up interview, the teacher reported having more time to walk around the classroom and check student progress because they no longer needed to answer every simple question.
findings.measure: Teacher workload and time available for classroom circulation, based on observation and interview

findings.finding_summary: The system had mixed effects on classroom equity. It helped more students complete tasks and may have narrowed completion gaps, but it also reduced questions from introverted students and made it harder for the teacher to identify common student difficulties because questions were split between the teacher and the AI.
findings.measure: Observed classroom participation, task completion, and teacher awareness of common difficulties

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-site, mixed-methods classroom deployment study rather than an experimental efficacy trial. The paper provides rich qualitative and descriptive quantitative evidence, but it does not report causal effect sizes or randomized comparison conditions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports meaningful classroom benefits and harms, but the paper does not provide standardized effect sizes. Overall impact appears important operationally and pedagogically, but the magnitude is unclear from the reported data.

paper_profiles.title: FEANEL: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Error Analysis in K-12 English Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of fine-grained, pedagogically useful error analysis for K-12 English writing, especially in the context of large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that existing work in automated essay scoring and grammatical error correction often provides either coarse feedback or surface-level corrections that do not capture the complexity of student writing errors.

To study this problem, they introduce FEANEL, a benchmark for Fine-grained Error ANalysis for English Learners. The benchmark contains 1,000 anonymized essays written by K-12 students, split evenly between elementary and secondary school, and annotated by experienced English education experts. Each edit is labeled with an error type, severity score, and explanatory feedback using a part-of-speech-driven taxonomy co-developed with educators. The paper evaluates multiple state-of-the-art LLMs under different prompting conditions, including zero-shot and one-shot settings.

The benchmark includes elementary school essays from students aged 9–11 and secondary school essays from middle school-aged learners aged 12–18, drawn from a global online education platform and the TECCL corpus. The setting is therefore educational and language-learning focused, not an intervention study in a classroom. Results show that current LLMs can perform some error classification, but they still struggle with complex errors, long-tail error types, and high-quality pedagogical explanations. Performance improves with richer prompts and examples, and larger reasoning-oriented models generally do better, but human teachers still outperform the models on the evaluated tasks.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General large language models used to analyze K-12 English writing errors and generate explanatory feedback, rather than a single named educational product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper benchmarks multiple LLMs on the FEANEL task: fine-grained error classification, severity rating, and explanation generation for K-12 English essays.

findings.finding_summary: Across LLMs, performance on fine-grained error analysis was substantially below human teachers, with strong variation by model and prompting condition. In the Zero-shot-naive setting, average classification performance was Acc=63.13 and F1=67.83, while human teachers reached Acc=79.90 and F1=76.66 on the same benchmark subset; explanation quality was also lower for LLMs than humans. The paper reports that one-shot detailed prompting improved performance across classification and explanation metrics, but no single LLM consistently outperformed others across all sub-tasks.
findings.measure: Error classification accuracy and Macro-F1; error severity MAE; explanation BLEU/METEOR/ROUGE-L
findings.sample_size: n=1000 essays (500 elementary, 500 secondary); 8,676 error analyses; human evaluation on 1,000 errors

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark study, but it is not an intervention study or meta-analysis. The design is systematic and clearly specified, yet the evidence is based on model evaluation rather than causal impact on learners.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows meaningful differences in model performance and clear gains from richer prompts, but it does not report learner outcome effect sizes. Reported results are primarily benchmark scores rather than demonstrated educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly expanding and poorly defined area of AI literacy education in the wake of generative AI. The authors ask how researchers conceptualize AI literacy in K-12 and higher education and what new trends have emerged since generative AI became publicly available. Their goal is not to evaluate a single intervention, but to synthesize the field and build a framework that clarifies the different ways AI literacy is being defined and taught.

The study uses an integrative review approach to examine 124 empirical and theoretical studies published between 2020 and July 2024. The review focuses on K-12 and undergraduate contexts and excludes graduate, adult, and discipline-specific professional training. The authors code each study by how it conceptualizes AI and literacy, identifying three AI perspectives (technical details, tools, sociocultural impact) and three literacy perspectives (functional, critical, indirectly beneficial). They then map how these combine across studies, including pre-generative-AI curricula centered on machine learning or AI ethics and post-generative-AI work emphasizing direct use of tools such as ChatGPT.

The review finds that AI literacy research has shifted notably after generative AI, with a sharp increase in studies focused on AI tools and prompt engineering, especially in higher education. In K-12, most studies still emphasize machine learning fundamentals and ethics, often combining technical and sociocultural content. The paper concludes that AI literacy is too broad a term for the current landscape and argues for more precise terminology that distinguishes technical, tool-based, ethical, and indirectly beneficial goals. It also identifies gaps, especially around critical and sociocultural use of AI tools and around comparable post-secondary curricula.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic category of generative AI / large language model tools used for language-based interaction, content generation, prompting, and instruction support, without a single named commercial product being the focus.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is an integrative review of AI literacy studies in K-12 and higher education. It synthesizes how recent studies conceptualize AI literacy in the wake of generative AI, including studies that discuss or teach use of ChatGPT and other generative AI tools, but it does not empirically evaluate one specific tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an integrative review and conceptual framework paper, not a primary empirical evaluation of a tool. It synthesizes prior studies rather than reporting a single study design with tool-level outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct outcome effects are reported for a specific AI tool, so there is no measurable intervention impact to rate. The paper is useful for framing the literature, but not for estimating student outcome gains.

paper_profiles.title: How University Disability Services Professionals Write Image Descriptions for HCI Figures Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how university Disability Services Office (DSO) professionals write alternative text (alt text) for complex academic figures and whether generative AI can improve that process. The central problem is that accessibility professionals are often asked to describe figures from technical fields outside their expertise, which can lead to generic, incomplete, or inaccurate descriptions. The authors argue that this is especially problematic for screen reader users who rely on alt text to access visual information in academic materials.

The study evaluates a human-AI workflow using ChatGPT-4o as a writing assistant. In Study 1, 12 DSO professionals from higher education institutions wrote alt text for HCI publication figures both with and without AI assistance, while thinking aloud and completing interviews and questionnaires. The figures were selected from CHI 2025 papers and intentionally varied in complexity. In Study 2, 11 HCI experts evaluated the resulting alt texts using a rubric that assessed figure type identification, message, key elements, trends, clarity, detail, and contextual relevance. The design combines qualitative interview/thematic analysis with quantitative comparisons of confidence, text length, and rubric scores.

The participants were adults working in higher education accessibility roles, located in the United States, and the context was institutional accessibility remediation rather than K-12 instruction. The main findings are that AI assistance helped DSO professionals produce longer, faster, and higher-quality alt text, especially for complex figures, and increased their confidence. However, some participants over-relied on the AI, accepted outputs with insufficient checking, and struggled to prompt the model precisely. The evaluation by HCI experts found that AI-assisted alt text was generally superior to human-only alt text, though both approaches still showed weaknesses in specificity, clarity, and contextual accuracy.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based generative AI chatbot used for text and image understanding, drafting, and revising responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a writing assistant to generate and refine alt text for HCI figures written by DSO professionals; participants uploaded articles and figures and prompted the model to draft accessibility descriptions.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1 with 12 DSO professionals, ChatGPT assistance helped participants write alt text more quickly and with less effort than writing without AI. All participants completed the AI-assisted writing task within 20 minutes, whereas without AI assistance all used the full 50 minutes and two could not complete descriptions of all figures.
findings.measure: Time to complete alt-text writing task; task completion

findings.finding_summary: Participants rated their confidence in AI-assisted alt text considerably higher than in self-written alt text. The paper also reports that ChatGPT-assisted descriptions were longer on average than human-only descriptions (mean=140.70 words, std=79.65 vs mean=104.16, std=66.21; t(36)=-2.09, p=0.044).
findings.measure: Perceived confidence in alt-text quality; alt-text word count

findings.finding_summary: In Study 2 with 11 HCI experts, AI-assisted alt text was rated superior in quality to human-only alt text, even when some inaccuracies were present. The evaluation also found that human-generated alt text lacked specific details and was inconsistent.
findings.measure: Expert-rated alt-text quality

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods user study with expert evaluation, not a randomized controlled trial or meta-analysis. The paper provides descriptive and limited quantitative comparisons, so the evidence is useful but not high-credibility experimental evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive effects on efficiency, confidence, and expert-rated alt-text quality, but effect sizes are mostly not reported and the study is small. The overall impact appears promising but modest and context-specific.

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how secondary EFL students engineer prompts when using ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots to complete a writing task. The authors focus on prompt content, prompt sequencing, and how students move through trial-and-error pathways while collaborating with generative AI in a machine-in-the-loop writing process.

The intervention/approach examined is not a formal instructional program but a first-time use of ChatGPT-compatible chatbots for a timed blog-writing task. Four high-achieving Form 1 students in a Hong Kong secondary school were asked to write a blog entry using their own words and AI-generated words, with no explicit instruction on prompt engineering or on how chatbots differ from other generative AI. Screen recordings of their iPads and the resulting Google Docs were analyzed qualitatively as four case studies.

The study identifies six distinct prompt types and shows that each student followed a different pathway, often exploring prompts by minor modifications, repeated attempts, and switching between chatbots. The authors conclude that students were largely unsophisticated prompt users and that prompt engineering education could help EFL learners use generative AI more strategically for writing. The paper also suggests that prompt pathways differ even for the same task and may reflect students’ prior experience, exploration, and attempts to unlock chatbot capabilities for idea generation.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot for conversational text generation and instruction following.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by secondary school EFL students as one of several chatbots to complete a blog-entry writing task; students prompted it during a machine-in-the-loop writing activity and one student switched between ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly.

findings.finding_summary: This qualitative case study did not test ChatGPT with an outcome measure or compare writing performance attributable to ChatGPT. It reported that students used ChatGPT as part of prompt-engineering pathways while composing a blog entry, including repeated prompts and prompt revisions, but no effect sizes or quantitative outcomes were reported.
findings.measure: Prompt content, prompt type, prompt sequencing, and student writing task completion process

identified_tools.name: POE
identified_tools.description: A mobile app/platform that provides access to multiple chatbots, including ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly.
identified_tools.use_case: Students used the POE app on iPads to access proprietary chatbots while completing a timed EFL blog-writing task in class.

findings.finding_summary: The paper did not evaluate POE as an intervention or report outcome effects. POE served as the interface through which students accessed multiple chatbots during the writing task, and the study reported only descriptive differences in how students used prompts across chatbots.
findings.measure: Prompt engineering behaviors during writing (descriptive case analysis)

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI chatbots used for human-language interaction and text generation, without a single named product focus.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied secondary EFL students' first-time use of generative AI chatbots for writing support and prompt engineering in a classroom blog-writing task.

findings.finding_summary: Across 4 cases and 36 coded turns, the paper found six distinct prompt-content types and described trial-and-error pathways in which students explored different prompt forms. The authors concluded that students were unsophisticated users who did not optimize chatbot use, and that prompt-engineering education would help them move beyond trial-and-error.
findings.measure: Prompt types, prompt quantity, prompt sequencing, and qualitative pathway patterns

findings.finding_summary: Students completed the same timed blog-writing task using chatbots, but the paper did not report quantitative writing-quality outcomes. It did note that students used different combinations of prompts and multiple chatbots, and that some pathways appeared more sophisticated than others.
findings.measure: Writing-task completion process and prompt pathway sophistication

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study with four participants and descriptive coding of prompt behavior, not an experimental design. The paper provides detailed process evidence but no causal estimates of learning or writing impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests possible instructional value for prompt-engineering education, but it reports no effect sizes or measured gains in literacy outcomes. Any impact remains descriptive and unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: Let AI Read First: Enhancing Reading Abilities for Individuals with Dyslexia through Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: CHI EA ’25 (Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that people with dyslexia often struggle with reading fluency, comprehension, and attention, while existing assistive reading tools can be costly, impractical in quiet settings, or may distort the meaning of the original text. The authors propose Let AI Read First (LARF), an AI-based reading presentation strategy that uses large language models to annotate text with HTML tags such as highlighting, bolding, and underlining so that important information is visually emphasized without changing the original content.

The study evaluated LARF in a between-subjects experiment with 150 adult participants recruited online through Prolific. Participants either had a medical diagnosis of dyslexia, were being assessed for dyslexia, or strongly suspected undiagnosed dyslexia. They were randomly assigned to read the same IELTS Academic passage in one of three conditions: unmodified text, a conventional Bionic Reading version, or LARF-generated GPT-4 annotations. Outcomes included reading time, recall questions, free-detail retrieval scored by GPT-4 and verified by humans, comprehension questions, and subjective usability/helpfulness ratings.

Results showed that LARF improved reading-related outcomes relative to the other conditions, especially retrieval performance, subjective satisfaction, and perceived helpfulness. Comprehension and recall trends also favored LARF, though some differences were not statistically significant. A post hoc analysis further suggested that LARF was particularly beneficial for participants with more severe dyslexia symptoms. The paper concludes that AI-generated annotations may be a promising accessibility technique for dyslexic readers and may extend to other reading scenarios, though the authors note several implementation and model-scale limitations.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT family / ChatGPT product used here as a large language model to annotate text with HTML tags and to score participant responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the annotation model in LARF to mark important information in reading passages; also used with human verification to score participants' retrieval responses.

findings.finding_summary: In a between-subjects experiment with participants who self-reported dyslexia (final analyzed sample n=148; LARF n=48), GPT-4-annotated text via LARF improved reading-related outcomes relative to control and Bionic Reading. For recall, LARF scored 3.71 (SD=1.20) vs 3.44 (SD=1.74) control and 3.53 (SD=1.64) conventional; for retrieval, LARF scored 5.87 (SD=2.30) vs 5.51 (SD=2.38) control and 4.96 (SD=2.89) conventional, with the retrieval difference statistically significant (F(2,128)=3.465, p=.034).
findings.measure: Recall questions and retrieval detail score
findings.sample_size: n=148 (recall n=131? not_reported; retrieval n=131? not_reported; final analysis reported n=148 overall, with 138 for reading time and 138/129 for some analyses)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary between-subjects experiment with randomized conditions and quantitative outcomes, but it is not a full K-12 study and uses adult participants with dyslexia. The design is fairly strong, though some analyses are modest and not all outcomes are statistically significant.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are positive but generally modest in magnitude, and the paper does not report standardized effect sizes for the key literacy outcomes. The statistically significant retrieval improvement is meaningful, but overall the impact appears small-to-moderate rather than large.

paper_profiles.title: “From Unseen Needs to Classroom Solutions”: Exploring AI Literacy Challenges & Opportunities with Project-Based Learning Toolkit in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the challenges and opportunities of supporting AI literacy in K-12 classrooms through a Project-Based Learning (PBL) toolkit. The authors ask how teachers understand AI literacy, how they adapt AI tools into lesson plans, and how teachers’ and students’ backgrounds shape perceptions of AI tools and classroom use. The motivation is to make AI education more accessible beyond computer science, especially in interdisciplinary subjects where teachers may have limited technical expertise.

The intervention studied is a prototype PBL AI literacy toolkit containing three tools: an AI Art Lab, AI Music Studio, and AI Chatbot. Teachers used a short demo video, explored the toolkit, and then participated in semi-structured interviews and co-design sessions. The study involved 13 middle- and high-school teachers teaching a range of subjects in North America and East Asia, across public, private, and charter schools. Teachers designed hypothetical classroom activities using the toolkit for subjects such as math, science, Chinese, social studies, art, biology, and IT.

Findings suggest teachers generally viewed AI as useful for self-directed learning, creativity, inquiry, and concept reinforcement, but they also worried about accuracy, trustworthiness, copyright, and uneven student readiness. The toolkit was seen as especially helpful for scaffolding student exploration, supporting personalized learning, and reducing barriers for teachers with limited AI knowledge. The authors conclude that modular, adaptable, and scaffolded AI tools can support AI literacy across diverse K-12 settings, while further teacher training and better onboarding are needed for broader adoption.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model/chatbot system used for conversational question answering, prompt evaluation, and generating text, images, music, and other AI-assisted outputs. The paper discusses it as part of a broader PBL AI literacy toolkit rather than naming a specific commercial product.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in the toolkit as an AI Chatbot for student Q&A, concept reinforcement, prompt evaluation guidance, and conversational tutoring; also discussed alongside other toolkit tools in teacher co-design interviews.

findings.finding_summary: In qualitative interviews with 13 middle and high school teachers, the AI chatbot was the most widely adopted toolkit component (n=9 for course designs). Teachers said it could function as a 24/7 tutor, help students clarify misunderstandings outside class, provide supportive non-judgmental practice, and save teacher time by answering questions or reviewing work.
findings.measure: Teacher interview themes on adoption, instructional utility, and perceived classroom support

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods formative study based on interviews and co-design sessions with 13 teachers, not an experimental evaluation. It provides useful design evidence but no causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived usefulness and adoption for classroom support, but does not provide measured learning gains or effect sizes. Impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Answers: Large Language Model-Powered Tutoring System in Physics Education for Deep Learning and Precise Understanding
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to provide effective personalized tutoring with large language models (LLMs) in physics education. The authors argue that generic LLM assistance can produce superficially correct answers without supporting deep conceptual understanding, especially for abstract and information-rich physics problems. To address this, they propose Physics-STAR, a prompting framework that structures LLM tutoring into three stages: knowledge explanation, error analysis, and review suggestion.

The study evaluated Physics-STAR in a controlled experiment with 12 high school sophomores in Shenzhen, China. Students were split into three groups: traditional teacher-led review, generic GPT-4o tutoring, and GPT-4o guided by Physics-STAR. Pre- and post-tests measured performance on conceptual, computational, and information-based physics questions about gravity and spaceflight. The Physics-STAR group performed best on the more demanding information-based items, while all groups improved similarly on conceptual and computational questions. The results suggest that prompt-structured LLM tutoring can better support reflective learning and error analysis than generic LLM use.

Overall, the paper concludes that LLM-powered tutoring is most valuable when designed to support student-centered learning rather than direct answer provision. It emphasizes that personalized scaffolding, step-by-step guidance, and explicit error analysis can help students build deeper understanding and improve efficiency on complex problems. The paper does not focus on K-12 literacy or subgroup comparisons such as multilingual learners or students with disabilities.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model used as a conversational tutoring/feedback system for generating explanations, analyzing errors, and suggesting review steps.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the general LLM baseline (GPT-4o) and also as the underlying model within the Physics-STAR prompting framework for high school physics tutoring.

findings.finding_summary: In a controlled experiment with 12 high school sophomores (n=12), the generic LLM tutoring group using GPT-4o performed similarly to traditional teacher lecture on conceptual and computational questions, but showed only minimal improvement on information-based questions. The paper reports information-based post-test scores of M=2.5 for both General LLM tutoring and Teacher lecture, compared with M=5 for the Physics-STAR-guided GPT-4o group.
findings.measure: Pre-test/post-test multiple-choice physics performance on conceptual, computational, and information-based questions; completion time on each question type

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system archetype that provides personalized, adaptive instructional support through dialogue, explanation, error analysis, and review.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes Physics-STAR as an LLM-powered tutoring framework for personalized physics instruction; the system was compared against teacher lecture and generic LLM tutoring.

findings.finding_summary: In a controlled experiment with 12 high school sophomores (n=12), Physics-STAR-guided GPT-4o produced the strongest gains on information-based physics questions. Post-test information-based scores were M=5 for Physics-STAR versus M=2.5 for both general LLM tutoring and teacher lecture, and the paper reports a more pronounced decrease in completion time for information-based questions under Physics-STAR.
findings.measure: Post-test scores and completion time on conceptual, computational, and information-based physics questions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small controlled experiment with only 12 students and no reported inferential statistics, effect sizes, or confidence intervals. The paper provides preliminary evidence rather than a well-powered or fully reported causal evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed benefit is promising and appears concentrated on information-based physics questions, but the study is very small and does not report effect sizes. The practical impact is therefore unclear/modest rather than clearly medium or large.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing to Improve Health Literacy and Communication in Pediatric Populations and Beyond
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can be used to improve health literacy by generating explanations of pediatric medical conditions at different reading-grade levels. The authors were interested in two related questions: whether models such as ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing can produce explanations from a basic prompt, and whether adding explicit reading-level instructions helps the models tailor output for younger readers.

To study this, the authors tested 288 childhood disorders and conditions using two basic prompts and two prompt styles that specified grade level, spanning first through twelfth grade. They evaluated the output with readability indices and word counts, comparing performance across models. The work was conducted using publicly available LLMs and did not involve human participants, instead focusing on the textual outputs generated by the systems.

The main finding was that all models struggled to consistently generate truly low-grade reading levels, especially below sixth grade. ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 showed the greatest ability to vary output by requested grade level, while Bing and Bard tended to stay closer to high-school-level readability. The authors conclude that LLMs have promise for generating patient education materials for pediatric audiences, but current models are limited in their ability to precisely target easy reading levels and should be used cautiously alongside other educational tools.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot system used to generate and adapt text responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 on their ability to explain pediatric medical conditions at different reading-grade levels in response to basic and grade-specified prompts.

findings.finding_summary: Across 288 childhood conditions, ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 produced outputs that could be shifted toward lower reading-grade levels when prompts specified grade level, but neither model reliably matched the requested target. For basic prompts, both models produced college-level text at baseline; with 'Explain {} to a __ grader' and 'Explain {} at a __-grade reading level' prompts, ChatGPT-3.5 ranged roughly from 6th/7th grade to college-freshmen/twelfth-grade levels and ChatGPT-4 ranged from about 6th grade to college-senior level, depending on prompt wording.
findings.measure: Average reading grade level (aRGL) of generated explanations; word count
findings.sample_size: n=288 conditions; ChatGPT-4 tested on n=150 conditions

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational large language model chatbot system (formerly Bard) used to generate text responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated Google Bard on its ability to explain pediatric medical conditions at different reading-grade levels in response to basic and grade-specified prompts.

findings.finding_summary: Google Bard generally produced high-school-level text and showed limited ability to precisely adapt to requested reading grade levels. Across prompts, Bard ranged from about 7th to 10th grade on grade-specified prompts, tended to stay near the high-school level, and failed to generate responses for some conditions on basic prompts (e.g., 11 failures for 'What is/are' and 19 failures for 'Explain').
findings.measure: Average reading grade level (aRGL) of generated explanations; word count; rate of failed outputs

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic large language model / chatbot system used for generating and simplifying text at different reading levels.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a generic category label for the study's evaluation of large language model outputs for health-literacy-oriented explanations, although the paper actually named specific products.

findings.finding_summary: The study found that LLM outputs could be adjusted somewhat by prompt specificity, but models struggled to consistently produce text below a sixth-grade reading level. The overall conclusion was that generative AI showed promise for tailoring patient education materials, while remaining limited in exact grade-level control and in some cases refusing to answer prompts.
findings.measure: Reading grade level of outputs; word count; prompt success/failure

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot system used to generate and adapt text responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper also evaluated ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 on word count variation across prompts and the relationship between prompt grade level and output length/readability.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 showed increasing word count as requested grade level increased in some prompt structures, but the relationship between word count and readability was inconsistent across prompts. ChatGPT-4 generally produced longer outputs than ChatGPT-3.5, with the study noting greater variation in word count for OpenAI models than for Bing or Bard.
findings.measure: Word count of generated explanations

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single descriptive evaluation of LLM output readability, not an experimental intervention study or meta-analysis. It provides useful comparative information but does not meet higher-evidence design standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical potential for tailoring reading level, but it reports no effect sizes and no direct learner outcomes. Impact is therefore suggestive and modest rather than demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Effects of Generative AI Assistance on Writing Self-efficacy
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines whether generative AI assistance changes students’ writing self-efficacy, and whether the effects depend on where AI intervenes in the writing process. The paper is motivated by concerns that AI can both support writing and potentially reduce learner agency, ownership, and confidence if overused or used at the wrong stage.

The intervention compared four conditions in a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment: no AI, ideation-stage AI only, sentence-level AI only, and full-process AI. ChatGPT was used as the AI tool, and the study focused on argumentative writing tasks completed by Korean undergraduates. Participants completed two writing cycles in an online session, with self-efficacy measured after each task using a continuous 0–100 scale.

The findings suggest that generative AI does not uniformly improve writing self-efficacy. Full-process AI produced high but mostly stable self-efficacy, though participants reported reduced ownership; sentence-level AI was associated with declines in self-efficacy over time; and ideation-only AI showed the most promising pattern, combining high self-efficacy with positive change across tasks. The authors conclude that the locus of AI support matters more than the amount of support, and that ideation-focused assistance may better preserve agency while supporting confidence.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot for text generation and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the generative AI writing assistant in four experimental conditions for Korean undergraduates' argumentative writing: sentence-level revision, ideation-only support, full-process support, and a no-AI control condition.

findings.finding_summary: In this pilot experiment with 13 Korean undergraduates, writing self-efficacy differed by AI configuration rather than simply by AI presence. Full AI showed the highest average self-efficacy (M=82.2) but also signs of reduced ownership; Ideation AI showed high self-efficacy (M=80.1) and the steepest increase over time (94M=+11.1); Sentence AI was associated with universal decline in self-efficacy (5/5 participants, 94M=-5.7); No AI was lowest overall (M=61.8). Pairwise effects included Full AI vs No AI g=1.23 (95% CI [-0.60, 3.07]) and Full AI vs Sentence AI g=0.73.
findings.measure: Writing self-efficacy (0-100 scale) across two argumentative writing tasks
findings.confidence_interval: [−0.60, 3.07] for Full AI vs No AI; other CIs not reported

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot experiment with n=13 and non-definitive confidence intervals, so the evidence is preliminary. It is empirical and structured, but the sample is too small for high-confidence causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect sizes are large in some comparisons (e.g., g=1.23) and the paper identifies meaningful differences across AI configurations. However, the practical significance is limited by the pilot nature and unstable estimates.

paper_profiles.title: Approaching the Limits to EFL Writing Enhancement with AI-generated Text and Diverse Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary school EFL students use generative AI text while composing a feature article, and whether different interaction patterns with AI-generated text are associated with writing quality. The central problem is that although generative AI may help students write longer and potentially better texts, it is unclear which kinds of AI-human text integration are actually beneficial, and whether the benefits differ for students with different academic achievement levels.

The study analyzed 59 compositions from Hong Kong secondary school students who attended a two-hour workshop on writing with ChatGPT support. Students were taught an explicit writing approach, prompt engineering, and then completed a feature article task using their own words plus AI-generated text; they highlighted AI-generated portions for later analysis. The researchers used content analysis, multiple linear regression, and cluster analysis to examine how the number, length, and distribution of AI-generated and human-written chunks related to human-rated scores for content, language, organization, and total quality.

Results showed that overall writing scores were mainly associated with the total number of words in a composition rather than the specific way AI text was chunked or integrated. However, the relationship differed by school academic band. Students from higher-banding schools appeared better able to use AI flexibly and still produce strong writing, while students from lower-banding schools did not benefit as much from more AI words and sometimes scored worse when revising AI output. The authors conclude that generative AI can support EFL writing, but the benefits are uneven and depend on students’ existing writing competence, suggesting a need for stronger writing pedagogy and AI literacy instruction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational generative AI chatbot for text generation and interactive assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the generative AI chatbot supporting EFL secondary students' feature-article writing; students could use ChatGPT or other chatbots, and the paper's declaration also states the authors used ChatGPT to improve readability and language.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of 59 Hong Kong secondary EFL students, ChatGPT-style AI-generated text was integrated into compositions with an average of 281.10 AI words per composition (63.39%). Across all 59 compositions, human- and AI-word counts were positively associated with content, language, organization, and total scores (partial correlations around 0.39-0.44, p<0.01), but chunk-level integration patterns were not generally significant. The authors conclude that more words, rather than the specific AI integration pattern, mainly predicted writing quality, and that benefits differed by school achievement band.
findings.measure: Human-rated HKDSE writing scores (content, language, organization, total) and composition word/chunk features
findings.effect_size: partial correlations approximately 0.387-0.437 for AI/human words with scores

identified_tools.name: POE
identified_tools.description: A platform/app that provides access to multiple chatbots and large language models.
identified_tools.use_case: Introduced in the workshop as the app featuring different chatbots; students could use POE and any chatbot software to complete the writing task.

findings.finding_summary: The paper does not isolate POE-specific effects from other chatbots, but reports that students were introduced to POE as a gateway to state-of-the-art chatbots and then used any chatbot software of their choice. The study's measured outcomes pertain to compositions written with AI-generated text generally, not POE alone.
findings.measure: Composition scores and AI/text-use patterns in human-AI writing

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational/mixed-methods study using content analysis, regression, and cluster analysis rather than an experiment. It provides useful subgroup evidence, but causal claims are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed associations are modest to moderate in size, with partial correlations around 0.4 between word counts and scores. The subgroup differences by school achievement band suggest practically meaningful variation, though effects are not uniformly positive.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching with ChatGPT as a Linguistically Responsive Tool for Multilingual Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines how K–12 teachers in U.S. public schools used ChatGPT and related AI tools to support multilingual learners’ language and literacy development. The paper is motivated by a gap in evidence about how generative AI can be used in linguistically responsive ways for multilingual learners, especially within translanguaging-oriented pedagogy. The author asks how teachers are using ChatGPT in instruction and whether those uses align with key dimensions of translanguaging pedagogy.

The study drew on classroom observations and post-observation interviews from two cohorts of in-service teachers enrolled in a professional development course on culturally and linguistically responsive pedagogy. Although 61 teachers participated in the broader PD, the analysis focused on 42 observed teachers and identified eight observations in which ChatGPT was used. These cases spanned primary and secondary grades and included general education, Spanish immersion, English as a second language, dual-language bilingual education, science, math, ELA, and special education contexts in Washington, DC public schools and public charter schools.

Findings showed that teachers mainly used ChatGPT to facilitate communication and differentiate content, such as translating texts, transcribing student speech, generating subtitles, simplifying or adapting texts, and creating exemplars for disciplinary writing. A smaller number of secondary teachers used the tool to scaffold student prompting and to support multimodal literacy experimentation with image generation. The paper concludes that these practices align most strongly with the translanguaging dimensions of affordances, production, and co-labor, but that assessment and reflection were notably absent. The author argues that generative AI may expand multilingual learners’ access and agency, but only if teachers use it critically and explicitly, with attention to bias, ethical concerns, and more robust support for multilingual assessment and metalinguistic reflection.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system used for text generation, translation, prompting support, and multimodal outputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a linguistically responsive tool used by K-12 teachers of multilingual learners to translate texts, transcribe speech, differentiate content, scaffold student prompting, and support multimodal literacy experimentation.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative/mixed-methods classroom observation study, ChatGPT was used by 8 of 42 observed teachers across grade levels and settings to facilitate communication, differentiate content, provide structured prompt supports, and support multimodal literacy experimentation. The paper reports no experimental effect sizes or outcome measures; instead, it documents instructional practices that aligned with translanguaging dimensions, especially affordances, production, and co-labor.
findings.measure: Observed instructional practices and post-observation interview reports
findings.sample_size: n=42 observed teachers; ChatGPT use identified in 8 observations

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative classroom observation and interview study, not an experimental design. It provides descriptive evidence of implementation and pedagogical alignment rather than causal evidence of student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful instructional use of ChatGPT for multilingual learners, but it does not report measured learning gains or effect sizes. Impact is therefore promising but unclear from the evidence presented.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how artificial intelligence is reshaping education and argues that effective use of AI in classrooms depends on three key competencies: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. Rather than evaluating a specific AI intervention with outcome data, the article develops a conceptual case for how educators and students should understand and use generative AI tools responsibly, especially in the context of AI-generated academic work and classroom activities.

The paper combines an informal case study from Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, with a narrative literature review. Its central institutional example is the development of internal AI guidelines for student academic writing: students are encouraged to use tools such as ChatGPT and other generative models, but must be transparent about which model they used, how they used it, how they evaluated outputs, and where AI contributed to the manuscript. The paper also sketches classroom uses of AI such as AI experiments, AI-generated case studies, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive environments.

The intended context is primarily higher education, with the author noting that the discussion may also be useful for children and school settings. The article concludes that AI should not be treated as a tutor, teacher, or ghostwriter, but as a sparring partner that can support brainstorming and exploration while still requiring human judgment. It recommends building an “AI culture” through workshops, institutional guidance, and dedicated support for educators and students, while teaching AI literacy and prompt engineering as part of broader efforts to improve responsible and critical use of generative AI.

identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a prominent AI chatbot used in education and cited as an example of an LLM students and teachers might use for academic writing and classroom activities; also named alongside other models in the university’s AI guidelines.

paper_profiles.title: The Manifesto for Teaching and Learning in a Time of Generative AI: A Critical Collective Stance to Better Navigate the Future
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a manifesto that critically examines the rapid integration of generative AI (GenAI), chatbots, and algorithms into education, with a particular focus on teaching and learning in higher education. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, the authors argue for a balanced, evidence-based, and ethically grounded stance toward GenAI, emphasizing that these systems are not neutral and may reshape pedagogy, assessment, agency, equity, and human relationships in education.

The paper uses collective writing and a modified Delphi process to synthesize the perspectives of a large international group of higher-education educators and researchers specializing in GenAI. The resulting themes outline both perceived benefits and risks: on the positive side, GenAI may save time, support personalized learning, assist lesson planning and formative feedback, improve accessibility, and foster creativity and innovation; on the negative side, it may deepen digital divides, amplify bias, undermine academic integrity, spread misinformation, reduce human connection, and weaken critical thinking and learner agency.

The context is explicitly higher education and broader educational policy/practice, not K-12 literacy instruction. The authors conclude that GenAI should be integrated cautiously, with human oversight, institutional support, transparent policies, and ongoing research. They argue that GenAI should augment rather than replace human teaching, and that educators should preserve care, equity, creativity, and critical reflection while adapting curricula, assessment, and professional practice to the realities of GenAI.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI / large language model chatbot systems that can generate text and other content, support conversation, and assist with tasks such as drafting, feedback, and personalization.
identified_tools.use_case: This manifesto discusses generative AI broadly, including chatbots and LLMs such as ChatGPT, as an educational technology that may support lesson planning, formative feedback, assessment, tutoring, and other teaching/learning functions. It does not evaluate a specific product or report empirical effects.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a manifesto/editorial and qualitative collective-writing piece, not an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. It offers critical discussion and thematic claims rather than measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues GenAI may have broad educational influence, but it provides no quantitative effect estimates or outcome data. Its influence is conceptual and field-shaping rather than evidence of measured impact.

paper_profiles.title: The Artificial Intelligence Assessment Scale (AIAS): A Framework for Ethical Integration of Generative AI in Educational Assessment
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how educational institutions should respond to the rapid spread of generative AI tools in assessment, especially the tension between banning these tools as academic misconduct and incorporating them in ways that support learning. The authors argue that a binary AI/no-AI stance is too simplistic and propose a practical framework for defining acceptable levels of GenAI use in assessments.

The main intervention is the Artificial Intelligence Assessment Scale (AIAS), a five-level scale ranging from no AI use to full AI use. The levels distinguish between idea generation/structuring, editing, task completion with human evaluation, and fully integrated use. The paper explains how the scale can help educators specify permitted AI use, support transparency, and guide students toward ethical and academically responsible use of GenAI in their work.

The paper is framed primarily around higher education assessment, but the authors state that the scale is flexible enough to be adapted for K-12 settings. It does not report an empirical study of student outcomes; instead, it synthesizes prior literature on GenAI, academic integrity, assessment design, and digital literacy. The paper concludes that institutions need clearer policies and more nuanced assessment designs that move beyond detection-and-punishment approaches toward structured, transparent integration of GenAI.

A relevant secondary contribution for K-12 and teacher-facing use is that the authors explicitly note GenAI's potential to support lesson planning, feedback, and assessment tasks, while also distinguishing educator use from student use in assessed work. However, the paper itself is not an evaluation of a classroom implementation or a teacher-training intervention.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative artificial intelligence / large language model tools capable of producing and revising text and other content, and supporting assessment-related tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) for regulating how generative AI may be used in educational assessment, and discusses teacher/student uses such as brainstorming, editing, task completion, and feedback/support in assessment contexts.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/framework paper proposing the AI Assessment Scale rather than reporting an empirical evaluation of a specific AI tool. No study design, sample, or outcome data are presented.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potential practical influence on assessment policy and GenAI integration, but it does not report measured impact on learning or operational outcomes. As a framework, its impact is suggestive rather than empirically demonstrated.

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review of literature reviews on artificial intelligence in education (AIED): a roadmap to a future research agenda
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of understanding the rapidly expanding but fragmented literature on artificial intelligence in education (AIED). Rather than reviewing primary studies directly, the authors conduct a systematic review of literature reviews to synthesize what prior reviews have found, identify dominant themes, and map gaps in the field. Their goal is to provide an overarching roadmap for future AIED research and practice.

The study uses PRISMA-guided systematic searching across major education and technology databases and includes 143 journal-based literature reviews on AIED. The analysis is organized using a technology-enhanced learning framework, coding each review by publication year, country, venue, stakeholder group, educational level, subject area, review method, educational objectives, technologies used, and reported advantages/challenges. Although the paper is broad rather than intervention-specific, it includes discussion of AI uses such as machine learning, chatbots, intelligent tutoring systems, and large language models/generative AI in educational settings.

The reviewed literature spans multiple educational contexts, with the heaviest emphasis on higher education, followed by K-12, and a much smaller set focused on special education and early childhood. Across the review corpus, students and teachers are the primary stakeholders, while administrators and researchers receive much less attention. The paper concludes that AIED is most often positioned to support teaching and learning, assessment, and personalization, but that major concerns remain around privacy, equity, reliability, lack of teacher training, and the risk that AI may be seen as a replacement for human judgment rather than an augmenting tool. The authors call for more work on K-12, special education, and ethical, collaborative human–AI use.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbots used in education for content generation, instructional support, questioning, and feedback rather than a specific branded product.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of reviews on AI in education. It synthesizes literature that includes teacher-facing and student-facing generative AI uses, especially chatbots and large language models, but does not evaluate one specific named product.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature reviews, generative AI and LLMs were discussed as increasingly important in education, with 19.5% of the reviewed studies focusing on LLMs/generative AI and 9.5% on chatbots. The paper notes that these tools are being used for teaching and learning support, including answering frequently asked questions and helping teachers plan and carry out lessons, but it does not report a pooled effect size.
findings.measure: Frequency of review coverage and described uses in the literature review corpus

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of literature reviews, so it synthesizes secondary evidence rather than reporting a primary causal estimate. The review is methodical and PRISMA-based, but the extract provides no quantitative effect estimate for a specific tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broad relevance of generative AI in education, especially for teacher support and instructional tasks, but it does not quantify impact on learner outcomes. Without an effect size, the magnitude of impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This reflection paper examines current debates and research on artificial intelligence (AI) in education, with a focus on how AI affects cognitive learning processes and outcomes. The authors argue that discussions around AI are often shaped by hype and overgeneralization, and they call for more evidence-based research that distinguishes between genuine learning gains and superficial performance improvements.

The paper proposes the ISAR model, which classifies AI effects on learning into four types: inversion, substitution, augmentation, and redefinition. Using this framework, the authors synthesize prior research on AI-enhanced learning, including intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI, large language models, teacher-facing tools, and student-facing applications such as conversational agents, feedback systems, dashboards, and AI-generated instructional materials. They emphasize that AI can support learning when it augments instruction or enables deeper learning tasks, but it can also reduce learning if students over-rely on AI or if the tool design is poorly aligned with instructional goals.

The paper is not an empirical study of a specific population or intervention, but a conceptual review aimed at educators, researchers, and designers working in AI-enhanced education. It highlights that successful AI integration depends on student and teacher prerequisites such as AI literacy, pedagogical skill, and contextual factors like infrastructure and regulation. The main conclusion is that AI should be treated as an instructional support that must be carefully designed, validated, and used in ways that preserve cognitive engagement and human involvement.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI / large language model chatbot used for general-purpose text generation, question answering, and interactive dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses ChatGPT as a non-educational generative AI tool used in educational settings, and cites studies using it for student tasks such as scientific inquiry, writing revision, and support in learning activities. It is contrasted with educational AI systems and with teacher-facing uses of generative AI.

findings.finding_summary: In the cited study by Stadler et al. (2024), students used ChatGPT during a scientific inquiry task on nanoparticles in sunscreen. ChatGPT simplified task processing by reducing extraneous and intrinsic load, but this did not improve learning effectiveness and was accompanied by reduced cognitive processing depth and lower cognitive learning outcomes, as reflected in the quality of arguments in a posttest justification task.
findings.measure: Quality of arguments in a posttest justification task; cognitive processing depth (germane load)

findings.finding_summary: In the cited study by Fan et al. (2024), ChatGPT was compared with a human expert chat, writing analytics tools, and no support during a writing task. ChatGPT improved task performance during the supported intervention phase, but there were no differences in posttest knowledge gain or knowledge transfer; learners also showed relatively low metacognitive processing, which the authors characterized as possible 'metacognitive laziness'.
findings.measure: Task performance during supported intervention phase; posttest knowledge gain; knowledge transfer; metacognitive processing

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a reflection/theoretical paper rather than a primary empirical evaluation of ChatGPT. The ChatGPT findings are reported secondhand from cited studies, without full methodological detail or direct effect estimates in this paper.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports both negative and mixed ChatGPT-related outcomes, including reduced learning effectiveness in one cited study and no posttest gains in another. Because effect sizes are not reported here and the evidence is indirect, the impact is best treated as modest/unclear overall.

paper_profiles.title: Developing and Validating the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Concept Inventory: an Instrument to Assess Artificial Intelligence Literacy among Middle School Students
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of reliable and valid instruments for assessing K-12 students’ artificial intelligence (AI) literacy, especially at the middle school level. The authors argue that without a general assessment tool, educators and researchers cannot clearly determine what AI concepts students can learn or how effective different AI literacy curricula and pedagogies are. To fill this gap, they developed the AI Literacy Concept Inventory (AI-CI), a multiple-choice assessment intended to measure middle school students’ conceptual understanding of core AI literacy topics.

The study combines qualitative and quantitative methods to design, refine, and validate the instrument. Qualitative work included expert panel reviews, observations of students in a pilot of the Developing AI Literacy (DAILy) curriculum, student interviews about their thinking, and cognitive validation interviews to identify misconceptions and improve item wording and distractors. Quantitative validation used responses from 981 middle school students across three U.S. public school districts, with a separate reliability sample of 108 students who took the AI-CI before and after learning with the DAILy curriculum. The assessment focused on AI general concepts, logic systems, machine learning, and supervised learning, and items were designed to be age-appropriate and technology-independent.

The authors conclude that the AI-CI is a valid and reliable tool for assessing AI literacy among middle school students. They also show that concept-inventory design can surface student misconceptions and provide more diagnostic information than standard multiple-choice tests, making the tool useful for both research and classroom assessment. Although the paper is not about teacher-facing generative AI tools, it is relevant to broader K-12 AI education because it clarifies how student learning of AI concepts can be measured and how misconceptions can be used to design better assessments.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / AI literacy context rather than a specific commercial product; in this paper it is discussed conceptually as AI systems that can generate content and as a topic in student AI literacy.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper does not evaluate a teacher-facing generative AI tool. It develops and validates an assessment of middle school students’ AI literacy, including concepts such as AI general, logic systems, machine learning, supervised learning, and mentions generative AI only as a concept students should understand.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary empirical validation study, but it does not evaluate an AI instructional tool or intervention. The main contribution is assessment development/validation, so evidence is indirect for AI tool effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s impact is methodological rather than tool-intervention impact. It provides a validated assessment that could support future AI education studies, but it does not report outcome effects of an AI tool.

paper_profiles.title: Potential Benefits and Risks of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.venue: Bartın University Journal of Faculty of Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the potential benefits and risks of artificial intelligence (AI) in education, with particular attention to the rapid spread of generative AI systems such as ChatGPT. The central question is how AI systems may support teaching, learning, assessment, and educational administration, while also creating ethical, privacy, bias, and equity concerns. The author positions the paper as a systematic review of prior studies and reports, using document analysis to synthesize relevant literature across educational contexts.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the paper surveys the broader landscape of AI uses in education. It discusses teacher-facing uses such as lesson planning, creating instructional materials, assessment support, grading, and feedback generation, as well as student-facing uses such as assignment support, translation, and personalized learning. The paper also includes school and policy-level uses, such as decision-making and educational management. The discussion explicitly distinguishes assistive teacher tools and intelligent tutoring / automated assessment systems from student misuse of generative text tools, emphasizing that AI may support instruction but should not replace teachers.

The paper is not based on a primary empirical sample; instead, it synthesizes claims from the literature to identify recurring opportunities and risks. It concludes that AI can reduce workload, personalize learning, and improve feedback and assessment processes, but may also intensify inequality, undermine academic integrity, reproduce bias, and create privacy and data-protection problems. The author recommends responsible AI use, stronger AI literacy for students, teachers, and administrators, updated teacher preparation and in-service training, and more robust assessment practices that can detect unethical use and better capture student learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT

identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses ChatGPT as an example of generative AI in education, including teacher uses such as lesson planning, preparing materials, creating exams, conducting assessments, providing feedback, and generating interactive learning scenarios; it also notes student use for assignments and exams.

findings.finding_summary: This systematic review reports that ChatGPT can support teachers with lesson planning, material generation, exam creation, assessment, feedback, and interactive learning scenarios, and can also help students with assignments, presentations, translation, and access to materials. The paper does not report original effect sizes or study-level estimates; it synthesizes potential benefits and risks from prior literature.
findings.measure: Narrative review of reported educational uses, benefits, and risks

findings.finding_summary: The review emphasizes risks including privacy and data protection concerns, academic integrity/plagiarism, bias in outputs, unequal access, and potential teacher workload increases or role displacement. It argues that uncritical use may deepen inequities and weaken assessment validity, but no quantitative estimates are provided.
findings.measure: Narrative review of reported risks and policy concerns

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review and policy-oriented discussion rather than an empirical evaluation of a single intervention. No original experimental design, effect sizes, or quantitative outcome estimates are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially substantial educational relevance for teacher workflow, assessment, and literacy instruction, but it provides no measured effect sizes. The impact is therefore conceptually meaningful yet empirically unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: On opportunities and challenges of large multimodal foundation models in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the emerging role of large multimodal foundation models (LMFMs) in education and asks how these systems differ from earlier large language models in their educational uses and risks. The authors frame LMFMs as models that can process and generate not only text, but also speech, images, and video, and they discuss how this multimodality expands opportunities for learning, teaching, research, and educational software development.

The paper is not an empirical intervention study; instead, it provides a conceptual overview of likely use cases. For learners, it highlights possibilities such as personalized learning assistants, multimodal feedback, support for language learning, image generation and interpretation, help with experimentation, code generation, and accessibility features for students with disabilities. For educators, it discusses lesson planning, classroom activity design, assessment creation and grading, dashboards, teacher training simulations, and administrative support. It also distinguishes teacher-facing uses from student-facing tutoring tools by emphasizing educator workflow support, task design, and feedback generation rather than direct instruction alone.

The paper is situated in K-12 and higher-education discussions broadly, but it does not report a specific participant sample, school setting, or country because it is a theoretical perspective. Its main conclusion is that LMFMs could substantially improve personalization, engagement, and efficiency in education, but only if educators and institutions address major concerns including hallucinations, bias, privacy, unequal access, overreliance, and the need for AI literacy and human oversight.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational generative AI family used for text generation, multimodal understanding, and task-oriented assistance via prompts and APIs.
identified_tools.use_case: This perspective discusses ChatGPT and GPT-4-Turbo/GPTs as teacher-facing and student-facing generative AI tools for lesson planning, assessment creation, feedback, tutoring, data analysis, and educational application development, but does not report an empirical evaluation in this paper.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective article rather than an empirical study, systematic review, or meta-analysis. It provides conceptual discussion of opportunities and challenges without reporting original data or evaluated outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ChatGPT/GPT-based tools may have broad educational utility, especially for lesson planning, feedback, and assessment support, but it does not present measured effects. Because no outcome data are reported, empirical impact is not established.

paper_profiles.title: The Potential Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Equity and Inclusion in Education
paper_profiles.venue: OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers / OECD Education Working Papers Series
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This OECD working paper examines how artificial intelligence may affect equity and inclusion in education, with a particular focus on school education. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, it reviews the current landscape of AI tools and policy guidance, and organizes the discussion around a taxonomy of learner-centred, teacher-led, and other institutional tools. The paper is motivated by concerns about both the potential benefits of AI for adapting learning and supporting diverse learners, and the risks of bias, exclusion, privacy harms, techno-ableism, and uneven access.

The paper uses desk-based research, mainly in English, and draws on examples of AI tools already used or emerging in schools, such as intelligent tutoring systems, AI-enabled simulations, chatbots, assessment assistants, classroom-management tools, and admissions or early-warning systems. It distinguishes tools primarily by who the main beneficiary or user is: students, teachers, or institutions. The teacher-led category includes tools that can support lesson-related work such as curation of materials, assessment, classroom management, and continuing professional learning, while the learner-centred category includes tools designed to support student learning and the institutional category includes administrative decision-support tools.

The paper’s main conclusion is that AI may support equity and inclusion if deployed carefully, but current evidence remains limited and uneven. Many benefits are presented as plausible opportunities rather than established effects, and the authors caution that adoption is often proceeding without systematic oversight or robust evaluation. They argue that policy should prioritize access, transparency, bias mitigation, teacher training, ethical safeguards, and further interdisciplinary research so that AI use in education does not reinforce existing inequalities.

identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI and chatbot tools used to produce, adapt, or support educational content and interactions without a specific commercial product named.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI in teacher-led and learner-centred education contexts, including examples such as ChatGPT and Google Bard, but the paper itself is a policy/review paper rather than an empirical evaluation of one specific product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a policy/review working paper that synthesises concepts, guidelines, and examples rather than reporting a primary empirical study or meta-analysis of a specific AI tool. It does not provide a clear evaluated intervention design or outcome data for a named product.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that generative AI may reduce teacher workload and support teaching, but it does not report effect sizes or direct outcome estimates. As a result, the practical impact is discussed qualitatively and remains uncertain rather than demonstrated empirically.

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers collaborate with an AI-assisted lesson planning system, Shiksha Copilot, in low-resource government schools. The central problem is whether and how large language models can support teachers who face heavy administrative workloads, limited instructional materials, multilingual teaching demands, and little time for planning. The authors focus on teacher-facing generative AI rather than student tutoring: the system is explicitly designed to help educators generate, review, adapt, and reuse lesson plans, as well as optionally generate questions and answer lesson-specific queries.

Shiksha Copilot was deployed in government schools across Karnataka, India, supporting English- and Kannada-medium lesson planning for Grades 5–10. The system used a two-stage workflow: 23 expert curators first reviewed and refined AI-generated learning objectives and lesson plans, then 1,043 teachers accessed the curated plans and customized them for their classrooms. The platform also included curriculum-grounded retrieval, bilingual translation, question generation, and chat tools. Deployment included a three-hour training session led by mentors, with ongoing support through WhatsApp, phone calls, and visits.

Using system logs, surveys, and 43 semi-structured interviews, the study shows that teachers used the tool both for instructional preparation and bureaucratic documentation. The system reduced planning time and stress, while helping teachers access curriculum-aligned materials and encouraging more activity-based pedagogy. However, teachers often made off-platform adaptations, and the Kannada translations required substantial human revision because of literal translation and terminology issues. The paper concludes that teacher-AI collaboration is most effective when human expertise, curation, and local contextual knowledge remain central, especially in multilingual and low-resource settings.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model-based teacher support system used for lesson planning, translation, question generation, and teacher Q&A; not a single named commercial product in the paper's main system.
identified_tools.use_case: Shiksha Copilot used LLMs with RAG and human-in-the-loop curation to generate and customize bilingual lesson plans for teachers, support lesson-specific and general pedagogical chat, and generate assessment questions.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that Shiksha Copilot reduced bureaucratic workload, lesson planning time, and teaching-related stress for teachers using the system. It also enabled teachers to access curriculum-aligned lesson plans and support both instructional and administrative documentation needs, based on mixed-methods data from 1,043 teachers and 23 curators.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers used AI-generated lesson plans for classroom instruction and bureaucratic documentation, and the tool supported a shift toward activity-based pedagogy.
