The paper also reports that teachers appropriated features such as question paper generators and AI chat to support classroom practice.
findings.measure: Observed teacher use of lesson plans and platform features; interviews and platform logs

findings.finding_summary: For the curation workflow, English lesson-plan content was largely reliable and required few edits: 96.13% of 7,744 content blocks were rated suitable for classroom use, with 3.53% needing minor adjustments and 0.34% unusable. This indicates the AI-assisted pipeline produced mostly usable English lesson-plan drafts after curator review.
findings.measure: Curator ratings of English lesson-plan content blocks

findings.finding_summary: Kannada lesson plans required extensive linguistic intervention despite sound pedagogical structure: 94.4% of content blocks in 26 Kannada-medium lesson plans were edited, with nearly all substantive edits related to language. The paper attributes this to literal translation problems and the need for domain-appropriate Kannada wording.
findings.measure: Curator edits to Kannada-medium lesson-plan content blocks

findings.finding_summary: Teachers rarely modified the curated lesson plans inside the system, but the authors interpret this low in-platform edit rate as reflecting off-platform adaptation rather than passive acceptance. Of 5,542 teacher-created lesson plans, only 85 (1.53%) were modified, and interviews showed teachers often adapted plans mentally or using peer resources.
findings.measure: Distribution-platform edit logs and teacher interviews

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods field study with interviews, surveys, and log analysis rather than an RCT or meta-analysis. The evidence is informative but observational, so causal claims are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful workload and workflow benefits, but it does not provide a quantified effect size for the main outcomes. Reported impacts are substantial qualitatively, yet the numeric impact is unclear or not reported.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-Assisted Lesson Planning for Children’s STEAM Arts Education: An Experimental Study on Benefits, Challenges, Methods, and a Prompt Framework
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can improve lesson planning for children’s STEAM arts education, with a specific focus on teacher-facing generative AI support rather than student tutoring or direct student text generation. The authors argue that lesson planning in children’s art and STEAM contexts is time-consuming and resource-intensive, especially when teachers must integrate interdisciplinary content, age-appropriate materials, and safety considerations. They investigate whether ChatGPT can help teachers generate, refine, and optimize lesson plans more efficiently and with higher quality.

The study was conducted with 13 children’s art teachers and 6 university professors in China. In Experiment 1, teachers created lesson plans using both traditional methods and ChatGPT-assisted methods for the same thematic lesson topic (“Color Art”) for K3 children aged 7–9. Teachers used GPT-4o and were guided by a prompt framework developed by the researchers. In Experiment 2, professors blind-rated the lesson plans using a rubric adapted from the 5E Inquiry Lesson Plan model across six dimensions, including introduction, teaching method, practical method, interdisciplinarity, after-class work, and core competencies. The study combined teacher questionnaires, interviews, ChatGPT interaction logs, observation notes, and professor ratings.

Findings suggest that ChatGPT improved lesson-planning efficiency, reduced planning time, and helped teachers generate richer content, images, and interdisciplinary ideas. Teachers generally rated ChatGPT positively and reported willingness to continue using it. However, they also identified important limitations: outputs could be overly idealized, insufficiently practical for day-to-day classrooms, and sometimes unsafe or poorly adapted to the age group. The authors conclude that ChatGPT is best understood as a collaborative tool for teacher-facing lesson planning, not a replacement for educators, and they propose a structured prompt framework to support more effective use in art education.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot / large language model system used for text generation, planning support, and interactive prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by teachers to assist with lesson planning for children's STEAM arts education, including generating, refining, checking, and optimizing lesson plans and related content/resources; the paper also developed a prompt framework for using ChatGPT in this context.

findings.finding_summary: In the experimental comparison of traditional versus ChatGPT-assisted lesson plans, ChatGPT-assisted plans received a higher average evaluation score than traditional plans (21.0 vs 17.0). The study reports that ChatGPT significantly improved lesson-planning quality, although the paper does not provide a test statistic or confidence interval in the excerpted text.
findings.measure: Professor-rated lesson plan quality using a six-dimension rubric adapted from the 5E Inquiry Lesson Plan framework
findings.sample_size: n=25 lesson plans (12 traditional, 13 ChatGPT-assisted); n=13 teachers; n=6 professors

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that ChatGPT improved lesson-planning efficiency, including faster topic selection, faster generation of instructional content, and reduced planning time. Mean ratings were 3.7 for accelerated topic selection, 3.8 for rapid generation of high-quality instructional content, and 4.2 for reduced lesson-planning time.
findings.measure: Teacher survey ratings on teaching efficiency and time savings

findings.finding_summary: Teachers rated ChatGPT positively for interdisciplinary integration, with 61% of respondents giving ratings of 4 or above on the interdisciplinary items. The paper describes ChatGPT as effective for rapidly generating interdisciplinary teaching resources, but no formal effect size is reported.
findings.measure: Teacher survey ratings on interdisciplinary integration

findings.finding_summary: Teachers generally agreed that ChatGPT improved lesson-plan content quality, including accuracy and alignment with their requirements. The reported average ratings were 4.0 for content accuracy and 3.9 for meeting teacher requirements, but the paper also notes limitations in practicality, personalization, and safety-related suitability.
findings.measure: Teacher survey ratings on content quality and fit to requirements

findings.finding_summary: Teachers were neutral on ChatGPT's ability to foster innovation: the paper states ChatGPT more often served as a source of inspiration than as a generator of wholly innovative content. The study frames this as a limitation of the tool and emphasizes that it cannot replace teachers' own observational and creative work.
findings.measure: Teacher survey ratings and interview themes on innovation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods experimental study with teacher and professor participants, but it is small and not randomized in the strict RCT sense. The evidence is useful yet limited by feasibility sampling, self-report measures, and the absence of full statistical detail in the excerpt.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are practically meaningful for teacher-facing lesson planning, including higher lesson-plan quality scores and improved efficiency. However, the evidence is mostly descriptive and the sample is small, so the overall impact is modest rather than large.

paper_profiles.title: Science Literacy: Generative AI as Enabler of Coherence in the Teaching, Learning, and Assessment of Scientific Knowledge and Reasoning
paper_profiles.venue: The handbook of generative AI in education: Implications for research and practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how generative AI could support science literacy across the K-16+ span, with a particular emphasis on K-12 science education. The central problem is the long-standing disconnect between science curriculum, instruction, and assessment, especially under contemporary standards that require students to integrate disciplinary core ideas, science and engineering practices, and crosscutting concepts. The authors argue that this challenge becomes even more important in the era of AI, because science education must now also prepare learners to understand and use AI in scientifically informed ways.

Rather than reporting a new empirical intervention study, the chapter proposes a human-in-the-loop architecture for integrating generative AI into science teaching, learning, and assessment. It discusses how AI can support teacher-facing work such as creating lesson plans, generating assessments, scoring student explanations and models, and providing formative feedback, while keeping teachers in control of pedagogical decisions. The paper distinguishes these teacher-facing uses from student-facing intelligent tutoring and open-ended learning environments that provide direct scaffolding to learners.

The discussion is grounded in K-12 science education frameworks such as the NRC Framework and NGSS, and it uses examples from recent science education AI systems, including AI-supported scoring and feedback tools and generative tools for instructional design. The authors conclude that generative AI has strong potential to improve coherence across curriculum, instruction, and assessment, but only if designed within transparent, ethical, and teacher-mediated systems that preserve human agency and align with disciplinary learning goals.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model-based educational assistant used to generate instructional materials, support feedback on student work, and assist with assessment and tutoring-like scaffolding.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a human-in-the-loop generative AI approach in K-12 science education to support teachers with lesson planning, formative feedback, and assessment design; the chapter also discusses teacher-facing use for creating lesson plans and scoring/explaining short-answer assessments.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical chapter rather than an empirical evaluation, and it does not report a study design, sample, or outcomes for a specific tool. The text discusses architectures and illustrative examples instead of measured effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter argues that generative AI could reduce teacher workload and support coherence across teaching, learning, and assessment, but it provides no direct outcome data or effect sizes. Impact is therefore plausible but unmeasured in this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Education Reform in Libya: Opportunities and Challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence could support education reform in Libya while protecting equity, privacy, and academic integrity. It is framed around the question of which AI uses are most promising for improving learning and teacher efficiency in a context marked by regional disparities, connectivity gaps, and limited Arabic-language digital content.

The paper combines a scoping review of recent empirical studies and policy documents with a Libya-focused desk review of governance, infrastructure, teacher capacity, and curriculum-aligned content. It also proposes a mixed-methods study design for Libya that would include teacher and student surveys, semi-structured interviews with policymakers, school leaders, and teachers, and a short pilot intervention. The proposed pilot targets Libyan K-12 and some early higher-education settings, especially public schools, with attention to foundational literacy, mathematics, and low-stakes writing support.

Across the reviewed literature, the paper concludes that curriculum-aligned intelligent tutoring, adaptive practice, and automated feedback can improve short-cycle learning outcomes and reduce teachers’ routine marking burden when teachers retain control and tools are embedded in formative routines. It argues that generative AI should be limited to drafting and support functions rather than answer generation, and that effective adoption requires professional development, local Arabic content, offline or low-bandwidth access, and strong governance safeguards. The paper ultimately proposes a staged roadmap for Libya emphasizing national guidance, teacher capacity building, targeted pilots, and evidence-based scaling.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: Intelligent tutoring systems are AI-driven educational tools that provide adaptive practice, guidance, and feedback tailored to learner responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper synthesizes prior evidence and proposes pilots using curriculum-aligned intelligent tutoring/adaptive practice in foundational literacy and mathematics; it does not evaluate a specific product.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that curriculum-aligned intelligent tutoring and adaptive practice are associated with improvements on short-cycle assessments in foundational literacy when embedded in lesson plans and formative routines. The synthesis does not provide a pooled effect size or sample size for these literacy findings.
findings.measure: Short-cycle literacy assessments

findings.finding_summary: The paper states that curriculum-aligned intelligent tutoring and adaptive practice consistently coincide with gains in mathematics short-cycle assessments when teachers integrate them into lesson plans and formative assessment routines. No pooled effect size, confidence interval, or sample size is reported in the paper's synthesis.
findings.measure: Short-cycle mathematics assessments

identified_tools.name: Adaptive Feedback System (General)
identified_tools.description: AI-supported feedback systems generate automated comments, hints, or rubric-based guidance for student work, especially low-stakes writing and quizzes.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses automated or AI-supported feedback for low-stakes writing and quizzes as a teacher-facing efficiency support and as a structured low-stakes drafting aid in the proposed pilot.

findings.finding_summary: The paper says automated feedback for low-stakes writing can reduce grading burden and provide individualized guidance on grammar, structure, or misconception patterns, supporting revision and metacognition when feedback is targeted. It also cautions that direct answers can short-circuit learning; no effect size or sample size is reported.
findings.measure: Teacher grading burden and individualized writing feedback quality

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers can spend less time on routine marking when automated feedback is limited to low-stakes tasks and teachers retain authority over high-stakes judgments. This is presented as a synthesis finding rather than a single study result, with no effect size or sample size reported.
findings.measure: Teacher workload/time spent on routine marking

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI assistants produce text and other content for drafting, brainstorming, language scaffolds, and similar tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper distinguishes generic generative assistants for drafting and coding from student-facing tutoring tools, and describes them as limited to low-stakes drafting support with disclosure and academic integrity guardrails.

findings.finding_summary: The paper warns that generative AI used for drafting can create performance illusions: short-run gains in assignment quality may coincide with reduced knowledge retention and task persistence when students outsource core thinking. It therefore frames GenAI as potentially useful for brainstorming and language scaffolds but risky when used as an answer engine; no pooled effect size or sample size is reported.
findings.measure: Assignment quality, knowledge retention, and task persistence

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a scoping review/policy synthesis with a proposed pilot framework, not a completed controlled evaluation of a specific AI product. The evidence described is mixed-method and secondary, so it does not meet high-causality criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for literacy, mathematics, and teacher workload, but no primary effect sizes are reported for the paper itself. Because the findings are synthesized and context-dependent, the impact is promising but still unclear.

paper_profiles.title: When ChatGPT joins the team: a mixed-methods study of AI-mediated collaborative lesson design
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how ChatGPT changes collaborative lesson-design work when it is positioned as a peer-like feedback provider rather than as a traditional tutor or external tool. The authors focus on a gap in AI-in-education research: much of the literature studies individual use, while less is known about LLMs functioning as active contributors in group learning processes and how that affects both collaboration and learning.

The intervention was a quasi-experimental, counterbalanced crossover study in which 102 in-service teachers in a one-year specialization program for special education completed two authentic group tasks in a single 240-minute session. In one task sequence, groups used ChatGPT 3.5 as a collaborative “team member” to help select and justify inclusive ICT tools and then to design a full lesson/intervention; in the other sequence they completed the same kinds of tasks without ChatGPT. The study combined individual multiple-choice knowledge tests, expert ratings of group-produced artifacts, and written group reflections, allowing the authors to compare learning gains, product quality, and collaborative processes across AI-assisted and non-AI phases.

The main findings suggest that ChatGPT support improved knowledge scores, especially on technology-related content, and that gains made during AI-assisted phases were not immediately lost when the AI was withdrawn. The authors describe this as a Post-Withdrawal Sustained Performance pattern, with stable performance after AI removal within the study window. ChatGPT also appeared to increase efficiency and help groups generate more technology-focused insights, but qualitative evidence showed trade-offs, including reduced peer-to-peer idea building in some groups and concerns about creativity. Overall, the paper argues that LLMs can support collaborative design when learners are scaffolded to critically evaluate AI output rather than accept it passively, but that designers should preserve opportunities for authentic peer dialogue.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot used for text generation, feedback, and general assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a peer-like feedback provider / collaborative team member during group lesson-design tasks; groups were instructed to treat ChatGPT as if it were a colleague and to use it for suggestions, clarification, and critique while designing lesson plans.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods quasi-experimental study with 102 preservice teachers in 21 groups (82 completed all tests and were included in final analyses), use of ChatGPT was associated with significant gains on the individual knowledge test when it was present in a task phase. For GT1, scores increased after Task 1 (p=0.015, rrb=-0.429) and technology knowledge increased more strongly (p=0.001, rrb=-0.692); for GT2, scores increased when ChatGPT was used in Task 2 (p=0.023, rrb=-0.371; technology subscore p=0.022, rrb=-0.442).
findings.measure: 13-item multiple-choice knowledge test (overall score and technology/methodology subscores)
findings.confidence_interval: GT1 overall: (-0.80, -0.06); GT1 technology: (-1.12, -0.26); GT2 overall: (-0.73, -0.01); GT2 technology: (-0.87, -0.02)
findings.sample_size: n=82 final analysis; GT1 n=38; GT2 n=45

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT support did not produce a detectable decline after withdrawal in the immediate next phase, indicating a post-withdrawal sustained performance pattern within the study timeframe. For GT1, knowledge remained essentially stable from T1 to T2 (overall p=0.451, rrb=-0.028), and task product quality also did not decline after AI removal (two-sided p=0.236; one-tailed test for decrease p=0.882; d=0.43).
findings.measure: Post-withdrawal knowledge test scores and group artifact quality after AI removal
findings.sample_size: n=38 for GT1 sequence; n=82 final analysis

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods quasi-experimental study with counterbalanced crossover assignment, but not a randomized controlled trial. It provides quantitative outcome data plus qualitative process evidence, so the methodological strength is moderate rather than high.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects on knowledge gains during AI-supported phases are statistically significant and in the modest-to-medium range (e.g., rrb about 0.37 to 0.69 in absolute value), while post-withdrawal performance is maintained rather than further improved. Overall impact is positive but not uniformly large across outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Task automation and instructional planning support with large language models: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the emerging literature on large language models (LLMs) in educational settings, focusing on whether they reduce teacher workload and support instructional planning. The review is framed around two questions: whether LLMs reduce the time spent generating educational content and improve the perceived quality of that content, and whether they automate teaching-related tasks and planning compared with traditional methods.

The review included 16 studies published between 2023 and 2025, consisting of 13 primary empirical studies and 3 secondary syntheses. The primary studies covered qualitative, quantitative, quasi-experimental, and mixed-methods designs and were concentrated mainly in higher education, with some evidence spanning mixed settings and teacher-training contexts. The LLMs studied included ChatGPT variants and other models such as GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude, LLaMA, PALM, and custom systems, and they were used for generating lessons, explanations, assessments, feedback, summaries, and other instructional materials.

Across the reviewed studies, LLMs were generally associated with reported time savings, quicker drafting of content, and perceived improvements in clarity or usefulness of generated materials. They also appeared useful for automating first-pass feedback, lesson planning, and task generation. However, the evidence was heterogeneous, often self-reported, and methodologically limited; the review highlights risks such as prompt sensitivity, hallucinations, privacy concerns, and weak reproducibility. The authors conclude that LLMs may support educators, but their use should remain human-in-the-loop and guided by clearer pedagogical frameworks and stronger evaluation designs.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based conversational generative AI tool used for text generation, feedback, and instructional support.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic review examined ChatGPT and other LLMs as teacher-facing tools for generating educational content, automated feedback, lesson planning, and assessment support. The paper explicitly distinguished teacher-facing uses from student-facing tutoring or learning assistance, noting that some included studies used ChatGPT for student learning tasks rather than teacher workflow support.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT-supported workflows were associated with reported reductions in time required to generate educational materials or produce feedback, but the magnitude of time savings varied by task and context and was not measured consistently. The review emphasizes that evidence is mostly self-reported, heterogeneous, and concentrated in higher-education settings, so conclusions should be interpreted cautiously.
findings.measure: Time devoted to content generation; reported efficiency/time savings for feedback and planning tasks

findings.finding_summary: The review found that ChatGPT was used for teacher-facing content generation, including lesson materials, outlines, guides, feedback, assessment items, and instructional planning support. Reported benefits were perceived clarity, usefulness, and convenience of generated resources, but outcomes were heterogeneous and often based on teacher or learner perceptions rather than objective measures.
findings.measure: Perceived quality/usefulness/clarity of generated educational materials; planning support; automated feedback generation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of mostly qualitative, mixed-methods, and quasi-experimental studies with heterogeneous measures and several unclear risk-of-bias domains. The paper does not provide pooled effect sizes for ChatGPT-specific outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review reports practical benefits such as time savings and improved perceived usefulness, but the effects are not quantified consistently and are largely based on self-report. That makes the impact direction favorable but the magnitude unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models in Education: Foundations, Customization, Applications, and Responsible Use
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter/paper provides a conceptual and technical overview of large language models (LLMs) in education, with emphasis on how they work, why they matter, and what limits and risks accompany their use. It explains the Transformer architecture, scaling laws, pre-training, instruction tuning, and alignment, then connects these foundations to educational uses such as tutoring, content generation, lesson planning, assessment creation, rubric design, differentiated texts, and simulated practice scenarios.

The customization section focuses on how educational institutions can adapt LLMs through prompt engineering, few-shot prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). It discusses these methods as ways to align model behavior with curriculum standards, reasoning transparency, age appropriateness, and institutional privacy requirements. The chapter also distinguishes between proprietary and open-source models, arguing that the choice affects cost, privacy, transparency, and deployment feasibility.

The paper is not an empirical study of a specific classroom intervention; rather, it is a framework-oriented discussion aimed at educators, developers, and institutions considering LLM adoption. It concludes that LLMs have strong potential as teacher co-pilots and scalable educational infrastructure, but their use must be cautious because of hallucinations, bias, finite context windows, privacy risks, and environmental and financial costs.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General-purpose large language models / generative AI systems that can tutor, generate content, provide feedback, and be customized via prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning.
identified_tools.use_case: This chapter discusses LLMs as a class of teacher- and student-facing generative AI tools for education, including tutoring, assessment support, lesson planning, feedback generation, and differentiated content creation. It does not evaluate a specific deployed product or report empirical results.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical chapter rather than an empirical study. It explains LLM capabilities, customization methods, and deployment considerations, but reports no study design, sample, or measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter argues that LLMs may reduce teacher workload and support tutoring, assessment, and lesson planning, but it provides no direct outcome data or effect sizes. As a framework paper, any impact claims are speculative and not empirically demonstrated here.

paper_profiles.title: Intelligent teaching design assistant for primary mathematics: A large language model-driven framework with retrieval-augmented generation and problem-chain pedagogy
paper_profiles.venue: International Electronic Journal of Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that primary mathematics teachers face substantial cognitive overload and weak support when designing lesson plans, especially under curriculum reform pressures. The authors argue that general-purpose large language models can help with lesson planning, but that they often produce generic, context-insensitive, and sometimes inaccurate outputs that are not well aligned to curriculum standards, student characteristics, or pedagogical goals.

To address this, the study develops an Intelligent Teaching Design Assistant built on large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and a multi-agent architecture. The system draws on three knowledge bases: curriculum standards, teaching strategies, and student profiles. It also includes a process planner and student simulator to support problem-chain pedagogy and make the design process more transparent and teacher-facing. The intervention was tested with 34 elementary school mathematics teachers in China, who used the tool to design a lesson on multiplying decimals by whole numbers and compared it with a generic large language model condition.

The results showed that the assistant improved lesson-plan quality across all evaluated dimensions, with especially strong gains in teaching objectives, analysis of teaching situation and textbook content, problem-chain design, usability, and overall ratings. Teachers also reported high ease of use, perceived usefulness, acceptance, and satisfaction. The paper concludes that pedagogically grounded generative AI can function as a teacher-facing cognitive partner for lesson planning, though it still needs better support for interdisciplinary knowledge integration and formative assessment design.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based generative AI chatbot and language model family used for conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the generic large language model in the control condition for lesson design, and also mentioned in the paper’s AI statement as a writing/readability aid during manuscript preparation.

findings.finding_summary: In the control condition, teachers used a general-purpose large language model via its standard web interface to create a lesson plan for 'Multiplying Decimals by Whole Numbers.' Compared with the purpose-built assistant, the generic model produced significantly lower-quality lesson designs across all evaluated dimensions; the overall rating was M=3.67 for Task 1 versus M=5.83 for Task 2 (p<0.01).
findings.measure: Lesson plan quality / instructional design evaluation

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental comparative study with 34 teachers and rated lesson-plan outputs, plus post-use survey data. It is empirical and reasonably designed, but not randomized and without reported effect sizes or full assumption checks.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The comparison shows statistically significant improvement in lesson-plan quality, but the paper does not report standardized effect sizes. The practical gains are clear, yet the absence of effect-size reporting makes the magnitude harder to classify precisely.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a system for generating middle-school English reading comprehension materials using ChatGPT and compares the quality of AI-generated passages and questions against human-written materials and a fine-tuned GPT-2 + PPLM baseline. The central problem is the labor-intensive production of up-to-date, personalized reading exercises for Chinese middle school English instruction. The authors argue that large language models can help teachers create richer and more tailored reading resources than traditional manual authoring.

The intervention is not a classroom efficacy trial but a prompt-engineered generation system that produces reading passages in zero-shot and one-shot settings, along with multiple-choice comprehension questions and answer options. The paper also includes a smaller baseline comparison using fine-tuned GPT-2 with PPLM. Evaluation relies on automatic text metrics, human ratings by Chinese college students and native English speakers, pairwise comparisons against human-written passages, and teacher feedback after one week of system use.

The population context is middle school English learning in Beijing, China, covering Grades 7–9 materials sourced from local schools and the municipal education commission. The results show that ChatGPT-generated passages were often rated higher than human-written textbook passages on readability, coherence, engagement, suitability, and overall quality, while the baseline GPT-2 model performed worse. For question generation, however, human-written items outperformed the generated items across all assessed dimensions, especially usefulness and suitability; the main weakness was distractor quality and limited variation. Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT is promising for generating reading passages, but question generation still needs improvement before broad classroom use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative chatbot/LLM system used to generate and adapt reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice questions from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate middle-school English reading passages in zero-shot and one-shot settings, and to generate multiple-choice reading comprehension questions and answer options for existing passages; compared against human-written passages and a GPT-2+PPLM baseline.

findings.finding_summary: In human evaluation of reading passage quality, ChatGPT-generated passages were rated higher than human-written passages on multiple dimensions by Chinese college students and native English speakers. On overall quality, ChatGPT scored 4.46 vs 4.18 for human-written passages among Chinese students and 4.06 vs 3.89 among native speakers (Table 2); in pairwise comparison, ChatGPT passages were preferred over human-written ones (0.87 vs 0.13 in zero-shot; 0.80 vs 0.20 in one-shot).
findings.measure: Human-rated passage quality, including readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, overall quality, and pairwise preference against human-written passages
findings.sample_size: n=9 Chinese college students; n=364 native English speakers; pairwise comparison n=9 additional students

findings.finding_summary: For multiple-choice reading exercise questions, human-written questions outperformed ChatGPT-generated questions across all four rated dimensions. Human questions were rated higher for match, usefulness, suitability, and appearing less model-generated; for example, match was 4.58 vs 4.38 and usefulness was 3.93 vs 3.25 (Table 7).
findings.measure: Human-rated exercise question quality: match to passage, usefulness for student training, suitability for middle school learners, and detectability as model-generated
findings.sample_size: 10 textbook exercises; human evaluation sample size not_reported

findings.finding_summary: In topic-coherence and suitability comparisons, ChatGPT was rated highly for following topic constraints and producing suitable reading materials. In topic coherence, ChatGPT scored 0.97 in both zero-shot and one-shot conditions versus 0.77 for human-written passages in the comparison setup (Table 5), and in suitability it scored 0.77 vs 0.40 and 0.77 vs 0.53 for human-written passages (Table 6).
findings.measure: Pairwise topic coherence and suitability scores for generated passages
findings.sample_size: n=10 human-written passages plus 30 generated passages in comparison set; evaluator n=9

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model/chatbot category used for educational text and exercise generation when no specific commercial or research product is named beyond ChatGPT-like systems.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper frames the work as an application of generative AI for creating personalized reading comprehension materials, but the empirical focus is on ChatGPT specifically.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an evaluation study of generated reading materials and questions, but not a randomized or quasi-experimental K-12 learning-outcome trial. The evidence is based on human judgments and comparative text-quality assessments, so it is informative but indirect for literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The strongest reported advantages are on passage-quality and suitability ratings rather than student achievement, and the paper does not report effect sizes on reading test outcomes. For question generation, performance is mixed or worse than human-written questions, so overall impact is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT Pass High School Exams on English Language Comprehension?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can solve a real high-stakes reading comprehension exam at the high-school level, and whether performance differs across model versions and prompting strategies. The motivation is not to test an instructional intervention, but to benchmark the capability of large language models on an authentic educational assessment in English reading comprehension.

The study applied GPT-3.5 and two versions of GPT-4 (March 2023 and June 2023 updates) to Dutch national VWO English reading comprehension exams from 2022. The exams included multiple-choice and open-ended items, and the author compared model scores to official scoring standards and to student performance on one exam. GPT-3.5 performed around the average student level overall, while GPT-4 outperformed the average student, with the best performance coming from GPT-4-0314.

A secondary analysis used repeated API sampling to examine self-consistency across 50 runs per exam item. This showed that GPT-4 was usually consistent, but inconsistency often coincided with incorrect answers. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can generate valid answers to reading comprehension questions at scale, raising concerns about assessment integrity and suggesting that future educational assessment may need to adapt to AI availability. The strongest evidence in the paper is on multiple-choice reading comprehension items, where GPT-4 showed the clearest improvement over GPT-3.5; there is no direct comparison to instructional interventions such as teacher-led literacy instruction or tutoring.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model chatbot system used to generate responses to user prompts and perform text-based question answering.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to answer Dutch national high school English reading comprehension exam questions, via the web interface for GPT-3.5 and via API for GPT-4; performance was compared across versions and against human student exam results.

findings.finding_summary: On Dutch national VWO English reading comprehension exams (2022), GPT-3.5 achieved an overall mean grade of 7.3 on the Dutch 1–10 scale (6.5 without re-prompting), compared with the average student grade of 6.99 on Exam 1. GPT-4-0314 and GPT-4-0613 scored higher, with overall mean grades of 8.3 and 8.1, respectively; no effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Exam score / converted grade on English reading comprehension national exams
findings.sample_size: n=124 questions across 3 exams; student comparison available for Exam 1 only (n=35,698 students)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single benchmark-style assessment study rather than an RCT, quasi-experiment, or classroom intervention study. It provides useful descriptive evidence about reading comprehension performance, but not causal evidence about instructional impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported exam grades suggest substantial performance on reading comprehension items, especially for GPT-4, but this is an assessment benchmark rather than an educational intervention effect. No effect size is reported, so impact is difficult to quantify beyond the raw scores.

paper_profiles.title: Investigating marker accuracy in differentiating between university scripts written by students and those produced using ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether experienced markers can distinguish student-written coursework from text generated by ChatGPT-3.5. The authors frame the study as a response to concerns that generative AI may disrupt academic assessment, especially in writing-intensive higher education settings.

The study used a mixed-methods cross-sectional survey with 34 experienced academic and clinical academic markers from a medical school in Wales, UK. Participants reviewed undergraduate reflective writing scripts and postgraduate extended essays; in each set, two scripts were human-written and one was ChatGPT-generated. Markers graded scripts on writing style and content, then judged whether each script was written by a student, generated by ChatGPT, or uncertain. Open-ended responses were also collected and analyzed qualitatively.

Results showed low marker accuracy in identifying ChatGPT-authored work: only 23% correctly identified the undergraduate ChatGPT script and 19% correctly identified the postgraduate ChatGPT script. A significant effect of suspected authorship was found for script content but not writing style, suggesting content cues influenced judgments more than style. Qualitative findings indicated that language, structure, reflective depth, and referencing were the main cues used by markers. The authors conclude that even experienced markers struggle to reliably detect AI-generated writing, with referencing and some content features offering the strongest clues, but overall discrimination remained poor.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model system used to generate text responses from prompts and to assist with writing tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the comparator-generated text source (ChatGPT-3.5) for undergraduate reflective writing scripts and postgraduate extended essays; markers were asked to distinguish ChatGPT-generated scripts from student-written scripts.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods cross-sectional study with 34 experienced markers, only 23% correctly identified the ChatGPT-generated undergraduate reflective script and 19% correctly identified the ChatGPT-generated postgraduate essay. Markers were significantly affected by suspected author identity for content ratings, X(4, n=34)=10.41, p<0.05, but not for writing style.
findings.measure: Marker accuracy in identifying ChatGPT-authored scripts; grading of writing style and content

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods cross-sectional study, not an RCT or quasi-experiment, and it evaluates marker accuracy rather than learner outcomes. The evidence is informative but methodologically limited for causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational achievement effect size is reported, and the main outcomes are author-identification accuracy and content/style judgments. Findings suggest notable marker difficulty, but the practical impact on K-12 literacy instruction is indirect and unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Construct Validity in Psychological Tests
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a classic theoretical treatment of construct validity in psychological testing. It addresses the problem of how psychological tests should be interpreted when no single external criterion fully captures the attribute of interest, and argues that validation must go beyond simple test-criterion correlations. The authors distinguish construct validity from predictive validity, concurrent validity, and content validity, and explain why construct validation is needed for many psychological traits and abilities.

The paper does not study a generative AI intervention, reading/literacy instruction, or any educational treatment. Instead, it develops a general framework for test validation using examples from anxiety, intelligence, personality, and other psychological constructs. The discussion emphasizes the use of multiple sources of evidence, including group differences, correlation matrices, factor analysis, internal structure, change-over studies, and process analyses.

The main conclusion is that construct validity is established through a nomological network linking test scores to theoretical constructs and observable outcomes, not by a single coefficient or one criterion measure. The authors stress that negative findings can be informative, that alternative interpretations must be considered, and that practical use of a test requires a strong empirical fit between predicted and observed relations. This is a methodological paper rather than an empirical intervention study.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system is an adaptive computer-based instructional system that provides individualized guidance, feedback, and practice based on learner responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a conceptual discussion of construct validity in psychological tests and does not study an AI tutoring tool; ITS is the closest relevant archetype only as a general category.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical paper about construct validity in psychological tests, not an empirical study of an AI tool. There is no direct evaluation design, no K-12 literacy intervention, and no outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No intervention effects are reported because no AI tool is tested. As a result, there is no evidence of impact on reading or literacy outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: LLaMA: Open and Efﬁcient Foundation Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces LLaMA, a family of large foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters. The main research question is whether it is possible to train competitive large language models using only publicly available data, while improving inference efficiency relative to much larger systems. The work is primarily about model design, training data composition, scaling, and efficiency rather than education or learning applications.

The authors pre-train the models on a mixture of publicly available web text, Wikipedia, books, code, scientific articles, and Stack Exchange data. They describe architectural changes such as pre-normalization, SwiGLU activations, and rotary positional embeddings, and they report zero-shot and few-shot benchmark results across common sense reasoning, question answering, reading comprehension, math, code generation, MMLU, bias, toxicity, and truthfulness tasks. They also briefly present an instruction-finetuned variant, LLaMA-I.

The paper does not study K-12 learners, educators, or instructional interventions, and it does not evaluate reading or literacy instruction outcomes in educational settings. Its closest reading-related result is model performance on the RACE reading comprehension benchmark, where larger models perform better than smaller ones, but this is a language-model benchmark rather than a direct comparison of instructional approaches. Overall, the paper concludes that open models trained on public data can be competitive with larger proprietary systems, though bias, toxicity, and hallucination remain concerns.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: A family of open-weight large language models developed by Meta, trained on large text corpora for general language understanding and generation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper introduces the LLaMA model family and evaluates multiple sizes on standard language modeling and reading comprehension benchmarks, including RACE reading comprehension.

findings.finding_summary: On the RACE reading comprehension benchmark, LLaMA was evaluated in a zero-shot setting. LLaMA-65B achieved 67.9 on RACE-middle and 51.6 on RACE-high, outperforming GPT-3 (175B) at 58.4 and 45.5 respectively, and slightly trailing PaLM-540B on RACE-middle but exceeding it on RACE-high.
findings.measure: RACE-middle and RACE-high zero-shot accuracy

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark paper on a general-purpose language model, not a K-12 instructional study. It does include an academic reading comprehension benchmark, but there is no classroom, randomized, or quasi-experimental evidence on literacy instruction.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong benchmark performance on RACE, with LLaMA-65B outperforming GPT-3 on both middle and high school reading comprehension sets. However, the outcome is not an educational intervention effect size, so practical instructional impact cannot be inferred.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Students to Question the Machine: An AI Literacy Intervention Improves Students Regulation of LLM Use in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a brief AI literacy workshop can improve how middle-school students use generative AI during problem solving. The core concern is that students may over-trust fluent but unreliable LLM outputs, accept suggested prompts uncritically, and fail to regulate their interaction with the system. The authors frame effective GenAI use as a metacognitive regulation problem involving prompt selection, response evaluation, and iterative control of the interaction.

The study tested a two-hour classroom workshop that combined conceptual instruction about how LLMs work and fail with procedural guidance on how to prompt, judge, and follow up on AI responses. The intervention was compared with a no-training control condition. Students then completed six science inquiry tasks using a generative AI chatbot, and the researchers measured final-answer quality as well as behavioral indicators such as prompt acceptance, follow-up questioning, and correctness judgments. The sample consisted of 116 French students in grades 8–9 in one middle school, and the work was conducted during regular class hours.

Results showed that the intervention group produced slightly better final answers and displayed stronger regulation of GenAI use. Trained students were less likely to accept underspecified prompts, more likely to replace prompts or ask follow-up questions when needed, and more accurate in judging whether AI responses were correct. The intervention effect appeared to operate through improved strategic responses to detected problems rather than better discrimination alone. In contrast, GenAI self-report scores and metacognitive self-reports did not predict performance, and the workshop did not change students’ self-reported GenAI attitudes or knowledge in any robust way. Overall, the paper concludes that brief, scalable AI literacy instruction can improve middle-school students’ regulation of LLM-supported learning tasks, though the study is limited to one school, a short follow-up window, and a science task rather than reading/literacy instruction.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / large language model chatbot used for question answering, prompt generation, and iterative response evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: Middle-school students used a generative AI system (primarily GPT-4o mini via DuckAI; sometimes GPT-4o, GPT-4.1-nano, or GPT-3.5-turbo) to support six science inquiry tasks after a brief AI literacy workshop or with no prior training.

findings.finding_summary: In a controlled classroom study with grade 8-9 students (n=116), the intervention group that received a 2-hour AI literacy workshop before using GenAI scored higher on final written answers than the control group with no training. Final-answer validity on a 0-20 scale was M=11.38 (SD=3.87, n=76) versus M=10.29 (SD=3.04, n=40), Mann-Whitney U=1871, p=.040, r=.19.
findings.measure: Final-answer validity / exercise score on a 0-20 scale

findings.finding_summary: The workshop improved students' interaction regulation with the GenAI system. Trained students accepted fewer suggested prompts overall and were less likely to accept underspecified prompts than controls (51.5% vs. 66.7%, p=.044); they also asked more follow-up questions when initial answers were underspecified (59.2% vs. 27.9%, p<.001).
findings.measure: Prompt acceptance, follow-up questioning, and prompt replacement behavior

findings.finding_summary: Trained students judged the correctness of AI responses more accurately, especially when prompts were well-specified; the condition-by-prompt-validity interaction for correctness judgments was significant (p=.012). In addition, when students asked follow-up questions after accepted underspecified prompts, the intervention group benefited in answer quality by approximately +5 points out of 20, whereas the control group did not (interaction p=.038).
findings.measure: Correctness judgments of AI answers; answer quality after follow-up questioning
findings.effect_size: approximately +5 points out of 20 (for follow-up questioning benefit)

findings.finding_summary: Self-reported GenAI attitudes/knowledge did not predict task performance. Across all students, GenAI self-report scores were not correlated with performance (r=0.01, p=.88, R2<.001, n=116), and pre-post changes in GenAI self-reports in the intervention group did not predict sensitivity to prompt specificity (all p>.05).
findings.measure: GenAI self-report questionnaire and its pre-post change scores

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled classroom study with an intervention and comparison group, but it is not a randomized controlled trial and some outcomes are behavioral/process measures rather than direct literacy outcomes. The paper reports modest but statistically significant effects, with additional null findings on self-report measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main performance effect is modest (r=.19; approximately small-to-moderate), and several process outcomes show meaningful practical improvement in how students use GenAI. However, the absolute achievement gain is limited and the study is narrow in scope (one school, short follow-up).

paper_profiles.title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether a brief AI literacy lesson can reduce high school students’ tendency to rely on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations. The authors focus on over-reliance: accepting a wrong AI suggestion when the correct answer is available. They note that AI literacy is often proposed as a way to help learners use generative AI more critically, but there is limited experimental evidence on whether such instruction actually reduces reliance on incorrect outputs from large language models.

The intervention was a short educational text about ChatGPT given to 12th-grade students in Estonia. The intervention text explained how ChatGPT works, its limitations and risks, and how to use it wisely; the control text included only a general introduction to ChatGPT. Students were randomly assigned to intervention or control and then solved eight math/language-reasoning puzzles using ChatGPT recommendations, half of which were intentionally incorrect. The study was conducted online with 36 final participants from 10 schools.

Results showed substantial over-reliance overall: students accepted incorrect ChatGPT recommendations in 52.1% of cases. The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance, though the intervention group showed significantly more under-reliance, meaning they were more likely to ignore correct ChatGPT advice. Self-reported AI literacy increased for ChatGPT’s working mechanism and usage, but not for limitations/risks. The authors conclude that a short AI literacy text is not enough to reduce over-reliance on ChatGPT and may even make students more skeptical of correct advice; they suggest future interventions may need to address both strengths and weaknesses of AI more carefully.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot that generates text-based responses and can assist with a wide range of tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the AI system in a randomized controlled study where high school seniors solved math puzzles with ChatGPT recommendations after reading either a short AI literacy text or a control text. The intervention text explained ChatGPT's working mechanism, limitations, prompt use, and risks.

findings.finding_summary: In this randomized study with 36 12th-grade students (19 intervention, 17 control), the intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations. Mean over-reliance was 48.68% in the intervention group versus 55.88% in the control group, Welch's t(28.78)=-0.73, p=.236, d=-0.25.
findings.measure: Over-reliance rate on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations while solving math puzzles

findings.finding_summary: The intervention significantly increased under-reliance, meaning students were more likely to ignore correct ChatGPT recommendations. Mean under-reliance was 36.84% in the intervention group versus 19.12% in the control group, t(34)=2.35, p=.025, d=0.78.
findings.measure: Under-reliance rate on correct ChatGPT recommendations while solving math puzzles

findings.finding_summary: Students in the intervention group reported greater perceived knowledge about how ChatGPT works and how to use it wisely. Self-reported knowledge in the 'Usage' category was higher in the intervention group (M=3.42) than control (M=2.77), t(34)=2.26, p=.030, d=0.76; 'Working mechanism' was also higher (M=3.37 vs 2.77), t(34)=2.09, p=.044, d=0.70.
findings.measure: Self-reported AI literacy gains: usage and working mechanism

findings.finding_summary: The intervention did not significantly improve self-reported knowledge of ChatGPT limitations and risks. Scores were slightly higher in the intervention group (M=2.95) than the control group (M=2.77), but the difference was not significant, t(34)=0.56, p=.577, d=0.19.
findings.measure: Self-reported knowledge of ChatGPT limitations and risks

findings.finding_summary: Perceived confidence when relying on ChatGPT recommendations was slightly lower in the intervention group (M=3.58) than control (M=3.67), but the difference was not statistically significant, U=188.50, p=.400, rrb=0.17.
findings.measure: Self-perceived confidence when relying on ChatGPT recommendations

findings.finding_summary: The intervention did not significantly change total initial decision time. Mean dttotal was 1.56 minutes in the intervention group versus 1.64 minutes in the control group, Mann-Whitney U=179.5, p=.560.
findings.measure: Total initial decision time across puzzles

findings.finding_summary: Across all participants, longer decision time on incorrect-recommendation puzzles was associated with less over-reliance (rs=-0.41, p=.013). Longer decision time on correct-recommendation puzzles was associated with more under-reliance (rs=0.35, p=.038).
findings.measure: Correlation between initial decision time and reliance

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an original randomized between-groups experiment with direct comparison to a control text, but the sample is very small (n=36) and the outcome is not a reading/literacy achievement measure. The design is experimental, yet the evidence is limited by size and by the fact that outcomes are self-report plus puzzle-based reliance behavior rather than K-12 literacy instruction outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main outcome is null for reducing over-reliance (d=-0.25), while one adverse outcome is statistically significant and moderate-to-large (under-reliance, d=0.78). Because the strongest effect is negative and the primary target outcome is null, the overall impact is modest/unclear rather than positive.

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school students regulate inquiry when using ChatGPT during science investigation tasks. The central question is whether students can effectively formulate prompts, evaluate AI-generated answers, and decide when to continue or stop asking follow-up questions in an AI-mediated learning activity.

The study is not an instructional intervention or reading/literacy experiment; rather, it is an observational study of student behavior while using ChatGPT 3.5 in a structured task-based setting. Sixty-three French students aged 14–15 from four schools completed six science problems. For each problem, they were shown either an efficient or inefficient suggested prompt, could use it or write their own prompt, interacted freely with ChatGPT, and rated each response they received. The researchers analyzed prompt discrimination, answer-evaluation sensitivity, follow-up behavior, and final written explanations, along with relationships to metacognition, prior knowledge, and attitudes toward AI.

Results showed consistently weak performance: students were near chance at distinguishing efficient from inefficient prompts, often rated low-quality AI answers as useful, and rarely asked follow-up questions even after unsatisfactory responses. Final task success was only moderate, and better outcomes were associated with receiving more high-level AI answers, being more sensitive to answer quality, and asking follow-up questions. Positive AI attitudes and higher self-reported prior knowledge were associated with poorer regulation, while metacognitive regulation and critical perceptions of AI were protective. The authors conclude that students need explicit AI literacy and metacognitive scaffolding to avoid over-reliance and the illusion of understanding.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot, used for generating and evaluating natural-language responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the LLM in six middle-school science investigation tasks; students prompted ChatGPT, evaluated its responses, and optionally asked follow-up questions.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of n=63 middle-school students, prompt-quality discrimination was at chance level (mean d'=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08), indicating that students could not reliably distinguish efficient from inefficient prompts for ChatGPT. Students also accepted inefficient prompts 75.9% of the time after judging them as inefficient.
findings.measure: Signal detection sensitivity for prompt-quality discrimination (d')

findings.finding_summary: Students showed near-zero ability to evaluate ChatGPT answer quality (mean d'=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65). They rated 71.4% of expert-coded low-level answers as clear/useful, and only 16 students exceeded 70% evaluation accuracy.
findings.measure: Signal detection sensitivity for answer-quality discrimination (d')

findings.finding_summary: Behavioral regulation was weak: only 14 of 63 students asked any follow-up questions, totaling 22 follow-up questions across six tasks. Even after low-level answers, students initiated follow-up only 31.8% of the time, suggesting premature termination of QA cycles.
findings.measure: Follow-up question behavior / QA-cycle regulation

findings.finding_summary: Task outcomes were modest overall: the average correct solution rate across six problems was Msuccess=0.51 (SD=0.25). The best-fitting model predicted success rate from the frequency of high-level answers received (beta=0.52, p=0.000), answer-evaluation sensitivity (beta=0.1, p=0.000), and follow-up questioning after low-level answers (beta=0.4, p=0.004); adjusted R2=0.81, F(5,57)=40.29, p<0.0001.
findings.measure: Final written explanation accuracy / conceptual understanding

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary empirical study with a clear within-subjects design, but it is observational/correlational rather than a randomized or quasi-experimental comparison against a control condition. It provides useful descriptive evidence about ChatGPT use in middle-school learning, but not causal literacy-instruction effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The strongest reported effects are on interaction quality and task success, with moderate associations in the regression model (e.g., beta=0.52 and beta=0.4) but no direct instructional effect size against a comparison group. Overall, the paper shows negative or null evidence about students’ ability to use ChatGPT effectively rather than positive learning impact.

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly expanding and still loosely defined area of AI literacy in education, especially in the wake of generative AI. The authors note that the term AI literacy has been used for very different educational activities, ranging from young children interacting with social robots to undergraduates learning prompt engineering for ChatGPT, and they argue that the field needs a more precise conceptual framework.

To answer this question, the paper conducts an integrative review of 124 AI literacy studies published from 2020 to July 2024. The review includes both K-12 and higher education studies, and examines how researchers conceptualize AI and literacy across interventions and theoretical work. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the paper synthesizes the literature into a framework with three perspectives on AI (technical details, tools, sociocultural) and three perspectives on literacy (functional, critical, indirectly beneficial).

The K-12 studies discussed in the review include machine learning curricula, AI ethics lessons, comprehensive AI literacy curricula, and newer generative-AI-related activities such as showing students ChatGPT outputs or having them interact with AI tools like DALL-E under supervision. In higher education, the review highlights both technical machine-learning primers and emerging tool-use curricula such as prompt engineering and ChatGPT-focused instruction. The main conclusion is that generative AI has shifted the field toward tool-oriented AI literacy, but many K-12 interventions still combine technical and sociocultural content, often aiming to build both functional skills and critical awareness. The paper also identifies research gaps, especially the relative scarcity of critical or sociocultural tool-focused work and the lack of comparable post-secondary AI literacy research.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General generative AI / large language model chatbots or related tools used for prompting, generating text, and interactive assistance, without a specific named commercial product identified as the sole focus.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is an integrative review of AI literacy studies in K-12 and higher education; it does not empirically evaluate a single AI tool. It discusses generative AI tools broadly, including ChatGPT as an example, but the paper’s focus is on conceptualizations of AI literacy rather than direct tool comparisons.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an integrative review and conceptual framework paper, not a primary evaluation of an AI intervention. It synthesizes prior literature rather than reporting a controlled study with reading or literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct effect size or outcome impact is reported for a specific tool in K-12 reading/literacy instruction. The paper does not provide comparative evidence on literacy outcomes, only a field-level synthesis of AI literacy concepts.

paper_profiles.title: Generating and Evaluating Tests for K-12 Students with Language Model Simulations: A Case Study on Sentence Reading Efficiency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of developing and calibrating K-12 reading assessment items more efficiently, focusing on silent Sentence Reading Efficiency (SRE), a timed true/false sentence-reading task used to measure reading fluency. The authors ask whether large language models can generate new reading test items and whether an item-response simulator trained on prior student response data can estimate item difficulty, ambiguity, and response time well enough to construct parallel test forms.

The intervention is not an instructional tool for students but an automated assessment-development pipeline. GPT-4 generates candidate true and false sentences following expert rules, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-based item-response simulator predicts how students would respond and how long they would take. The simulator is then used to filter items and, in one part of the study, to build parallel AI test forms matched to a human-authored Lab form. The paper compares AI-generated forms against human-generated items in crowdworker testing and in a school deployment, and also compares simulator predictions against a readability baseline (Flesch-Kincaid) for unseen item properties.

The population includes students from grades 1 through high school in the simulator training data, with the main school deployment conducted with 234 students in grades 2-8 in a California public school; there is also a smaller Prolific adult crowdworker evaluation. The key finding is that AI-generated, simulator-filtered test forms produced highly similar total scores to the human-generated Lab form (r = 0.92 with crowdworkers and r = 0.93 in the school study), while ambiguous AI items reduced similarity. For predicting item properties, the simulator outperformed Flesch-Kincaid on both accuracy and median response time, suggesting that LLM-based simulation can support scalable assessment construction for reading fluency tasks.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used to generate and filter educational text items and to simulate student responses for item calibration and test-form construction.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate true/false sentence items for a K-12 silent sentence reading efficiency task, and to support filtering via an item-response simulator built on LLaMA; GPT-4 also generated safety/appropriateness judgments for crowdworker experiments.

findings.finding_summary: In the school student evaluation (n=234 students in grades 2-8; 3 removed for random guessing), the filtered GPT-generated AI test form produced total scores highly correlated with the human-generated Lab form (r=0.93). The paper reports that the two forms also matched closely in difficulty, indicating comparable reading-efficiency measurement.
findings.measure: Total scores on silent sentence reading efficiency test forms

findings.finding_summary: For predicting unseen item parameters in the school student study, the GPT-generated item set combined with simulator-based filtering was evaluated against human ratings and readability baselines. The paper reports stronger prediction of median response time than Flesch Kincaid (r=0.509 vs r=0.254) and stronger prediction of item accuracy (r=0.316 vs r=-0.001), showing the AI-filtered items aligned better with observed reading-efficiency properties.
findings.measure: Prediction of item median response time and item accuracy for unseen sentences

findings.finding_summary: In the crowdworker evaluation (n=50 recruited; 6 removed), the parallel AI test form based on GPT-generated items achieved a high correlation with the human Lab form (r=0.92). A separate ambiguous-AI form correlated less strongly (r=0.75), suggesting the filtering pipeline improved equivalence to the human-developed reading test.
findings.measure: Total scores on Lab form vs parallel AI form; Lab form vs ambiguous AI form

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta open-weight large language model family used here as the student-response simulator to predict item responses and response times for unseen reading items.
identified_tools.use_case: Fine-tuned with LoRA on student response data to simulate how prior participants would answer new sentence-reading items, estimate item difficulty/ambiguity, and support selection of parallel test forms.

findings.finding_summary: On a held-out evaluation subset of the response dataset, the item-response simulator’s aggregated predicted response times correlated with true aggregated response times at r=0.50, and predicted vs actual aggregate response probabilities correlated at r=0.76. This indicates the simulator could reasonably estimate reading-item properties used for test calibration.
findings.measure: Predicted vs true item-aggregated response time; predicted vs actual aggregate response probabilities

findings.finding_summary: In the school student study, the simulator outperformed Flesch Kincaid in predicting unseen item properties. For median response time, the simulator achieved r=0.509 (95% CI 0.427-0.586) versus Flesch Kincaid’s r=0.254 (95% CI 0.149-0.351); for item accuracy, the simulator achieved r=0.316 (95% CI 0.215-0.410) versus Flesch Kincaid’s r=-0.001 (95% CI -0.109 to 0.106).
findings.measure: Prediction correlations for unseen item accuracy and median response time

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical study with K-12 student data and a comparative school evaluation, but it is not a randomized controlled trial of instruction. The evidence is useful for tool calibration and assessment equivalence, yet it is primarily correlational/validation-based rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported correlations are modest-to-large for test-form equivalence and item-prediction tasks, especially r=0.93 for total scores and r=0.509 for response-time prediction. However, the study measures assessment generation/calibration rather than direct gains in reading instruction or achievement, so the educational impact is indirect.

paper_profiles.title: How Motivation Relates to Generative AI Use: A Large-Scale Survey of Mexican High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how high school students’ motivational profiles relate to their use of generative AI tools for learning in math and writing. The central question is whether students with different levels of self-concept and perceived subject value use AI in different ways, rather than whether AI improves learning outcomes.

The study used an anonymous online survey with 7,739 public high school students in Chihuahua, Mexico, narrowing to 6,793 students who had prior experience with generative AI and passed attention checks. Students reported motivation indicators and their frequency of using AI for different math and writing tasks, such as formula retrieval, step-by-step help, brainstorming, grammar improvement, and feedback. The researchers used K-means clustering to identify motivational profiles separately for math and writing, then compared AI-use patterns across profiles.

The analysis identified three profiles in both domains: Aspirational, Confident, and Disengaged. In math, Aspirational students most often used AI for step-by-step guidance and interpreting problems, Confident students used it more selectively, and Disengaged students showed the strongest shortcut-seeking pattern, including the highest direct answer copying. In writing, Aspirational students mainly used AI for brainstorming and outlining, Confident students for language and grammar improvement and feedback, and Disengaged students reported the lowest overall use. The paper concludes that AI use is domain-specific and shaped by motivation, arguing against one-size-fits-all AI integration and for more targeted, motivation-informed educational support.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbots or large language model-based tools used for producing, transforming, or supporting text and language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed high school students’ self-reported use of generative AI tools in writing tasks (e.g., brainstorming, outlining, grammar improvement, feedback) and math tasks; the paper did not name a specific product.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a large-scale survey study with self-reported usage patterns, not an experimental evaluation of instructional impact. It provides descriptive correlational evidence rather than causal evidence on reading or literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No achievement effect sizes or literacy outcome improvements were reported. The paper’s contribution is about patterns of AI use by motivational profile, so instructional impact on literacy is unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant, can support K-12 students’ writing development by providing formative feedback aligned with teachers’ rubrics, instructional materials, and expectations. The study is motivated by concerns about declining writing performance and the need for scalable, timely feedback in middle and high school classrooms.

CyberScholar was piloted in four public schools in the United States across grades 7, 8, 10, and 11, in English Language Arts, social studies, and world history classes. The project used an exploratory multiple case study design with qualitative data from classroom observations, surveys, and interviews involving 121 students and 4 teachers. Students used the tool to generate feedback on writing drafts and revise their work; teachers received training before implementation, and the system was customized through retrieval-augmented generation using classroom materials and rubrics.

Findings were based on thematic analysis of participant perceptions rather than a controlled comparison.
