Students generally viewed the tool positively, especially for detailed feedback, interactivity, perceived writing improvement, and rubric-based scoring. Some students reported inconsistent ratings when resubmitting the same paper. The authors conclude that CyberScholar has potential to support writing instruction and formative assessment, but it complements rather than replaces teacher feedback. The study does not provide direct comparative evidence against business-as-usual instruction or other writing interventions.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI writing assistant that provides automated or semi-automated formative feedback, content refinement, and rubric-aligned suggestions for student writing.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as CyberScholar, a piloted GenAI assistant for K-12 writing in grades 7, 8, 10, and 11. The paper examined students’ and teachers’ perceptions of how the tool provided formative feedback aligned to teacher rubrics and classroom materials.

findings.finding_summary: This was a qualitative multiple case study, not an experimental comparison. Across 121 participating students and 4 teachers, students reported that CyberScholar provided detailed, specific, and interactive feedback that helped them revise writing and better understand rubric criteria. Some students reported improved rubric scores after revisions (for example, one student improved a 'Compare' and 'Contrast' rubric score from 0 to 2), but no causal effect estimate was reported.
findings.measure: Student/teacher perceptions, post-survey themes, interviews, and observed rubric score changes after revision
findings.sample_size: n=121 students; n=4 teachers (post-survey n=54 students, n=3 teachers; interviews n=8 students, n=1 teacher)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The paper is a qualitative exploratory multiple case study with convenience sampling and no random assignment or comparison group. It provides useful implementation insights but not causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceptions and anecdotal rubric-score improvements, but no effect size or experimental estimate is available. Impact is therefore suggestive but unclear rather than demonstrably large or modest.

paper_profiles.title: LLMs’ Reading Comprehension Is Affected by Parametric Knowledge and Struggles with Hypothetical Statements
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a fundamental evaluation problem in large language model (LLM) reading comprehension: when models answer questions from a text prompt, their responses can be influenced by parametric knowledge acquired during pretraining rather than by the provided context. The authors argue that this makes standard reading-comprehension evaluation misleading, because a correct answer may reflect memorized world knowledge rather than actual text understanding.

To address this, they propose an evaluation framework based on "imaginary" reading-comprehension instances, in which real-world entities and facts are replaced with fictitious ones so that the examples neither match nor contradict the models’ internal knowledge. They test multiple LLMs, including GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA 2, and Mixtral, on extractive QA tasks with supported, contradicting, and imaginary contexts. They then extend the benchmark to non-affirmative constructions such as negation, negative non-factives, modals, and conditionals to see whether models can correctly abstain when the text does not answer the question.

The results show that performance on ordinary affirmative contexts can be inflated or distorted by knowledge alignment/conflict effects. Across models, hypothetical constructions, especially modals and conditionals, are much harder than simple affirmatives or negations, and they also trigger stronger susceptibility to knowledge conflicts. The paper concludes that LLMs are not reliably context-faithful, particularly for semantically complex or hypothetical text, and that evaluation of text understanding should use imaginary data to separate linguistic comprehension from memorized knowledge.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family chat-based large language models used for zero-shot question answering and extractive reading comprehension.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as ChatGPT/GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 models on imaginary, supported, and contradicting reading-comprehension contexts to test context-faithfulness and handling of non-affirmative statements; also used in prompt-mitigation experiments.

findings.finding_summary: Across supported affirmative QA, models achieved near-perfect F1 on the supported set, but performance dropped on contradicting contexts (first GPT-4 prompt and both GPT-3.5 prompts fell below 70% F1). On the imaginary set, performance was near-perfect, indicating that the apparent supported-set success may be inflated by parametric knowledge rather than text understanding.
findings.measure: SQuAD F1 on supported, contradicting, and imaginary context-question pairs

findings.finding_summary: On non-affirmative imaginary contexts (negation, unlikely, modals, conditionals), ChatGPT showed a pronounced performance drop for hypotheticals, especially modals and conditionals, and often failed to abstain. Manual error analysis found that 94.64% of errors involved ignoring entailment-cancelling modifications and answering as if the context were affirmative.
findings.measure: F1 on non-affirmative imaginary benchmark; manual error analysis of errors

findings.finding_summary: In re-assessing context-faithfulness, ChatGPT was often affected by knowledge conflicts: supported contexts tended to suppress abstention and contradicting contexts often triggered abstention, especially for hypotheticals. Prompting strategies improved average performance but did not eliminate the gap; instructed prompting and two-step prompting helped most, while chain-of-thought was inconsistent across non-affirmative sets.
findings.measure: Average non-affirmative performance across supported, contradicting, and imaginary sets under different prompts
findings.sample_size: n=50 per condition; 2880 manually analyzed responses

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta LLaMA-family large language models used here as zero-shot extractive QA systems.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated in LLaMA 2 chat form on the same reading-comprehension benchmarks to test text understanding, abstention, and susceptibility to knowledge conflicts.

findings.finding_summary: LLaMA 2 achieved near-perfect performance on supported affirmative items and near-perfect performance on the imaginary set, but was vulnerable to knowledge-conflict effects on contradicting contexts. On non-affirmative contexts, it handled simple negation relatively well but showed much weaker performance on modals and conditionals, with the largest gaps between supported, imaginary, and contradicting sets among the more semantically complex cases.
findings.measure: SQuAD F1 on supported, contradicting, and imaginary context-question pairs; non-affirmative F1 by semantic condition

findings.finding_summary: In context-faithfulness tests, LLaMA 2 was noted as an exception among models on hypothetical contexts: contradicting-set performance was not higher than imaginary-set performance and was sometimes lower. Manual inspection suggested that LLaMA 2 more often produced parametric answers instead of abstaining, which reduced performance on contradicting data.
findings.measure: Relative performance across supported, contradicting, and imaginary sets; manual error analysis
findings.sample_size: n=50 per condition; 2880 manually analyzed responses

identified_tools.name: Mistral
identified_tools.description: Mistral AI large language model used as a zero-shot extractive QA system.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as Mixtral 8x7B Instruct on reading-comprehension benchmarks with imaginary, supported, and contradicting contexts, plus non-affirmative variants.

findings.finding_summary: Mixtral performed near perfectly on supported affirmative items and on the imaginary set, but showed a large decline on contradicting contexts and especially weak performance on non-affirmative items. It was among the models with the biggest drop on negative non-factives and had a very dramatic decrease on modals and conditionals.
findings.measure: SQuAD F1 on supported, contradicting, and imaginary context-question pairs; non-affirmative F1 by semantic condition

findings.finding_summary: On context-faithfulness, Mixtral was described as practically unaffected by parametric knowledge on affirmative and negative contexts, but the issue resurfaced for hypothetical contexts. Prompting strategies improved average accuracy somewhat, but chain-of-thought with instructed prompting negatively impacted some non-affirmative cases.
findings.measure: Relative performance across supported, contradicting, and imaginary sets under different prompts

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark/evaluation paper, but it is not a K-12 instructional intervention study and does not test educational outcomes. The evidence is about general LLM reading-comprehension behavior rather than classroom literacy effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No K-12 reading or literacy instruction impact is measured here, and no effect sizes for educational outcomes are reported. The paper is therefore not evidence of instructional impact in the requested sense.

paper_profiles.title: FEANEL: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Error Analysis in K-12 English Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces FEANEL, a benchmark for fine-grained error analysis in K-12 English writing. The authors argue that while large language models have shown promise for educational applications, their ability to provide detailed, pedagogically useful feedback on student writing remains underexplored. FEANEL is designed to evaluate whether LLMs can classify individual writing errors, rate their severity, and generate explanations that are accurate and instructional rather than merely corrective.

The benchmark contains 1,000 anonymized essays written by K-12 learners, split evenly between elementary-school students and secondary-school students, and annotated by English education experts. The data were collected from a global online education platform and the TECCL corpus, then cleaned to remove off-topic, nonsensical, incomplete, or error-free essays. Experts developed a 29-category error taxonomy and produced gold-standard labels for error type, severity, and explanatory feedback. The paper evaluates multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, including GPT-4o, o1, o3, Gemini-2.5-pro, Claude-3.7, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-3, and Llama-3 variants, under zero-shot and one-shot prompting conditions.

The main finding is that current LLMs remain substantially below human teachers on this fine-grained writing-analysis task, especially for classification of complex errors and for generating high-quality explanations. Performance improves with richer prompts and examples, and larger or reasoning-oriented models often do better, but no model dominates across all sub-tasks. The paper concludes that fine-grained educational feedback for K-12 writing is still a difficult problem and that better task-specific model alignment, prompting, and evaluation methods are needed.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic large language model/chatbot systems used to analyze writing errors and generate pedagogically oriented explanations or feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper benchmarks multiple state-of-the-art LLMs on a K-12 English writing benchmark (FEANEL) for fine-grained error classification, severity rating, and explanation generation.

findings.finding_summary: On the FEANEL benchmark, current LLMs showed substantial limitations in fine-grained writing error analysis for K-12 English essays. Human teachers outperformed all evaluated models on error classification and explanation, and the paper reports that LLM explanations had low BLEU/METEOR/ROUGE compared with other generation tasks, indicating weak pedagogical feedback quality. No effect sizes or CIs were reported.
findings.measure: Error classification accuracy/Macro-F1, severity MAE, and explanation quality (BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE-L) on 1,000 essays

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark and model-evaluation paper, not a randomized or quasi-experimental study of instructional impact in classrooms. The evidence is methodological/benchmarking in nature rather than causal evidence about reading or literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear model-performance differences on error-analysis metrics, but no educational effect size is provided and the results do not establish impact on student literacy outcomes. The strongest evidence is descriptive: LLMs perform below human teachers, especially on explanation quality and complex error classification.

paper_profiles.title: Read Quietly, Think Aloud: Decoupling Comprehension and Reasoning in LLMs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is not about K-12 reading or literacy instruction. Instead, it investigates a machine learning problem: how to improve large language models’ reasoning by separating an initial comprehension stage from later response generation. The authors argue that current LLM methods focus heavily on explicit reasoning traces, but underemphasize an earlier ‘silent reading’ phase in which the model internalizes the input context before generating an answer.

The paper proposes two techniques. READQ applies loss masking to the first K tokens of a sequence during training so the model can process context without immediate next-token prediction pressure. READQBUDDY adds an auxiliary model that reads the full input in parallel and passes contextual embeddings to the main generation model, aiming to sustain comprehension throughout generation.

The experiments are conducted on Llama 3.1 and Llama 3.2 models and evaluated on standard NLP benchmarks such as ARC Challenge, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, PubMedQA, WinoGrande, MedQA, MedMCQA, GPQA, and MMLU. The authors report consistent accuracy gains over baseline models in these benchmark settings, including some multi-point improvements, but the paper does not involve human learners, classrooms, teachers, or literacy outcomes. As a result, it provides no direct comparative evidence relevant to generative AI tools for K-12 reading or literacy instruction.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: A family of open-weight large language models from Meta used for text understanding and generation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and evaluates READQ and READQBUDDY on LLaMA 3.2 3B Instruct/Base and LLaMA 3.1 70B models to test whether a silent-reading phase improves benchmark accuracy.

findings.finding_summary: On benchmark accuracy, READQ improved LLaMA 3.2 3B Instruct from 37.2 to 45.82 on ARC Challenge, 57.56 to 72.64 on HellaSwag, 34.0 to 40.8 on OpenBookQA, 65.0 to 75.4 on PubMedQA, and 62.35 to 69.22 on Winogrande. READQBUDDY further improved ARC Challenge to 49.06 and slightly changed other tasks (e.g., 73.03 on HellaSwag, 40.8 on OpenBookQA, 75.6 on PubMedQA, 68.82 on Winogrande).
findings.measure: Accuracy on ARC Challenge, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, PubMedQA, and Winogrande

findings.finding_summary: In ablations on LLaMA 3.2 3B Base, adding READQ improved accuracy from 37.97 to 45.56 on ARC Challenge, 61.98 to 71.6 on HellaSwag, 35.4 to 40.0 on OpenBookQA, 67.6 to 70.8 on PubMedQA, and 64.4 to 67.4 on Winogrande. For LLaMA 3.1 3B Instruct with READQBUDDY plus a sliding window, ARC Challenge improved to 47.18 (SW16) or 47.7 (SW64), HellaSwag to 72.64 or 73.0, OpenBookQA to 40.8 or 41.0, PubMedQA to 75.4 or 75.6, and Winogrande to 70.4 or 70.32.
findings.measure: Accuracy in ablation comparisons on the same benchmark suite

findings.finding_summary: For the larger LLaMA 3.1 70B model on scientific-domain benchmarks, READQ improved MedQA from 66.8 to 74.7, MedMCQA from 69.1 to 69.7, PubMedQA from 79.6 to 80.0, GPQA from 37.37 to 38.38, and MMLU from 78.9 to 79.2. The largest gain reported was on MedQA, an 8-point accuracy increase.
findings.measure: Accuracy on MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, GPQA, and MMLU

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical preprint on LLaMA model architecture/training, not an education study and not an RCT/QED in K-12 learners. The reported results are benchmark accuracies on NLP tasks, with no classroom, literacy, or student outcome evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports model accuracy changes in benchmark tasks, not educational impact. It provides no evidence of K-12 reading or literacy effects, and no effect sizes, sample sizes, or confidence intervals are reported.

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Generation of Inference Making Questions for Reading Comprehension Assessments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for scalable generation of diagnostic reading comprehension questions that target specific kinds of inference making. The authors argue that existing reading comprehension assessments often treat inference as a single construct, even though bridging inferences, pronoun resolution, text-connecting relations, and gap-filling inferences reflect different reading processes relevant to instruction and diagnosis.

The study develops a taxonomy of inference question types for multiple-choice reading comprehension assessments and validates it against an operational in-house item bank of grade 3-12 reading questions. The paper then uses GPT-4o to generate new reading comprehension items for expository passages adapted from Simple English Wikipedia, comparing standard few-shot prompting with chain-of-thought prompting and varying the number of training examples. Human experts evaluated generated items for general quality, correctness of the intended inference type, and quality of the model's reasoning.

The main finding is that GPT-4o can generate many acceptable-grade reading comprehension questions for grades 3-12, but it often fails to target the intended inference type precisely. More training examples improved item quality somewhat, but chain-of-thought prompting did not clearly outperform standard prompting. Gap-filling items were easiest to generate, text-connecting items were hardest, and the overall distribution of generated item types roughly resembled the distribution in the operational item bank. The paper concludes that LLM-based item generation may be promising for diagnostic assessment, but human review remains necessary to ensure valid inference-type targeting and operational quality.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used for generating and evaluating text-based content.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as GPT-4o to automatically generate multiple-choice reading-comprehension questions targeting pronominal bridging, text-connecting, and gap-filling inference types for grades 3-12 diagnostic assessment items.

findings.finding_summary: In a human evaluation of 357 GPT-4o-generated items, 93.8% were judged good-quality and suitable for operational use in grade 3-12 contexts. However, only 42.6% of generated questions matched the requested inference type, and only 37.2% had adequate reasoning overall, indicating strong item quality but weak type-control and reasoning fidelity.
findings.measure: Human ratings of general item quality, inference-type accuracy, and reasoning quality

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single study of automated item generation with human ratings, not a randomized or quasi-experimental study of student reading outcomes. Evidence is useful for tool evaluation but does not establish instructional effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports high operational item-quality rates, but the key instructionally relevant outcome is inference-type accuracy, which is only 42.6% overall. No effect size is reported and there is no demonstrated student learning impact.

paper_profiles.title: Generating AI Literacy MCQs: A Multi-Agent LLM Approach
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 56th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V. 2 (SIGCSE TS 2025)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of scalable, reliable assessment materials for AI literacy in K-12 education. The authors ask whether a multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflow can generate high-quality multiple-choice questions (MCQs) aligned to learning objectives, grade level, and Bloom’s taxonomy for AI literacy instruction.

The proposed intervention is a generator-and-critic workflow built with LangGraph and OpenAI’s gpt-4o-mini model. A generator agent creates MCQs from user inputs, and two critique agents review them for language/grade-level appropriateness and item-writing flaws. A supervisor agent either approves items or sends them back for revision. The system produced 40 MCQs for grades K7-9, and three K-12 AI literacy experts evaluated the items using a rubric covering correctness, clarity, relevance, Bloom’s level, grade-level fit, and classroom usability.

The evaluation found generally strong expert agreement that the questions were understandable, answerable, grammatical, clearly worded, and closely related to the learning objectives. Experts also largely judged the items to be usable in class, though there was some disagreement on whether certain items needed rephrasing, matched the intended Bloom’s level, or were appropriate for the target grade level. Overall, the paper concludes that the multi-agent approach shows promise for producing pedagogically sound AI literacy assessment items, but it remains an early-stage system requiring classroom testing and further validation.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model-based AI system used to automatically generate and critique multiple-choice questions for educational assessment.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a multi-agent workflow to generate and refine AI literacy multiple-choice questions for grades K-9, with critique agents checking readability, grade-level alignment, and item-writing flaws.

findings.finding_summary: This paper is not an empirical classroom or learning-outcome study. In a preliminary expert review of 40 LLM-generated AI literacy MCQs, three experts judged the items to be generally well formed and aligned with learning objectives, with high agreement on correctness (97.5%, 85%, and 85%) and strong ratings for understandability, answerability, grammaticality, clarity, and relevance. However, the study reports disagreement on rephrasing, Bloom's level, and grade-level appropriateness, and notes that classroom effectiveness has not yet been tested.
findings.measure: Expert rubric ratings of generated multiple-choice questions

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a framework/prototype paper with expert evaluation only, not a randomized, quasi-experimental, or classroom-based study of reading or literacy outcomes. It does not provide direct comparative evidence against instruction or other tools.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No student outcome effect size is reported, so instructional impact cannot be estimated. The paper suggests potential utility for assessment generation, but the evidence is limited to expert judgments rather than measured learning effects.

paper_profiles.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Persian: A Preliminary Study Focusing on ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper benchmarks large language models for Persian across a set of NLP tasks, asking how GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, and OpenChat-3.5 perform on classic, reasoning, and knowledge-based language tasks in a low-resource language setting. The authors are motivated by the lack of comprehensive Persian evaluation and by the question of whether instruction prompting, few-shot examples, and translation into English improve model performance.

The evaluated tasks include sentiment analysis, emotion recognition, named entity recognition, reading comprehension, machine translation, textual entailment, multiple-choice QA, elementary-school math questions, and mathematical problems. The study compares LLMs against task-specific fine-tuned SOTA models on subsets of 200 examples for several tasks, and also tests prompt language (Persian vs English), zero/one/three-shot settings, and translated examples. The educationally relevant portions are the newly created elementary school and 7th/10th grade math question benchmarks, but these are used as language/reasoning benchmarks rather than an instructional intervention study.

Overall, GPT-4 performs best among the tested LLMs and often improves with more shots, while GPT-3.5 is less consistent and sometimes degrades with additional demonstrations. In classic tasks, task-specific fine-tuned models remain stronger for NER, emotion recognition, and reading comprehension; in some reasoning tasks, GPT-4 approaches or exceeds SOTA. Translating prompts/examples into English generally improves GPT-3.5, suggesting strong language sensitivity. This paper does not evaluate K-12 reading or literacy instruction interventions, nor does it provide comparative evidence on generative AI used in classrooms.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI generative large language model chatbot based on GPT-family models used for instruction-following, question answering, translation, and text generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated as GPT-3.5-turbo-0613 and GPT-4 on Persian NLP benchmarks, including reading comprehension, with comparisons against task-specific SOTA models and across Persian vs. English prompts and few-shot settings.

findings.finding_summary: On the reading comprehension task (ParsiNLU), ChatGPT models scored below the task-specific SOTA model. GPT-3.5 achieved F1=.535/.643/.642 in Persian prompts (0/1/3-shot) and .588/.644/.644 in English prompts; GPT-4 achieved .564/.646/.659 in Persian and .603/.673/.687 in English, compared with SOTA F1=.691. The paper reports that one-shot results improved over zero-shot by large margins, but even the best ChatGPT result remained below SOTA.
findings.measure: Reading comprehension F1 on ParsiNLU

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark study, but not a randomized or quasi-experimental K-12 literacy intervention study. It provides direct comparative evidence on a reading comprehension benchmark, yet the work is primarily NLP evaluation rather than educational impact evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational effect size is reported, and the paper does not evaluate classroom literacy outcomes or instructional impact. The closest relevant result is a benchmark F1 comparison showing ChatGPT below SOTA on reading comprehension.

paper_profiles.title: Can Large Language Models Make the Grade? An Empirical Study Evaluating LLMs Ability to Mark Short Answer Questions in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably mark short-answer responses in K-12 education, focusing on the educational assessment task rather than direct instructional use. The authors ask whether GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 can classify student responses as correct or incorrect on open-response questions, and whether performance varies by subject, grade band, and item difficulty.

The study uses a newly assembled dataset of 1,710 student responses from the Carousel online quizzing platform, spanning Science and History questions across Key Stages 2, 3, and 4 (ages 5-16). Human expert teachers first rated the responses, establishing ground truth and interrater agreement, and then the same items were evaluated by LLM configurations using zero-shot and few-shot prompting. The comparison is direct but not an intervention study; it benchmarks model scoring against human raters.

Results show that GPT-4 with few-shot prompting performed best, reaching Cohen's kappa of 0.70, which was close to human agreement at 0.75. GPT-3.5 performed substantially worse (kappa 0.44-0.45), and few-shot prompting offered only a modest improvement. Performance was relatively stable across subjects, key stages, and question difficulty, suggesting potential utility for low-stakes formative assessment support in K-12 settings. The paper's strongest evidence is for GPT-4 as an automated scoring aid, while also highlighting that human agreement sets a practical ceiling for performance on ambiguous short-answer items.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used for zero-shot and few-shot automated scoring/grading of short-answer student responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Evaluated whether GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 and GPT-4-0125-preview could mark K-12 student short-answer responses as correct or incorrect, compared against expert human raters and the rater ground truth.

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,710 short-answer responses from K-12 Science and History questions, GPT-4 with few-shot prompting achieved Cohen's kappa=0.70 against the expert-human ground truth, compared with human rater agreement of kappa=0.75. The paper reports this as close to human-level performance for automated marking.
findings.measure: Agreement with expert human ground truth on correct/incorrect grading; Cohen's kappa

findings.finding_summary: GPT-3.5-turbo performed substantially worse than GPT-4 for the same grading task, with kappa=0.44 in zero-shot and 0.45 in few-shot conditions. The authors note the improvement was mainly due to GPT-4's much higher recall.
findings.measure: Agreement with expert human ground truth on correct/incorrect grading; Cohen's kappa

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational model-evaluation study, not an RCT or quasi-experiment on student learning outcomes. The paper does report clear quantitative agreement statistics, but the methodology concerns and absence of causal inference keep it below experimental tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported agreement for the best model is moderate-to-strong (kappa=0.70) and close to human raters, but the paper evaluates grading accuracy rather than instructional impact. That makes the educational impact indirect and not clearly tied to learning gains.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether ChatGPT can be used to generate high-quality reading comprehension materials for middle school English learners, and how those materials compare with existing human-written exercises. The core problem is the labor-intensive and difficult task of creating current, customized, and pedagogically appropriate reading passages and multiple-choice questions for English reading practice in Chinese middle schools.

The authors build a reading exercise generation system using ChatGPT, with both zero-shot and one-shot prompting, and compare it against a fine-tuned GPT-2 + PPLM baseline and human-written textbook materials. The system generates reading passages and accompanying multiple-choice questions, includes a toxicity filter, and is designed for use by teachers and students through a graphical interface. The evaluation is primarily offline and human-centered rather than instructional: passages and questions are rated by Chinese college students, native English speakers, and experienced middle school teachers.

The study population and context are middle school English materials in Beijing, China, drawing on textbook passages and supplemental reading materials from Grades 7-9. The paper reports that ChatGPT-generated passages are often rated higher than human-written passages on readability, coherence, engagement, overall quality, and topic matching, while the generated multiple-choice questions are relevant but still weaker than human-written questions, especially in distractor quality and variation. The system is presented as a promising educational authoring tool, but not as a learner outcome study.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational LLM chatbot/product used to generate and adapt text and questions from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate middle-school English reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice exercise questions in zero-shot and one-shot settings, and compared against a fine-tuned GPT-2 + PPLM baseline and human-written textbook materials.

findings.finding_summary: In human evaluation of reading passages, ChatGPT-generated passages were rated higher than human-written passages across readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, and overall quality by Chinese college students and native speakers. In pairwise comparison, ChatGPT zero-shot passages were preferred over human-written ones (human 0.13 vs generated 0.87), and one-shot passages were also preferred (human 0.20 vs generated 0.80); sample sizes were 30 passages in the main set and 10 passages in the pairwise set, with multiple raters per passage.
findings.measure: Human-rated passage quality; relative quality score; model-generated score; topic coherence; suitability
findings.sample_size: n=30 passages (main passage evaluation), n=10 passages (pairwise comparison), 9 Chinese college students + 364 native speakers in one evaluation; 9 Chinese college students in pairwise comparison

findings.finding_summary: For exercise question generation, human-written questions outperformed ChatGPT-generated questions on all four rated dimensions: match, usefulness, suitability, and whether they appeared model-generated. The paper reports that generated questions were highly aligned with passage content (Match=4.38/5) but were judged less useful (3.25 vs 3.93), less suitable for middle-school learners (3.48 vs 3.92), and more likely to look model-generated (0.67 vs 0.27).
findings.measure: Human-rated exercise question quality
findings.sample_size: n=10 textbook exercises; 20 generated question sets; n not otherwise reported

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / large language model chatbot system with no specific product named beyond the general category.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses generative AI for reading comprehension exercise generation in general terms, but its empirical system is specifically ChatGPT.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical comparative study, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental literacy intervention study with student learning outcomes. The evidence is based on human ratings of generated materials rather than K-12 reading achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests strong perceived quality for some generated passages, but it does not report learning gains or effect sizes on reading outcomes. For question generation, the results are mixed and sometimes negative relative to human-written materials, so overall educational impact remains unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Generation and Evaluation of Reading Comprehension Test Items with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically generating and evaluating multiple-choice reading comprehension items. The authors argue that manual item development is time-consuming and that common automatic metrics for generated questions are poorly suited to reading comprehension tasks, so they propose a new evaluation approach based on answerability and guessability.

The intervention studied is the use of large language models, specifically Llama 2 Chat and GPT-4, to generate German reading comprehension items in a zero-shot setting and to evaluate those items by answering them with and without the source text. The paper introduces a new metric, text informativity, defined as the difference between answerability and guessability. It also compares human judgment with LLM-based evaluation and reports item quality ratings and inter-annotator agreement.

The dataset came from German online language courses offered by Deutsche Welle, targeting non-native speakers at about CEFR B1 level. Human annotators were six native German-speaking university students or recent graduates who judged items from ten texts, while automatic evaluation was run on fifty texts. The authors find that GPT-4-generated items generally outperform Llama 2 items and are closest to human-written items in text informativity and quality ratings. GPT-4 is also the most human-like evaluator, while Llama 2 is less reliable. The paper concludes that zero-shot LLMs are promising for reading-comprehension item generation and that text informativity is a useful evaluation metric, though it does not capture all aspects of item quality.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: A large language model/chat model family used for zero-shot text generation and response evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of two instruction-tuned LLMs to generate multiple-choice reading comprehension items from German texts and to automatically evaluate item answerability/guessability with and without the text.

findings.finding_summary: On zero-shot generation, LLaMA 2 produced acceptable-quality items but clearly underperformed GPT-4 on text informativity and human quality ratings. For text informativity, LLaMA 2 generated items scored 0.160 with human evaluators and 0.129 with GPT-4 as evaluator; these were the lowest among the generators. Human raters also gave LLaMA 2 the lowest average quality, including 11/180 unusable ratings.
findings.measure: Text informativity; human quality ratings; response accuracy with/without text
findings.confidence_interval: [0.109, 0.213] (human evaluator text informativity); [0.082, 0.178] (GPT-4 evaluator text informativity)
findings.sample_size: generation test set n=50 texts; human evaluation subset n=10 texts

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical study with a small human-evaluation subset and no randomized or quasi-experimental comparison in an educational intervention sense. It is methodologically careful for item-generation/evaluation, but evidence for K-12 instruction outcomes is indirect.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects concern item quality and evaluability rather than learner achievement. The only numeric differences are modest-to-medium in the item-quality domain, but they do not translate to direct reading gains.

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to teach K-12 students how to use generative AI chatbots responsibly and effectively for learning, with a focus on prompting literacy rather than general AI awareness. The authors argue that as students increasingly encounter tools like ChatGPT, they need instruction on when to use AI, how to ask useful questions, and how to avoid inappropriate or overly direct requests that could undermine learning.

To meet this need, the paper presents a web-based prompting literacy module built around scenario-based practice. Students interact with an LLM chatbot, write prompts for hypothetical learning scenarios in secondary-school subjects, and receive immediate, elaborated feedback from an AI auto-grader. The module was designed using learning-by-doing and experiential learning principles, with grading rubrics derived from prompting guidance and the CLEAR framework.

The empirical work includes two classroom deployment studies in 11 authentic secondary-education classrooms in East Asia. Study 1 (111 students) examined auto-grader accuracy, student prompt performance, confidence changes, and student perceptions via surveys and open-ended responses. Study 2 reused the same setting with revised assessment items to improve measurement quality. The findings suggest that the auto-grader was reasonably accurate overall, students improved mainly in embedding background/context in prompts, and confidence in using AI for learning increased after the activity. However, the study did not compare the module against business-as-usual instruction or another AI literacy intervention, so it does not provide direct comparative evidence about effectiveness versus alternative instruction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model chatbot and related LLM services used for interactive text generation, feedback, and automated evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper used OpenAI GPT-4o as the LLM for student interaction and as the AI-based auto-grader for student-written prompts in the prompting literacy module.

findings.finding_summary: The AI auto-grader using GPT-4o achieved an average accuracy of 0.92 against human labels when assessing student prompts, and was able to generate high-quality, detailed feedback. Accuracy was especially high for Relevance, Background, and Elaboration dimensions (>0.90), with lower accuracy for Purpose (0.85) and No Direct Answer (0.88).
findings.measure: Auto-grading accuracy of student-written prompts compared with human grading

findings.finding_summary: In a classroom deployment with 111 students, the module supported immediate feedback and was associated with improved prompt-writing performance on the Background dimension from Q1 to Q3 (McNemar p=.039), but no significant improvement was found for Relevance (p>.90), Conciseness (p=.286), or Purpose (p=.617). The post-test showed no significant gain overall (mean=4.4 pre and post; p=.377) because of a ceiling effect, although self-reported confidence in using AI for learning increased by 10.4% on average (p<.001).
findings.measure: Prompt-dimension performance, post-test score, and self-reported confidence
findings.effect_size: 10.4% confidence increase; no significant effect on overall post-test; significant improvement on Background only
findings.sample_size: n=111 (classroom deployment); n=98 for pre/post test comparison

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical classroom study with mixed-methods and descriptive/statistical analyses, but it is not a randomized controlled trial or quasi-experimental comparison against a control condition. Evidence is useful for feasibility and measurement, but causal claims are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The strongest reported effect is on confidence (10.4%) and one prompt dimension (Background), but the paper does not report standardized effect sizes or a direct comparison to alternative instruction. Overall impact is promising but modest and uneven across outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Generating and Evaluating Tests for K-12 Students with Language Model Simulations: A Case Study on Sentence Reading Efficiency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of creating and validating parallel reading-assessment items for K-12 students more efficiently using large language models (LLMs). The authors focus on silent Sentence Reading Efficiency (SRE), a timed true/false sentence-reading task used to assess reading fluency and efficiency, and propose an item-response simulator that predicts how students will answer new items and how long they will take. The system uses GPT-4 to generate candidate sentences, then filters and calibrates them with a fine-tuned LLaMA-based simulator trained on prior student response data.

The intervention studied is not a reading instruction tool, but an AI-assisted assessment-generation pipeline. The paper evaluates whether AI-generated test forms can match a human-authored, expert-calibrated Lab form in terms of score distributions and item properties. It includes a crowdworker comparison and a school deployment with 234 students in grades 2-8 from a California public school, comparing human-generated items against GPT-generated items filtered by the simulator and reviewed by experts.

The main findings are that filtered AI-generated test forms closely match human-generated forms on total scores, with very high score correlations in both crowdworker (r=0.92) and school (r=0.93) evaluations. The simulator predicts item response time and accuracy better than simple readability metrics such as Flesch-Kincaid, though the evidence is strongest for response-time prediction rather than accuracy. Ambiguous AI-generated items reduce reliability and produce weaker agreement, showing the value of simulator-based filtering. The paper concludes that LLMs can support scalable generation and calibration of reading-assessment items, but human review remains necessary for classroom use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI generative large language model system used to generate and evaluate educational text items.
identified_tools.use_case: Used GPT-4 to generate true/false sentence items for a K-12 silent sentence reading efficiency test, and in some experiments used GPT-4 to filter items for safety/appropriateness and identify ambiguous items.

findings.finding_summary: In a school student evaluation with 234 students in grades 2-8, the filtered GPT-generated AI test form produced total scores highly correlated with the human-generated Lab test form (r=0.93). The paper also reports that the AI and Lab forms matched closely in difficulty, and the AI test form outperformed Flesch Kincaid for predicting unseen item response time and difficulty.
findings.measure: Total test score correlation between filtered AI test form and human-generated Lab form; item prediction correlations for accuracy and median response time
findings.effect_size: r=0.93; item prediction r=0.316 (accuracy), r=0.509 (median RT)

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta open-weight large language model family used here as the base model for fine-tuning an item-response simulator.
identified_tools.use_case: Fine-tuned as an item-response simulator to predict student responses and response times to unseen sentence items, and to evaluate/flag ambiguous items for reading assessment test construction.

findings.finding_summary: The fine-tuned LLaMA-based item-response simulator showed moderate predictive performance on held-out items, with correlations of r=0.76 for predicted vs actual aggregate response probabilities and r=0.50 for predicted vs actual aggregate response times on the model evaluation set. In the school student study, the simulator outperformed Flesch Kincaid for predicting unseen item accuracy and median response time (Table 2).
findings.measure: Predicted vs actual aggregate response probabilities; predicted vs actual aggregate response times; prediction of unseen item accuracy and median RT
findings.sample_size: n=1962 training participants; held-out evaluation sample not_reported

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical study, but it is primarily about test-item generation/calibration rather than a randomized or quasi-experimental literacy intervention. The evidence is correlational/model-evaluation plus a school deployment, not a causal comparison of instruction.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported correlations are moderate to high, especially the AI vs. Lab score correlation (r=0.93), indicating meaningful but not instructional effect size evidence. However, the findings concern assessment item quality and prediction, not direct student literacy gains.

paper_profiles.title: Accessible Computer Science for K-12 Students with Hearing Impairments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of making K-12 computer science instruction accessible to Deaf and hard-of-hearing (D/HH) students, who often rely on American Sign Language (ASL) and may have limited access to computer science resources in ASL. The authors argue that captions alone are often insufficient because of language complexity and accessibility barriers, and they motivate the need for sign-language-rich, visually supported instructional materials for technical computing concepts.

The paper presents an early-stage project for an accessible block-based coding web application and a set of ASL video resources covering introductory programming topics such as commands, conditionals, loops, variables, functions, debugging, and object-oriented programming. The design also includes accessibility features such as captioned videos, visual feedback, sign-language tooltips, controllable video speed, and alternative text/tool modes. The planned content is intended for middle-school D/HH learners, although the broader framing is K-12 accessibility.

This is not an evaluation study of learning outcomes; rather, it is a design and project description that outlines future work. The authors state that they plan to conduct a study with middle-school deaf students after the videos are produced, but no results are reported in this paper. The main conclusion is that ASL-based, multimodal, and accessible CS instruction is needed and should be built into block-based environments for D/HH learners.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI or AI-assisted content generation system; in this paper, the relevant focus is on ASL video content and accessible instructional media rather than a named AI product.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a future-facing possibility in the broader context of automated virtual human sign technologies and reading assistance technologies; the paper itself proposes human-made ASL instructional videos and does not evaluate a generative AI tool.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/project-design paper with no empirical evaluation of an AI tool, no comparative design, and no reading/literacy outcomes measured. The paper discusses planned accessibility features and future study intentions only.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No impact can be established because there are no reported outcome data, effect sizes, or head-to-head comparisons. The paper does not test any generative AI intervention against instruction or another tool.

paper_profiles.title: LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to better extract semantically meaningful information from e-book lecture slides and how to use that content information alongside reading logs to support personalized student interventions. The authors argue that conventional reading-activity features alone are limited because they show how students engage with materials but not which topics they are reading about. To address this, they introduce LECTOR, an AI/NLP model that estimates slide-topic relationships from lecture slides and can be combined with reading logs to produce topic-preference features.

The study evaluates LECTOR in two experiments. First, it compares LECTOR against TF-IDF, a binary reader-modeling method, TextRank, and AttentionRank on keyphrase extraction from 2,255 lecture slides from a programming theory course. It also includes a human evaluation with 28 students using slides from the 2023 course cohort. Second, it tests whether topic preferences derived from LECTOR improve identification of at-risk students compared with traditional reading-time/activity features, using reading logs from 218 students across 2019–2022 cohorts and logistic regression as the prediction model.

The population is undergraduate students in a university engineering course at Kyushu University in Japan. The context is an e-book reading platform (BookRoll) used in a programming theory course delivered over 7–8 weeks. No K-12 learners or school-based literacy instruction were studied, and the paper does not evaluate generative AI for reading instruction in grades K–12.

Main findings are that LECTOR outperformed the TF-IDF baseline in the human evaluation and achieved the best overall technical keyphrase-extraction results at larger cutoffs, while attention-based models did not uniformly dominate in this domain. For the at-risk prediction task, topic-preference features generally matched or outperformed traditional reading features, especially for out-of-class data, but effects were mixed rather than uniformly significant across all cases. The strongest evidence in the paper concerns keyphrase extraction and the alignment of LECTOR outputs with student judgments; the student-risk prediction results are suggestive but not consistently superior across all comparisons.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / transformer-based NLP system used for keyphrase extraction and topic-related feature construction from e-book lecture slides, rather than a specific commercial product.
identified_tools.use_case: LECTOR, a proposed attention-based NLP model, was evaluated for extracting keyphrases from lecture slides and for deriving topic-preference features from reading logs to support at-risk student prediction.

findings.finding_summary: In technical keyphrase extraction on lecture slides, LECTOR outperformed baseline methods at larger cutoffs, achieving the highest reported performance at @15 with F1=33.44%, and the best overall F1 of 37.92% (n not reported beyond the set of 9 syllabus keyphrases). In the human evaluation with 28 students, LECTOR also outperformed TF-IDF, with mean F-scores of 61.8% (slide-level) and 46.5% / 44.4% (student-level groups ST-1/ST-2), all with very small p-values.
findings.measure: Keyphrase extraction performance against syllabus keyphrases and student-validated keyphrases; Precision, Recall, F1-score
findings.sample_size: n=28 students for human evaluation; 390 slides in slide-level evaluation; 9 ground-truth keyphrases

findings.finding_summary: Against traditional reading-time features, topic-preference features derived from LECTOR showed higher Fisher's Discriminant Ratio (FDR) in all reported grade-comparison cases, indicating stronger separability of student groups. In the downstream logistic-regression prediction task over 60 cases, topic preferences were often equal or better than traditional features; however, the paper reports many null comparisons and only a few statistically significant wins, with no performance degradation in OUT-CLASS data.
findings.measure: Fisher's Discriminant Ratio; logistic regression AUC and F-score for at-risk student prediction
findings.sample_size: n=218 students for reading logs; 60 prediction cases

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical study with comparative evaluations, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experimental instruction study in K-12 literacy. The evidence is primarily technical/observational and uses university programming-course data rather than K-12 reading outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains in keyphrase extraction and prediction are positive but modest-to-unclear in educational impact terms, and the paper does not report classroom reading achievement effects. Because there is no clear effect size for literacy outcomes and the setting is non-K-12, impact on the target use case remains uncertain.

paper_profiles.title: Observation of post-soliton expansion following laser propagation through an underdense plasma
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates the late-time expansion of electromagnetic post-solitons formed after a high-intensity laser pulse propagates through an underdense deuterium plasma. The central question is how these post-soliton structures evolve temporally and whether their expansion follows existing analytical models.

The study combines proton radiography experiments with analytical snowplow-model calculations and 2D/3D particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations. The experiment used the VULCAN Nd:glass laser at Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, firing 30 ps, 3 × 10^18 W cm−2 pulses into a supersonic deuterium gas jet. Proton radiography captured bubble-like structures interpreted as post-solitons, and their diameters were tracked over time. The authors compared the observed scaling with spherical and cylindrical post-soliton models and found the cylindrical scaling fit the data better than the spherical prediction.

The paper concludes that the observed structures are consistent with post-solitons whose expansion is better described by cylindrical than spherical theory, likely because of polarization-dependent laser-plasma dynamics. The 3D PIC results support this interpretation, showing that soliton formation depends on laser polarization and that non-spherical early-time structure can explain the observed expansion behavior. This is a physics/plasma paper and does not study education or AI interventions.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI/large language model chatbot system for natural-language text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: No AI tool was studied. The paper is an experimental plasma physics paper about post-soliton expansion following laser propagation through an underdense plasma.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is not an education research study and does not evaluate any AI tool, let alone a K-12 literacy intervention. It is a physics experiment with no relevant educational methodology.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There are no K-12 reading or literacy outcomes and no AI intervention effects to assess. The paper provides no evidence relevant to the requested topic.

paper_profiles.title: Mapping data literacy trajectories in K–12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a systematic literature review of K–12 data literacy research rather than an intervention study. The authors ask how learning experiences across K–12 data literacy activities can be mapped using a common framework, especially as AI and machine learning increasingly require students to understand data-driven systems rather than only traditional rule-based programming. They propose a two-dimensional “data paradigms” framework based on logic (knowledge-based vs. data-driven) and explainability (transparent vs. opaque) and use it to characterize existing activities.

The review synthesizes 84 empirical studies published from 2019 to 2024 across computing education, mathematics education, STEM, and learning sciences contexts. The paper identifies four learning trajectories: keeping transparent, keeping data-driven, jumping, and bridging. Most activities remained within a single paradigm, especially data-driven/transparent or data-driven/opaque tasks, while comparatively few studies bridged multiple paradigms or moved learners gradually from rule-based to opaque ML systems.

The main conclusion is that K–12 data literacy instruction is fragmented and often lacks a shared vocabulary for describing progression across paradigms. The authors argue that making epistemic differences between rule-based and data-driven reasoning explicit could help educators design better learning progressions and scaffolds. Because this is a literature review and position paper, it does not provide direct comparative evidence on outcomes for reading or literacy instruction, nor does it evaluate generative AI tools in K–12 classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / machine learning conversational or data-driven systems used in K–12 learning; in this paper, the focus is on data literacy trajectories rather than a specific educational product.
identified_tools.use_case: Systematic literature review of K–12 data literacy interventions, including examples that involved AI/ML tools such as Teachable Machine, StoryQ, Zhorai, Machine Learning for Kids, and other ML-based learning environments.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper/systematic literature review that synthesizes prior K–12 data literacy studies but does not report a new empirical comparison of an AI tool against instruction or control conditions. It provides conceptual framing and categorization rather than causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct outcome effects are reported for a tool in this paper, so there is no measurable instructional impact to rate. The paper does not provide effect sizes, comparative results, or student learning outcomes for reading or literacy.

paper_profiles.title: Vocalnayno: Designing a Game-Based Intervention to Support Reading Development in Primary Schools
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 6th European Conference on Games-Based Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical problem in primary-school reading support: how to help pupils develop reading skills while also giving teachers and teaching assistants better information about individual progress. The author argues that paper-based reading records and informal support from volunteers can be inefficient and may not provide timely, detailed feedback about specific phonics or reading weaknesses.

To explore this problem, the paper proposes and prototypes Vocalnayno, a game-based reading intervention intended for use on a laptop or tablet. In the game, children read letters, words, and phonics aloud to power gameplay, and the system records performance as an assessment metric that can be shared with teachers and parents. The design is framed as a supplement to existing primary-school practice, particularly the work of teaching assistants and parent volunteers.

The population and context are primary-school pupils in the UK, but the paper does not report a classroom deployment or a controlled evaluation. Instead, it describes an action-research-inspired design process, informal consultations with teachers, teaching assistants, parents, and children, and a very small pilot test of the prototype. The main conclusion is that the idea is promising as a way to combine engagement with objective assessment, but the current prototype is not yet ready for classroom use and needs a more accurate voice-recognition component and further development.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI or speech-enabled educational system without a specific commercial/product name. In this paper, the discussed concept is a game-based reading assessment and support tool that uses voice recognition to evaluate children reading letters/words aloud and provide feedback to teachers/assistants.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a design/prototype paper proposing 'Vocalnayno' as a game-based intervention for primary school reading development and assessment. It was not evaluated in a classroom trial; the author reports only informal discussions and a very limited pilot test of the prototype's voice recognition with the author and one primary school pupil.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/design-oriented paper with no classroom deployment and no empirical evaluation of reading outcomes. The only testing mentioned is a prototype pilot focused on voice recognition functionality, not literacy impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No outcome effects on reading or literacy are reported, so there is no demonstrated educational impact. The paper proposes a tool and describes design considerations rather than measured results.

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Teachers to Co-Design Integrated AI Curriculum for K-12 Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how artificial intelligence education can be made more accessible and relevant when embedded into existing K-12 subject areas. Rather than studying student learning outcomes, the authors focus on the design process itself and on teacher perspectives about integrating AI concepts into core curricula.

The study used a two-day remote co-design workshop with 15 K-12 educators and educational directors. Participants first discussed AI concepts and tools, then worked in small groups with researchers to draft integrated lesson ideas for social studies, ESL, and literacy for students with learning disabilities. The workshop also included pre-work, presentations on AI and AI ethics, card sorting, and reflective discussions.

The main findings were that teachers valued curriculum supports for evaluation, engagement, logistics, and collaboration, and that AI could be integrated into core subjects through data, reflection, and ethics. The literacy-related example was a curriculum for students with learning disabilities centered on vocabulary and image classification, but the paper does not evaluate learner outcomes or compare the AI curriculum against any control condition. The authors conclude that teacher co-design is important for making K-12 AI curriculum more accessible and implementable, especially outside computer science classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general artificial intelligence tool or system for K-12 AI education, including machine learning and AI learning tools used in classrooms rather than a specific commercial chatbot or named LLM product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper did not evaluate a literacy AI tool in an instructional experiment. It described a co-design workshop where teachers designed an integrated literacy/AI curriculum concept using Google Teachable Machine and discussed other AI learning tools such as Machine Learning for Kids, Google Quick Draw, and MIT App Inventor.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative co-design/workshop paper rather than an experimental evaluation of a literacy AI tool. It provides design insights and proposed curricula, but no direct comparative outcome evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No student outcome effects were measured, and there are no effect sizes or comparative literacy results reported. The paper does not provide evidence of instructional impact for a specific tool.

paper_profiles.title: An XAI Social Media Platform for Teaching K-12 Students AI-Driven Profiling, Clustering, and Engagement-Based Recommending
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents Somekone, an explainable AI (XAI) educational tool for K-12 classrooms that teaches students how social media platforms use data collection, profiling, engagement metrics, clustering, and recommendation algorithms. The authors motivate the tool as a response to the need for children and adolescents to understand the data-driven mechanisms behind social media rather than only learning general social media literacy or safety rules.

The intervention is an Instagram-like browser-based platform with real-time visualizations that show students how their actions generate data, shape profiles, and affect recommendation outputs. The system includes teacher-facing analytics views and student-facing views for browsing, profiling, and recommendations. The paper emphasizes collaborative classroom use, with students typically working in pairs and teachers projecting class-level visualizations.

The reported evidence is a case example and analytics from 12 two-hour test sessions with 209 children in grades 5 and 8 across schools in Finland. The paper does not report a controlled comparison against business-as-usual or another instructional condition; instead, it analyzes usage patterns through latent profile analysis and sequence analysis. The main conclusion is that the tool appears feasible and engaging for classroom use, and that the action logs can support research on student interaction patterns and learning analytics. The paper explicitly notes that future research is needed to evaluate learning outcomes more rigorously.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI-enabled educational tool for explaining and simulating social media platform mechanisms, including data collection, profiling, engagement, clustering, and recommendation with real-time visualizations and classroom analytics.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the basis for the Somekone XAI tool, an Instagram-like classroom platform for grades 4-9 to teach AI-driven profiling, clustering, engagement-based recommending, and social media data mechanisms.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a tool/resource description with a case example and usage analytics, not an experimental study comparing learning outcomes. It does not report causal evidence, randomized assignment, or literacy outcome measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect sizes or comparative outcome data are reported for reading/literacy instruction. The paper discusses intended learning outcomes and pilot usage only, so instructional impact cannot be assessed.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the piloting of CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant designed to provide formative feedback on K-12 student writing. The study asks whether and how the tool can support writing development across subject areas by giving detailed, rubric-aligned feedback and enabling interactive revision cycles. The authors frame the work around formative assessment and metacognition, emphasizing AI as a complement to teacher guidance rather than a replacement for it.

CyberScholar was piloted in four public schools in the United States with students in grades 7, 8, 10, and 11 across English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History classes. Participants included 121 students and 4 teachers, though only 54 students and 3 teachers completed the post-survey and 8 students plus 1 teacher were interviewed. The implementation involved teacher-provided rubrics, prompts, and class materials being integrated into the AI system through retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering, with training provided to teachers and students before use.

The study used qualitative case-study methods and thematic coding of surveys, interviews, and classroom observations. Findings were broadly positive: students reported that the tool gave detailed and specific feedback, supported revisions, improved grammar and clarity, and made rubric expectations more visible. Some students noted improved rubric scores after revising, while others reported inconsistent ratings when re-submitting the same text. Overall, the paper concludes that CyberScholar has potential to support K-12 writing instruction, especially when aligned with teacher expectations and used for iterative feedback, but it does not provide direct comparative or causal evidence against business-as-usual or other instructional conditions.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI writing assistant/chatbot used to generate formative feedback and support writing revision in K-12 contexts.
identified_tools.use_case: CyberScholar is described as a GenAI-based writing assistant; the paper also notes use of ChatGPT and Grammarly in the authors’ acknowledgments for manuscript polishing, but the studied K-12 tool itself is presented generically as a GenAI assistant rather than a separately evaluated named commercial product.

findings.finding_summary: This was a qualitative, exploratory case study of 121 students and 4 teachers across grades 7, 8, 10, and 11 in four U.S. schools. No controlled comparison or standardized outcome effect was reported; instead, students and teachers perceived the GenAI tool as helpful for writing revision because it provided detailed feedback, interactive clarification, and rubric-aligned ratings.
findings.measure: Student/teacher perceptions from surveys, interviews, and classroom observations; rubric-based revision changes mentioned anecdotally
findings.sample_size: n=121 students, n=4 teachers; post-survey n=54; interviews n=8 students and n=1 teacher

findings.finding_summary: Students reported perceived improvements in writing quality, including grammar, transitions, sentence clarity, and more professional phrasing. The paper gives illustrative examples of rubric-score improvement after revision (e.g., one student improved a 'Compare'/'Contrast' rubric item from 0 to 2), but does not report group-level quantitative literacy effects.
findings.measure: Perceived writing-quality improvement and rubric-based draft revisions
findings.sample_size: n=121 students (qualitative reports); no comparison group

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: The study is qualitative and exploratory, with convenience sampling and no randomized or quasi-experimental comparison group. It provides implementation evidence and user perceptions, but not causal evidence for reading or literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived usefulness for writing support, but it does not provide experimental effect sizes or direct comparative impacts. Any evidence of impact is anecdotal and rubric-based rather than a quantified treatment effect.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating Reading Comprehension Exercises Generated by LLMs: A Showcase of ChatGPT in Education Applications
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of generating high-quality, personalized reading comprehension materials for middle school English learners using large language models, especially ChatGPT. The authors argue that existing reading exercises are often outdated, repetitive, and difficult for teachers to customize, and they explore whether LLMs can help produce more engaging and suitable passages and multiple-choice questions.

The intervention is a reading exercise generation system built around ChatGPT. The system uses carefully designed prompts to generate reading passages in zero-shot and one-shot settings, as well as multiple-choice questions and answers for those passages. It also includes a toxicity filter before materials are released. As a baseline, the authors fine-tune GPT-2 with PPLM control on teacher-provided middle school reading datasets. Teachers can edit generated content through a graphical interface, making the system teacher-facing rather than student-facing in primary use.

The study context is Chinese middle schools, specifically Grade 7 to Grade 9 English reading instruction in Beijing. Evaluation combines automatic text metrics, human ratings from Chinese college students and native English speakers, and feedback interviews with three experienced middle school teachers who used the system for a week. The results suggest ChatGPT-generated passages are often judged as comparable to or better than human-written passages on readability, coherence, engagement, and suitability, while the generated multiple-choice questions are relevant but still weaker than human-written ones in distractor quality and variety. Teachers reported that the system could reduce time and cost while supporting personalized resource creation, but also noted the need for better question generation.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational LLM chatbot used to generate and adapt reading comprehension passages and multiple-choice questions from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Implemented in a reading exercise generation system for Chinese middle school English learners to produce zero-shot and one-shot reading passages, generate multiple-choice questions and answers, and support teacher editing; also evaluated for passage and question quality and suitability in school use.

findings.finding_summary: In human evaluation 1, ChatGPT-generated reading passages were rated higher than human-written passages across readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, and overall quality by 9 Chinese college students and 364 native English speakers. Reported mean scores for Chinese students were 4.61 vs 4.52 in readability and 4.46 vs 4.18 overall quality; for native speakers, overall quality was 4.06 vs 3.89.
findings.measure: Human-rated passage quality across readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, and overall quality
findings.sample_size: n=9 Chinese student evaluators; n=364 native English speakers; 30 passages rated in this evaluation

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise comparison, evaluators preferred ChatGPT passages over human-written passages and judged them as more likely to be human-written than the true human passages. Relative quality scores were 0.87 for ChatGPT zero-shot and 0.80 for ChatGPT one-shot versus 0.13 and 0.20 for the human-written counterparts in the paired comparisons.
findings.measure: Pairwise relative quality judgments and model-generated-versus-human discrimination for reading passages
findings.sample_size: n=9 additional student evaluators; 10 human-written passages plus 30 generated passages in this evaluation

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT passages showed high topic coherence with the given prompts, scoring 0.97 in both zero-shot and one-shot conditions, compared with 0.40 for the fine-tuned GPT-2 + PPLM baseline. This indicates strong prompt-following and topic control for reading passage generation.
findings.measure: Topic coherence of generated passages relative to specified topics
findings.sample_size: n=9 student evaluators; 10 topic pairs in the pairwise evaluation

findings.finding_summary: Evaluators judged ChatGPT passages to be suitable for middle school English learners, with suitability scores of 0.77 in both zero-shot and one-shot settings, compared with 0.37 for the baseline and 0.53 for human-written passages in the comparison task. The authors conclude the materials were largely suitable for real educational use.
findings.measure: Suitability of generated passages for middle school English learners
findings.sample_size: n=9 student evaluators in the suitability comparison

findings.finding_summary: For generated multiple-choice questions, ChatGPT produced items that aligned well with passage content (match score 4.38/5), but scores were lower than human-written questions on usefulness (3.25 vs 3.93) and suitability (3.48 vs 3.92). Evaluators also found generated questions more obviously model-like (0.67 vs 0.27), suggesting the questions were useful but still in need of teacher selection and refinement.
findings.measure: Human-rated quality of generated multiple-choice reading questions (match, usefulness, suitability, and whether they appeared machine-generated)
findings.sample_size: n=multiple human evaluators; 10 textbook exercises compared with 20 generated question sets

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary evaluation study with multiple human-judgment tasks, but it is not an RCT/QED and does not report causal effects or robust experimental classroom outcomes.
