The evidence is nevertheless useful because it includes implementation details and direct user feedback from teachers in a school-oriented setting.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong positive quality judgments for generated reading passages, but no effect sizes or student learning gains are reported. The impact appears promising for instructional material generation, though the evidence is limited to prototype and evaluation data rather than demonstrated classroom achievement effects.

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines whether ChatGPT can function as a feedback tool to improve foreign language writing for students with refugee/migrant backgrounds. The paper is motivated by the growing interest in generative AI for language learning and by the specific needs of socially vulnerable learners who may face additional barriers in second-language acquisition.

The intervention took place over two weeks in a Junior High School (Gymnasium) in Patras, Greece, with eight 15-year-old students in a German-as-a-foreign-language class. Students first wrote a personal email, then the researchers used ChatGPT to revise the texts specifically for vocabulary and grammar. Students received the improved version, discussed the revisions, and then wrote a second, similar email on a related topic intended to encourage transfer of the new language forms.

The study compared pre- and post-intervention texts using objective textual measures such as total words, unique words, and average words per sentence. Results showed increases on these measures for most students, suggesting that ChatGPT-supported feedback may help strengthen writing performance in this setting. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support language learning in multilingual classrooms, while also emphasizing the need for teacher supervision, critical checking of outputs, and further research in larger and more diverse contexts.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI language model/chatbot that generates and revises text from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a feedback tool to improve students' foreign-language writing by correcting/enhancing vocabulary and grammar in their initial email drafts, with students then revising a similar writing task after reviewing the AI-improved version.

findings.finding_summary: In a pilot classroom study with 8 junior high school students (age 15) in a German-as-foreign-language class, ChatGPT-assisted revision was associated with longer and lexically richer post-intervention texts. The authors report increases in total words (mean increase 38%, ranging from 2% to 62%), unique words (mean 19.1 more per student, with one decrease), and average words per sentence (mean about 42%, with one student decreasing), but no inferential statistics were reported.
findings.measure: Total words, unique words, average words per sentence in students' pre- and post-intervention German emails

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot classroom study with observational pre/post comparison and no control group or inferential testing reported. It provides implementation detail but limited causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported changes are moderate in magnitude at the text level (e.g., mean 38% increase in total words and about 42% increase in words per sentence). However, the evidence is based on a very small sample and descriptive analysis only.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT and related GPT-style systems, for education. Rather than reporting an empirical study, the authors synthesize early research and offer a conceptual overview of how these models may support learning and teaching, while also identifying major risks and governance concerns.

The paper discusses student-facing uses such as generating quizzes, flashcards, summaries, explanations, reading-comprehension questions, tutoring support, and language-learning assistance. It also discusses teacher-facing uses such as lesson planning, adaptive feedback, assessment support, exercise generation, and professional development. The discussion spans elementary, middle/high school, university, remote learning, and professional learning contexts, with special attention to language learning, reading comprehension, writing, and problem solving.

The main conclusion is that large language models can improve personalization, efficiency, and access to instructional resources, but only if they are used with strong human oversight, curriculum alignment, fact-checking, bias mitigation, privacy protections, and clear pedagogical strategies. The paper emphasizes that these systems are not replacements for teachers and should be integrated as complementary tools within responsible educational design.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based large language model chatbot for generating, answering, and revising natural language text.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a general-purpose LLM for education; the paper highlights potential uses for reading comprehension support, quiz generation, summaries, explanations, feedback, lesson planning, and assessment, but does not report an empirical classroom study of ChatGPT itself.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper, not an empirical evaluation. It offers conceptual discussion and recommendations rather than a study with measured outcomes or implementation data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No outcome data, effect sizes, or classroom impact measures are reported, so there is no basis for estimating impact from this paper.

paper_profiles.title: Integrating Generative AI in Knowledge Building
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can be integrated into K-12 classroom knowledge-building activities and what this integration reveals about students’ emerging AI literacy. The authors focus on a high school World Religions course and ask how students used ChatGPT in their knowledge-building work and how their understanding of AI changed through that experience.

The intervention was a teacher-designed pedagogical approach embedded in an elective high school course. The teacher introduced ChatGPT, modeled its use, and structured student activity in two phases: first, using ChatGPT to generate ideas and questions that students critiqued and built upon; second, using a steering prompt so students could converse with ChatGPT, fact-check responses, discuss them with peers, and incorporate them into group notes and final essays. Students were encouraged to use prompts in English or Spanish, and the teacher provided guidance on prompt engineering, citation, and ethical use. Data came from student interviews, classroom artifacts, and teacher planning/reflection documents.

Findings show that students used ChatGPT in multiple ways: for information search, idea generation, support for writing, rapid access to information during discussion, and brainstorming questions. Students also reported challenges such as hallucinations, limited reliability, difficulty with prompt design, and the need to verify and contextualize outputs. The study concludes that mindful classroom use of ChatGPT, paired with teacher scaffolding and explicit attention to limitations, can support both knowledge building and AI literacy. It also suggests that educators need to create structured opportunities for students to reflect on AI’s strengths, weaknesses, risks, and appropriate use in schoolwork.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot powered by GPT-family large language models, able to answer questions, generate text, and support interactive prompting/dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a high school world religions course to support knowledge building and writing. Students used it for information search, idea generation, question generation, essay drafting, and answering student questions via a teacher-designed steering prompt; the teacher also modeled ethical use, prompted fact-checking, and required transcript citation when used in final essays.

findings.finding_summary: In qualitative interviews with 10 high school students, ChatGPT was used in multiple ways to support knowledge building: 70% reported it improved information-search efficiency, and about 60% used it to keep up with class discussion by getting quick information. Students also reported benefits for brainstorming, generating questions, and reducing workload on writing tasks, but they emphasized that outputs required fact-checking and sometimes led to shortcut use rather than learning.
findings.measure: Semi-structured student interviews; student writing/artifacts; teacher planning/reflection notes

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods single-case classroom study with interviews and artifacts, not an experimental design. It provides implementation detail and observational evidence, but not causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports perceived benefits and classroom use patterns rather than measurable learning gains. The evidence suggests useful support for literacy-related tasks, but the impact is unclear and not quantified.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and its implications for higher education, especially assessment, learning, and teaching. Rather than reporting a classroom study, it provides a desktop review of early ChatGPT-related literature and the authors’ own experimentation with the tool. The central question is how generative AI should be understood within the broader history of AI in education and what risks and opportunities it presents for teaching, assessment, and institutional policy.

The paper describes ChatGPT’s functionality, training background, access model, capabilities, and limitations. It also situates ChatGPT within a three-part AIEd framework: student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing applications. Within this framing, the paper discusses uses such as tutoring, writing assistance, automated essay scoring, feedback generation, plagiarism detection, and administrative analytics. The authors emphasize that ChatGPT can generate fluent prose quickly, but its factual reliability, reasoning, and handling of citations are limited and error-prone.

The population most directly referenced is higher-education students and instructors, with some discussion of institutions and assessment systems. The paper is not an implementation study in a specific classroom or school-based setting; instead, it is a conceptual and review-based article focused on higher education. The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is likely to become mainstream and should not simply be banned; instead, educators and institutions should adapt assessment practices, develop guidance for responsible use, and anticipate both productive and harmful applications of generative AI.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational AI chatbot built on GPT-family large language models, designed to generate text and answer prompts in natural language.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviewed ChatGPT’s capabilities and limitations and experimented with it directly for drafting essays, explanations, multilingual text generation, and plagiarism-related rewriting in a higher-education context; it did not study K-12 classroom implementation.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/review-style article with author experimentation, not an empirical classroom study. It provides no K-12 implementation data, no controlled evaluation, and no reported outcomes for student learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measurable impact estimates are reported, and the paper does not evaluate effects in real classrooms. The discussion is about potential opportunities and risks rather than demonstrated educational impact.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching with ChatGPT as a Linguistically Responsive Tool for Multilingual Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how teachers of K–12 multilingual learners in U.S. public schools are using ChatGPT and related AI tools to support language and literacy instruction. The paper is motivated by concerns about how generative AI is actually implemented in real classrooms, especially for multilingual learners whose linguistic resources are often marginalized by monolingual school norms. Using a translanguaging lens, the study asks how teachers use ChatGPT in instructional practice and whether those uses support linguistically responsive pedagogy.

The study draws on classroom observations and post-observation interviews with in-service teachers enrolled in a professional development course on culturally and linguistically responsive pedagogy. Across two cohorts over two academic years, the researcher observed 42 teachers in DC public and charter schools; instances of ChatGPT use were identified in 8 observations. The observed teachers worked across elementary and secondary levels and across content areas including general education, ESL, dual-language bilingual education, Spanish immersion, science, math, and English language arts.

Findings show that teachers mainly used ChatGPT to facilitate communication and differentiate content, such as translating text, generating bilingual explanations, transcribing oral language, simplifying or re-leveling texts, and creating exemplar disciplinary writing models. In a smaller number of secondary classrooms, teachers also scaffolded students’ own prompting of ChatGPT and experimented with Dall-E for multimodal literacy activities. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support translanguaging affordances, production, and some co-labor, but that assessment and reflection were notably absent. It also emphasizes the need for explicit teacher mediation, critical AI literacy, and safeguards against bias, overreliance, and inappropriate or inaccurate outputs.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI system that generates and transforms text and other outputs from prompts; here used for translation, text simplification/differentiation, transcription, prompt scaffolding, and image generation via DALL·E integration.
identified_tools.use_case: Observed in K–12 multilingual learner classrooms and teacher interviews as a teacher-facing tool to translate texts and vocabulary, transcribe and translate student speech, create differentiated and leveled texts, generate exemplar disciplinary texts, scaffold student prompting for writing support, and support a multimodal literacy activity using image generation.

findings.finding_summary: Across 42 observed K–12 teachers, ChatGPT was used in 8 observations to support language and literacy instruction for multilingual learners. Reported classroom uses included translation, transcription, text differentiation, prompt scaffolding, and a multimodal image-generation activity; the paper reports no experimental effect sizes or test-score outcomes.
findings.measure: Classroom-observed instructional uses of ChatGPT in literacy/language teaching
findings.sample_size: n=42 observed teachers; 8 observations with ChatGPT use

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative classroom-observation study with post-observation interviews, not an experimental or quasi-experimental impact study. It provides implementation evidence, but no causal evidence or quantified learning effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful instructional uses of ChatGPT for multilingual literacy support, but it reports no effect sizes or student outcome data. Impact is therefore promising but unquantified.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation of the Effect of Generative AI in English Writing
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Education, Humanities and Social Sciences
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can improve English writing instruction and student writing outcomes in high school classrooms. The central question is how AI-assisted writing evaluation and support affect writing quality, student perceptions, and teachers’ ability to provide personalized feedback and lesson planning.

The intervention involved the Spark Desk AI tool from Iflytek, along with other generative AI tools mentioned in the classroom (Sora, Quillbot, Grammarly, ChatGPT). In the experimental condition, teachers used AI to evaluate writing, generate diagnostic feedback, and support essay instruction; in the control condition, the teacher conducted writing lessons and feedback without AI support. The study also collected semi-structured interview data from students to understand their experiences with AI-assisted writing lessons.

The participants were students from two first-year high school classes in China, with teachers who had prior EFL and English writing experience. The setting was classroom-based English writing instruction focused on the Chinese college entrance exam genre of “continue the story.” Quantitative comparisons of writing performance and error patterns, combined with interview responses, suggested that AI-assisted instruction improved writing outcomes, reduced some error types, and was viewed positively by students, though participants also noted limitations such as mechanical feedback and difficulty using resources. The paper concludes that generative AI can support personalized writing feedback and teacher planning, but it should be used carefully to avoid bias and to preserve human guidance and students’ higher-order thinking development.

identified_tools.name: SparkDesk
identified_tools.description: An AI writing analysis and feedback system by iFlytek that provides diagnostic reports, personalized writing suggestions, and whole-class performance summaries.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a high school English writing classroom as the generative AI tool for evaluating student essays, generating personalized feedback/resources, and supporting teacher analysis in an experimental comparison with a non-AI control condition.

findings.finding_summary: In the short-run comparison, the AI-assisted class showed a downward trend in writing error frequency and number of errors relative to the traditional class, especially for verb tense and verb form errors. The paper also reports that SparkDesk produced individualized diagnostic reports and teacher-facing whole-class summaries, but it does not provide a formal effect size.
findings.measure: Writing error frequency and number of errors in composition tasks; diagnostic feedback quality
findings.sample_size: 100 samples collected for evaluation; two first-year high school classes

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot used for text generation, feedback, and language support.
identified_tools.use_case: Listed among the generative AI tools used to support students in explaining and improving essay writing during the experimental group lesson; the paper does not isolate ChatGPT-specific implementation details or results.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbot/writing assistance tools used for grammar checking, paraphrasing, content generation, and writing feedback when no single product is being distinguished.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a general label for several AI writing tools discussed in the paper, including AI chatbots and automated writing assistance functions in English writing instruction.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods classroom study with pre/post and interview data, but the paper reports limited methodological detail and no formal statistical effect sizes in the text provided. The evidence is useful for implementation context, but the causal strength is modest.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper claims improved writing performance and reduced errors in the AI-assisted class, but the magnitude is not quantified clearly enough to judge as modest or large. Based on the reported classroom gains and personalized feedback effects, the impact appears potentially meaningful but still uncertain.

paper_profiles.title: Effects of the English language intervention as a foreign language for struggling elementary readers in South Korea: a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how effective English language interventions are for struggling elementary school readers learning English as a foreign language in South Korea. It is not a generative AI literacy study; rather, it is a meta-analysis of reading and English-learning interventions for underachieving or learning-disabled elementary students. The authors also examine whether certain intervention and context variables moderate outcomes, including outcome type, intervention component, interventionist, dosage, classroom type, and grade level.

The review synthesized 22 studies published from 2000 to 2021, including both experimental between-group studies and quasi-experimental within-group pre-post studies. Eligible studies had to measure English achievement and/or affective outcomes and be conducted in general education or inclusion classroom settings. The review excluded qualitative and single-subject studies, as well as studies in special schools or self-contained settings.

Results showed medium-to-large overall effects, with larger mean effects in within-group studies than between-group studies. Moderator analyses suggested stronger effects for affective outcomes such as confidence, interest, and motivation, and for some achievement measures such as reading comprehension, phonological awareness, letter recognition, and vocabulary. Phonics, shared reading, growth mindset, and small-group instruction were among the more effective intervention types, and higher dosage generally produced stronger effects. The authors also found larger effects in general education classrooms than inclusion classrooms and a larger effect for lower elementary grades than upper elementary grades in the within-group analysis. The paper concludes that English intervention can benefit struggling elementary readers, but results should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity, design differences, and some small subgroup sizes.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A general intelligent tutoring system or adaptive instructional system that provides individualized tutoring, practice, or feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Not studied in this paper. The paper is a meta-analysis of English language interventions for struggling elementary readers in South Korea, not an AI-tool evaluation.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis with systematic search, explicit inclusion criteria, quality appraisal, and subgroup analyses. However, it does not evaluate an AI tool, so the evidence tier reflects study rigor rather than tool-specific evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI tool is actually studied, so there is no direct tool impact to rate. The paper reports literacy intervention effects in general, but those are not attributable to an AI system.

paper_profiles.title: Under the world of AI-generated feedback on writing: mirroring motivation, foreign language peace of mind, trait emotional intelligence, and writing development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examines whether AI-generated feedback on writing affects multiple outcomes in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners: writing proficiency, motivation, foreign language peace of mind (FLPoM), and trait emotional intelligence (EI). The paper is not focused on literacy subgroups or accessibility, but rather on whether AI feedback improves learners’ writing development and related affective variables.

The intervention compared two groups in a quasi-experimental design: an experimental group received online writing development with AI-generated feedback, while a control group completed the same online writing activities without AI-generated feedback. The study was conducted at the College of Languages, Nawroz University in Duhok, Kurdistan Region, Iraq, with 322 intermediate-level EFL learners aged 16–30. Quantitative instruments included pretest/posttest writing assessments and validated scales for FLPoM, trait EI, and motivation; qualitative semi-structured interviews were also conducted with 29 participants.

The quantitative results are internally inconsistent in the article’s narrative, but the inferential tables indicate significant posttest group effects for writing, FLPoM, EI, and motivation after controlling for pretest scores. The qualitative interviews similarly describe perceived gains in motivation, calmness, emotional regulation, and writing quality among students in the AI-feedback group. However, the study does not report subgroup analyses, differential effects for emergent readers, multilingual learners, students with disabilities, or any other accessibility-related subgroup. Claims about broader benefit are based on the overall sample rather than subgroup outcome data.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general generative AI / LLM chatbot or feedback system used to generate writing feedback and support language learning, without a specific named product identified in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as AI-generated feedback during online EFL writing development; feedback was immediate, personalized, and addressed grammar, vocabulary, coherence, and structure.

findings.finding_summary: In this quasi-experimental mixed-methods study (n=322; EG=153, CG=169), AI-generated feedback improved writing performance on the posttest. The paper reports a statistically significant group effect in ANCOVA for writing (F=61.18, p=0.00, partial eta squared=.16), with the EG scoring higher than the CG on the writing posttest (EG M=58.05, CG M=48.88).
findings.measure: Writing posttest / writing proficiency rubric (coherence, grammar, vocabulary, structure)

findings.finding_summary: AI-generated feedback significantly improved Foreign Language Peace of Mind (FLPoM). The ANCOVA for FLPoM posttest showed a significant group effect (F=94.05, p=0.00, partial eta squared=.22), and the EG scored higher than the CG on the posttest (EG M=34.06, CG M=28.27).
findings.measure: FLPoM posttest scale

findings.finding_summary: The study reports a significant positive effect of AI-generated feedback on trait emotional intelligence (EI). For the EI posttest, the group effect was significant (F=15.26, p=0.00, partial eta squared=.04), and the EG mean was higher than the CG mean (EG M=99.13, CG M=92.19). The effect size was small.
findings.measure: Trait EI Questionnaire posttest

findings.finding_summary: Motivation improved significantly for learners receiving AI-generated feedback. The ANCOVA for motivation posttest reported a significant group effect (F=31.77, p=0.00, partial eta squared=.09), with the EG scoring higher than the CG (EG M=34.06, CG M=29.41).
findings.measure: Language Learning Motivation posttest scale

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods quasi-experimental study with a comparison group, but not a randomized trial. The evidence is still useful, though the design and the paper's limited reporting of subgroup analyses constrain causal certainty.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The writing outcome shows a medium effect (partial eta squared=.16), and FLPoM shows a larger effect (.22), while motivation is modest (.09) and EI is small (.04). Overall impact is best characterized as modest-to-medium, with the strongest effects on writing and FLPoM.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses the role of artificial intelligence in education, with a focus on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It asks how educators and institutions can respond to the rapid adoption of large language models such as ChatGPT and how students can be guided to use them responsibly in academic work and classroom learning.

The paper combines a conceptual discussion with informal observations from the author’s experience at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences (Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences) and a narrative literature review. It describes an institutional response in the form of AI guidelines for student writing, emphasizing transparency about model use, prohibition of direct copy-pasting, and the need for critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs. It also proposes workshops, updated guidance, and dedicated staff support as ways to build an AI culture at the institution.

A second major focus is pedagogical: the paper lays out what AI literacy should include, such as understanding AI basics, limitations, bias, ethics, and practical use, and it presents prompt engineering methods as instructional tools for improving learning and critical thinking. The paper concludes that simply allowing or banning AI is insufficient; instead, schools should teach students and teachers how to use AI critically and responsibly. It also suggests that AI literacy should be accessible to all learners, though this is presented as a recommendation rather than an evaluated intervention.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based generative AI chatbot for conversational text generation and assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as a major AI chatbot used in education and as an example of an LLM students and teachers might use for academic work, prompt engineering, and classroom activities. The paper also mentions GPT-4 and other OpenAI models under this umbrella.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review, not an empirical K-12 study with comparison groups or measured outcomes. It contains no subgroup analyses or outcome data for literacy effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No quantitative effects are reported, so there is no measurable impact on literacy or subgroup outcomes to assess.

paper_profiles.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This working paper examines the potential labor-market impact of large language models (LLMs), including GPT-family systems, rather than studying an educational intervention. The core question is how much of the U.S. workforce’s task content could be affected by LLMs and by software built on top of them. The authors develop a rubric for scoring task exposure and apply it to O*NET occupational task descriptions.

The paper uses two annotation sources: human raters and GPT-4 as a classifier. It evaluates 19,265 O*NET tasks and 2,087 detailed work activities, then aggregates task-level scores to occupations. Exposure is defined as the extent to which access to an LLM or LLM-powered software could reduce task completion time by at least 50% while maintaining quality. The analysis is conducted in the U.S. labor market context using O*NET and Bureau of Labor Statistics data.

The main findings are that LLMs appear broadly applicable across occupations, with stronger exposure in higher-wage, writing- and programming-intensive work and weaker exposure in manual or highly physical work. The paper also finds moderate to strong agreement between human and GPT-4 labels and reports that complementary software substantially increases estimated exposure. However, this is a conceptual/exposure-mapping paper with no student sample, no reading or literacy outcome measures, and no subgroup analysis of K-12 learners, emergent readers, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model/chatbot used for text generation, classification, and other language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a classifier in the paper's exposure rubric to annotate occupational tasks and detailed work activities for potential LLM impact, alongside human raters.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a methodological working paper about labor-market exposure measurement, not an empirical study of K-12 educational outcomes or subgroup effects. No literacy intervention, comparison group, or student-level outcome data are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured educational impact on reading, literacy, or subgroup outcomes. The paper offers no effect sizes or outcome evidence relevant to K-12 learners.

paper_profiles.title: A survey on large language model based autonomous agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of large language model (LLM)-based autonomous agents. It asks how recent work has designed, equipped, and evaluated autonomous agents built on top of LLMs, rather than studying any educational intervention or learner outcome. The review organizes the field around three pillars: agent construction, application domains, and evaluation strategies.

The paper proposes a unified framework for agent architecture with four modules: profiling, memory, planning, and action. It then reviews how different works build agent capabilities through prompt-based strategies, external tools, memory systems, and fine-tuning on task-specific data. The survey also summarizes applications in social science, natural science, and engineering, along with common evaluation approaches.

The paper does not report a participant-based study, an intervention, or any K-12 literacy outcomes. No population of human learners is studied, and there are no subgroup analyses or accessibility-specific findings. Its main contribution is conceptual: taxonomy building, synthesis of prior work, and discussion of challenges and future directions in LLM-based autonomous agents.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model-based autonomous agent system or archetype, not a specific commercial product.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a review of LLM-based autonomous agents and discusses their architectures, memory, planning, action, and evaluation at a field level. It does not evaluate a specific educational AI tool or K-12 literacy intervention.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a broad review article on LLM-based autonomous agents, not an empirical study of a K-12 AI tool or literacy intervention. It contains no participant-level educational outcomes, comparison groups, or subgroup analyses relevant to literacy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact is measured in the paper, so there is no outcome-based effect to assess. Any subgroup or accessibility claims are absent from the empirical record because no such study is reported.

paper_profiles.title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether a short AI literacy intervention can reduce high school students’ tendency to over-rely on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations. The authors motivate the work by arguing that as large language models are introduced into education, students may accept AI outputs uncritically, which could undermine critical thinking and learning. The paper focuses on reliance behavior rather than literacy outcomes such as reading comprehension, and it does not report subgroup or accessibility analyses.

The intervention was a short educational text about ChatGPT’s working mechanism, limitations and risks, and how to use it wisely. A control group read a shorter introductory text about ChatGPT without the literacy-focused content. Participants were 12th-grade students in Estonia, randomly assigned to intervention or control conditions in an online survey experiment. After reading, they completed self-reported AI literacy items and then solved eight math puzzles with ChatGPT recommendations, half of which were intentionally incorrect.

The main findings were that students showed substantial over-reliance overall, adopting incorrect recommendations about half the time. The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance; instead, it increased under-reliance, meaning students were more likely to ignore correct recommendations after the literacy text. The intervention also increased students’ self-reported understanding of ChatGPT’s working mechanism and usage, but not limitations. The authors conclude that brief AI literacy texts may not be sufficient to reduce reliance on flawed LLM advice among secondary students.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model/chatbot used for text-based question answering, content generation, and recommendation of responses to user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in a randomized experiment read a short AI literacy text about ChatGPT and then solved math puzzles with ChatGPT recommendations; the study tested whether the intervention reduced adoption of incorrect ChatGPT recommendations.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized comparison of an intervention text versus a control text (n=36), the mean over-reliance rate was lower in the intervention group (M=48.68, SD=24.26) than in the control group (M=55.88, SD=33.69), but the difference was not statistically significant, t(28.78)=-0.73, p=.236, d=-0.25. The authors report widespread over-reliance overall (52.1% of cases), but the intervention did not reduce over-reliance.
findings.measure: Over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations during math puzzle solving

findings.finding_summary: The intervention increased under-reliance on correct ChatGPT recommendations: intervention group M=36.84 (SD=24.11) versus control group M=19.12 (SD=20.78), t(34)=2.35, p=.025, d=0.78. The paper interprets this as a moderate-to-large effect indicating greater tendency to ignore correct ChatGPT recommendations after the literacy text.
findings.measure: Under-reliance on correct ChatGPT recommendations during math puzzle solving

findings.finding_summary: Self-reported AI literacy increased for 'Usage' and 'Working mechanism' after the intervention. Usage ratings were higher in the intervention group (M=3.42, SD=0.77) than control (M=2.77, SD=0.97), t(34)=2.26, p=.030, d=0.76; Working mechanism ratings were also higher in the intervention group (M=3.37, SD=0.76) than control (M=2.77, SD=0.90), t(34)=2.09, p=.044, d=0.70.
findings.measure: Self-reported perceived knowledge of ChatGPT usage and working mechanism

findings.finding_summary: Self-reported knowledge about ChatGPT limitations did not differ significantly between groups: intervention M=2.95 (SD=0.91) versus control M=2.77 (SD=1.03), t(34)=0.56, p=.577, d=0.19. Thus, the intervention did not clearly improve participants' perceived understanding of limitations and risks.
findings.measure: Self-reported perceived knowledge of ChatGPT limitations and risks

findings.finding_summary: Participants' confidence in their answers after using ChatGPT was slightly lower in the intervention group (M=3.58, SD=0.46) than in the control group (M=3.67, SD=0.76), but the difference was not statistically significant, U=188.50, p=.400, rrb=0.17.
findings.measure: Self-perceived confidence after relying on ChatGPT recommendations

findings.finding_summary: Initial decision time across puzzles did not differ significantly between groups. The intervention group had mean dttotal=1.56 minutes (SD=0.77) versus control mean dttotal=1.64 minutes (SD=1.12), U=179.5, p=.560. The authors use this to argue that the intervention did not measurably increase slow, analytical thinking.
findings.measure: Initial decision time across all puzzles

findings.finding_summary: Within-person correlations showed that longer initial decision times were associated with less over-reliance on incorrect recommendations (rs=-0.41, p=.013) and more under-reliance on correct recommendations (rs=0.35, p=.038). This suggests a tradeoff: slower deliberation reduced acceptance of wrong advice but also increased rejection of correct advice.
findings.measure: Correlation between decision time and reliance outcomes

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled experiment with a clear comparison group and pre-specified outcome measures, which supports relatively strong internal validity. However, the sample is very small and subgroup analyses were not reported, so confidence is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced a large positive self-reported literacy effect for some measures (d=0.70-0.76) and a large negative effect on under-reliance (d=0.78), meeting the threshold for medium/large impact. The main target outcome, over-reliance, did not improve significantly.

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Learning Experiences for K-12: Emerging Works, Future Opportunities and a Design Framework
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2020 ACM Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '20)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging need for K-12 artificial intelligence (AI) literacy resources and asks how existing AI education work can be organized into practical guidance for educators and researchers. Rather than testing a new intervention with participants, the authors conduct an exploratory review of K-12 AI and AI-literacy-related literature and tools to identify common patterns, gaps, and promising design directions.

The paper synthesizes 49 works spanning elementary, middle school, high school, and unspecified K-12 contexts. It organizes these works using AI literacy competencies and design considerations adapted from Long and Magerko’s framework, then extends that framework with nine future opportunities and eleven additional design guidelines tailored to K-12 learning. The review includes a range of tools, curricula, workshops, and classroom activities, many of which involve block-based programming, tangible/robotic systems, visualizations, and guided activities for students and teachers.

Its main conclusion is that current K-12 AI learning experiences tend to emphasize accessibility, engagement, and hands-on programming, but often under-address ethics, gradual scaffolding, identity/backgrounds, parental support, and explicit explanations of AI capabilities and limitations. The paper argues that future AI education efforts should more deliberately support diverse learners, involve teachers and parents more fully, and integrate AI learning into broader K-12 subjects. It is a conceptual and survey-based contribution intended to guide future design rather than report outcome effects from a single study.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI literacy / AI learning experience category rather than a specific commercial or research product.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a conceptual review and design framework for K-12 AI literacy experiences. It surveys many AI education tools and curricula, but does not evaluate a single named generative AI product or chatbot.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual and exploratory review/design framework paper, not an empirical study evaluating an AI tool with participants. It synthesizes prior work and proposes guidelines rather than reporting outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No quantitative impact estimates or subgroup outcome data are reported in this paper. The paper does not test interventions or measure effects, so there is no evaluable impact on literacy outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a small group of secondary school English as a foreign language (EFL) students crafted prompts while using ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots to complete a blog-writing task. The central question is not whether the chatbot improved writing scores, but what kinds of prompt content students used and how their prompt sequences unfolded as they tried to get useful output from the tools.

The study is a qualitative case study of four high-achieving Form 1 students in a Hong Kong secondary school. Students completed the same timed writing task in a classroom after school, using iPads and the POE app, and their screen activity was recorded. The authors coded 36 valid prompt turns and identified six distinct prompt types, including auto-complete, search-engine style prompts, greetings, questions, natural-language instructions, and combined instruction-plus-example prompts. They also mapped each student’s pathway across chatbots to show how prompting evolved through trial-and-error.

The main conclusion is that students used a limited range of prompting strategies and did not receive explicit prompt-engineering instruction, suggesting they were experimenting rather than using a mature repertoire of techniques. The authors argue that prompt-engineering education could help EFL students use chatbots more effectively for writing tasks. The paper does not report subgroup outcome analyses for emergent readers, multilingual learners, students with disabilities, or other accessibility-related groups; any discussion of learner differences is speculative and not tied to comparative outcome data.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on large language models, designed for conversational text generation and instruction following.
identified_tools.use_case: Used alongside other POE-hosted chatbots by secondary school EFL students to generate text while completing a blog-writing task; students experimented with prompts across chatbots, including ChatGPT.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study of four students’ prompt engineering pathways, not an experimental evaluation of learning outcomes. It provides descriptive evidence about chatbot use in EFL writing, but no comparative outcome data or subgroup analyses.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests ChatGPT may support EFL writing and prompt-engineering learning, but it reports no effect sizes or measured impacts on literacy outcomes. Any subgroup-related comments are speculative and not supported by outcome data.

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Prompt in the Classroom to Understand AI Limits: A pilot study
paper_profiles.venue: AIXIA 2023 (22nd International Conference of the Italian Association for Artificial Intelligence)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study asks whether a classroom-based AI literacy workshop can help high school students better understand the limits of ChatGPT and reduce fear or negative attitudes toward AI. The intervention is grounded in the idea that users need explicit literacy instruction about large language model limitations, especially hallucination, incomplete understanding, and the need for effective prompting.

The workshop was delivered in a high school in Palermo, Sicily, to 21 students aged 16 to 18. It consisted of a two-hour session with an introductory presentation about AI, LLMs, and human vs. artificial intelligence, followed by two hands-on ChatGPT activities. In the first activity, students attempted to make ChatGPT act as a teacher explaining democracy without being taught prompting strategies; after that, the instructor explained ChatGPT’s limits and introduced prompting techniques, and students repeated the same task in a second activity.

The study used pre/post questionnaires and open-ended responses to examine perceived realistic and identity threat, emotions, interaction quality, and perceptions of ChatGPT functionality. Results suggested reduced perceived AI threat, more positive emotions, and better perceived interaction quality after prompting instruction. Students also reported that the second interaction felt clearer and better than the first. The authors conclude that guided classroom exposure to generative AI can improve students’ understanding of ChatGPT’s capabilities and limitations, though the findings are preliminary and based on a small single-site pilot.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on large language models, designed for conversational text generation and instruction following.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a high-school AI literacy workshop where students interacted with ChatGPT to teach it to act as a personal teacher for democracy concepts, first without prompting strategies and then again after being introduced to prompting techniques, to explore AI limitations and improve prompt quality.

findings.finding_summary: In this pilot with high school students (n=21; analysis n=20 or 21 depending on measure), the workshop was associated with lower perceived AI threat after the intervention. Realistic threat decreased from m=4.17 (SD=1.39) pre to m=3.73 (SD=1.42) post, and identity threat decreased from m=4.08 (SD=1.39) to m=3.57 (SD=1.54), both reported as significant at p<0.05. Participants also reported significantly higher positive than negative emotions after interacting with ChatGPT (mPositive=3.48 vs mNegative=1.35, p<0.05).
findings.measure: Perceived realistic threat, perceived identity threat, and self-reported emotions after interaction

findings.finding_summary: After the prompting instruction, students rated the second ChatGPT interaction as better, clearer, and more natural than the first attempt. The paper reports mean scores for the comparison items (e.g., better m=2.45, SD=1.19; clearer m=5.25, SD=1.11; more natural m=4.55, SD=1.61), but no effect sizes or subgroup analyses were provided.
findings.measure: Post-intervention comparison of first vs second ChatGPT interaction quality and perceived functionality

findings.finding_summary: The intervention improved students' understanding of ChatGPT limits, with qualitative and questionnaire evidence that they better grasped unreliability, limited understanding of commands, and presentation flexibility limits. The authors also noted that prompting strategies improved interaction quality, but this was not tied to a literacy or reading assessment and was not analyzed by subgroup.
findings.measure: Perceived understanding of ChatGPT capabilities and limitations; open-ended reflections on interaction

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot field study with mixed quantitative and qualitative measures, not a controlled literacy trial. The paper reports pre-post changes and descriptive outcomes, but no subgroup or moderator analyses and no explicit reading outcome assessment.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects are positive but modest and largely descriptive, with no effect sizes and a very small sample. The strongest outcomes are attitudinal and interaction-quality improvements rather than direct literacy gains.

paper_profiles.title: Effects of the English language intervention as a foreign language for struggling elementary readers in South Korea: a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether English language interventions improve outcomes for struggling elementary readers in South Korea, and whether effects differ by outcome type, intervention characteristics, classroom context, and grade level. It is a meta-analysis of studies published from 2000 to 2021 that examined English interventions for elementary students identified as underachieving, low achieving, or having learning disabilities.

The authors synthesized 22 studies, separating analyses by study design: 7 between-group experimental/quasi-experimental studies and 15 within-group pre-post studies. The included interventions covered phonics, shared reading, growth mindset, small group instruction, English songs, vocabulary/sentence supports, and related instructional formats. Outcomes were grouped into affective measures such as confidence, motivation, and interest, and achievement measures such as phonological awareness, fluency, vocabulary, reading comprehension, listening comprehension, and writing.

Results showed medium effects for between-group studies and large effects for within-group studies, with substantial heterogeneity. Moderator analyses suggested stronger effects for affective outcomes and several achievement outcomes, with particularly large effects for listening comprehension, letter recognition, and phonological awareness in some subsets. Effects were generally larger for interventions delivered more frequently, across 20–29 sessions or more, and sometimes when teachers were involved. The authors also report larger effects in general education classrooms than inclusion classrooms, and for lower elementary grades than upper grades in the within-group analyses.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system or adaptive instructional system that provides individualized instruction, practice, and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a meta-analysis of English language interventions for struggling elementary readers, not an AI-tool study. No specific AI system is named; the intervention literature is educational reading/English instruction.

findings.finding_summary: This meta-analysis synthesized 22 experimental and quasi-experimental studies of English language interventions for struggling elementary EFL readers in South Korea. The pooled effects were medium for between-group studies (g=0.684, SE=0.26, CI95=0.18, 1.18; p<0.01) and large for within-group studies (g=1.39, SE=0.67, CI95=0.08, 2.69; p<0.05).
findings.measure: Overall English language intervention effects on English achievement/affective outcomes

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis with a defined search, coding, and random-effects synthesis, so it meets the highest evidence tier for study design. However, it is not an AI-tool evaluation and does not report evidence on generative AI literacy specifically.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effects reported are medium to large (g=0.684 and g=1.39), which qualifies as high impact by the stated threshold. Still, these effects pertain to English intervention generally, not AI literacy or a named AI tool.

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing the Power of Generative AI to Support ALL Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper examines how teachers perceive generative AI, especially ChatGPT, as a tool for supporting multilingual learners and students with disabilities through Universal Design for Learning (UDL). The authors were interested in whether teachers viewed ChatGPT as helpful or harmful, what benefits and drawbacks they associated with it, and how it might be used to support language learning and accessibility.

The study was conducted during a summer 2023 professional development institute with 137 educators, including elementary, secondary content, ESOL, special education, pre-service teachers, administrators, and other school staff. Participants all worked with multilingual learners in suburban school districts in the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States. Data came from plenary-session polls, small-group workshop artifacts, and teacher reflections, followed by descriptive summarization and categorization of perceived benefits and drawbacks within UDL principles.

Findings were entirely perceptual rather than outcome-based: teachers were split on whether generative AI was a "friend" or "foe," and many believed it could improve accessibility, language support, translation, feedback, and differentiated materials, while also raising concerns about cheating, bias, reduced critical thinking, and overreliance. The paper does not test student achievement or reading/literacy outcomes and does not report subgroup comparisons for emergent readers, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities beyond qualitative, teacher-reported implications. Its main conclusion is that generative AI may help teachers create more flexible UDL-aligned materials for multilingual learners, but further research is needed.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s generative AI chatbot/large language model system for natural-language generation, question answering, drafting, translation, and feedback generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the focal generative AI tool in a teacher professional development study. Teachers explored ChatGPT 3.5 for lesson planning, generating tables, creating responses to writing assignments, creating factual questions, providing feedback on writing, lowering reading level, adding citations, translating responses, and discussing how it could support multilingual learners and UDL.

findings.finding_summary: This exploratory study did not test student outcomes. Among 137 teachers working with multilingual learners, 43% agreed or strongly agreed before the ChatGPT workshop that ChatGPT and other generative AI would help make instruction more accessible for all learners (including those with disabilities), while 23% disagreed/strongly disagreed and 32% were undecided. After exploring the tool, teachers generated more positive (54%) than negative (46%) perceived aspects, but these were perception data rather than literacy outcome data.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions of accessibility/support for multilingual learners and perceived benefits/drawbacks

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/exploratory professional development study with teacher perception data, not a controlled evaluation of student literacy outcomes. The paper includes no subgroup outcome analyses or causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No effect size or student outcome impact is reported. The paper suggests potential accessibility benefits for multilingual learners and students with disabilities, but only at the level of teacher perceptions and brainstormed uses.

paper_profiles.title: Writing growth among non-English learners and English learners in grades 6–8 using automated writing evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether an automated writing evaluation (AWE) system, MI Write, can serve as a benchmark assessment for monitoring middle-school students’ writing growth over an academic year and whether growth differs for English learners (ELs) and non-ELs. The paper is framed as a response to the need for efficient, scalable, and informative literacy assessment tools within a multi-tiered system of supports (MTSS), especially for identifying and tracking diverse learners in writing instruction.

The study used three benchmark argumentative writing assessments administered in fall, winter, and spring to 3,299 students in Grades 6–8 in one Mid-Atlantic U.S. district, including 464 ELs. Essays were scored by MI Write on an overall writing score and six analytic traits, and the system also generated 81 NLP-derived features representing subskills such as syntax, vocabulary, spelling, and cohesion. Growth was modeled using multilevel longitudinal analyses with reading proficiency, grade, race/ethnicity, special education status, and school effects as covariates. The paper is not an intervention trial; it evaluates assessment performance and subgroup growth patterns in an existing instructional context.

Findings showed modest but significant growth in overall writing quality across the year, with no meaningful difference in total gain between EL and non-EL students once covariates were controlled. However, subgroup patterns emerged at the trait and feature levels: EL students showed relatively faster growth in sentence fluency and some foundational skills such as sentence complexity and spelling accuracy, while non-EL students showed faster growth in more advanced language features such as sophisticated grammar, verb forms, vocabulary, and error reduction. The authors conclude that MI Write can capture distinct developmental pathways among middle school writers and may be useful for monitoring diverse learners, but the subgroup findings are based on outcome data from writing assessments rather than any experimental accessibility or instructional accommodation study.

identified_tools.name: MI Write
identified_tools.description: An automated writing evaluation (AWE) system that uses NLP and machine learning to score student writing analytically across traits and provide feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the benchmark writing assessment to score middle-school argumentative writing across fall, winter, and spring and to derive 81 NLP features for growth modeling.

findings.finding_summary: Across 3,299 middle-school students (n=464 ELs), MI Write Total Score increased significantly over the school year. The average gain was about 1.6 points from fall to spring, corresponding to d=0.32 (95% CI [0.19, 0.45]).
findings.measure: MI Write Total Score (overall writing quality) across fall, winter, and spring benchmark argumentative writing prompts

findings.finding_summary: No significant difference in overall writing growth was found between EL and non-EL students, and English language proficiency did not predict growth. However, at the trait level EL students showed significantly faster growth in development (β=0.050, p=.041) and sentence fluency (β=0.053, p=.031), while time×EL interactions for organization, word choice, style, and conventions were positive but not statistically significant.
findings.measure: MI Write analytic trait scores (development, organization, sentence fluency, style, word choice, conventions) over time and time×EL interactions
findings.effect_size: β=0.050 to 0.053 for significant trait interactions; other interactions not significant

findings.finding_summary: At the NLP feature level, 58 of 81 features changed significantly over time, and 7 features showed differential growth by EL status. EL students grew faster in sentence complexity (β=0.141, p<.01) and spelling accuracy (β=0.081, p<.05), while non-EL students grew faster in subordinate conjunctions, perfect aspect verbs, advanced content words, and reductions in misspellings and homophone errors.
findings.measure: 81 proprietary NLP features derived from student essays; time effects and time×EL interactions
findings.effect_size: β=0.141, 0.081 for EL-favored features; β=-0.090 to -0.151 for non-EL-favored features

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical longitudinal multilevel growth study with a large sample and explicit subgroup analyses, but it is observational rather than randomized. The methodology is strong for detecting differential growth patterns, yet causal claims are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main overall gain is modest (d=0.32 across the year), with subgroup differences mostly small and feature-level. The paper reports meaningful but not large differential effects for some writing subskills.

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to teach K-12 students how to use generative AI chatbots responsibly and effectively for learning, with a specific focus on prompting literacy. The authors argue that as AI tools such as ChatGPT become more common in school and home settings, students need instruction not only on what AI can do, but also on how to ask better questions, when AI is appropriate for learning, and how to avoid overreliance on direct answers.

To address this, the paper presents a web-based AI literacy module built around scenario-based practice with an LLM chatbot and an automatic grader. Students complete prompt-writing tasks in three secondary-school learning scenarios (biology, geography, and math) and receive immediate feedback on dimensions such as relevance, purpose, conciseness, background/context, and whether the prompt asks for a direct answer. Study 1 was deployed in six secondary classrooms in East Asia with 111 students and used pre/post surveys, multiple-choice prompting-literacy questions, and open-ended reflections. Study 2 revised the assessment into true/false and open-ended items and re-used a similar classroom sample to evaluate item quality.

Findings suggest that the AI auto-grader generally rated prompts with high accuracy, students improved in including background/context in prompts, and self-reported confidence in using AI for learning increased after the activity. However, conceptual test scores showed a ceiling effect, other prompt dimensions improved less clearly, and the paper notes that some challenges were related to students’ basic typing and computer skills rather than prompting knowledge itself. The authors conclude that the module shows promise for classroom AI literacy instruction, but more extensive and comparative studies are needed to establish learning effectiveness and assessment quality.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model chatbot used for interactive prompting practice and AI-based auto-grading/feedback in a K-12 AI literacy module.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the underlying LLM via GPT-4o for student prompt generation, chatbot responses, and automatic grading of student-written prompts in classroom deployments.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1, the GPT-4o-based auto-grader was compared against human labels on 483 unique student-written prompts and achieved an average accuracy of 0.92 overall. The paper reports high pass/fail accuracy for relevance (0.98), background (0.96), and elaboration (0.90), with lower accuracy for purpose (0.85) and no-direct-answer (0.88), indicating mostly strong grading performance with some rubric-specific weaknesses.
findings.measure: Accuracy of AI-based automatic grading against human labels for student-written prompts

findings.finding_summary: The prompting literacy module was associated with improved student performance on one prompt dimension: the proportion of students correctly including background/context in prompts increased significantly from Q1 to Q3 (p = .039). Students also reported increased confidence in using AI for learning, with self-reported confidence rising by 10.4% on average (SD = 0.92; Wilcoxon p < .001).
findings.measure: Prompt-dimension performance and self-reported confidence in using AI for learning
findings.effect_size: 10.4% increase in confidence; r=0.27 for prior AI use and first-question performance
findings.sample_size: n=111 valid Study 1 students; n=98 pre/post test completers

findings.finding_summary: Study 2 compared the original multiple-choice assessment with a revised assessment using True/False and open-ended items. The revised version improved item quality: none of the MCQs fell in the desired difficulty range, whereas 60% of open-ended items and 30% of True/False items did; Cronbach’s alpha was 0.68 for the original assessment and 0.58 for the iterated version.
findings.measure: Assessment difficulty, discrimination, and internal reliability for prompting literacy assessment items

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical classroom study with mixed methods and clear procedures, but not a randomized controlled trial. Evidence includes descriptive statistics, nonparametric tests, and item analysis rather than a strong causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are modest-to-unclear in scope: one significant improvement in background/context prompting, a self-reported confidence increase, and improved assessment item quality. No standardized literacy outcome or large effect size is reported.

paper_profiles.title: The Agency Gap: How Generative AI Literacy Shapes Independent Writing after AI Support
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether students’ generative AI (GenAI) literacy is associated with stronger independent writing performance after AI support is removed. The authors frame this as an “agency gap,” asking when GenAI literacy matters most and whether its effects persist beyond immediate AI-assisted performance.

The study experimentally compares two GenAI chatbot support styles: a reactive chatbot that responds only to user questions and a proactive chatbot that scaffolds learners through structured questions and feedback. Seventy-nine higher education participants completed multimodal academic writing tasks based on visual data, first with either reactive or proactive AI support and then again on a parallel task without AI support. Writing was scored on insightfulness, visual data integration, organisation and coherence, linguistic quality, critical thinking, and a composite score. GenAI literacy and visualisation literacy were measured as predictors and possible confounds.

Results showed that GenAI literacy predicted independent writing performance mainly in the reactive condition, especially after AI support was withdrawn. In the proactive condition, performance was more equal across GenAI literacy levels, suggesting that proactive scaffolding reduced reliance on individual literacy differences. The study also found no meaningful indirect effect through AI-supported writing performance, implying that GenAI literacy functioned as a direct, transferable competence rather than merely boosting performance during AI use. The paper concludes that proactive scaffolds may mitigate disparities, while GenAI literacy becomes more consequential when learners must self-initiate and self-regulate.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI chatbot system providing reactive question-answering or proactive scaffolding, using multimodal GPT-4o with retrieval-augmented generation to support academic writing tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a reactive versus proactive GenAI chatbot supporting multimodal academic writing from visual data, followed by a parallel independent writing task without AI support.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of n=79 higher education medical and nursing students, GenAI literacy positively predicted independent writing performance after AI removal in the reactive chatbot condition, but not in the proactive condition. Significant associations in the reactive condition were reported for insightfulness (rs=.41, p=.010), visual data integration (rs=.40, p=.013), organisation and coherence (rs=.44, p=.005), linguistic quality (rs=.32, p=.045), critical thinking (rs=.37, p=.019), and composite score (rs=.44, p=.005); partial correlations controlling for visualisation literacy remained significant.
findings.measure: Spearman correlations and partial correlations between GenAI literacy and writing rubric scores at AI-removal; rubric dimensions plus composite score

findings.finding_summary: Median-split comparisons showed that in the reactive condition (low n=21, high n=18), the high GenAI literacy group scored higher at AI-removal on insightfulness (U=99.00, p=.021, rrb=.34), visual data integration (U=87.50, p=.012, rrb=.36), organisation and coherence (U=67.50, p=.002, rrb=.46), and composite score (U=83.50, p=.009, rrb=.41). At AI-support, only linguistic quality differed significantly (U=120.50, p=.038, rrb=.28). No significant GenAI literacy group differences were found in the proactive condition (low n=23, high n=17).
findings.measure: Mann-Whitney U tests comparing low vs high GenAI literacy groups on writing rubric scores at AI-support and AI-removal

findings.finding_summary: Ordinal logistic regression predicting AI-removal writing found that higher GenAI literacy significantly predicted better visual data integration (b=0.13, SE=0.06, z=2.07, p=.039, OR=1.14), critical thinking (b=0.14, SE=0.07, z=2.18, p=.029, OR=1.15), and composite score (b=0.10, SE=0.05, z=2.15, p=.032, OR=1.11). GenAI literacy did not significantly predict insightfulness, organisation and coherence, or linguistic quality, and chatbot type and visualisation literacy were not significant predictors.
findings.measure: Ordinal logistic regression of AI-removal writing outcomes

findings.finding_summary: Mediation analyses did not support an indirect pathway from GenAI literacy to independent writing through AI-supported performance in either condition. In the reactive condition, the indirect effect was 0.032 with 95% CI [-0.022, 0.108]; in the proactive condition, the indirect effect was 0.022 with 95% CI [-0.055, 0.102].
findings.measure: Bootstrapped mediation of AI-support score between GenAI literacy and AI-removal score

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary mixed-method/experimental study with clear comparison conditions and quantitative analyses, but it is not a randomized educational efficacy trial on a named product and the evidence is limited to a small higher-education sample. The paper is correlational/experimental within-task rather than a full K-12 intervention study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported associations and group differences are modest to medium in magnitude, with several effects around r=.32-.45 and rrb=.28-.46. The findings suggest meaningful differences in independent writing after AI support, but they are context-specific and not directly K-12.

paper_profiles.title: What is prompt literacy? An exploratory study of language learners’ development of new literacy skill using generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study asks whether a new form of literacy—“prompt literacy”—emerges when language learners use generative AI to complete a vocabulary-image creation task. The authors define prompt literacy as the ability to craft precise prompts, interpret generative-AI outputs, and iteratively revise prompts to achieve desired results.

The intervention was an AI-powered image creation project in which 30 EFL undergraduate students majoring in English Language and Literature used ChatGPT for vocabulary exploration and Bing Image Creator for generating images tied to the sociocultural or historical meanings of English words. Students read about word origins, researched further, sketched images, wrote prompts, revised them repeatedly, and compared generated images across iterations. Data sources included the generated artwork, a post-project survey adapted from a vocabulary learning questionnaire, and students’ reflection papers.

Findings show that students used repeated prompt revision to better specify context, character actions, and other details needed to generate intended images. Survey responses suggested high self-perceived gains in vocabulary-learning strategies such as visualization, attention to word origins, hidden meanings, and use in context. Reflections indicated that students viewed prompt literacy as enjoyable, useful for communication and problem-solving, and relevant to future human-AI collaboration. The paper argues that prompt literacy is an emerging AI-era literacy that can support vocabulary learning and creative language tasks, but it is an exploratory study rather than a controlled efficacy test.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/LLM system used for conversational text generation, question answering, and assistance with drafting prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by EFL students to confirm word meanings, research additional information, and iteratively refine prompts for AI-generated images in a vocabulary-image creation project.

findings.finding_summary: The study reports qualitative evidence that students used ChatGPT iteratively to refine prompts and understand vocabulary origins and contexts, but it does not report a controlled comparison or outcome data isolating ChatGPT effects. The paper notes perceived improvement in vocabulary learning strategies after the project (n=30), but no tool-specific effect sizes or subgroup analyses are provided.
findings.measure: Self-perceived vocabulary learning strategies; reflection-based prompt literacy development

identified_tools.name: Bing Image Creator
identified_tools.description: Microsoft's text-to-image generative AI system for creating images from natural-language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate and revise images representing the socio-cultural meanings and historical origins of English vocabulary items through iterative prompt refinement.

findings.finding_summary: Participants demonstrated prompt literacy by repeatedly revising prompts to better match intended images, indicating development of the ability to generate, interpret, and refine prompts for generative AI. The paper reports no experimental comparison group, no subgroup moderation, and no direct literacy test scores beyond self-reports and qualitative analysis.
findings.measure: Prompt revision behavior; qualitative analysis of generated images and reflections

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small qualitative/mixed-methods exploratory study with descriptive survey data and no true comparison group or causal estimate. It provides useful evidence about how students used generative AI in a literacy task, but not high-causal-credibility subgroup or differential-effects evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive but unquantified development of prompt literacy and self-perceived vocabulary strategy use, with no effect sizes. Any impact appears educationally meaningful but is not measured in a way that supports medium-or-large impact classification.

paper_profiles.title: Trust and Reliance on AI in Education: AI Literacy and Need for Cognition as Moderators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students’ trust in a generative AI assistant relates to their appropriate reliance on the assistant during problem-solving, and whether that relationship differs by learner characteristics. The central question is whether higher trust helps or harms selective use of AI suggestions, especially when the AI sometimes provides intentionally misleading advice.

The study used a single-session laboratory experiment with 432 undergraduate students enrolled in computing-related courses at the University of Florida. Participants completed 14 Python output-prediction problems while interacting with an AI chatbot that delivered a mix of correct and incorrect recommendations and explanations.
