Reliance was measured behaviorally by whether students accepted correct recommendations and rejected incorrect ones; surveys measured AI literacy, need for cognition, programming self-efficacy, programming literacy, and post-task trust.

Results showed that higher trust was associated with lower appropriate reliance and lower task accuracy, indicating more frequent acceptance of AI suggestions without sufficient discrimination between correct and incorrect advice. The trust–reliance relationship was nonlinear but did not show a clear optimal middle range within the observed data. AI literacy and need for cognition significantly moderated the association: students higher on those traits tended to show better selective reliance when trust was low, but the trust–reliance slope became more negative as those moderator values increased. The paper concludes that instruction and tool design should support more explicit verification of AI outputs during learning tasks.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family conversational generative AI chatbot/assistant.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as an AI chatbot assistant in a single-session laboratory experiment for Python output-prediction problems. The platform integrated OpenAI's API (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125) to generate follow-up responses after the pre-programmed initial recommendations.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of 432 undergraduates, higher post-task trust in the AI assistant was associated with lower appropriate reliance on the chatbot's recommendations during Python output-prediction problems. The regression was significant (b = -3.65, SE = 0.39, t(430) = -9.48, p < .001, R2 = .173), indicating less selective acceptance/rejection of correct versus misleading advice.
findings.measure: Appropriate reliance on AI recommendations during programming problem-solving

findings.finding_summary: A quadratic model fit the trust-to-appropriate-reliance relation slightly better than the linear model (R2 = .185 vs. .173; 94R2 = .012). Both the linear trust term (b = -3.18, p < .001) and the squared term (b = 0.56, p = .011) were significant, suggesting a steep decline in appropriate reliance from low to moderate trust that attenuated at higher trust values, but without reversal within the observed range.
findings.measure: Nonlinear association between trust and appropriate reliance

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI chatbot/assistant with no uniquely identified commercial product name in the text.
identified_tools.use_case: The study used a general AI chatbot interface with intentionally correct and misleading recommendations to examine selective reliance in a programming task. The paper names the underlying API (OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo-0125) but treats the system functionally as an AI assistant rather than evaluating a distinct branded educational product.

findings.finding_summary: AI literacy significantly moderated the trust-appropriate reliance relationship (interaction b = -1.03, p = .014). The authors report that the conditional trust slope became more negative as AI literacy increased, with estimated slopes of about -3.59 at -1 SD, -4.62 at the mean, and -5.65 at +1 SD AI literacy, suggesting higher AI literacy supported more selective reliance when trust was lower but not when trust was high.
findings.measure: Moderation of the trust-appropriate reliance relationship by AI literacy

findings.finding_summary: Need for cognition also moderated the trust-appropriate reliance relationship (interaction b = -0.99, p = .040). The conditional trust slope was approximately -3.38 at -1 SD, -4.37 at the mean, and -5.36 at +1 SD need for cognition, indicating that more cognitively reflective students showed higher predicted appropriate reliance when trust was low, but the trust-reliance association became more negative as trust increased.
findings.measure: Moderation of the trust-appropriate reliance relationship by need for cognition

findings.finding_summary: Programming self-efficacy did not significantly moderate the trust-appropriate reliance relationship (interaction p = .121), and programming literacy also did not significantly moderate it (interaction p = .437). The authors describe this as limited evidence that these characteristics altered how trust related to appropriate reliance in this task.
findings.measure: Moderation of the trust-appropriate reliance relationship by programming self-efficacy and programming literacy

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-session correlational laboratory experiment with regression and moderation analyses, not a randomized comparison trial. The methodology is clear and the measures are defined, but the evidence is observational rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main trust effect is moderate in magnitude (R2 = .173), but the study does not report educational achievement gains from the AI tool itself. The most relevant findings concern reliance behavior and moderator effects, not direct literacy outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Students to Question the Machine: An AI Literacy Intervention Improves Students Regulation of LLM Use in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a brief AI literacy workshop can improve middle-school students’ ability to use a generative AI system effectively during science problem solving. The central question is whether teaching students how large language models work, why they fail, and how to regulate interactions with them leads to better task performance and better interaction strategies.

The intervention was a two-hour classroom workshop given two days before the main task. It combined conceptual instruction about LLM limitations such as hallucinations, bias, and sycophancy with procedural guidance on prompting, evaluating responses, and asking follow-up questions. The comparison group received no training. Students then completed six science inquiry exercises using an LLM-supported interface, where researchers measured prompt acceptance, rejection of underspecified prompts, correctness judgments of AI answers, follow-up questioning, and final written answer quality.

The study was conducted in one French middle school with 116 students in grades 8–9 (ages 13–15). The authors report that trained students performed better overall, were more selective about prompt use, made more accurate judgments of AI output quality, and asked follow-up questions more often when initial answers were inadequate. The intervention improved behavioral regulation of LLM use, but self-report measures of GenAI attitudes/knowledge and metacognitive awareness did not predict performance, and the workshop did not meaningfully change self-reported GenAI beliefs. The paper concludes that brief, scalable AI literacy instruction can improve middle-school students’ use of generative AI in school-like science tasks.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general-purpose generative AI / large language model chatbot used for interactive question answering, prompt response generation, and iterative answer evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by middle-school students as a support tool during six science inquiry tasks; students prompted the system, judged responses, iterated follow-up queries, and wrote final answers. The intervention trained students on how to regulate these interactions.

findings.finding_summary: In this controlled classroom study (N=116), students who received the 2-hour AI literacy workshop achieved higher final-answer performance than controls on the six science tasks. Mean final-answer score was 11.38 (SD 3.87, n=76) versus 10.29 (SD 3.04, n=40), with Mann�adWhitney U=1871, p=.040, r=.19.
findings.measure: Final written answer quality / exercise score on a 0-20 scale

findings.finding_summary: Trained students showed stronger interaction regulation: they accepted fewer suggested prompts overall, were less likely to accept underspecified prompts (51.5% vs. 66.7%, p=.044), judged AI answer correctness more accurately, and asked follow-up questions more often when initial prompts were underspecified. The paper reports that these behavioral changes translated into higher-quality answers in the intervention group for accepted underspecified prompts, with an interaction p=.038.
findings.measure: Prompt acceptance, correctness judgments, follow-up-question behavior, and associated performance effects

findings.finding_summary: The workshop did not produce significant changes in students' GenAI self-report scores. Repeated-measures MANOVA showed no overall pre-post effect in the intervention group (Pillai's trace=0.116, F(6,62)=1.36, p=.247), though two dimensions had small non-robust increases (Attitude and Fairness & ethics, both pFDR=.054).
findings.measure: GenAI self-report questionnaire dimensions
findings.sample_size: n=72 intervention; n=40 control for baseline comparison

findings.finding_summary: Across all students, GenAI self-report scores were not correlated with task performance (r=0.01, p=.88, R2<.001, n=116). Metacognitive self-report scores were also unrelated to exercise scores (r=0.04, p=.65, R2=.002, n=116), and within the intervention group pre-post changes in GenAI self-reports did not predict prompt-discrimination sensitivity.
findings.measure: Correlation between self-report measures and performance

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled classroom study with a comparison group and behavioral outcomes, providing relatively strong causal evidence for a brief AI literacy intervention. However, subgroup analysis was not possible because demographic data were not collected.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main performance effect is modest (r=.19; mean difference about 1.1 points on a 20-point scale), and several related outcomes are behavioral/process gains rather than large achievement effects. The intervention appears meaningful but not large in magnitude.

paper_profiles.title: Specializing Multilingual Language Models: An Empirical Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how to better adapt pretrained multilingual language models to low-resource languages, especially when the target language uses a script that is poorly represented in the model’s original vocabulary. The authors focus on two specialization strategies: vocabulary augmentation, which adds new wordpieces to MBERT’s vocabulary and continues pretraining, and script transliteration, which converts target-language text into Latin script before additional pretraining.

The experiments evaluate these approaches on three NLP tasks: part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, and named entity recognition. The study uses nine low-resource languages across three scripts (Latin, Cyrillic, and Perso-Arabic), with downstream benchmarks drawn from Universal Dependencies and WikiAnn, and reports results over five random seeds. The paper also analyzes tokenizer coverage and the relationship between unknown-wordpiece rates and downstream gains.

The main conclusion is that vocabulary augmentation generally improves performance, with especially strong gains for unseen languages and non-Latin scripts where the original multilingual tokenizer has poor coverage. The improvement is associated with reduced unknown-token rates, particularly for Type 2 and Arabic-script languages. However, when vocabulary augmentation is combined with transliteration, the two methods can interact negatively, and transliteration does not consistently add benefit beyond either method alone. The paper frames these findings as evidence that model specialization is most useful at the mix-in stage between initial and continued pretraining, but it does not study K-12 learners or literacy outcomes.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic pretrained multilingual language model / transformer-based NLP system (MBERT) specialized via vocabulary augmentation and transliteration for low-resource language processing.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies MBERT as the base model, comparing unadapted MBERT, language-adaptive pretraining (LAPT), vocabulary augmentation (VA/TVA), transliteration, and their combination on POS tagging, dependency parsing, and named entity recognition in low-resource languages.

findings.finding_summary: Across nine low-resource languages and three tasks, vocabulary augmentation (VA) generally improved performance over unadapted MBERT and usually over LAPT. The paper reports that VA was especially beneficial for unseen low-resource languages and non-Latin scripts, with the largest gains on Uyghur (e.g., up to a 57% relative error reduction over LAPT on one task).
findings.measure: POS tagging accuracy, UD parsing LAS, and NER macro F1

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that transliteration and VA both improved MBERT-based models, but they interacted negatively when combined. For Uyghur and Meadow Mari, VA with transliteration often underperformed the best single mix-in or LAPT with transliteration, especially on NER, suggesting the two augmentation strategies can conflict.
findings.measure: POS tagging accuracy, UD parsing LAS, and NER macro F1 after transliteration

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a controlled empirical NLP study with clear comparative evaluation, but it is not an education study and does not involve learner outcomes or human subjects in the K-12 sense. The evidence is experimental rather than qualitative, but the educational relevance is indirect.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are substantial for the NLP tasks studied, particularly for low-resource and unseen-script languages, but there is no direct educational intervention or reading/literacy impact. The paper’s impact for the requested K-12 literacy question is therefore unclear.

paper_profiles.title: Digital Literacy and Reading Habits of the Central University of Tamil Nadu Students: A Survey Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the digital literacy skills and reading habits of students and research scholars at the Central University of Tamil Nadu in India. The authors ask how familiar respondents are with digital tools, how frequently they use digital environments and applications, and whether they prefer print or electronic reading formats. It is primarily a descriptive survey of current habits and self-perceived skills rather than an intervention study.

Data were collected with a structured questionnaire distributed through email, WhatsApp, and Telegram to 135 respondents drawn from undergraduate, postgraduate, integrated UG/PG, and research scholar groups. The survey covered self-ratings of typing, web search, computer, internet, and digital literacy skills; use of tools such as email, the web, databases, language apps, and video conferencing; and attitudes toward digital devices and digital literacy. The paper also asked about reading enjoyment, sources of reading recommendations, and format preferences for different reading situations.

The main conclusion is that respondents generally reported good digital literacy and comfort with digital tools, but they still preferred print books for many reading purposes, especially pleasurable reading and reading in bed or with children. Electronic formats were favored for quick access, travel, sharing, and maintaining large collections. The study argues that digital literacy is widespread among these university students, yet print remains the preferred medium for deeper or recreational reading. Because the study is self-report and descriptive, it does not test causal effects or compare literacy outcomes across subgroups beyond simple demographic descriptions.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI or chatbot system for producing and processing language-based outputs without a specific named product identified.
identified_tools.use_case: No generative AI tool was studied. The paper is a survey of university students' digital literacy, digital device use, and reading habits, including preferences for print versus electronic formats.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey study about digital literacy and reading habits, not an evaluation of an AI literacy intervention or AI tool. There is no comparison group, no moderator analysis, and no subgroup outcome analysis for emergent readers, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI tool effect was measured, so there is no estimable impact on literacy outcomes. Reported results are descriptive self-reports only and do not support causal or subgroup effect claims.

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Financial Literacy, Social Capital, and Financial Technology on Financial Inclusion of Indonesian Students
paper_profiles.venue: IRJEMS International Research Journal of Economics and Management Studies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether financial literacy, social capital, and financial technology are associated with financial inclusion among Indonesian students. The motivation is that students are often treated as key agents of financial inclusion, yet the authors argue that many still fall victim to fraud and do not fully use formal financial services. The study is framed around a perceived gap between students’ financial inclusion and their financial literacy, and it discusses how social networks and digital finance may also shape students’ access to and use of financial services.

The study uses a quantitative survey design with primary data from 100 active economics-faculty students in Tangerang, Indonesia, across seven private universities. Respondents were fifth-semester students in management, business, and accounting programs. The paper uses questionnaire measures for financial literacy, social capital, financial technology, and financial inclusion, and analyzes the data with descriptive statistics, reliability/validity checks, and multiple regression in SPSS.

The main findings are that financial literacy, social capital, and financial technology each have positive and statistically significant associations with financial inclusion. The authors conclude that greater knowledge, trust, networked support, and use of fintech are linked to better financial inclusion among these students. The discussion emphasizes that the gap between literacy and inclusion remains substantial and that students are still vulnerable to fraud, but these claims are interpretive and not based on subgroup or experimental outcome comparisons. No differential effects for emergent readers, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities are reported.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI or large language model chatbot, without a specific named product identified in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: No generative AI or AI literacy tool is studied. The paper examines financial literacy, social capital, and financial technology as predictors of financial inclusion among economics students.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quantitative correlational study about financial inclusion, not an evaluation of an AI tool or AI literacy intervention. There is no AI system, comparison condition, or subgroup analysis related to generative AI literacy outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI tool was studied, so there is no tool impact to assess. The reported outcomes concern financial inclusion rather than literacy or AI-related educational effects.

paper_profiles.title: ActiveAI: Enabling K-12 AI Literacy Education & Analytics at Scale
paper_profiles.venue: Companion Proceedings 15th International Conference on Learning Analytics & Knowledge (LAK25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for larger-scale, more replicable evidence in K-12 AI literacy education. The authors note that prior work has produced promising learning materials and summer programs, but that large-scale learning data remain scarce. To address this gap, they developed ActiveAI, an online learning platform designed to deliver AI literacy modules, assessments, and standardized logging for secondary analysis.

The platform includes a survey, pre-test, interactive learning module with an AI agent, and post-test. It was deployed across 12 secondary schools and used by over 1,000 learners, with 426 completing all components across four implemented modules. The system was built to support students, teachers, and researchers, and to make de-identified data downloadable for tools such as DataShop and LearnSphere. The study does not test a randomized intervention; instead, it reports preliminary analysis of collected usage and assessment data.

The main findings are that some AI literacy objectives showed significant pre/post gains, and that these gains were associated with more interactive activities rather than passive reading. The paper also reports gender differences in one module: non-male students scored higher on both pre- and post-tests than male students and showed slightly higher gains. The authors emphasize that the dataset and platform are intended to support future secondary analyses and improvements to AI literacy instruction across diverse educational contexts.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI / LLM-based online learning platform with AI Literacy modules, interactive AI-agent activities, assessments, and data logging; built using OpenAI APIs but not a specific named product in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to deliver K-12 AI literacy learning modules, pre/post tests, and interactive activities such as identifying LLM hallucinations in simulated scenarios; the platform also supported teacher/researcher data access and analytics.

findings.finding_summary: Across 7 learning objectives in 4 modules, the paper reports significant learning gains in 4 objectives based on Wilcoxon tests on pre- and post-test scores. The paper does not provide effect sizes for these gains; it states that objectives with significant gains involved interactive activities, while those with smaller gains were linked to passive reading.
findings.measure: Pre-test vs post-test scores on AI literacy learning objectives
findings.sample_size: n=426 completed all components (over 1,000 unique learners used the platform)

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI-supported K-12 AI literacy learning environment that includes interactive activities and assessment data for analysis.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied for subgroup patterns in assessment performance, including gender differences in the latest experiment (module 4: Identify LLM Hallucinations).

findings.finding_summary: In module 4, non-male students achieved significantly higher pre-test scores (f=6.97, p<0.01, one-way ANOVA) and post-test scores (f=6.80, p=0.01, one-way ANOVA) than male students, with slightly higher learning gains. The paper reports this as a gender difference, but it is not a literacy-subgroup analysis for emergent readers, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities.
findings.measure: Pre-test and post-test assessment scores by gender

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-data study of a K-12 AI literacy platform, but the evidence reported here is preliminary, correlational/subgroup-based, and lacks effect sizes or full experimental controls. The paper includes quantitative pre/post testing and ANOVA, but not a rigorous design focused on literacy subgroup effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported learning gains are statistically significant for some objectives, but no effect sizes are given and subgroup findings are limited to gender differences. For the literacy-subgroup question posed, the paper provides no direct evidence of differential effects for emergent readers, multilingual learners, or students with disabilities.

paper_profiles.title: Situationally-Induced Impairments and Disabilities Research
paper_profiles.venue: CHI’19 Workshop: Addressing the Challenges of Situationally-Induced Impairments and Disabilities in Mobile Interaction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper argues for more systematic research on situationally-induced impairments and disabilities (SIIDs) in mobile interaction. The authors focus on the problem that many prior SIID studies have examined contextual impairments in an ad hoc way, making it difficult to compare effects across conditions or to design sensing and adaptation techniques that address the most consequential impairments.

Rather than testing a new educational intervention, the paper proposes a research agenda and summarizes the authors’ prior empirical work on smartphone interaction under different situational impairments such as cold environments, stress, and ambient noise. They describe a reusable experimental protocol built around three core mobile tasks: target acquisition, visual search, and text entry, with baseline conditions and task training to support fair comparisons across studies.

The paper does not study K-12 learners or reading/literacy outcomes. Its main contribution is conceptual: it argues that understanding the magnitude and comparability of SIID effects is foundational for later sensing, modeling, and interface adaptation work. The authors conclude that future work should examine combined situational impairments and more complex tasks, especially where cognitive demands are higher.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: No AI tool or educational generative AI system is studied. This is a position paper about situationally-induced impairments and disabilities in mobile interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: Not applicable; the paper does not evaluate an AI literacy tool or generative AI system.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/position paper, not an empirical study of an AI tool. It provides no participant-level outcomes, comparison groups, or literacy measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No AI intervention or educational outcome is evaluated, so there is no measurable impact to assess.

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy in K-12 and Higher Education in the Wake of Generative AI: An Integrative Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly expanding but still loosely defined area of AI literacy, especially in the period after generative AI became widely available. The authors argue that the field contains many different uses of the term “AI literacy,” ranging from technical machine-learning instruction to prompt engineering with ChatGPT to critical discussions of AI ethics and societal impact. Their main goal is not to evaluate a single intervention, but to synthesize and organize the conceptual diversity in the literature.

Using an integrative review method, the paper examines 124 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and July 2024 that focused on AI literacy in K-12 or undergraduate contexts. The authors code studies according to how they conceptualize AI (technical details, tools, sociocultural impact) and literacy (functional, critical, indirectly beneficial). They identify established pre-generative-AI patterns, such as K-12 machine-learning curricula and ethics-focused lessons, and emerging post-generative-AI patterns, especially the teaching of generative AI tool use and prompt engineering.

The review includes K-12 and higher education studies across multiple countries, but it is not a primary outcome study and does not test subgroup effects or literacy outcomes directly. Its main conclusion is that the field needs more precise terminology and that generative AI has shifted AI literacy toward more tool-oriented and functionally framed instruction, while critical and sociocultural work remains important but less common in some areas. The paper also notes several research gaps, including limited postsecondary research, relatively few critical uses of AI tools, and the need for clearer conceptual boundaries within AI literacy research.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic large language model / generative AI chatbot or tool used for interactive text generation, prompting, and AI literacy instruction; no single commercial product is the focus of the review.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is an integrative review of 124 AI literacy studies in K-12 and higher education published since 2020, synthesizing how studies conceptualize AI and literacy. It does not evaluate a single AI tool; rather, it discusses generative AI tools in general, including unnamed LLM-based tools and examples such as ChatGPT.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an integrative review and conceptual framework paper, not an empirical evaluation of an AI intervention. It does not report primary outcome data, subgroup analyses, or effect estimates for a specific tool.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper is influential for framing AI literacy research and identifying trends, but it does not present measurable student outcome effects. As a review, its impact is conceptual rather than intervention-based.

paper_profiles.title: Accessible Computer Science for K-12 Students with Hearing Impairments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to make K-12 computer science instruction more accessible for Deaf and Hard of Hearing (D/HH) students, especially those with hearing impairments and limited access to computer science resources in American Sign Language (ASL). The authors argue that many existing captions and text-based explanations are too difficult or linguistically mismatched for some D/HH learners, and that accessible programming instruction should better align with Deaf culture, ASL, and visual learning preferences.

The paper presents an early-stage project design for an accessible block-based computer science curriculum and web application. The intervention concept includes ASL video explanations of core programming topics, captions, and accessibility features such as visual feedback, ASL tooltips for blocks, adjustable video speed, and user choice between ASL and text tooltips. It also describes a companion robot-based programming environment intended to support hands-on learning.

The intended population is middle-school D/HH students within a broader K-12 accessible computing initiative, along with teachers and sign language experts who may use the materials in classrooms. The paper is primarily a design and position paper rather than an evaluation study; it reports no outcome data from student use. Its main conclusion is that ASL-centered, multimodal accessibility features are needed and promising for D/HH students, and that future work will test the impact of these videos and tools with middle-school deaf learners.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI/chatbot system that produces text and instructional content; no specific commercial or research product is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Not actually studied as an AI literacy intervention. The paper is a conceptual/design paper about accessible block-based K-12 computer science resources for Deaf/Hard of Hearing students, including ASL videos and accessibility features.

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/future-work paper with no empirical comparison groups, no outcome data, and no evaluated AI literacy intervention. The paper proposes accessibility supports for K-12 CS learning rather than reporting study results.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measured effect on reading, literacy, or subgroup outcomes is reported. Claims about Deaf/Hard of Hearing learners, post-lingual vs. pre-lingual students, and accessibility benefits are speculative or design-oriented rather than evidence of impact.

paper_profiles.title: AI Literacy, Safety Awareness, and STEM Career Aspirations of Australian Secondary Students: Evaluating the Impact of Workshop Interventions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a one-day workshop-based AI literacy intervention changes Australian secondary students’ knowledge, confidence, ethical understanding, and STEM career aspirations. The study is motivated by concerns about adolescents’ exposure to synthetic media such as deepfakes and the need for schools to provide more explicit AI literacy rather than leaving learning to incidental exposure.

The intervention was the Day of AI Australia workshop sequence, delivered in three New South Wales government high schools to Years 7–10 students. The program covered AI foundations, ethics, safety and privacy, misinformation/deepfakes, and AI in careers. Data came from anonymous pre- and post-surveys, with quantitative analysis of changes in AI knowledge, AI recognition in everyday tools, and career interest, plus thematic analysis of open-ended reflections.

Results showed that students reported significantly higher AI knowledge and confidence after the workshops, and they became better at identifying AI in platforms such as Netflix, Spotify, TikTok, and Face Unlock. Students also showed increased interest in AI, computer science, and engineering careers, though these effects were small. The authors conclude that short AI literacy workshops can produce immediate gains in conceptual understanding and awareness, but sustained and longitudinal instruction is likely needed to influence longer-term aspirations and durability of learning.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General generative AI tools and chatbot-like systems used for text, image, and other content generation, without a single named product focus.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper discusses students’ use of general generative productivity tools and AI chatbots as part of baseline AI exposure and literacy (e.g., ChatGPT, Canva Magic Write/Design, Google Gemini), but the intervention itself is a workshop-based AI literacy curriculum rather than a study of a single generative AI product.

findings.finding_summary: Students reported higher self-reported AI knowledge after the workshop intervention, with the largest effect size for "Knowledge about AI" (p < .001, r = .445; pre n=200, post n=158). This is a mixed-methods pre/post comparison using separate samples rather than paired individuals.
findings.measure: Self-reported knowledge about AI

findings.finding_summary: Students also showed improved understanding of how AI systems are trained and how AI bias/errors work, with medium effect sizes. The paper reports "Understand AI training" (p < .001, r = .399; pre n=201, post n=160) and "Understand AI bias/errors" (p < .001, r = .302; pre n=200, post n=160).
findings.measure: Understanding of AI training and AI bias/errors
findings.sample_size: pre n=201/post n=160; pre n=200/post n=160

findings.finding_summary: Recognition of AI in everyday tools increased for some platforms after the workshop, including Spotify (+16.2%), TikTok (+12.8%), Netflix (+27.1%), and Face Unlock (+11.2%). The paper interprets this as students better recognizing AI within algorithmic recommendation systems rather than only in overt chatbots.
findings.measure: Proportion identifying tools as using AI
findings.effect_size: percentage-point change: Spotify +16.2, TikTok +12.8, Netflix +27.1, Face Unlock +11.2
findings.confidence_interval: reported for proportion differences in table, but not summarized as a single CI
findings.sample_size: N=368 total responses (pre n=205 + post n=163)

findings.finding_summary: Interest in AI-related careers increased significantly after the workshops, but the reported effect sizes were small. The paper reports increased interest in AI (p < .001, r = .189; pre n=175, post n=157), Computer Science (p = .005, r = .115; pre n=176, post n=157), and Engineering (p = .029, r = .119; pre n=178, post n=157).
findings.measure: STEM career interest (AI, Computer Science, Engineering)

paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods pre/post workshop study with separate pre and post samples rather than paired student-level data, so it is observational/QED-like rather than a randomized trial. The evidence is useful but has notable design limitations and no subgroup moderator analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: Several literacy-related outcomes show medium effects, including AI knowledge (r = .445) and understanding AI training (r = .399), which meet the medium-impact threshold. Although some outcomes are small, the main literacy gains are substantial enough to place the study in blue for impact.

run_graph_section:
## Research Architecture & Open Questions

### Field Anchors
The citation structure does not show a single dominant pre-2023 foundation for generative AI in K–12 literacy. Instead, later work appears to draw from several adjacent traditions. One anchor is computer-assisted early reading intervention, represented here by Headsprout Early Reading, which established that AI-adjacent or automated instructional systems could be evaluated against business-as-usual literacy support for elementary students with specific literacy difficulty [15]. A second anchor is the pre-generative AI review literature on artificial intelligence in education and on teacher-facing AI use. Reviews of AI applications in higher education and of AI for teachers helped define the main categories of use—feedback, tutoring, planning support, and implementation concerns—that later generative AI studies inherit even when the setting differs [22][23]. A third anchor is the broader shift from conventional AI to large language models and chatbots in school contexts, visible in early post-2022 school-based studies and reviews that operationalize chatbot practice, prompt engineering, and ChatGPT use as educational interventions rather than merely technical tools [7][21][18].

Methodologically, the field is building less on a settled literacy-specific theory than on reusable intervention formats: automated feedback, tutoring systems, chatbot-mediated practice, and teacher support tools. Theoretically, the strongest continuity is with L2 and writing-oriented work, where generative AI is treated as a scaffold for production, revision, and feedback rather than as a reading-comprehension intervention per se [7][16].

### Intellectual Lineage
| Foundational Paper | Year | What It Established | Extended By (papers from this run that build on it) |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Headsprout Early Reading for Specific Literacy Difficulty [15] | 2020 | Demonstrated that an automated reading program could be tested as a literacy intervention for elementary students with reading difficulty. | [4], [9] |
| Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education [22] | 2019 | Organized early AI-in-education uses into core functions such as feedback and tutoring, shaping later review frameworks. | [10], [14], [27] |
| The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers [23] | 2022 | Established teacher-facing AI uses and implementation concerns in K–12, including planning and instructional support. | [20], [26] |
| The application of chatbot as an L2 writing practice tool [7] | 2023 | Showed that chatbot-based literacy practice could be tested experimentally with elementary learners in a school setting. | [16], [18], [27] |

### Research Gaps
The clearest gap is that K–12 literacy research on generative AI remains concentrated in writing, feedback, and adjacent literacy domains, with little direct experimental evidence on reading outcomes. The source pool contains school-based work on L2 writing practice [7], secondary writing feedback [16], AI literacy [11][17], and media literacy [19], but no modern RCTs testing generative AI for reading comprehension, decoding, fluency, or vocabulary growth in classroom literacy instruction. This is especially notable for emergent readers, struggling readers, multilingual learners, and students with disabilities, all named as priority populations but only partially represented in the available evidence [1][8][24].

A second gap is comparative design. Multiple studies share L2 or literacy-support logic, yet there are no direct head-to-head comparisons of common generative AI uses such as chatbot tutoring versus AI feedback, or student-facing supports versus teacher planning supports [7][16][23][26]. A third gap concerns teacher-mediated classroom implementation. Reviews identify teacher support and planning as important AI use cases [23][20], but teacher-planning evidence in the pool comes from teacher education rather than K–12 literacy classrooms [26]. Modern extensions into school-based literacy outcomes are largely absent.

### Hypothesis Surfaces
Among elementary multilingual learners receiving literacy instruction, chatbot-based generative AI practice will produce larger gains in standardized reading comprehension and vocabulary outcomes than business-as-usual instruction, tested in a classroom-level randomized controlled trial. This hypothesis follows from the existing L2 writing chatbot evidence [7] and the broader unmet need for reading-focused trials in school literacy.

Among struggling readers in grades 3–5, a generative AI tutoring intervention that provides guided questioning and text summarization support will improve reading comprehension more than a non-generative digital reading program, evaluated through an individual- or classroom-randomized trial using curriculum-aligned comprehension measures. The rationale comes from the older automated reading intervention base [15] and recent tutoring-system reviews showing activity without literacy-specific RCT consolidation [4][9].

Among secondary students, combining an AI literacy lesson with AI-assisted writing feedback will yield stronger independent writing quality and lower uncritical acceptance of incorrect AI suggestions than AI-assisted writing feedback alone, using a randomized controlled design with writing-performance rubrics and measures of over-reliance on erroneous outputs. This hypothesis is directly grounded in the coexistence of writing-feedback studies and AI-literacy interventions that have not yet been integrated in K–12 literacy work [11][16][17].
